stories.Headline: Getty appeals to the Court of Appeal over whether AI models can be infringing copies
stories.Summary:
Getty Images is appealing to the Court of Appeal in its dispute with Stability AI, the developer of the Stable Diffusion image generator. The appeal is being heard over two days, Wednesday and Thursday, in the week of 11 November 2026. The High Court gave its first instance judgment in November 2025 and largely favoured Stability AI. Getty succeeded on only a small part of its trade mark claim, and its copyright claim failed. Getty's barrister told the court that Stability "doesn't think it should have to pay" for Getty's content.

The central question is whether an AI model can be an "infringing copy" under section 27(3) of the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988, even if the model never contained copies of the works. Stable Diffusion was trained outside the UK, so Getty dropped its primary copyright claims during the trial and kept only a secondary infringement case. That case argued that the model was an infringing copy imported into, and distributed in, the UK. The High Court accepted that an intangible AI model can be an "article", but held that an infringing copy must actually be a copy. Because the model weights had never stored Getty's images, the High Court ruled that the model could not be an infringing copy.

Getty says that "making" a model includes training it, which involves copying images, and that the finished model need not itself contain copies. In its view, if making the article in the UK would have infringed copyright, the article is an infringing copy whether or not it holds copies. Getty's barrister said Stability wants to separate what was done with the copyright works from the act of training, but can only do so by mischaracterising the facts. Stability AI argues that whether something is a copy depends on what is actually produced, not on how it was developed. It says Getty's approach would produce odd results, such as making it unlawful to import the model but lawful to copy it once it is in the UK.

The British Recorded Music Industry Limited, known as BPI, represents the UK recorded music industry and has permission to intervene in support of Getty. It warns that the High Court's approach could let developers train models offshore and bring them back into the UK, with significant consequences for the music and wider creative industries. BPI also notes that Getty accepted at trial that the versions of Stable Diffusion did not contain copies, and cites two recent German cases in which the Munich Court found that models had memorised works they were trained on. On that basis BPI says the Getty judgment has "no wider significance" on whether models contain copies, because the question depends on the facts of each model. Stability AI also argues that extending the law to models trained overseas is a matter for Parliament, not the courts, and it has cross-appealed two findings that went against it.

The High Court case was heard in June 2025, and Getty dropped one of its primary copyright infringement claims just two weeks into the trial. The claims that remained before Mrs Justice Joanna Smith were secondary infringement, trademark infringement and passing off. The court found that Getty succeeded in part on trademark infringement, but only for older models and on isolated examples. Getty had alleged that Stability copied and processed millions of copyrighted images to train Stable Diffusion in the US. Stability's directors include the filmmaker James Cameron, and Stability argues that the images were downloaded and stored in data centres outside the UK, so UK copyright law does not apply.

Stability AI is asking the Court of Appeal to overturn two findings that went against it at first instance: that an intangible model can be an "article", and that Stability itself imported or distributed the model in the UK. Getty disputes both points. If Getty succeeds, developers could face UK copyright claims over models trained abroad on unlicensed works, even where the imported model stores no copies. If Stability succeeds, where a model is trained and whether it stores copies will remain key to any claims. The judgment has not yet been handed down, and the Government continues to consider its approach to copyright and AI following its March 2026 report.

stories.Headline: US labor authorities launch PERM actions against Microsoft, Adobe and six IT firms
stories.Summary:
United States authorities in October initiated administrative action under the Permanent Labor Certification program against Microsoft, Adobe and six major technology outsourcing firms, including Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, Wipro, HCL Technologies, Cognizant and Capgemini, according to TechGig. The actions have disrupted the processing and acceptance of these firms' PERM applications, creating uncertainty for foreign professionals awaiting permanent residency. The federal inquiry centers on allegations that certain employers used immigration programs to replace American workers with lower-paid foreign personnel. Officials noted that the ongoing investigations and administrative actions do not constitute a final finding of guilt. The PERM program is a critical step for US employers seeking to sponsor foreign workers for employment-based green cards, and employers must certify that insufficient qualified US workers are available and that hiring a foreign national will not adversely affect American employees.

The Trump administration has introduced a requirement of $100,000 for certain new H-1B petitions while extending related visa restrictions through September 2027. The H-1B program allows US companies to temporarily employ foreign professionals in specialty occupations and has long been central to the Indian IT sector across software development, cloud services, cybersecurity and technical consulting. The administration has not formally announced a complete shutdown or overhaul of the H-1B program, focusing instead on audits, employer accountability and strict compliance. US Department of Labor Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito warned that temporary work visas cannot be treated as a permanent business strategy, stating that visas like the H-1B should only be used when qualified and willing American workers are unavailable for a given role. D'Esposito indicated that the probe is likely to widen and warned that similar actions could soon target additional companies and academic institutions.

His office is coordinating closely with the White House Fraud Task Force, led by Vice President JD Vance, which aims to identify systemic irregularities and abuse within visa programs. The heightened scrutiny directly affects major Indian IT service providers whose US operations rely heavily on deploying specialized talent from abroad. For Indian IT firms, the immediate challenge lies in balancing business continuity in their largest market with rigorous adherence to evolving immigration rules. If federal investigations expand and PERM restrictions persist, Indian service providers could face significant hurdles in talent deployment, foreign hiring and green card sponsorship for employees in the United States. The articles do not say what further steps, if any, the firms or the administration will take next.

stories.Headline: Flagstar Bank uses Windows 11 and Intune to secure devices and run AI agents
stories.Summary:
Flagstar Bank built a secure, manageable foundation for AI with Windows 11, Microsoft reported on November 16, 2026. The bank invested in Microsoft Surface devices to bring a more secure foundation to employees. Windows 11 anchors Flagstar’s modernization, with Microsoft Entra for identity, Intune for device management, and Windows Autopilot for setup. Flagstar needed to unify a fragmented technology environment, simplify employee access and device management, and protect customer information as it introduced AI. Headquartered in New York, Flagstar Bank serves consumers and business clients across the United States.

Following mergers that brought together three organizations and six data centers, Flagstar needed a more consistent approach to employee access, device management, and AI. Its starting point was a patchwork of on-premises Active Directory systems and a legacy domain-join model for deploying devices. The bank is consolidating its Active Directory systems, with the goal of using Microsoft Entra as the authoritative source for employee identities and group membership. With Windows Hello for Business, employees sign in with a PIN or biometrics instead of relying on passwords. Microsoft Intune gives IT a single place to govern, control, and secure devices across the environment.

Kevin Kilbride, engineering manager at Flagstar Bank, said the Windows environment consisted of different hardware models and software versions, and that joining that with a domain legacy deployment system made it difficult to manage. Kilbride said moving to Windows as the secure foundation takes the bank from a fragmented environment to a more manageable IT experience, which translates to teams, employees, and then customers. Jason Pope, Flagstar’s chief technology and data officer, said that in a highly regulated organization you need to be able to show who, what, where, when, and how a specific user accessed an application, and that Windows together with Microsoft Entra and Intune gives the bank that ability. Kilbride said getting new devices imaged and shipped to employees used to take days, and that now the bank ships new Surface devices directly to employees and, with Windows Autopilot, employees are online in less than 15 minutes. Pope said using agentic AI on the Windows platform has enabled the bank to spend more time with customers and remove repetitive sequences, specifically in banking where there is a lot of duplication of entry.

Under the legacy domain-join model, IT spent at least a day or two getting each device ready before shipping it out, and employees had to wait for equipment to arrive before they could start work. Now the end-user support team simply allocates a device and gets it to the employee, and when the employee signs in with company credentials, Windows Autopilot and Intune automate the remaining setup. Employees across the bank already use StarIQ, the bank’s AI tool built on Microsoft Copilot, which Flagstar CEO Joseph Otting says has an adoption rate of about 83 percent. Within its Windows 11 environment, Flagstar also runs a custom small language model on Microsoft Surface devices, and its purpose-built agent, BranchIQ, uses the device’s neural processing unit to help bankers perform know-your-customer activities and accelerate onboarding customers. Localizing the AI model on the device supports the bank’s security priorities and enables offline access to policies, procedures, and customer-onboarding assistance.

When onboarding a customer, bankers must verify identity as part of know-your-customer and anti-money-laundering checks, which in the past meant jotting down details from a driver’s license or passport or keying them into a legacy system over and over. With BranchIQ, a banker can instead take a photo of the ID that stays on the device, and the agent extracts the details and enters them automatically into the systems of record used to set up the new customer and account. Windows supplies the operating environment and guardrails for this agent workflow with Microsoft Execution Containers, while Surface provides the neural processing unit and mobile form factor that bring it to branch colleagues’ flow of work. Agents on Surface devices are given their own identity in the Entra Suite, which lets the bank track an agent’s actions apart from a person’s. Microsoft Execution Containers, built into Windows 11, add control over what each agent can access and do, and give the bank a way to account for those actions to regulators.

Pope said that with the bank’s agents using Microsoft Execution Containers on its Windows platform, the bank was able to ascertain how an agent is working and control it, then prove how and why it controlled it and produce that report for regulators. Flagstar is now exploring how to expand its use of the containers as part of its Windows 11 AI work. Pope said the principle behind the bank’s Windows modernization is making work easier while keeping it secure, manageable, and compliant, and that from how employees sign in and get their devices to running AI locally on Surface, Windows is the foundation, and it is the same foundation the bank will use as it brings governed agents into the bank. Centralized policy management helps IT identify settings that need attention, resolve issues, and keep devices aligned as the bank’s security and compliance standards evolve. Together, these modern identity and device management tools help Flagstar document application access and demonstrate policy enforcement to auditors.

Articles.Title: Flagstar Bank builds a secure, manageable foundation for AI with Windows 11

stories.Headline: Digital News Publishers Association challenges India's data protection law in Supreme Court
stories.Summary:
The Digital News Publishers Association challenged the Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023 before the Supreme Court of India. This group represents twenty one news publishers who are concerned about the law and its associated rules. A Bench led by Chief Justice Surya Kant issued a notice to the Union Government on 27 October 2026. The court declined to grant interim relief without first hearing the government side of the legal dispute. A further hearing on this matter is scheduled to take place on 17 November 2026.

The DPDP Act received presidential assent on 11 August 2023 and regulates digital personal data and digitised non digital data. It defines Data Fiduciaries as entities determining processing means and Data Principals as the individuals whose data is processed. The DPDP Rules, 2025, were notified on 13 November 2025, with principal compliance starting on 13 May 2027. Financial penalties for contraventions can reach Rs. 250 crore, and children under eighteen require verifiable parental consent for processing.

The challenge targets Sections 7, 17, 18, 19, 27, 29, 36, 37, 44(3), and specific provisions of the 2025 Rules. The publishers argue that the law lacks a specific journalistic exemption, which could hinder the collection of information for investigations. They claim that requiring prior consent from individuals under investigation would undermine the work of journalists investigating public office misuse. The publishers also question Section 44(3), which amends Section 8(1)(j) of the Right to Information Act of 2005 regarding personal information. They believe Section 17 raises concerns about the scope of exemptions available to the State for national security purposes.

These groups seek to balance individual dignity with the public right to information and the freedom of the press. Journalists and citizens are affected by this law, as it impacts the ability to scrutinize public institutions and government power. The articles suggest that privacy should not be a shield against legitimate scrutiny, nor should journalism justify publishing every detail. The debate involves the constitutional relationship between Articles 14, 19(1)(a), and 21 of the Indian Constitution regarding expression and privacy. In Jammu and Kashmir, digital rights are significant because platforms are essential for banking, education, employment, and public services.

The region has a specific history with internet restrictions that makes these data protection and privacy issues particularly important. The 2017 case of Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India established that privacy is a constitutionally protected fundamental right. The 2020 Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India case emphasized proportionality and transparency regarding internet suspensions in Jammu and Kashmir.

Internationally, the European Union uses the GDPR, while the United States uses fragmented laws like the California Consumer Privacy Act. China implemented the Personal Information Protection Law in 2021, which includes specific provisions regarding State organs and national security. These global examples show different ways of balancing individual autonomy, state surveillance, and the right to information or erasure. The Supreme Court will now determine if the law adequately distinguishes public interest journalism from the commercial misuse of data.

It must decide if the legislation protects citizens from information misuse or protects power from the scrutiny of the citizens. The court will examine if State interference with privacy satisfies standards of legality, legitimate purpose, necessity, and proportionality. The articles leave open whether the Data Protection Board will provide an independent and accessible remedy for those affected. It remains unclear how the court will reconcile the right to informational privacy with the public right to know.

stories.Headline: John Langford resigns from Microsoft after AI Frontiers restructuring
stories.Summary:
John Langford, a veteran machine learning researcher at Microsoft, has resigned from the company, and his departure follows the dissolution of the AI Frontiers research group, which was established in 2023. The 50-member team focused on exploring new approaches to artificial intelligence, working on projects like Microsoft's AutoGen multi-agent framework and Fara, a computer-use agent. A restructuring in September 2026 moved AI Frontiers from Microsoft Research into Microsoft AI, the company's commercial AI division. Langford stated that this change created differences over how AI development should progress within Microsoft.

The commercial division prioritised scaling existing models using larger datasets and computing resources, while AI Frontiers focused on developing alternative algorithms, optimisation techniques, and model architectures. Langford reported that the team's research was considered "aggressively not research" by the product organisation, which reportedly left several projects without a clear path towards adoption within Microsoft. The research group explored alternative AI technologies including Next Latent, Dion3, and Full Bandwidth Transformers, and these projects aimed to improve AI training and computational efficiency rather than relying on increasing model size. Langford's departure reportedly coincided with other senior researchers leaving the group, which highlights the differences between exploratory AI research and commercial product development.

Langford said the restructuring created differences over how AI development should progress within Microsoft, and he reported that the product organisation viewed the team's research as "aggressively not research." The commercial division's focus on scaling existing models with larger datasets and computing resources stood in contrast to the group's work on alternative algorithms, optimisation techniques, and model architectures. The projects explored by the group, including Next Latent, Dion3, and Full Bandwidth Transformers, aimed to improve AI training and computational efficiency rather than relying on increasing model size. His departure reportedly coincided with other senior researchers leaving the group, and the articles do not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: Researchers review how AI can cut emissions across iron and steelmaking
stories.Summary:
A comprehensive academic review published in Carbon Neutral Systems examines how artificial intelligence can accelerate decarbonization across the iron and steel industry by optimizing process efficiency, enabling feedstock substitution, and supporting carbon capture, utilization, and storage. The study was authored by Xidi Shang, Wuliang Yin, Jianxin Pan, Min Wang, Hua Wang, Kai Yang, and Qingtai Xiao. It synthesizes findings from 133 representative investigations identified through structured database searches covering research published between 2000 and 2025. The review was published on November 16, 2026, according to bioengineer.org. The article appeared under the site's Technology section with a reading time of five minutes.

The authors highlight that the global steel sector accounts for approximately 7 to 9 percent of direct industrial carbon dioxide emissions. Traditional blast furnace and basic oxygen furnace configurations generate roughly 70 percent of global crude steel output. Electric arc furnace operations currently produce approximately 41.5 percent of crude steel in the European Union and 68.0 percent in the United States. The review maps five technological pathways under evaluation across global producers, ranging from conventional coal-fed blast furnace systems paired with carbon capture to scrap-fed electric arc furnaces, hydrogen-based direct reduction, and electrolytic ironmaking. The article's subject of research is artificial intelligence applications in low-carbon iron and steel metallurgy.

The authors observe that current industrial applications remain predominantly confined to isolated processing units operating within narrow parameter boundaries. They state that most models lack comprehensive representations of dynamic cross-unit couplings among material, energy, and carbon flows, which restricts route-wide optimization across entire industrial complexes. They note that industrial datasets suffer from noise, missing values, regime drift, and a scarcity of validated operational logs for emerging hydrogen or electrolytic pilots. Because metallurgical operations depend strictly on thermodynamic conservation laws, the authors say unconstrained black-box learners risk outputting nonphysical predictions when extrapolating outside training domains. The review concludes that future progress depends on physics-informed, multi-scale gray-box architectures that embed conservation equations and transport kinetics directly into deep neural frameworks, supporting verifiable, plant-wide carbon reduction across the steel industry.

The authors highlight that broad deployment of newer hydrogen and electrolysis technologies faces substantial hurdles, including capital requirements, infrastructural bottlenecks, and high operational costs, requiring system-wide optimization within existing facilities while cleaner routes mature. They report that multimodal perception frameworks combining two-dimensional photographic images with three-dimensional point clouds have achieved material granularity recognition rates exceeding 90 percent. Vision-based monitoring tools detect bosh pressure channel anomalies eight to sixteen minutes prior to operational disruptions, according to the review. Digital-twin structures integrated with deep residual networks identify carbon emission deviations, categorizing operational anomaly severity with reported classification accuracies exceeding 97 percent.

In electric arc furnaces, artificial neural networks estimate endpoint carbon concentrations, achieving reported hit rates of 96.67 percent within an error margin of 0.05 percent carbon. The review delineates the baseline operating structure of integrated steelmaking, where raw-material preparation, blast furnace reduction, converter refining, and rolling units share significant energy flows and off-gas networks. Sintering, pelletizing, and coking supply the burden materials required for blast furnace operation, wherein fossil carbon acts simultaneously as a chemical reducing agent and an energy source. Conventional chemical analyses remain accurate but require offline sampling that cannot provide high-frequency process feedback.

Echo state networks, variational mode decomposition, and swarm intelligence algorithms generate multi-step forecasts of blast furnace gas production and gasholder storage levels, driving root-mean-square errors below 0.05 across benchmark industrial datasets. The article's references cite Shang, X., Yin, W., Pan, J., Wang, M., Wang, H., Yang, K., & Xiao, Q. (2026), published in Carbon Neutral Systems, volume 2, issue 1. The review states that future progress depends on physics-informed, multi-scale gray-box architectures that embed conservation equations and transport kinetics directly into deep neural frameworks. The authors observe that current industrial applications remain predominantly confined to isolated processing units operating within narrow parameter boundaries.

The article does not state when or whether such plant-wide architectures will be deployed. It does not give a timeline for the five technological pathways it maps. The article does not report any response from steel producers or policymakers to the review. It does not state the review's conclusions on costs for the hydrogen and electrolysis routes beyond the hurdles it lists.

stories.Headline: Urban Legend pays right-wing influencers to promote Nvidia chip sales to China and pro-AI articles
stories.Summary:
Urban Legend paid over 80 right-wing influencers on X to promote pro-AI industry articles for more than one year. These campaigns pushed Nvidia chip sales to China and attacked AI doomers. The most recent of these coordinated campaigns ended on November 10. Many influencers also posted these links on Facebook, Instagram, YouTube, and Truth Social. The operation used shortened links and redirects to track clicks and payments.

The campaigns promoted Nvidia H200 chip sales to China and the company's open-weights AI letter. One ad mentioned Build American AI, which connects to Greg Brockman, Marc Andreessen, and Ben Horowitz. Other links promoted Jordan Schachtel, a policy advisor for Innovation Council Action linked to David Sacks. Lyceum launched on June 9, 2026, and published four policy editorials tied to these campaigns. Upward News also ran a byline-free piece praising Nvidia sales to China.

Urban Legend declined to comment on the investigation into its influencer marketing practices. The company uses a system where creators are paid fees for conversions tracked through digital content. One influencer, Kaya Jones, shared over one hundred links and encouraged others to sign up. Another creator, Ash Saves USA, admitted she was helping drive traffic to a Washington Examiner article. Buzz Patterson promoted a Lyceum article backing former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

The campaigns targeted Anthropic and OpenAI, calling them woke and insufficiently aligned with the Trump administration. Four of five Trending Politics pieces were marked as sponsored, affecting readers who saw paid partnerships. Lyceum claims it is editorially independent despite its house editorials being tied to Urban Legend. Most of Lyceum's other editorials were rated as AI-generated by a detector called Pangram. Only three of the promoted articles took a pro-safety or cautionary stance toward AI.

Urban Legend has conducted various conflicting campaigns across many topics for an eclectic array of clients. Donald Trump Jr. and FBI Director Kash Patel stopped posting Urban Legend links in November 2024. The firm used the domain mycreator.studio, which was registered on May 29, 2021. The first link routing through that domain appeared on July 27, 2021. WIRED previously identified the domain exc.to as part of the Urban Legend network in 2022.

Urban Legend registered a new domain, bitlicustom.com, after being contacted for comment on Tuesday. Eight new links began routing through this new domain by the following afternoon. The articles do not name the specific clients who paid for the Nvidia and crypto campaigns. It remains unclear how many other non-AI campaigns the firm is currently running. The investigation leaves the total amount of money paid to influencers undisclosed.

stories.Headline: New Jersey assembly committee advances bills to regulate AI in insurance and tenant screening
stories.Summary:
New Jersey lawmakers advanced legislation to regulate artificial intelligence in insurance, housing and the workplace at a November 16, 2026 meeting of the Assembly Science, Innovation and Technology Committee. The committee took up bills limiting AI use in insurance claim denials, regulating automated tenant screening and imposing new requirements on electronic monitoring of employees. Lawmakers also considered measures requiring greater transparency from data center developers. Assemblyman Chris Tully (D-Bergenfield), the committee chairman, said the legislation reflects the need to protect consumers as AI becomes more widely used. The proposals drew concerns from businesses about higher costs and restrictions on emerging technology.

One bill, A5494, would prohibit certain uses of artificial intelligence in denying homeowners, automobile and flood insurance claims. It advanced with Assemblyman Chris DePhillips (R-Wyckoff) abstaining and every other committee member voting in favor. A second bill, A5495, would regulate automated tenant screening systems used to evaluate prospective renters. It also advanced with DePhillips abstaining and the remaining committee members voting in favor. The committee held a discussion-only hearing on A4981, which would regulate AI-based electronic monitoring systems used in employment and public services.

Assembly members Heather Simmons (D-Glassboro) and Cody Miller (D-Monroe) are sponsoring that proposal, along with 16 other Democratic co-sponsors. Tully said AI systems can improve efficiency and tackle fraud, but that people must be protected from automatic denial by algorithms. He said that when a major decision affects someone's life, there must always be a human in the loop. Tully said mandating human oversight establishes common-sense guardrails to use these powerful tools responsibly. DePhillips said he abstained on both bills because proponents and opponents did not seem that far apart and he saw an opportunity for both sides to collaborate.

Assemblyman Balvir Singh (D-Burlington) said he felt like he was learning to ride a bike while riding it. Assemblywoman Carmen Morales (D-Bloomfield) defended the insurance proposal as a consumer protection measure and said it really is about transparency. Insurance industry representatives raised concerns that the restrictions could limit their ability to use new technology and leave companies at a competitive disadvantage. Nicholas Kikis, vice president of legislative and regulatory affairs for the New Jersey Apartment Association, did not take a position on the tenant screening bill but warned that AI has made it increasingly difficult for landlords to detect fraudulent applications. Kikis pointed to income verification, saying documents landlords previously could verify with relative ease can now be altered using AI.

Jeff Kolekowski of the New Jersey Builders Association raised similar concerns without taking a formal position on the bill. Anthony Russo of the Commerce and Industry Association of New Jersey said the monitoring bill would add a high cost to companies that invent those technologies and that they would have to pay to have it approved. Russo said that if the bill goes through, it just adds to the cost of doing business. Jack Ramirez of the New Jersey Business and Industry Association said the bill's definition of artificial intelligence was too broad and could subject ordinary business tools to additional regulation. Eric Richards, legislative affairs coordinator for the New Jersey AFL-CIO, said AI has the power to change the very nature of work and that without oversight AI companies pose tremendous risk to working people.

Richards said the bill puts clear common-sense ground rules for how AI can be used in the workplace and makes sure an employer can't spy on you when you're off the clock. A5224 would require data center developers to disclose certain information to the public and elected officials before preliminary site plan consideration under the Municipal Land Use Law. S4304, sponsored by State Sens. Linda Greenstein (D-Plainsboro) and Brian Stack (D-Union City), would prohibit agreements intended to conceal certain information about data center developments, and its Assembly counterpart is A2774. Greenstein said that if you don't play by the rules of open government, you don't get to build in New Jersey, and that confidentiality agreements could prevent residents and local officials from learning the full extent of a project's electricity demands and environmental effects.

Chris Sotiro of the Climate Revolution Action Network said the developers are not interested in transparency but are interested in hiding. A2774 advanced with bipartisan support, with DePhillips, the only Republican present at the hearing, voting in favor, and Assemblyman Greg McGuckin (R-Toms River) was absent. Earlier this year, Gov. Mikie Sherrill signed legislation sponsored by Assemblyman Andrew Macurdy (D-Summit) that redirected $250 million in unused data center tax credits to the New Jersey Economic Development Authority. The measure passed the Legislature with nearly unanimous support.

The hearings illustrate the competing pressures facing lawmakers as they try to establish protections for consumers, tenants and workers without imposing restrictions that businesses say could discourage innovation or make new technologies more expensive to use. The articles do not say when the full Assembly or Senate might vote on the bills. The articles do not say what happens to A4981 after the discussion-only hearing. More to follow.

stories.Headline: AI Lawsuit Jersey 2026: Settlements, Eligibility and Filing
stories.Summary:
New Jersey faces three major AI class actions in 2026, according to lawfold.com, with the largest, Martinez v. TechHire Solutions, covering over 15,000 job applicants in the Newark metro area who claim an AI tool scored them lower based on zip code. The second, Doe v. SocialAI Corp, involves 8,000 New Jersey residents whose likenesses were used without consent to generate synthetic media. The third targets automated lending platforms and alleges AI loan denials disproportionately affected Black and Latino borrowers, with a class estimated at 12,000 applicants.

The Martinez case was certified by Essex County court in January 2026, the SocialAI Corp motion to dismiss was denied in February 2026, and the lending case began discovery in March 2026. The state attorney general filed two enforcement actions this year, both targeting AI vendors selling untested hiring tools to New Jersey employers. The cases invoke the 2025 AEDT Act, which gives workers a private right of action and requires a bias audit within 12 months of use, annual re-audits every 12 months, public disclosure, and candidate notification before AI use. Penalties run $500 per day for a missed initial audit, $1,000 per day for a missed re-audit, $500 per violation for non-disclosure, and $250 per applicant for missing notification. Deepfake victims can sue for statutory damages of $1,000 per incident under the 2025 privacy expansion, and the updated privacy framework took effect in January 2026, requiring explicit opt-in consent for AI data use.

Damages range from $500 to $2,500 for unauthorized data scraping under the NJ Consumer Fraud Act, $1,000 per violation for hidden AI data use, $1,000 to $5,000 for biometric misuse, and $5,000 per child for children's data harvesting. A 2025 state study found a 34% disparity in AI-driven loan approvals, against a 9% gap for human loan officers. The articles attribute the claims to New Jersey workers who say automated systems denied them jobs unfairly, and to plaintiffs who argue that non-compliance with the AEDT Act itself proves negligence. The articles state that employers must now prove their AI tools are bias-free and that companies that fail face penalties under the 2025 AEDT Act. The articles say the state attorney general filed the two enforcement actions, that penalties could exceed $10 million per case, and that the NJ Division on Civil Rights is actively investigating.

The articles state that the EEOC has referenced New Jersey cases in its own guidance. The articles say staffing agencies are the biggest targets and are named as co-defendants in multiple suits, and that at least four Fortune 500 firms paid undisclosed sums to New Jersey applicants. The articles state that over 20,000 workers have reported suspicious rejections since 2024, that over 40,000 New Jersey workers may be owed compensation, and that most claimants can expect between $200 and $5,000. The articles say the combined class size exceeds 35,000 people, that tech, finance, and staffing face the most exposure, and that the lead court is Essex County Superior Court. The articles state that retail chains face class actions over facial recognition data collected in New Jersey stores and offices.

The articles state that New Jersey passed the AEDT Act in 2025, that it was the first law of its kind in the state, and that the state leads the nation in AI regulation enforcement. The articles say New Jersey expanded its privacy laws in 2025 to cover synthetic media and that the updated privacy framework took effect in January 2026. The articles state that the claims fall under the NJ Law Against Discrimination, the NJ Consumer Fraud Act, the NJ Fair Housing Act, the NJ Biometric Privacy Act, and a NJ COPPA Extension. The articles say the law does not require proof of intentional discrimination and that disparate impact alone is enough under New Jersey law. The articles state that many employers missed the first audit deadline, creating a wave of new claims in early 2026.

The articles state that filing deadlines are approaching fast for several claims and advise workers rejected by AI systems to keep all emails, and deepfake victims to document screenshots, URLs, and timestamps. The articles do not name the defendants in the lending case, the employers or agencies named as co-defendants, the four Fortune 500 firms, or the retail chains facing biometric claims. The articles do not give the filing deadlines, the amounts paid in the undisclosed settlements, or the outcomes of the two enforcement actions. The articles do not state when the three class actions will next be heard or how the 34% disparity study was conducted.

stories.Headline: Trump launches five billion dollar Genesis Mission to advance science through AI
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump launched a five billion dollar government effort to advance science through artificial intelligence. This initiative, called the Genesis Mission, began in November 2025 via an executive order. It started at the Energy Department and now includes more than 15 federal agencies. The president also issued a second order in June to speed up quantum technology development. These actions occurred during the second term of President Donald Trump.

The Genesis Mission uses Energy Department data, computing power, and facilities to build shared AI tools. In 2025, federal agencies spent about 4.2 billion dollars on AI research and development. The White House Office of Science and Technology Policy released a 123 page report in July. The Energy Department aims to develop error corrected quantum computers by 2028. The Office of Science has a total budget of 8.4 billion dollars for fiscal year 2026.

Darío Gil is the undersecretary for science at the U.S. Department of Energy. He called AI, quantum science, and supercomputing the three legs of a transforming stool. Gil stated that 400 million dollars for Genesis is small compared to the total budget. John Sarrao is the director of SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory in Menlo Park, California. Sarrao said Genesis created an inflection point for scientists who already used AI.

Rachel Mandelbaum of Carnegie Mellon University leads a project combining huge datasets from observatories and instruments. She said the idea is conceptually powerful but noted her cosmology grant was reduced. Brad Marston is a physicist at Brown University and president of the American Physical Society. Marston said he wants all fields supported because AI and quantum were once backwaters. Researchers in public health and climate research have faced funding cuts and delays.

The National Science Foundation and National Institutes of Health launched Genesis efforts in biology, health, and space. SLAC is involved in 20 Genesis projects and leads two of them. The Energy Department funded nearly 300 projects this year, including nuclear fusion and electric grid simulations. Celia Merzbacher of the Quantum Economic Development Consortium said quantum computing is at the start of a marathon. Some Genesis funding came from a 2025 budget law and some from the department budget.

The government will continue using AI to speed up the development of nuclear reactors. Agencies will keep lining up research spending with the priorities of the current administration. Scientists will continue working on quantum sensors, quantum materials, and quantum error correction. The articles do not say how the government will balance funding for other science fields. It remains open whether the department will talk with scientists about these budget trade-offs.

stories.Headline: Kenyan High Court Justice Andayi sets aside ODPC compensation award and questions commissioner's power to decide damages
stories.Summary:
Justice Francis Andayi of the High Court set aside a KSh1.25 million compensation award against a Nairobi healthcare business on a complaint by a patient identified as GW about CCTV cameras in a clinical examination room. The patient argued the cameras compromised her privacy, and the healthcare provider disputed the ODPC's findings and presented forensic evidence on the footage. The High Court did not decide whether the alleged privacy violation occurred, and instead examined whether the Commissioner had legal authority to order compensation. The judgment questioned whether the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner can independently determine damages payable to individuals under the Data Protection Act. The decision came after the ODPC built a record of financial enforcement, with more than KSh30 million paid to individuals during 2025.

The dispute centred on Section 65 of the Data Protection Act and Regulation 14(3)(e) of the subsidiary legislation, and Section 65 gives individuals a right to compensation for damage from a contravention of the Act. Justice Andayi observed that Section 65 does not expressly assign the Commissioner the job of deciding whether damage occurred or calculating compensation payable. He distinguished the regulator's powers to investigate complaints, impose administrative penalties and issue enforcement notices from the separate function of deciding monetary claims between parties. He questioned whether Regulation 14(3)(e) could introduce a substantive power Parliament had not expressly provided in the parent legislation. He relied on the principle that statutory agencies and tribunals can exercise only powers conferred on them by law.

Justice Andayi also questioned the procedure followed when the ODPC issued the award, after the regulator investigated the complaint, considered the provider's response and issued a monetary determination. He was concerned the process had not provided an adequate hearing at which both sides could contest the evidence and address the compensation claim. He questioned whether the same Commissioner could investigate an alleged violation, effectively prosecute the complaint and then determine the financial remedy without safeguards required by natural justice. He said: "Even if a hearing were to be conducted, I again doubt that it would be by the same Data Commissioner to be the one investigating, then prosecuting it and then deciding." He said that would be against all the rules of natural justice.

The patient and the Data Commissioner maintained that Section 65, read with Regulation 14, authorised the watchdog to issue compensation orders, and they relied on previous High Court decisions supporting the regulator's administrative remedies. Justice Andayi found the earlier authorities had not adequately addressed whether the compensation provision in the regulations exceeded the powers granted under the Act. He declined to strike down Regulation 14(3)(e) or declare all previous ODPC compensation awards unlawful, saying such a challenge required proceedings directed at the validity of the subsidiary legislation with the Attorney-General given an opportunity to participate. The judgment does not invalidate previous awards, and the underlying right of individuals to seek compensation under Section 65 remains. The ODPC's compensation decisions have affected financial services, healthcare, lending and digital commerce.

Standard Investment Bank was ordered to pay Andrew Endovo KSh50,000 after sending him an unsolicited promotional email without his consent, and Platinum Credit was ordered to compensate Philip Bolo KSh900,000 after continuing direct marketing despite his objection. Moja Expressway Company, which operates the 27-kilometre Nairobi Expressway, was ordered to pay former employee Cyrus Mwaniki Ndung'u KSh500,000 for using his photograph to promote electronic toll collection services without permission. Tech Limited faced a KSh2.6 million compensation order, which it subsequently challenged at the High Court. In April 2026 the regulator ordered St. Luke Orthopaedic & Trauma Hospital Eldoret to pay Merceline Akoth Odeyo KSh525,000 after she received medical test results belonging to another person on two occasions and her medical information was shared with an external laboratory without her knowledge or consent.

The hospital attributed the incident to human error and argued the information shared was limited to identification details, and the Commissioner found it had not demonstrated explicit and informed consent or adequately protected her personal information. TechTrendsKE reported in April 2025 that the ODPC issued 51 determinations in 2024, with average fines of approximately KSh522,308 per case, and those administrative fines serve a different purpose from compensation awarded to individuals. Immaculate Kassait, the country's first Data Commissioner, is preparing for a leadership transition after a six-year tenure, and a November 13, 2026 assessment listed more than 13,000 complaints handled, 459 determinations issued and 206 enforcement and penalty notice actions. The regulator had also registered approximately 28,000 data controllers and processors, and Kassait has called for amendments to the Data Protection Act on artificial intelligence, sensitive personal information, penalties and data governance.

President William Ruto nominated Lydia Sitienei Chelagat, formerly Director of Legal Services at the Communications Authority of Kenya, to succeed Kassait on November 10, 2026, and her nomination was forwarded to the National Assembly for consideration. In the EU, Ireland's Data Protection Commission found that Tinder's "Download My Data" tool omitted certain categories of personal information or provided only summaries without clearly informing users, and the EU fined Match Group, the owner of Tinder, €11 million. The investigation into Match Group was launched in 2020 and resulted in an order requiring the company to bring its data processing practices into compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation within three months. Match Group rejected the findings and announced plans to appeal, insisting that Tinder maintains strong privacy protections for its users.

The ODPC's ability to investigate complaints and enforce compliance remains intact, and the unresolved issue concerns the legal route through which it can determine compensation. The eventual determination of whether the Commissioner can independently award those damages will depend on a direct judicial examination of the regulation underpinning that authority. The judgment provides businesses grounds to scrutinise the statutory basis and procedures behind compensation orders, while Section 65 continues to recognise the right of individuals to seek compensation when personal information is mishandled. The incoming Commissioner will inherit an institution with a substantial enforcement record and an expanding regulatory mandate.

stories.Headline: Nearly 70% of aides and lobbyists expect AI safety rules to pass in the 120th Congress
stories.Summary:
A Canvass survey published by Punchbowl News on November 15, 2026 found that nearly 70% of respondents expect artificial intelligence safety rules to pass in the next Congress, which will be the 120th. The survey combined senior congressional aides with leaders of the wider lobbying world, drawing on top Capitol Hill staff and K Street professionals. Those respondents see the next Congress as the time for action on artificial intelligence safety. The article presenting the survey was dated November 15, 2026, and appeared in Punchbowl News. The survey result points to a shift in expectations for AI guardrails, with nearly 70% of those polled saying they view safety rules as likely to pass in the next Congress.

The 120th Congress is the body the respondents identified as the one that would take up the issue. The article did not give a specific date for when a vote might occur or what the rules would contain. It also did not say how many people took part in the survey beyond describing them as senior congressional aides and leaders of the wider lobbying world. Democrats have rallied behind the idea that artificial intelligence needs legal guardrails, according to the same article, but they are divided on how to tax the tech. That division is the only detail the article offered on the substance of the debate, and it did not say where Republicans stand.

The article also linked to separate coverage on Florida asking a court to stop OpenAI development and on what the Trump-Xi meeting means for tech. No lawmaker or staffer was named as responsible for the push, and the article carried no direct comment from any official. The article did not say what happens next beyond the survey finding, and it did not give a timeline for when AI safety legislation might be introduced or voted on. It presented the 120th Congress as the window respondents expect, without naming a committee, a sponsor or a draft bill. The piece was a preview of premium tech coverage, and the full story was available only to subscribers.

stories.Headline: St. Paul student says Turnitin flag gave her a zero as district lacks AI policy
stories.Summary:
A St. Paul Public Schools student wrote in a MinnPost opinion piece published on November 16, 2026, that she received a zero on an English essay that Turnitin flagged as 32 percent AI-generated, dropping her grade to a D on the night before her last day of sophomore year. She said she had earned a 98 percent in the class before that and had not used AI for any part of the essay. When she offered the next morning to rewrite sections with pen and paper, her teacher said that was not necessary because she knew the student's writing style and believed the work was original. The teacher had previously raised concerns about Turnitin, an AI detection tool used by the district.

The piece says the district has no official school board AI policy, although Phil Wacker, the district's high school curriculum supervisor, acknowledged Turnitin's limitations in September 2025, particularly for students whose first language is not English, according to St. Paul Publishing. At that time nearly 30 percent of the district's students were English learners. The SPPS Board of Education recently announced a goal of adopting an AI policy by the end of the 2027-28 school year, with details still vague and the board saying the policy will include expectations for how the district prepares students and staff to use, question, evaluate and create with AI. Wacker said conversations about a policy are happening.

The student argues that administrators, not students, should fix the problem, and that she sees a lack of urgency. She writes that the time spent debating a policy means the conversation will take her class's entire high school career, and that some students use AI and have found ways to avoid detection. Turnitin assigns a score based on the percentage of suspected AI sentences, measuring burstiness, or spontaneity of word choice, and sentence length, and the company claims human writing tends to be inconsistent and idiosyncratic. The student notes that her flagged essay was about how high school writing structure strips individuality from students' work.

stories.Headline: Pierre school officials draft AI classroom procedures after survey
stories.Summary:
The Pierre School District has spent the past several months working to address the growing use of artificial intelligence in classrooms, with district officials meeting alongside a staff committee to develop procedures for AI use after a community survey was conducted earlier this year. Superintendent Donavan DeBoer said he entered the role knowing that discussions about AI would be necessary as the technology becomes increasingly common, not just in schools, and he noted that AI has been a frequent topic at education conferences and professional retreats because of how quickly the technology evolves. Drawing a comparison to the introduction of cellphones in schools, DeBoer said educators learned that simply allowing students unrestricted access often created challenges that continue today, and he said the district needs to put guardrails on AI sooner rather than later because having some sort of plan is better than having no plan at all. District conversations began earlier this year with an AI-focused survey sent to staff, students and parents, and about 1,655 responses gave the district a starting point for committee discussions as members work toward establishing AI procedures for the 2027-28 school year. Eighty percent of students surveyed said they had used AI before, and nearly half of those students said they use it monthly or more often, while of the 832 student respondents, 309 said they use AI for homework help and 412 said they use it for research, with others reporting use for writing assistance and studying.

Of the 209 staff members who responded, about half said they had used AI for tasks including lesson planning, and most respondents agreed AI can help teachers save time, though many also expressed interest in additional training, recommended tools and established expectations for student use. Across all respondent groups, students, staff and parents expressed awareness that AI tools can sometimes produce inaccurate information, and DeBoer said many students also voiced concerns about academic integrity similar to those expressed by adults in the community. The district has since formed an AI committee that has met twice, and the group includes principals representing the elementary, middle and high school levels as well as Technology Director Bryan Linn, with DeBoer saying he and Linn are currently working to draft procedures and protocols for AI use. The committee plans to meet again in January to further develop those ideas before sharing them with building leadership teams for additional feedback, and DeBoer said he hopes to bring a proposal to the school board this spring and receive approval before the next school year. Currently, websites such as ChatGPT and Gemini are blocked on student devices because of privacy concerns, though DeBoer said the district may have opportunities to incorporate more secure AI tools into classrooms for activities such as project brainstorming or creating renderings in technical education courses.

DeBoer said he does not intend this to be a hard and fast policy because the world is moving at warp speed and the district's AI expectations and protocols will change as things change, and he said the district is looking at a set of processes and procedures to guide staff on consistent expectations for students rather than a policy that would constantly need revision. DeBoer said he expects AI use to be more common at the high school level than in elementary or middle school classrooms, particularly as students prepare for college, technical school and future careers where the technology is becoming increasingly prevalent, and he noted that AI-detection tools used during grading are not always accurate, prompting some teachers to return to pen-and-paper assignments to avoid concerns about misuse. While the district continues to develop expectations for classroom use, officials also hope to help teachers identify effective AI tools, provide additional training and continue evaluating the technology as it evolves, and results of the district's AI survey are available on the district website. AI policy is expected to remain a topic of discussion at Pierre School Board meetings, and the board meets at 5:30 p.m. on the second Monday of each month at the district administration building, with meetings open to the public.

stories.Headline: Former Commerce officials allege Howard Lutnick failed to act on sensitive computer chip smuggling
stories.Summary:
Former Commerce officials allege Howard Lutnick failed to act on evidence of sensitive computer chip smuggling during his tenure as secretary. These ex-employees describe his leadership as chaotic and marked by micromanaging. The accusations surfaced as scrutiny grew following the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Huang admitted to an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. China has denied these spying accusations, calling them a smear attempt.

The department stopped adding firms to the Entity List, which bans advanced chip sales to adversaries. No companies were added between October 9, 2025, and the present, the first such gap since 2008. In May 2025, Lutnick rolled back an interim final rule from January 2025 to avoid stifling innovation. A new rule now requires licenses for exports to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand. This rule was directed by the National Security Council and the Department of Treasury.

Howard Lutnick and his deputy, Jeffrey Kessler, are responsible for the department's export control enforcement. Former staff claim Kessler micromanaged every minor decision and blocked enforcement against suspected smugglers. They allege the career workforce felt stymied and unable to perform their duties. The Commerce Department and the White House did not respond to requests for comment. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent expressed frustration that Lutnick failed to follow through on chip ban enforcement.

Jensen Huang and Nvidia are affected by the scandal involving suspected agent Alice Huang. Reports suggest $7.5 billion in Nvidia chips reached Chinese firms through her links since 2023. An OpenAI researcher found evidence that banned Nvidia chips trained top Chinese AI models. Epoch estimated between 290,000 and 1.6 million chips were smuggled into China in 2024 and 2025. These smuggled chips provided roughly a quarter of China's acquired computing power.

The Biden administration first issued AI chip export controls in 2022 and 2023. Lutnick began running the department in February 2025, shortly after firing veterans Matthew Borman and Eileen Albanese. This sparked an exodus of up to 50 skilled staff members over 18 months. Departed experts included specialists in AI, Russia, diversion, and chips. The department also pivoted to allow sales of Nvidia H20 and H200 chips to China.

Key roles in the Bureau of Industry and Security remain vacant, including the chief of staff. The principal deputy assistant secretary roles for export administration and export enforcement are also unfilled. It remains unclear if the department will fill these positions or change its enforcement approach. The articles leave open whether the decision to sell H20 chips was made by Trump. They do not state if further investigations into Alice Huang will occur.

stories.Headline: South Korea and other allies sign a security pact to protect AI technologies and supply chains
stories.Summary:
South Korea joined the United States, Japan, and other allies on Sunday, November 16, 2026, to sign a security pact for artificial intelligence. This agreement, known as the San Francisco Declaration on the Secure Foundations of Enduring Prosperity, aims to protect critical AI technologies and supply chains from hostile actors. The move occurred just before U.S. President Donald Trump is scheduled to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping this Wednesday and Thursday in Shenzhen. The pact is part of a larger State Department initiative called Pax Silica, which seeks to help allied supply chains withstand shocks.

The declaration was signed by the United States, Korea, Japan, Australia, Israel, Britain, India, Singapore, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates. It requires these nations to safeguard sensitive technologies that could provide a military or intelligence advantage if stolen or illicitly transferred. Participating countries plan to establish working groups, including one dedicated to creating economic hubs that attract AI investment. Jacob Helberg, the U.S. under secretary of state for economic affairs, expects Germany, the Netherlands, and Sweden to sign the agreement this week. Second Vice Foreign Minister Kim Jin-a signed the document in person as the head of the Korean delegation.

Jacob Helberg described the declaration as historic because partners agreed to treat the security of technology and infrastructure as a shared responsibility. He noted that chip design, equipment, and shipping ports are often located in different countries, necessitating this joint approach. While some view the bloc as an effort to isolate China, a source familiar with the matter stated that the text does not single out any specific country. Victor Gao, vice president of the Center for China and Globalization, warned that using recent scandals to pressure China would be a total miscalculation.

The timing of the pact coincides with a tariff truce between Washington and Beijing that lasts until January 10, 2027. Upcoming talks in Shenzhen may focus on a trade-off between Chinese rare earths and American AI technology. Tensions have also risen following allegations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. These concerns about technology leaks have led to bipartisan calls in Washington for stricter export controls on AI chips. If no deal is reached this week, China may use its control of rare earths to pressure the United States.

This initiative is called the Law and AI Certificate Lab, which is designed as a three-day course for building legal tools. The intensive program will take place from December 1 to December 3 for a small group of participants. It provides a condensed version of the AI curriculum that the law school typically offers its students over a full semester. The course requires the participation of up to 24 individuals, including lawyers, government officials, academics, and technologists.

These attendees will use specialized technology provided by companies such as Legora, Harvey, and the website builder Replit. The curriculum focuses on the actual development of artificial intelligence tools while addressing important ethical considerations. This training allows professionals to build and evaluate their own software solutions within a short timeframe. Adjunct professor Damien Charlotin, who created the AI Hallucination Cases database, is directing the program alongside adjunct professor Erin Fraser.

Fraser also serves as an associate at the firm McDermott Will & Schulte while helping to lead this lab. These directors intend for the course to support professionals in navigating the complexities of modern legal technology. They aim to bridge the gap between theoretical knowledge and the practical application of AI in legal settings. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Equity secures UK actors rights to consent and payment for digital replicas in new AI deal
stories.Summary:
Actors in the UK are to be given more rights over their digital replicas under a new agreement on AI protections with TV and film producers, secured by the actors' union Equity after a growing on-set backlash and years of talks with the production body Pact. The three-year deal gives performers the right to be paid when their digital replicas are used and to consent to whether their replica is used at all. Approval must be secured from an actor if a digital double or digital alteration is used to make substantive changes to scenes involving agreed levels of nudity or simulated sexual activity. The agreement also states that producers may not use a digital replica during a strike in any circumstance where consent is required for such use.

Contracts will now make clear that producers only obtain permission for a specific project rather than blanket consent to an actor's digital replica, and producers must limit access to replicas to people with a legitimate business need and use commercially reasonable efforts to protect them from unauthorised access, use or copying. The deal also includes a 24% increase in pay rates for major films and a 9% increase for TV projects, along with a commitment to safe casting and audition spaces, training and reporting on sexual harassment, and adequate hair and makeup provision for artists of all ethnicities and cultures. The three-year deal will be put to a vote among 8,000 Equity members, with the union's leadership recommending they approve it. It comes after Equity members voted 99% in favour of taking industrial action and refusing to be scanned on set without further AI protections in an indicative ballot last December.

Paul W Fleming, Equity's general secretary, said the union set out to radically improve and modernise the terms and conditions for performers across UK TV and film and called the result groundbreaking. He said the deal achieved the best AI provisions in the business, protecting performers and ensuring that human performance is valued and prioritised across the industry. Equity said that despite its efforts the new agreement did not establish explicit contract protections regarding the use of actors' performances for training AI systems, and it noted that digital replicas could be made using the same photography captured for the production itself without the need to scan artists. Equity also said there were areas a new agreement simply could not cover, such as digital scanning traditionally undertaken in production for digital effects added later.

The deal follows mounting concerns on set about the use of AI, which has made many actors more wary of undergoing body scans, with many fearing the data could be used to train AI models on their likenesses or poses and pave the way for the technology to take away work. Last year the actor Olivia Williams told the Guardian that actors should have as much control over the data harvested from scans of their body as they do over nudity scenes, saying she and other actors were regularly pressed to have their bodies scanned by banks of cameras while on set with few guarantees about how the data would be used or where it would end up. The agreement now goes to the 8,000 Equity members for a vote, with the union's leadership recommending approval.

stories.Headline: Democratic control of Congress shifts AI policy toward risk-based oversight, Carrillo, Ellison and Braithwaite write

Democratic control of Congress will shift the national debate regarding artificial intelligence policy on November 16, 2026. This political change moves the focus away from the deregulatory agenda previously established by the Trump administration. The new leadership intends to implement a risk-based approach that emphasizes accountability for various impacts. This strategy specifically targets the economic, consumer, and public safety consequences of deploying these technologies. The new policy framework requires a stronger focus on consumer harms, fairness, safety, and transparency.

Congress may also increase its scrutiny of cybersecurity measures and the power costs associated with data centers. Businesses must prepare for a higher volume of investigations even if no new laws are passed. Companies are encouraged to demonstrate that they have implemented strong safeguards to protect the public. Pablo Carrillo, Bradford Ellison, and Dominic Braithwaite are the authors responsible for analyzing these upcoming regulatory shifts.

They suggest that the government will likely push for tougher oversight to ensure that AI systems remain safe. The authors indicate that the shift toward accountability will redefine how technology companies operate within the United States. stories.Headline: Foreign investors withdraw nearly US$50 billion from Asian equities over AI and cash burn concerns
stories.Summary:
Foreign investors withdrew nearly US$50 billion from Asian equities during October, marking the largest monthly outflow since June. This sell-off targeted tech-linked stocks in South Korea, Taiwan, India, Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam, and the Philippines. The retreat was driven by concerns over the cash burn of hyperscalers and fears that US midterm elections would bring tougher artificial intelligence regulations. These worries persisted after Democrats won elections in states where opposition to new data centers has increased.

The net withdrawal totaled US$49.8 billion, with Taiwanese stocks seeing a net loss of US$30.7 billion, the highest since January 2008. South Korean shares experienced a net outflow of US$14.6 billion, while Indian stocks lost US$3.6 billion for a second straight month. Indonesian and Thai markets saw outflows of US$938 million and US$199 million, though Vietnam and the Philippines gained US$122 million and US$109 million. In early November, foreigners offloaded another US$22.6 billion, including US$19.8 billion from Taiwan and US$8.3 billion from South Korea.

Wael Makarem of Exness stated that the outflows showed a retreat from AI positions due to doubts about profitability and infrastructure spending. He noted that tighter environmental reviews and regulations were expected to hinder chip demand and data center construction. Scarlett Liu from BNP Paribas suggested that investors were drawn to the resilience of the S&P 500 compared to the MSCI Asia ex-Japan index, which fell 6.9 per cent in October. She also mentioned that some investors moved money into US Treasuries as the 10-year yield reached 5.3 per cent in early October.

Herald van der Linde of HSBC upgraded India to overweight on Monday, citing reasonable valuations and resilient earnings. This positive outlook is reflected in the fact that cross-border investors have put a net US$5.7 billion into Indian equities so far this month. Other analysts believe investors are reallocating capital from Asia toward developed markets. This shift follows a period where the MSCI All Country World Index declined by only 1.7 per cent during October.

During mid-November 2026, primary and middle school students across China participated in popular study tours focused on artificial intelligence and robotics. These educational trips took place at industrial bases, museums, and science centers to bring emerging technologies closer to younger generations. In Jinan, Shandong Province, an embodied intelligence industrial base expected over 5,000 young visitors during the autumn break and the following weekend. Meanwhile, a science carnival in Qingdao, Shandong, attracted more than 2,000 students through twelve interactive challenges and six inquiry-based courses.

These programs require a shift from simply operating high-tech products toward a deeper understanding of the underlying logic of artificial intelligence. Effective learning should cover core AI aspects such as perception, reasoning, learning, decision-making, and interaction to help students recognize both capabilities and limitations. From November 6 to 10, the Jiangsu Science and Technology Museum offered science experiment shows and maker activities to encourage broader exploration. Other families visited the Shanghai Science and Technology Museum for AI-themed programs that combined hands-on crafts with guided tours of astronomy and ecosystems.

Li Qingdu, an AI and robotics researcher and educator, stated that these programs should develop problem-solving skills through practice rather than basic operation. Li cautioned that educational frameworks for these tours remain immature because the trend has only developed rapidly over the past three years. Parents like Qiu Shuhua from Jiangsu Province noted that while previous generations focused on history, today's children use these events to imagine the future. Su Zizhou, a mother from Shenzhen, emphasized the importance of combining hands-on learning with professional explanations to introduce technology in an age-appropriate way.

stories.Headline: Criminals steal about €100 million from Crédit Mutuel Arkéa in a cyberattack
stories.Summary:
A highly organized criminal group targeted the French banking and insurance group Crédit Mutuel Arkéa in a major cyberattack during late 2026. The attackers first compromised a third-party service provider on October 27 to infiltrate the bank's infrastructure. Starting on Sunday, November 1, the hackers siphoned approximately €100 million, or about $112 million, from the organization's accounts. They used instant payment systems to move the funds into legitimate European bank accounts before transferring the money to cryptocurrency platforms.

The heist required the creation of fake Fortuneo IBANs to initiate payment orders from the bank's accounts to external destinations. On Tuesday, November 3, the bank discovered the fraud and immediately blocked external access to its information system. To stop the theft, the organization disconnected from the interbank payment system, deleted the fake accounts, and updated its credentials. Blockchain analyst ZachXBT recorded suspicious withdrawals over $106 million on November 2, later raising that estimate to over $133 million. Bitquery tracked $108.8 million in USDC moving through OKX, Crypto.com, and Kraken within 21 hours.

Julien Carmona and the bank's chairman described the incident as a new type of robbery carried out by a well-equipped group. The chairman stated that artificial intelligence was very likely involved in the attack, although he provided no specific technical details. Carmona suggested that advanced AI might have supported the criminals, but the bank has not yet provided concrete evidence of its usage. The bank noted that customer accounts and Fortuneo systems remained unaffected by the breach.

The security breach began outside the bank's network, and the name of the compromised provider remains undisclosed to protect similar companies. Most of the methods used, such as credential theft and money mules, existed long before the mass adoption of artificial intelligence. Experts believe AI could have assisted the group with reconnaissance, coding, or creating documents to open the fraudulent accounts. No criminal group has claimed responsibility for the theft at this time.

This agreement, known as the China-ASEAN Free Trade Area 3.0 Upgrade Protocol, was signed in October of last year. The new rules are scheduled to enter into force on December 1 to bolster regional supply chains. This initiative aims to lower business costs by deepening the coordination of regional standards and rules.

The protocol expands cooperation into behind-the-border areas including the digital economy, green development, and artificial intelligence. It encourages both sides to recognize conformity assessment results to eliminate the need for duplicate testing and certification. New systems for electronic payments, invoicing, and bills of lading will improve compatibility and reduce expenses for companies. Enhanced digital customs procedures and better transport links are intended to shorten clearance times and resolve logistics bottlenecks. These changes follow a period where two-way trade between the partners exceeded 1 trillion dollars in 2025.

An official from the Ministry of Commerce stated that these measures enhance product competitiveness more effectively than tariff preferences alone. The ministry explained that the upgrade reflects a shared commitment to free trade and multilateralism during a time of global economic uncertainty. They noted that the agreement provides fresh impetus for economic integration across the Asia-Pacific region. To ensure businesses can utilize these new arrangements, the ministry plans to organize targeted training sessions.

The ministry will continue to work with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations to advance practical cooperation. This future collaboration will include further consultations regarding the digital economy and the implementation of artificial intelligence. By focusing on these high-tech sectors, the partners hope to create more resilient and efficient regional supply chains. These ongoing efforts seek to maintain the status of China and ASEAN as each other's largest trading partners.
