stories.Headline: Scott Loughlin says AI agents on personal devices test whether BYOD programs can survive
stories.Summary:
Employees who use personal devices for work are increasingly running artificial intelligence agents that can read work email, open files and act across applications without a person at the keyboard, and Scott Loughlin, a partner at Hogan Lovells Cadwalader in Washington, DC, wrote in a Bloomberg Law column published on November 16, 2026, that this raises the question of whether bring-your-own-device programs can survive agents in their current form. In a Gartner survey conducted in early 2026, 88% of employees with an enterprise AI tool also used personal AI tools for work, and those tools will likely increasingly include AI agents. Loughlin wrote that the core controls of a BYOD program, a company-managed container for work apps, monitoring of corporate systems and the ability to remotely wipe work data, were designed for apps that people operate and may not work as well for devices running AI agents. Because an agent works inside the employee's logged-in session, company records may show the employee doing what the agent did, and the agent's history and memory sit in the provider's cloud under the employee's account, beyond the reach of a remote wipe. Loughlin wrote that none of this requires hacking, but the exposure is real and no new AI statute is needed to create it, with personal data given to an unapproved agent raising issues under the GDPR and US state privacy laws, protected health information entered into a personal agent possibly being a HIPAA breach, and routine flows of source code or pricing undercutting trade-secret protection.

He wrote that EU law restricts the scope of employee monitoring and may require works-council consultation, and that US laws can limit employers' access to employees' personal accounts. He described three models likely to be applied role by role: access-only BYOD, in which personal devices reach corporate data only through a managed browser, app or virtual workspace; a sanctioned agent, in which an enterprise agent lets the organization control the agent even when it does not control the device; and company-owned devices for people in the most sensitive roles. He noted that the May 2026 guidance on agentic AI from CISA, the NSA and other governments recommends giving agents their own short-lived credentials and requiring human approval for high-impact actions. Loughlin recommended that organizations assign ownership at the leadership level, naming an accountable executive, adding personal and unsanctioned agents to the enterprise risk register and reporting on them to the board committee that oversees cybersecurity risk. He also recommended revisiting the BYOD agreement to address which agents may touch company data, employee disclosure duties, a narrow commitment to preserve and produce work-related agent data, and offboarding certification that connectors are revoked and work-related memories deleted, covering phones and tablets and calibrated to local employment and privacy law.

He advised updating legal-hold and e-discovery playbooks to add agent prompts, outputs, logs and memory to custodian questionnaires and hold notices, mapping roles and controlling the connection points where the law allows, updating incident response with scenarios for a hijacked or misused personal agent, and aligning related policies so they cross-reference each other. Loughlin wrote that organizations that plan ahead will be better positioned to demonstrate reasonable governance to regulators, courts and customers, and that agent risks are developing quickly enough that organizations are changing their BYOD programs in the short term before settling on a longer-term model. He wrote that it is a good idea to make the sanctioned path easier than the personal one and to focus controls on the connection points the organization owns. He wrote that BYOD rests on the premise that a company can manage the risk of devices it does not own, that agents using employees' credentials on those devices test that premise, and that BYOD is unlikely to disappear but programs are likely to change.

stories.Headline: Fractal evaluates 20 to 25 startups for acquisitions to strengthen enterprise AI capabilities
stories.Summary:
Fractal is evaluating 20 to 25 startups for potential acquisitions across healthcare, agentic AI and AI engineering, according to a Reuters report cited by TechGig on 17 November 2026. The company is looking to strengthen its enterprise AI capabilities ahead of an expected scale-up in enterprise AI adoption. CEO Srikanth Velamakanni said the merger and acquisition focus is on acquiring specialised engineering talent. The company also aims to strengthen relationships with large cloud computing firms and frontier AI labs.

Fractal is open to deals worth up to ₹1,000 crore, with a preferred acquisition size of $50-100 million, Velamakanni said. The company evaluated around 800 potential targets over the past 12 months. Fractal reported record revenue from operations of ₹956.5 crore in Q2 FY27, up nearly 20 per cent year-on-year, while net profit more than doubled 139 per cent year-on-year to ₹79.2 crore in the same quarter. Earlier in November, Fractal acquired Geneva-based analytics firm PricingOne for 1.32 million Swiss francs ($1.57 million), which Velamakanni described as an acqui-hire providing a foothold in Europe.

Velamakanni expects enterprise AI to scale significantly over the next year as foundation models become more capable and cheaper. He noted the cost of fixed intelligence from a foundation model could fall 93 per cent over a year. This shift should make large-scale AI deployment compelling for enterprises, with impact becoming meaningful as early as FY28. Fractal aims for acquisitions that accelerate its ability to build and deploy complex enterprise AI solutions.

The company reorganised its business in April around three pillars: AI-led Transformation, AI Foundations, and AI Work & Workforce. This structure enhances its enterprise AI offerings and builds capabilities in agentic AI governance. stories.Summary:
Massachusetts state Rep. Lindsay Sabadosa, a Democrat from the 1st Hampshire district, and state Sen. Cindy Friedman, a Democrat from the 4th Middlesex district, filed bills in the House and Senate to outlaw algorithmic rent pricing in the state. The Joint Committee on Housing reported the bills out favorably in March, and the proposals now sit before the Committee on Ways and Means. The bills respond to rent-pricing software, often called revenue management software, that many of Massachusetts’ largest landlords use at their properties. The software draws on nonpublic leasing data from nearby properties to recommend how high rents can go. Landlords using such programs have been accused of unfair pricing, intentionally leaving units vacant and colluding with others to reduce competition.

The bills would ban rent-pricing algorithms in Massachusetts, and the session ends Jan. 5. The biggest industry player is Texas-based RealPage, which claims on its website that its customers outperform competitors who do not use the service by up to 7%. RealPage’s algorithm analyzes nonpublic data from landlords using its software, including listed rent, the actual price tenants agree to after discounts and lease length, for new leases and renewals. The software also accesses data on a unit’s future demand and occupancy, including inquiries and applications from prospective tenants. A 2023 report by the Metropolitan Area Planning Council found that 21% of Greater Boston properties sold between 2004 and 2018 were purchased by an investor or speculator, and a 2025 study by the Lincoln Institute of Land Policy found that 8.9% of residential parcels nationwide are owned by a corporation.

Sabadosa compared traditional rent-setting to selling a used car, where the seller checks prices for the same or similar models and sets an asking price accordingly. She said the algorithm is a much more sophisticated way of looking at all the rents than trying to understand the maximum the market will bear in a given community. She said that for someone just trying to make money it is surely a great idea, but for thriving communities where people can afford to live it is a terrible idea, because it is constant upward pressure that pushes everybody out. Friedman said the problem is that it is distorting the market and called it kind of immoral, saying people are taking rental places where people can live and need to live off the market. Friedman said it becomes much more insidious much faster than a landlord going through Zillow or Redfin.

Demetrios Salpoglou, CEO of the real estate platform Boston Pads, said frequent price fluctuations he sometimes sees on the website cause unnecessary issues for renters and landlords. He said he has seen out-of-state landlords rely too heavily on algorithms without understanding neighborhood nuances, and has heard from confused consumers or their agents about a unit’s price changing twice daily. He said it is like over-engineering a Hyundai and calling it a Porsche, and that he has never really had a landlord say the rental software is incredible. Salpoglou said most small- and mid-sized or independent property owners he works with use real-time pricing data on his platform and may lower rent near the lease date but otherwise rarely change prices unexpectedly. He theorized corporate landlords may use the software to satisfy obligations to owners and investors, which he called, in the nicest way he could say it, a CYA.

In 2024 the U.S. Department of Justice and several states, including Massachusetts, sued RealPage and some of the largest landlords in the country, alleging the practice illegally decreases competition. In November of last year RealPage and the DOJ reached a settlement requiring the company to stop using non-public competitor data in price recommendations, not to use active lease data to train its models and to remove or redesign features that limit price decreases. RealPage did not admit wrongdoing and said in court documents that it continues to believe the use of non-public data led to more efficient and procompetitive pricing and reduced vacancies. Massachusetts and other states continued their case, and two landlord defendants, Greystar Management Services and LivCor, have settled, while the case against RealPage, Camden Property Trust, Pinnacle Property Management Services and Willow Bridge Property Company is ongoing. Attorney General Andrea Campbell said in January 2025, when the state joined the case, that her office will seek to hold accountable those who betray renters’ trust and undermine a fair and competitive housing market.

Neither Sabadosa nor Friedman was optimistic the state legislation would pass this session, and Friedman said she thinks the proposal could make it into larger housing-related legislation next session. New York was the first state to ban the technology, with the prohibition taking effect in December 2025, and California and New Jersey have since followed suit. RealPage sued New York seeking to overturn the law, arguing it violated the company’s First Amendment rights to free speech and dissemination of information, and in late September a federal judge issued a preliminary injunction blocking the law while the case plays out. New York Attorney General Letitia James has appealed the decision. Sabadosa said one advantage of Beacon Hill being a little slow-moving is seeing the laws pass in other states and the immediate legal challenges, and that they are looking at what the courts identified as issues and redrafting to be responsive.

Articles.Title: Massachusetts Lawmakers Target AI-Driven Rent Hikes - GovTech

stories.headline_source: Massachusetts Lawmakers Target AI-Driven Rent Hikes

stories.Headline: NTT Data publishes IDC InfoBrief on sovereign AI for manufacturers and automotive firms
stories.Summary:
NTT DATA published an IDC InfoBrief on sovereign AI for manufacturing and automotive, dated November 12, 2026, and a related page the next day. The company also held a webinar on November 8, 2026, about the same subject. The material is aimed at manufacturers and automotive firms that want to move AI from pilot to production. It focuses on protecting proprietary data, AI models and industrial IP across connected IT and OT environments.

The InfoBrief sets out five areas for manufacturers to explore. These are secure shop-floor intelligence and predictive AI for operations, governed AI workflows to strengthen supply chain resilience, and protection of industrial IP while accelerating innovation. It also covers scaling AI securely across edge, on-premises and cloud environments, and moving from pilot to production with governance built in. NTT DATA's AI Factory is described as helping organizations move from isolated AI pilots to secure, governed AI at scale with measurable business outcomes. The page offers a data sheet and the IDC InfoBrief, with chapters by industry, through a form asking for name, business email, job title, country, contact number and company.

NTT DATA presents sovereign and private AI as the way for manufacturers to scale innovation securely while keeping control and resilience. The company says its AI Factory delivers measurable business outcomes and helps organizations reach governed AI at scale. The InfoBrief is offered as IDC guidance for the manufacturing and automotive sectors, with a chapter for each industry. NTT DATA also points readers to related material, including its 2026 Global AI Report Playbook and blogs on industrial AI and workforce readiness.

The articles do not say what happens next beyond the offer of the InfoBrief, the data sheet and the webinar. They also list related insights, including a research report dated December 10, 2025, and blogs dated August 12 and August 13, 2026. The page invites readers to contact NTT DATA and lists careers and contact links. No further steps or timelines are given.

stories.Headline: AI drafts legal briefs but lawyers still hold responsibility for judgment
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence now drafts legal briefs and organizes case law in minutes. This technological shift occurred by November 15, 2026, according to Seoul Economic Daily. Junior lawyers previously spent entire nights reading records and revising drafts manually. Now, these colleagues receive completed drafts before their morning coffee even cools. The technology replaces the long hours once required for building basic legal skills.

The system can sort through tens of thousands of emails overnight without pay. It can also instantly pull together manuals for handling Fair Trade Commission inspections. In cartel cases, the first leniency applicant has its fine waived entirely. The second applicant to come forward receives a 50 percent reduction in fines. These specific rules mean a single order can change a company's fate.

Lee Chang-hoon is an attorney at the law firm Shin and Kim. He says that responsibility for brief contents cannot be handed to machines. Lee believes lawyers now sell professional judgment rather than just providing information. He notes that AI delivers wrong answers with composure and fabricates rulings. He argues that AI cannot take the blame for a lawyer's mistakes.

Some lawyers in the United States were sanctioned for citing invented case law. These fabricated rulings are described as plausible but are disasters for clients. Flustered employees may try to delete emails during on-site inspections by investigators. Commissioners at plenary hearings do not read AI prepared answers before asking questions. Clients are affected because they need advice on which options to choose.

Lawyers used to believe that working longer hours helped them build more skill. AI can now write opinion letters and prepare anticipated questions for hearings. However, it cannot stop an employee from deleting evidence during a raid. It cannot grasp the true intent of a commissioner's question during a hearing. AI cannot walk a chief executive through reputational damage or employee fallout.

Lawyers must still recommend decisions amid uncertainty and take responsibility for outcomes. They must guide executives on whether to rush into a leniency application now. The articles leave open whether the lawyer's job will disappear with late nights. They do not state if more lawyers will be sanctioned in America. The future of the profession depends on the value of human judgment.

Articles.Title: AI Can Draft Legal Briefs, But Lawyers Still Carry the Judgment - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Roanoke County students question teachers' heavy AI use as school board adopts AI policy
stories.Summary:
Students in Roanoke County Public Schools are questioning how heavily their teachers rely on artificial intelligence for classroom materials, even as the school board adopted a formal AI policy on Thursday that restricts student use of generative technology. Student Advisory Council representative Addy Weaver told board members that teenagers are noticing an influx of AI-generated content from teachers while students face strict limits on when they can use the same tools for assignments. Weaver said students understand that AI is a very helpful tool for teachers and administrators who might need help with lesson plans or social media graphics, but she said the overwhelming influx of AI-generated content in schools has been a little jarring to students, and many wish for a more balanced approach. She raised these concerns during Thursday's meeting of the Roanoke County School Board.

The school board formally adopted Policy 6.42c on Thursday, codifying rules around artificial intelligence alongside the division's existing three-zone learning framework to prevent what the division calls cognitive offloading by students. District guidelines allow teachers to use AI for routine tasks such as lesson planning and administrative work, while students default to a no-AI zone for most assignments. Some coursework falls into intermediate zones where AI research tools are permitted with proper attribution, and the policy requires students to cite AI assistance when permitted while warning against letting technology replace original thinking. Superintendent Jamie Soltis asked student leaders to bring policy recommendations to their Dec. 9 meeting at the Roanoke County Career and Technology Center.

Weaver also addressed student frustration with Copyleaks, the AI plagiarism detection tool integrated into the Canvas learning management system, saying students reported that the software has been largely ineffective and creates unfair accusations with few ways for students to disprove AI-use claims. She said concerns about Copyleaks were addressed at the meeting, noting that students accused of using AI have few ways to disprove the claim within the tool's current system. Weaver said the discussion helped the council better understand how the use of certain AIs in the county is necessary and benefits both teachers and administrators, and she thanked Soltis for listening to the students' thoughts and discussions. More information is available at the schools website.

Articles.Title: Problems with AI use in Roanoke County schools: It’s not the students - WFIR News

stories.Headline: Banks seek to curb AI debt exposure as backlash against the technology mounts
stories.Summary:
The Financial Times reported on 17 November 2026 that banks are seeking to curb their exposure to debt linked to artificial intelligence, as a public backlash against the technology mounts, though the article itself sits behind a paywall and its full contents are not available. The report carries a headline stating that banks want to limit how much AI-related debt they hold while criticism of the sector grows. No further details, including which banks are involved or what specific measures they are taking, appear in the accessible text. The date of the report is the only precise figure the available material gives.

The accessible portion of the article contains no numbers on the scale of AI debt, no names of institutions beyond the general reference to banks, and no dates other than the publication date of 17 November 2026. It does not say what the banks require of borrowers, what rules or limits they are changing, or how much exposure they currently carry. The only change it signals is a stated intention among banks to curb AI debt exposure in response to a mounting backlash. Nothing in the available text describes a completed action, a decision by a named regulator, or a figure attached to any institution.

The article names no individual as responsible and carries no direct statements from bank executives, regulators or critics, so there is no one whose remarks can be paraphrased. Responsibility for the reported move rests with banks as a group, according to the headline, but the text does not identify which ones. No spokesperson is quoted and no explanation is offered for why the backlash is growing or who is driving it. The accessible material therefore cannot support any account of what was said by anyone involved.

The context the available text provides is limited to the existence of a backlash against AI and a parallel concern among banks about their lending and holdings tied to the sector. It does not say what happens next, whether the banks have set targets, whether regulators are involved, or how the story might develop. Because the articles carry too little to support a longer account, this is a breaking story and further reporting will follow as details emerge. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Uber's legal AI agent cuts contract review time by over 20 per cent at 91 per cent accuracy
stories.Summary:
Uber's Legal Redlining Agent has cut the average contract review time by more than 20 per cent while reaching 91 per cent accuracy in its AI-generated decisions, the company said in a report dated 17 November 2026. The system sits directly inside Microsoft Word, where it analyses proposed contract changes and assesses the legal risks they carry. It then recommends policy-aligned responses by drawing on retrieval-augmented generation, historical lawyer feedback and deterministic rules. Lawyers stay responsible for reviewing and approving every recommendation the agent makes.

The agent spots edits made by external parties, works out their intent and compares the changes against legal policies. It suggests whether a clause should be accepted, rejected or modified, and it writes comments explaining each recommendation. Uber began building the first generation in early 2024 and piloted it with its Legal team in 2025. An initial RAG setup pulled relevant sections from legal playbooks to guide the language model's responses, and a later feedback loop captured lawyers' decisions, reasoning and final edited text.

At runtime, similarity search and metadata filtering narrow thousands of historical interactions down to about 20 candidates, and a second language model-based filtering stage checks their relevance. Exponential decay weighting, with a configurable half-life set to 365 days, gives priority to recent decisions. The architecture pairs a React and TypeScript Word add-in with a Python backend orchestrated through LangGraph, while OpenSearch stores vectorised legal rules and historical feedback and Redis keeps session state for follow-up questions. A deterministic rules engine enforces non-negotiable legal requirements and can override the model's recommendations.

Uber is also exploring agentic harnesses, including Claude Code and OpenCode, alongside skills to structure and automate workflows.

Articles.Title: Uber legal AI agent cuts contract review time by 20 per cent

stories.Headline: Karen Nyamu denies viral Senate thumb-sucking video and says AI fabricated it
stories.Summary:
Nominated Senator Karen Nyamu denied on November 16, 2026, that a viral video showed her sucking her thumb while scrolling through her phone during a Senate sitting, and she told TNX Africa that the footage had been fabricated using artificial intelligence. The clip, which drew considerable attention on social media, appeared to show the senator seated in the chamber, seemingly distracted by her phone before putting her thumb in her mouth. Nyamu spoke exclusively to TNX Africa and insisted she was being targeted through manipulated digital content. She challenged viewers to examine her manicure, arguing that her nail polish would not have remained intact had she been sucking her thumb as the video portrayed. Nyamu asked whether she could have kept her polish if she had been sucking her thumb, and she said the footage was made using AI.

She added that another one of her posts had recently been doctored as well. She challenged those questioning her conduct to consult the official parliamentary recordings, insisting the footage would expose the alleged fabrication. Nyamu said she had been on the floor debating very serious issues and urged people to check the Senate live feed for any such thing. The denial comes against a backdrop of previous controversies involving the senator and viral footage of her conduct. A month before the November 2026 denial, she trended online after yet another video showed her sucking her thumb on the floor of the house mid-session.

In March 2024, Nyamu was captured on camera scrolling through her phone during a Senate sitting as Nakuru Senator Tabitha Keroche addressed the House, and the footage sparked online criticism from Kenyans who questioned her attentiveness during parliamentary proceedings. In April 2026, an ordinary photograph of Nyamu standing alongside Busia Senator Okiya Omtatah was transformed into a fabricated intimate video that circulated widely online. Nyamu is also the sponsor of the proposed Artificial Intelligence Bill, 2026, which seeks to establish a framework for regulating the development and use of AI in Kenya. The articles do not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: Karen Nyamu denies sucking thumb during Senate session, says video was AI generated - TNX Africa

stories.Headline: Kodivo launches free interactive lessons to help developers direct and verify AI coding agents
stories.Summary:
Kodivo launched free, browser-based interactive lessons on November 17, 2026, to help developers work effectively with AI coding agents. The platform's AI Coding path teaches developers how to give agents clear tasks, select the necessary context, and verify the work the agents produce. The lessons include examples and practice questions that show how to turn vague requests into verifiable tasks. One scenario shows an agent changing code for a Save button, after which the saved note disappears when it is reopened.

The lessons present explanations in short, interactive cards that let developers practice the decisions they make while coding with AI. Users can try a lesson without creating an account, and the platform supports connecting external agents such as Codex or Claude Code through MCP. Developers who prefer learning with their own tools can use their own provider account for those connections. The free lessons do not include an external AI subscription or provider usage.

Kodivo is responsible for the platform, and its lessons focus on giving clear instructions and verifying agent output before developers trust the results. The stated aim is to improve developer proficiency in AI-assisted coding workflows. The lessons teach that verifying a requirement means following the interaction through saving and reopening, rather than solely inspecting the code. The articles do not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: Schneider Electric unveils Reference Design 115 for modular AI factories supporting 227 kW racks
stories.Summary:
Schneider Electric introduced its RapidScale Modular Data Center Reference Design 115 on October 21 at NVIDIA GTC Berlin, outlining a modular AI factory architecture engineered for the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform. The design supports AI rack power reaching 227 kW, according to the company. A study conducted with Compass Datacenters documents an approximately 80% reduction in selected onsite installation activities through prefabricated white-space modules. Schneider describes the design as a 10, 20 MW, Tier III-targeted modular AI factory architecture developed to ANSI standards. The published example concentrates on one deployment unit containing four scalable units, designed around four NVIDIA Vera Rubin clusters with 1,008 GPUs each.

That translates to 4,032 GPUs distributed across 56 AI computing racks, supported by another 32 networking racks. The documented configurations support approximately 10.4 MW to 11.4 MW of active IT load, with total peak facility power of approximately 13.25 MW. The reference design assigns approximately 33,518 square feet to the deployment unit, divided between IT space and supporting utility infrastructure. Reference Design 115 uses four 3.75 MW RapidScale powertrains to serve the IT environment, providing a 3+1 distributed redundant UPS architecture. Each powertrain includes a 5,000-amp QED-2 switchboard, three parallel 1,250 kW Galaxy VXL UPS units, and associated distribution infrastructure, and the UPS systems provide five minutes of runtime at rated load.

Separate 2.5 MW powertrains provide 2N electrical infrastructure for the mechanical systems, with UPS support for critical coolant distribution units and pumps. The design continues to use 480V AC distribution for AI racks, with 415V distribution for networking equipment. At the Max-P operating point, each AI rack draws approximately 227 kW, while at Max-Q power consumption falls to approximately 188 kW per rack. In the tabulated Max-P configuration, 42 AI racks operate with approximately 10.4 MW of total IT demand, including networking equipment, and the Max-Q configuration supports all 56 AI racks with approximately 11.4 MW of aggregate IT demand.

The Max-P configuration operates with three of the four IT electrical powertrains, while the full 56-rack Max-Q configuration uses all four. Schneider's design assumes that liquid cooling removes approximately 96% of the heat generated by the liquid-cooled racks, with the balance handled by air-cooling infrastructure. Motivair liquid-to-liquid coolant distribution units connect the computing equipment to a high-temperature technology cooling loop designed for approximately 108°F supply and 126°F return temperatures. A separate chilled-water system supplies 64°F water to Uniflair fan walls, which manage residual rack heat and other air-cooled equipment.

Schneider models annualized power usage effectiveness at approximately 1.1 under the San Francisco and Dallas conditions examined in the reference design. The companies first announced their jointly engineered EcoStruxure white-space module in September 2025, and their October 2026 White Paper 238 examines the installation sequence for integrated IT pods at a Compass hyperscale campus. In the configuration studied, an approximately 1,000-square-foot pod accommodates up to 42 rack positions with a maximum electrical capacity of 1.2 MW. The study reports that selected onsite activities required 15 hours for the prefabricated pod, compared with 75.5 hours for the conventional approach.

Compass also documented improvement through repetition, with one earlier installation requiring 18 hours compared with 15 hours for the later deployment examined in the study. In September, UL Solutions announced that Schneider had achieved the first certification under its UL 2140 program for specified prefabricated power distribution assemblies. The comparison excludes offsite manufacturing activities and does not measure total data center construction or commissioning time, and it also excludes certain conventional overhead-support installation work. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Schneider Electric's AI Factory Strategy Moves Beyond the Modular Data Hall

stories.Headline: US, Israel, UAE and Qatar sign pact to protect AI supply chains and infrastructure
stories.Summary:
The United States, Israel, the United Arab Emirates, and Qatar signed the San Francisco Declaration on Sunday to protect critical infrastructure and AI supply chains. This agreement strengthens regional cooperation with Washington as the Trump administration attempts to reduce the technological advantages currently held by China. The pact was finalized just before President Donald Trump is scheduled to meet with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping this Thursday. These diplomatic efforts occur while a major scandal involving the chipmaker Nvidia creates further tension in the global race for artificial intelligence.

This accord is a component of Pax Silica, a broader initiative launched in December 2025 to secure advanced manufacturing, energy, semiconductors, and critical minerals. The San Francisco Declaration establishes a common understanding regarding sensitive technologies and proposes the creation of five specific working groups. These groups will focus on resilience, security hubs, supply-chain cooperation, AI adoption, and the development of policy frameworks. While the document does not explicitly name China, it aims to coordinate global partners to challenge Beijing's dominance over the industries that support AI.

The United States State Department is responsible for the agreement and issued a press release explaining the need to safeguard the foundations of AI. Officials indicated that the pact creates a shared understanding of the critical infrastructure and sensitive technologies required for the modern economy. The initiative seeks to build a new grouping of partners specifically tailored for the AI economy to ensure long-term economic security. This strategic move is intended to stabilize the technology race during a period of uncertainty caused by the crisis at Nvidia.

Articles.Title: Middle East allies sign US AI pact as Nvidia crisis clouds chip race

stories.headline_source: Middle East allies sign US AI pact as Nvidia crisis clouds chip race

stories.Headline: Progress Software's Ed Keisling says AI token costs now come out of salaries and bonuses
stories.Summary:
Ed Keisling, chief AI officer at Progress Software, said in a November 15, 2026 CDOTrends article by Winston Thomas that the era of nearly free tokens ended as little as nine to 12 months earlier. He said that money must now come from somewhere, such as employee salaries, bonuses or travel. He described the gap between expectations and reality in AI deployment as far more complicated than executives expect. He compared it to his early career, when his team shipped finished Sun hardware and Oracle software stacks to banks instead of letting each bank install them. He said that work was much more difficult in practice than on paper.

Accenture surveyed 750 executives in 17 countries and found they expect per-token prices to fall 19% over two years while consumption grows 78%. GitHub moved every Copilot plan to token-based billing on June 1, 2026. Accenture found only about one dollar in five of token spend can be tied to a financial return. One in three organizations ran out of its annual token budget before year-end, and fewer than one in 12 use chargeback. By April 2026 Uber had used its full-year budget for AI coding tools and now limits each employee to USD1,500 a month in token spending per agentic coding tool.

Keisling said employees should see their own spend and managers their team's, with budget thresholds that force a conversation about whether work justifies the money. He said nothing should be deployed to a production or even test environment without cost controls in place. He said Progress wired cost telemetry into every agent before release and shut down internal agents after comparing spend with output, saying there was no ROI there. He called dumping everything into a growing context window probably the most expensive route and pointed to retrieval-augmented generation instead. He said getting data ready for a small language model takes months and that governance and observability tooling simply does not exist as a complete package.

The FinOps Foundation notes provider bills show spend by API key or project, not by business unit or cost center, and tooling around a production agent can make up 40% to 60% of feature spend. Gartner predicts companies will use small, task-specific models at least three times as much as general-purpose LLMs next year. IBM found high levels of shadow AI added USD670,000 to the average breach cost, and Ramp data reported by Axios showed 28% of corporate OpenAI chat spending in February flowed through personal consumer plans. Keisling said there is a good chance some data sent to frontier models ends up training them, while OpenAI states it does not train on API or enterprise data by default. Accenture's research suggests only about one-third of workloads must stay sovereign.

Progress describes itself as providing context and control for AI, including control over cost, and bought agentic RAG startup Nuclia in 2025. Progress sells agentic RAG as a service starting at USD700 a month. TypeSafe AI's Jev launched with USD5 in starter credit, which the company says buys about 120 million tokens. Keisling said newer small models are orders of magnitude cheaper than mid-tier ones, and he pins cheap models to routine tasks while saving frontier models for hard ones. He also points to a new class of decision models that classify and choose rather than write.

Keisling scores agents that act on four dials: the access the agent holds, the financial impact of its decisions, how fast a bad change can be reversed and the damage to reputation. He said companies should put a dollar on it and test the agent before it ships. He said what matters is how big a box you were able to put the agent in, in terms of tools, skills and budget. The article says most companies are still drawing theirs. The article ends by saying tokens got cheaper but ready did not.

stories.Headline: Knit Health raises a $35 million Series A led by NEA to guide patient referrals with AI
stories.Summary:
Knit Health, a startup that uses an AI world model to predict patient care needs, forecast treatment impacts and optimize referrals, raised a $35 million Series A round led by NEA, CEO Jonathan Kolstad told Axios Pro exclusively. The round was reported by Will Maddox of Axios in a story published on November 16, 2026. The company's stated aim is to guide patient referrals with artificial intelligence. Investors are betting on AI that predicts patients' next health needs rather than simply documenting their current ones.

The $35 million Series A was led by NEA, according to the report, and the funding is intended to support Knit Health's work guiding patient referrals with AI. The company uses its AI world model for three stated purposes, which are predicting patient care needs, forecasting treatment impacts and optimizing referrals. The report frames the investment as a bet on prediction over documentation, meaning AI that anticipates what patients will need next instead of only recording what they currently need. The articles give no further terms of the deal, no total valuation and no list of other participating investors.

Jonathan Kolstad, the CEO of Knit Health, confirmed the $35 million Series A round to Axios Pro exclusively, and the report attributes the funding news to him. The articles do not include any further direct statements from Kolstad beyond his confirmation of the round and its amount. No other executives, investors or NEA representatives are named or quoted in the material provided. The report also does not say what Knit Health plans to do with the proceeds beyond its existing focus on AI-guided referrals.

The context given is that investors are placing bets on AI that predicts patients' next health needs rather than simply documenting their current ones, which is how the report describes the big picture behind the round. The articles do not say when the round closed, how the company will spend the money, or what happens next for Knit Health beyond the funding itself. No details are given about the company's customers, its market, or any prior funding. The report was published by Axios on November 16, 2026, with Will Maddox as the author.

stories.Headline: Microsoft report guides workplace AI security priorities as IT teams face identity risks from agents and user-built apps
stories.Summary:
The article, published by Cybersecurity Insiders on November 16, 2026, sets out practical steps for containing and securing artificial intelligence in the workplace, and it draws heavily on Microsoft's yearly Digital Defense Report as a guiding priority list for the next twelve months. The author argues that the protection of AI use is not vastly different from the security work IT teams already do, despite the large amount of hysteria surrounding the technology. The piece notes that end users are increasingly building their own apps through vibe coding and then expecting IT to handle hosting, security and support. It also observes that attacks are often described as sophisticated when the root cause is simply someone misconfiguring a basic control that every product has. The article says identity is the surface that matters most, and that the core failure is too much standing access that is too loosely enforced, a weakness red teams have exploited for years.

It explains that AI agents operate like virtual users, with an identity, access to files and resources, and the ability to carry out digital tasks on a computer, so identity must remain a priority. The author advises against blocking all AI tools, because users have become very dependent on them, and instead recommends discovering what is being used, most easily through tools that inspect network traffic and show which domains and categories are visited. Presenting that data to business owners can shock them about where data is going, which typically convinces them that AI governance is not optional. The author, writing from an IT management perspective, says technology is the quicker and easier part of the job, while understanding and working with people is what separates one professional from the rest. The article asks whether the rest of the business received adequate training on approved AI tools and understands what not to do with business data, and whether some parts of the organization would be more productive with specialized tools routed through strong security controls.

It recommends asking people what business problem they are trying to solve, rather than accepting an answer that begins with a request for AI to do something. The author also sets out an order to follow, starting with identity and seeing how far an organization can get, because that path aligns with the failures that lead to most business compromises. The article notes that few IT staff have worked in environments where they are involved with all aspects of the cybersecurity strategy, and that starting at an MSP can make it difficult to know where to begin. It says all steps have their own merits, but some matter more than others, and it gives the example that starting with data governance while allowing all users to access stored data on any device has less impact than first preventing that action within the identity project. The conclusion states that the priority remains ensuring businesses implement the fundamental security controls long considered essential, since getting these basics right creates a stronger foundation and better prepares organizations for the risks of emerging technologies.

stories.Headline: Lawyers say generative AI gives narcissistic family litigants speed and false authority
stories.Summary:
A law.com expert opinion piece published on November 16, 2026, by Elisa Reiter of Calabrese Budner and Daniel Pollack of Yeshiva University's Wurzweiler School of Social Work describes how generative AI has affected narcissistic behavior in family litigation. The authors say that generative AI did not create narcissistic behavior in family litigation, but it has given that behavior speed, scale and a veneer of authority. They describe the litigant who treats the courthouse as a stage and files a dozen motions in a month. They describe the opposing party who rewrites the history of the marriage with unshakable confidence and frames every parenting exchange as proof of the other parent's unfitness. They describe the litigant who reacts to any adverse ruling as a personal insult.

The full text of the article sits behind a subscription paywall on Law.com, so the specific requirements, changes, numbers and dates it sets out are not available. The visible portion gives no figures, no court dates and no named cases beyond the authors themselves. The page does list related coverage, including a November 16, 2026, article by Laura Lorek reporting that court filings containing hallucinations have fallen for two straight quarters while subtler errors may be harder to catch. It also lists an October 22, 2026, report by Avalon Zoppo on the Fifth Circuit reassigning a case after a judge misused AI to draft a ruling, with Judge Jerry Smith writing for the appellate court. Those items are separate stories and are not part of the Reiter and Pollack piece.

The authors are responsible for the opinions in the article, and the visible text attributes the described litigation behavior to anonymous litigants rather than to any named person or firm. The article's own framing is that AI supplies speed, scale and a veneer of authority to behavior that already existed. Beyond that framing, the paywalled article does not disclose what the authors recommend or what they say should change. The surrounding coverage suggests that courts and practitioners are watching AI errors in filings, but the articles do not say what happens next in family law specifically. More to follow.

stories.Headline: AMD completes its 8.2 billion dollar World Labs acquisition and names Fei-Fei Li chief scientist
stories.Summary:
AMD completed its acquisition of World Labs on Monday, November 16, 2026, for a total of 8.2 billion dollars. The chip giant gained immediate access to the research and artificial intelligence models developed by the acquired firm. Fei-Fei Li, who is widely known as the godmother of AI, will join the company as chief scientist. She will also take on the role of executive vice president to help guide the organization. The deal integrates World Labs' specialized AI models that simulate 3D environments to train robots for virtual and real worlds.

This strategic move allows AMD to better compete with Nvidia, which currently holds a strong position through its open-weights models. The acquisition requires the integration of pioneering model research into the future hardware, software, and systems of the company. These new capabilities aim to help developers and researchers push the boundaries of what artificial intelligence can achieve. AMD Chief Executive Officer Lisa Su expressed her excitement about welcoming Fei-Fei Li and her exceptional team to the company.

Su stated that optimizing compute platforms and models together is necessary to provide the infrastructure for the next era of super intelligence. She believes that the research from World Labs will be essential in shaping the future of their technical ecosystem. This announcement follows the recent recognition of Su as the Yahoo Finance CEO of the Year for 2026. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Study finds AI-generated ad labels reveal only that AI played some role
stories.Summary:
A study published on November 16, 2026, in a TechXplore article republished from The Conversation examines what an "AI-generated" label in advertising actually communicates to consumers, concluding that such a label reveals only that artificial intelligence played some role without clarifying how large or small that role was. The article explains that AI might have served as one tool in a largely human-led creative process, perhaps editing an image or refining text, or it might have generated much of the finished advertisement with limited human input, and a single label can cover both extremes and everything in between. The authors note that advertising has long used disclosures, such as the "#ad" tag influencers place on social media or labels marking sponsored content, which help consumers recognize the commercial side of what they are watching or reading. Their research indicates that AI disclosures serve a different purpose, because traditional disclosures tell consumers why content is being shown to them while AI labels draw attention to how it was produced without revealing the respective roles of humans and machines.

The article reports that the distinction matters because evidence suggests disclosing AI involvement can reduce levels of trust, and other research points to overall consumer resistance to AI, although reactions vary considerably depending on what the technology is used to create. It notes that AI blurs the line between editing existing content and creating new content, since a person may still develop the idea and refine the result while the balance between human and machine contribution varies considerably, and disclosing AI involvement can invite judgments about who or what created the content, how much human input was involved and whether the use of AI was appropriate. The article says this may help explain criticism of AI-led campaigns by brands such as Coca-Cola and Gucci, and it describes how governments and platforms are beginning to address these questions through new approaches to AI transparency. The EU wants providers of certain generative AI systems subjected to strict disclosure requirements, and technology is emerging that allows digital content, including ads, to carry accessible information about its provenance and editing history.

The article reports that Meta acknowledged its "Made with AI" label appeared on content involving only minor AI modifications and did not provide sufficient context, and the company replaced that wording with "AI info" before later making the label less prominent when AI had been used to edit rather than generate content. It also describes the same ambiguity appearing in reverse, with labels reading "human-made" and "no AI" emerging to signal human authorship, and it asks whether these mean no AI whatsoever or a predominantly human process in which AI played a supporting role, since both kinds of label can obscure as much as they reveal. The authors advise consumers to take a little time to consider how they interpret AI labels, saying the term "AI-generated" tells us something but not everything about how content was produced and does not by itself mean the result is fake, poor quality or untrustworthy. They add that the label will not spell out the human role, including who developed the idea, selected and refined the output, checked its accuracy and decided what ultimately appeared, and they conclude that an AI label should be a starting point for evaluating content rather than the end.

stories.Headline: Democrats win Congress as voters reject data centers over rising power bills
stories.Summary:
Democrats won both houses of Congress during the midterm elections in November 2026. Many candidates campaigned by criticizing the proliferation of gigantic data centers across the nation. Voters expressed strong opposition to the industry through various local ballot measures. This blue wave was partly driven by public anger over rising power bills. Some Republicans also distanced themselves from pro-AI rhetoric to match their constituents.

Voters rejected data center measures in 40 out of 41 cases across 10 states. A March Gallup poll showed 71 percent of Americans opposed local data centers. Wholesale electricity prices near some centers rose as much as 267 percent in five years. Cornell researchers found operators pay only about 38 percent of linked infrastructure costs. The four largest cloud companies expect to spend 720 billion to 740 billion dollars in 2026.

Representative Yassamin Ansari of Arizona wants a pause on advanced AI development on day one. Senator Bernie Sanders advocated for democratic oversight instead of an outright ban on the technology. Representative Greg Casar wants AI CEOs to testify under oath during congressional hearings. Senator Ed Markey warned executives about the large number of subpoenas they will face. These leaders seek to address voter complaints about electricity, water, and jobs.

Building trade unions view data centers as a jobs bonanza for their members. Some voters fear that AI will cause job losses or create doomsday scenarios. The general public opposes data centers more than they oppose nuclear power plants. Tech leaders have grown used to a free hand and often chafe at regulation. Many of these leaders now court President Trump as close allies and donors.

The Create AI Act would make a National Science Foundation computing program permanent for researchers. The AI Whistleblower Protection Act would protect workers who report risks from AI. The AI LEAD Act would create a federal right to sue over harmful products. Governor Kathy Hochul of New York and Governor Greg Abbott of Texas previously halted permits. Elon Musk reportedly spent almost 500 million dollars supporting Republican candidates in the midterms.

State utility regulators may force data centers to cover the grid upgrades they trigger. Democrats must balance voter demands for relief with the need for economic growth. AI investment currently accounts for 37 percent of United States GDP growth according to ING. It remains unclear if Democrats can demand accountability from executives who support President Trump. The articles leave open whether voluntary corporate pledges will become binding through state law.

Articles.Title: Voters want relief from rising power bills. Democrats must find a way to deliver without stalling the AI investment helping drive the economy

stories.Headline: Corporate leaders use vague language to hide AI-driven job losses
stories.Summary:
Corporate leaders are increasingly using vague euphemisms like delayering and efficiency to hide the impact of artificial intelligence on job losses during 2026. Companies such as Chime, Boston Scientific, and CRH have utilized this consultant-speak to describe transitioning to smaller teams or reducing expenses. These linguistic shifts occur as tech-enabled headcount reductions draw more public ire and political pushback from the general population. This trend masks the true scale of economic changes and makes it difficult to pinpoint which industries are hardest hit.

Better monitoring tools are required to avoid catastrophic disruption, including expanded funding for the Bureau of Labor Statistics and the Census Bureau. According to Challenger, Gray & Christmas, companies cited AI in 121,400 job cut announcements in 2026, compared to 54,800 in 2025. The government must improve the frequency of the Displaced Worker Supplement report to better track these shifts. Such data is necessary to deploy retraining programs and relocation support for families affected by these technological changes.

Jonathan Levin argues that lawmakers must address these blind spots before a massive avalanche of job losses arrives. He suggests that the Trump administration and the newly elected Democrats should increase government budgets to improve labor data. Andy Challenger noted that companies will likely become even more careful with announcements, making the impact of AI more opaque. Meanwhile, executives like Charles Scharf of Wells Fargo and Brian Moynihan of Bank of America have emphasized using attrition and careful hiring instead of formal layoffs.

The current labor market remains stable, with unemployment dipping to 4.1 percent in October from 4.2 percent in September. However, Goldman Sachs economist Pierfrancesco Mei noted that workers displaced by AI often take longer to find new employment. If the government response is too slow, the United States risks a repeat of the China shock from the 2000s. Policymakers must now act to ensure the labor market is not automated into oblivion before the full impact is understood.

Articles.Title: Corporate-speak is masking the impact of AI on job losses—here's why that's a problem

stories.Headline: UAE lawyer says companies face liability for harm from AI-generated advice under civil law
stories.Summary:
Under UAE law, liability for AI-generated advice or decisions that cause financial loss, legal violations or harm may be considered under general principles of civil liability, contractual obligations and any applicable sector-specific legislation, according to Ashish Mehta, founder and managing partner of Ashish Mehta & Associates, writing in Khaleej Times on 15 November 2026. The UAE Civil Transactions Law does not establish a separate liability regime specifically for AI-generated outputs or advice or work rendered on the basis of AI-generated advice, he wrote. Article 245(1) of Federal Decree-Law No. 25 of 2025 promulgating the Civil Transactions Law provides that, subject to special legislations, the chapter applies to liability arising from a harmful act committed by a natural or legal person. Article 246 provides that every act causing harm to another obligates its perpetrator to compensate for the damage, even if the perpetrator lacks discernment. Article 247 distinguishes harm caused directly, where a guarantee is due without any condition, from harm caused by causation, where no guarantee is due unless the perpetrator was a transgressor or acted intentionally, or the act led to the harm.

Liability may depend on the role each person played in the development, deployment or use of the AI system, the nature of the act or omission involved, and whether a sufficient connection can be established between that conduct and the damage suffered. Using AI as a tool would not by itself necessarily exclude liability on the part of the person or entity responsible for its use. A company may be liable where an AI system is used in its business operations and the resulting harm can be attributed to the company's acts or omissions, including inadequate assessment of the system, insufficient safeguards or a failure to appropriately monitor its use. Article 645 of the Civil Transactions Law defines a professional company as a company established by one or more persons licensed to practice a liberal profession, or thereby with others, whose purpose is to practice that profession, unless the law or the agreement provides otherwise. Article 651 provides that each partner is personally liable for their professional faults towards the professional company and the rest of the partners, and the professional company is liable for the faults of the partners vis-à-vis third parties.

Article 651 also provides that the professional company is liable for any act or conduct carried out by the manager or managers in the ordinary course of management, and for any act carried out by one of its employees or agents whenever such person has the authority to act on its behalf and the third party has relied on such authorization in dealing with it. Any provision in the articles of association of a professional company permitting approval of the exemption of any person from any personal liability borne thereby in their capacity as a current or former manager shall be void. Professional companies remain liable under UAE law for professional services they provide, regardless of whether rendered by a manager acting in the ordinary course of business or an authorised employee, and regardless of whether the service deliverables relied on advice generated by artificial intelligence. Such liability may not be expelled by the professional company's constitutional documents or other agreements. Article 3.2.1 of the AI Ethics: Principles and Guidelines (December 2022), issued by the UAE Ministry of State for Artificial Intelligence, Digital Economy and Remote Work Applications, provides that accountability for the outcomes of an AI system lies not with the system itself but is apportioned between those who design, develop and deploy it.

Article 3.2.2.1 of the AI Ethics Guidelines states that AI operators and AI developers should consider designating individuals to be responsible for investigating and rectifying the cause of loss or damage arising from the deployment of AI systems. Article 3.5.1 provides that AI developers should ensure AI systems will not cause any unintentional harm and adverse impacts. The AI Ethics Guidelines also provide procedures through which individuals affected by significant AI-assisted decisions may challenge those decisions and seek human review, but the Guidelines expressly describe themselves as non-binding and should be read as policy guidance rather than as a standalone basis for imposing legal liability. Where AI-generated advice or decisions by a company result in financial loss, legal violations or harm to an individual, the individual shall have a right of recourse against the company itself, and if the service was rendered by a partner, the partner remains personally liable to the company for any loss suffered as a result of such third-party claim or action.

As to a manager who was not acting in the ordinary course of business or an unauthorised employee acting in bad faith, the company may subsequently take action against such partner, manager or employee, including termination of employment. Article 614 clause 3 of the Civil Transactions Law provides that if the manager of the company exceeds the powers specified in the contract, he shall be liable for any damage that befalls the company as a result of such act. Clauses 2, 3, 4 and 9 of Article 44 of Decree Law No. 33 of 2021 on the Regulations of Employment Relations allow an employer to dismiss an employee without prior notice, after a written investigation and by a written and reasoned decision, in specified events. These include an employee committing an error resulting in gross material losses to the employer, or deliberately causing harm to the employer's property and admitting the same, provided the employer notifies the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation within 7 working days of being aware of the occurrence.

They also include violation of the establishment's bylaws on work and workers safety, where such instructions are in writing and posted in a visible place and the employee has been advised thereof, and failure to perform main duties under the employment contract despite a written investigation and two warnings of dismissal in case of recidivism. Clause 9 covers an employee abusing his position with the aim of obtaining personal gains and profits. Any claims by a company against an AI developer shall be subject to the contractual terms governing their relations. The applicable provisions cited are Federal Decree-Law No. 25 of 2025 promulgating the Civil Transactions Law and the AI Ethics: Principles and Guidelines (December 2022).

Ashish Mehta is qualified to practise law in Dubai, the United Kingdom and India, and full details of his firm are on www.amalawyers.com. Readers may e-mail their questions to news@khaleejtimes.com or send them to Legal View, Khaleej Times, PO Box 11243, Dubai. The article states that the information provided is intended for general guidance and does not constitute legal advice, and recommends seeking formal legal counsel. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Anthropic buys 3.4 billion dollars of gas-fired engines from OnePWR Solutions for its AI data centers
stories.Summary:
Anthropic signed a contract to buy gas-fired engines for its AI data centers in November 2026. The AI company behind Claude entered this deal with OnePWR Solutions, a Texas-based energy firm. This purchase is reported to be worth 3.4 billion dollars for the power generation equipment. The Financial Times says this is the largest known single purchase of its kind by an AI lab. These engines will provide the data centers with an enormous amount of off-grid electricity.

The deal requires gas-fired engines to power facilities that Anthropic describes as relying on dedicated on-site generation. This setup exposes the company to fuel price volatility and supply disruptions that it bears on a pass-through basis. Anthropic mentioned natural gas five times in one paragraph of its S-1 filing to highlight this bottleneck. The company notes that constraints on pipeline capacity and firm fuel transportation are necessary to deliver the gas. Failure to secure these supplies could cause a planned site to be delayed or abandoned entirely.

Anthropic's AI bot, Claude, stated that gas plants are less harmful than coal but more harmful than most alternatives. It explained that natural gas plants emit roughly 400 to 500 grams of CO2 per kilowatt hour. The bot noted that methane leaks during drilling and transport can erode the advantage gas has over coal. It further stated that building new plants can lock in emissions for 30 to 40 years. Claude added that carbon capture could reduce emissions but is currently costly and not widely deployed.

Futurism stated that the AI industry has turned its back on the climate crisis in favor of pollution-spewing generators. The Sierra Club estimated that upcoming AI data centers could release 2.1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide by 2030. This amount of pollution could wipe out nearly 15 years of greenhouse gas reduction efforts. Voters are showing they are fed up, as only one of 41 recent ballot measures favored data centers. These environmental impacts affect the global climate through increased air pollution and global warming emissions.

The articles note that 26.8 percent of U.S. businesses used AI in October 2026, up from 3.7 percent in 2023. Energy Transfer operates over 140,000 miles of pipelines across 44 states and has a debt of 68.8 billion dollars. This company signed agreements to supply natural gas to Oracle and a Nexus Data Center hyperscale campus. It also has a 20-year binding agreement with Entergy Louisiana, which partners with Meta Platforms for a facility. Energy Transfer grew its adjusted EBITDA by 31 percent to 5 billion dollars in the third quarter of 2026.

OpenAI may go public in 2027 and is currently burning through billions of dollars every quarter. Analysts have a median one-year price target of 25 dollars for Energy Transfer stock as of November 2026. The articles leave open whether the AI industry will continue to prioritize gas over solar and wind power. It remains unclear if the high debt of pipeline companies will yield the expected long-term financial returns. The future prognosis for the environment remains grim as AI companies race to secure necessary utilities.

stories.Headline: Sound Ventures holds a $7 billion stake in Anthropic from a $435 million investment
stories.Summary:
Bloomberg reported on November 15, 2026, that Sound Ventures, the firm co-founded by music manager Guy Oseary and actor Ashton Kutcher, holds a stake in Anthropic worth $7 billion based on private market valuations rather than any public share price. The relationship began in spring 2023, when Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei visited Oseary's Beverly Hills home and met with Oseary and Kutcher across the table. Sound Ventures made its first bet on Anthropic that spring with a $35 million investment in the company's Series C round, which valued the AI lab at roughly $4.6 billion before the new money arrived. Google and Spark Capital also participated in that round, giving the deal a mix of Big Tech strategic money and established venture backing.

Over several later rounds, Sound Ventures' total commitment to Anthropic grew to approximately $435 million, and the reported stake works out to roughly 16 times the total cash invested, though those are paper gains rather than realized returns. Sound Ventures was founded in 2015 out of A-Grade Investments, a collaboration between Oseary and Kutcher, and in 2023 it established a dedicated AI fund of nearly $240 million. Anthropic is preparing for an IPO anticipated for late 2026, which would give investors like Sound Ventures a public market for their shares and test the private valuations. Until then, the $7 billion figure is best read as a mark rather than a payout, since lockup periods, share price swings and the timing of any sales would all shape what the firm actually brings home.

The article attributes the reporting to Bloomberg and notes that the $7 billion figure rests on private market valuations, not on a public share price. It describes concentration as a quieter risk for Sound Ventures, because if one holding is worth far more than everything the firm put into it, a lot of the fund's results depend on that single company. The article says a few things are worth tracking from here, including whether Anthropic's IPO plans hold to the anticipated late 2026 timeline and how public markets value the company compared with its last private round. It adds that a third thing to watch is whether Sound Ventures decides to cut its position once there is a market to sell into.

The article notes that Anthropic was a young AI lab started by former OpenAI executives and was still proving it could compete with its old employer when Sound Ventures first invested. It observes that plenty of early backers make one bet and watch later rounds dilute them, while Sound Ventures kept investing, which helps explain how a $35 million opening check became a position measured in billions. It closes by noting that in 2023 Amodei may have been the least famous person in that Beverly Hills living room, and judging by the reported value of the stake, he may also have been the most consequential one for the people sitting across from him. The article carries a disclosure that it was edited by Diego Almada Lopez.

stories.Headline: European leaders meet in Dublin to discuss coordinating US and EU AI safety efforts
stories.Summary:
European leaders including Prime Minister Micheal Martin, Antonio Costa, and Roberta Metsola met in Dublin, Ireland, on November 13, 2026, to discuss artificial intelligence. This gathering highlighted the need for the United States and the European Union to coordinate on AI safety to prevent catastrophic risks. While the Trump administration has shown little interest in this engagement, recent cybersecurity incidents from American frontier labs may encourage narrower cooperation. Progress is more likely to occur through legislatures, specifically by creating a joint AI safety working group within the Transatlantic Legislators’ Dialogue.

This proposed coordination would utilize the Transatlantic Legislators’ Dialogue, which has met twice a year since 1999 to discuss security and trade. The effort would focus on interoperable incident reporting and establishing designated points of contact within regulatory and law enforcement agencies. It would build upon the October 2026 White House Accord on Super Intelligence and the bipartisan FRONTIER Act currently in the United States. European efforts include the AI Act and the Digital Omnibus, which entered into force in July 2026 to adjust compliance requirements.

The European Parliament's steering committee and a bipartisan US delegation are responsible for managing these legislative exchanges. These officials suggest that focusing on cybersecurity measures first would avoid contentious issues like data privacy or content moderation. They argue that an early dialogue with the incoming Democratic majorities in Congress would ensure that new enforcement measures are compatible. This approach aims to avoid previous failures where dialogues were dismissed as talk shops or seen as attempts to export regulatory regimes.

The current US policy is a patchwork of state laws and voluntary commitments, while the EU uses a formal legal framework. Unresolved questions remain regarding the oversight of restricted models, such as the Mythos rollout by Anthropic through Project Glasswing. Legislators face pressure from constituents to deliver meaningful safety measures that address risks extending across international borders. Future efforts will seek common definitions for incident reporting, drawing on the NIS2 Directive and the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act.
