During the 2026 Double 11 shopping festival, AI Token packages went on sale through e-commerce platforms and livestreaming rooms. This shift occurred as AI inference data volume in China exceeded training data volume for the first time. Chip manufacturers and cloud vendors have also changed their layout strategies to focus on inference. These developments reflect a broader industry trend where inference is becoming the mainstream study. New risks have emerged, including unregulated gray market data transfer hubs.

JD.com saw Token sales increase 20 times month-on-month during a November 2 livestream. On Tmall, Austin Li sold 100,000 Qianwen Office cards for 0.01 yuan each within thirty minutes. Intel and Qualcomm showcased agent phones and AI PCs at the China International Import Expo. AMD released the Ryzen AI Max PRO 400 series in September 2026.

Wang Zhicong of Intel China stated that more computing power will deploy on the inference side. He noted that Intel is extending applications to laptops and small AI Box edge devices. Qualcomm's Wan Weixing said end-side AI is evolving toward intention understanding and task orchestration. AMD's Michael Nordquist revealed that agent PCs running 100-billion-parameter models have shipped over 500,000 units. UCloud's Liu Hua believes cloud service delivery units are shifting toward the Token.

Consumers are affected by varying model capabilities and a lack of standardized refund rules. Some users reported that gray market tokens cost more than official prices or caused server congestion. These unofficial transfer stations may cause privacy leakage, data outflow, and malicious implantation. MediaTek and NVIDIA's RTX Spark chip now allows offline processing for ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft, and MSI. The Zhipu Coding Personal Edition GLM-5.3 monthly card is a bestseller on JD.com.

The industry is moving toward edge-cloud collaboration to reduce dependence on networks for real-time performance. stories.Headline: Numa raises a $45M Series C led by Blue Cloud Ventures at a $500M valuation
stories.Summary:
Numa, an Oakland-based company that builds an AI platform for car dealership customer service, announced on Monday a $45 million Series C round led by Blue Cloud Ventures, according to Fortune. The round brought Numa's total funding to $96 million, with Threshold Ventures, Costanoa Ventures, Touring Capital, Gradient Ventures, Mitsui and Tokio Marine also participating. A source familiar with the company said the investment valued Numa at $500 million after the round. Founded in 2017, Numa previously raised seed and Series A funding from investors including Draper Fisher Jurvetson.

Numa's AI agents connect to a dealership's software to check inventory down to a car's trim and features, pull repair updates and log sales leads alongside conversation transcripts. The platform also handles routine warranty paperwork and flags exchanges that may signal an unhappy customer for managers to review. CEO Tasso Roumeliotis told Fortune that filling out warranty paperwork is a drudgery of a job that nobody wants to do and that people do it poorly, and that AI can do it instantly. The company has about 160 employees across its Bay Area headquarters, a sales and marketing office in Kansas City and an AI development office in Montreal, and more than 1,500 dealerships in the U.S. and Canada use its software, including Longo Toyota, Norm Reeves Honda and Gold Coast Cadillac.

Roumeliotis previously built Location Labs, a mobile technology company that used GPS-enabled cellphones to help people track one another's locations, and after selling the business in 2015 he joined Draper Fisher Jurvetson as an entrepreneur-in-residence. Former colleagues from Location Labs then approached him wanting to build another company together, and in 2017 they launched Number AI to help small businesses receive and respond to texts through their existing landline numbers. As they worked with car dealerships they found problems beyond missed messages, with employees juggling calls, paperwork and manual follow-ups while customers waited, so the team narrowed its focus to the automotive industry and renamed the company Numa. Mir Arif, managing partner of Blue Cloud Ventures, told Fortune that he looks at the auto dealership as a little bit like jumbo shrimp, a massive niche, and that all of them are still working off legacy software or literally pen and paper.

A KPMG survey of roughly 2,100 senior leaders across 20 countries and industries ranging from automotive to healthcare, accounting and consulting found that 34% reported widespread employee adoption of AI agents in the third quarter of 2026, up from 25% in the first quarter. In a separate announcement on Friday, AI agent management startup LangChain raised $300 million in a Series C round led by CapitalG, with participation from Singapore's GIC, DFJ Growth, IVP and Sapphire Ventures. That investment valued LangChain at $3 billion, more than double its $1.25 billion valuation from a year earlier when it raised $125 million. LangChain began in 2022 as an open-source project and later shifted its focus to managing AI agents, and it reports 7,000 LangSmith customers, including Harvey, Rippling, Clay, Nvidia, Toyota and Salesforce.

stories.Headline: Democratic election wins and data center moratoriums push AI buildouts out of the US
stories.Summary:
Democrats won sweeping victories and local voters approved data center moratoriums during the recent midterm elections. These political shifts embolden opponents of artificial intelligence buildouts across the United States. Successful Democratic candidates campaigned on restricting new construction due to water and electricity use. Other Democrats seek broader AI regulations to prevent job losses and dystopian outcomes. These promises will be enacted in January when Democrats control Congress and several state capitals.

Democratic control will extend to state capitals in Texas, Ohio, Georgia, and Iowa. Goldman Sachs analysis indicates that moratoriums could delay as many as 45 percent of planned U.S. data centers. Alphabet announced a 15 billion dollar data center push in Malaysia the day after the elections. Anthropic mentioned reducing U.S. concentration risks in its initial public offering filing. The Senate previously voted for the GAIN AI Act in October 2025 to limit export control revisions.

Stanislav Kazanov of Innowise stated that the election accelerated a pre existing move of computing power outside the U.S. He noted that 26 percent of 633 gigawatts of tracked U.S. capacity is in states with planned halts. Kazanov explained that programs serving American users must stay close to them in accommodating states or federal lands. Mike Intrator of CoreWeave told CNBC on November 11 that he wants to build responsibly. He expressed hope that the election results would not cause a seismic slowdown in domestic construction.

President Donald Trump worries that these restrictions put the United States at a disadvantage in the global AI race. Thomas Anglero of MerkabaPhi AS said frontier model owners like OpenAI and Anthropic still need local U.S. centers. He argued that centers in Asia or Europe would hurt them due to latency issues. Aaron Henry of Foundeast Asia Co. Ltd. expects Thailand, India, and Malaysia to capture more market share. These regions can provide the reliable power and water that developers struggle to find in the U.S.

The U.S. currently holds 45 percent of global data centers, while Europe has 28 percent and Asia has 15 percent. McKinsey and Company reports that Amazon, Microsoft, Oracle, and Alphabet are already investing in Asian infrastructure. Asia is projected to account for 34 percent of global data center demand by 2030. Kearney sees European demand shifting toward Scandinavia, Greece, Portugal, and Hungary while slowing in France, Germany, and the United Kingdom. Arnold Platz of General Future Holding noted that the core capital and chips remain in the U.S.

Future growth may occur in Vietnam and Indonesia as developers seek more accommodating international locations. The new Democratic Congress may push for renewed AI export controls on chips and infrastructure. This focus follows a potential Chinese intelligence operation involving Alice Huang and former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Huang resigned as CEO after reports of a second affair with an executive at the chip company. The articles leave open whether the U.S. can maintain its lead despite these domestic buildout challenges.

The same reporting described plans to direct roughly $30 million from treasury resources toward an AI-related marketplace scheduled for December. The articles do not name the executives who made the decision or give the exact date the cuts took effect. They also do not say how many employees were affected in absolute numbers. The reported figures include value locked in the MegaETH ecosystem at about $8.8 million, down from an earlier period above $240 million.

The articles note that total value locked can move for many reasons, including token prices, rewards programmes and the exit of a few large liquidity providers, so it is not a complete measure of adoption or revenue. Reporting also referenced a planned decentralisation milestone in March 2027, which the articles say matters because it speaks to who controls upgrades and critical infrastructure. The articles stress that the $30 million allocation and the December marketplace are plans, not proof of an operating product or revenue. The articles do not quote MegaETH executives directly and do not attribute specific statements to named company officials. They frame the open questions instead: whether applications are attracting repeat users without incentives, whether the network delivers the promised speed and reliability, and whether independent developers can ship products people want.

On the AI marketplace, the articles say it would need to answer ordinary product questions about customers, the service being sold, the business model and why this particular blockchain improves the experience. They add that a broad trend toward blockchain and AI connections is not a commercial plan in itself. The articles place the situation against difficult market conditions for Ethereum, including ETF outflows covered in a separate NewsBTC report, and describe MegaETH's case as a company-specific test on top of that. They say the next meaningful update will be evidence of both product execution and the original network commitments, rather than a new roadmap graphic. The articles do not say what MegaETH has announced about next steps beyond the December marketplace plan and the March 2027 milestone.

stories.Headline: Former Wall Street regulator warns AI bubble will burst and cause recession by 2028
stories.Summary:
A former top Wall Street regulator said in mid November 2026 that the artificial intelligence bubble will likely burst and cause a recession by the 2028 election, according to CNN. The warning came as a survey reported by the Chosun Ilbo on November 15, 2026 found that 87% of Wall Street experts cite AI as a major risk. The two reports together frame a market that has risen sharply on AI enthusiasm while professionals increasingly flag the danger. The CNN report identifies the speaker as Wall Street's former top cop, a reference to a senior enforcement official, though the supplied text does not name the person.

The CNN account says the expected burst would be severe enough to tip the economy into recession before voters go to the polls in 2028. The Chosun Ilbo figure of 87% is the share of Wall Street experts who named AI as a major risk in the survey it reported on November 15, 2026. Both dates fall in November 2026, which places the warnings roughly two years before the 2028 election. The articles give no further numbers, no specific forecast dates beyond the election, and no named companies or individuals beyond the former official described in the CNN headline.

Responsibility for the warning rests with the former enforcement chief, who according to CNN expects the bubble to pop and drag the broader economy down with it. The Chosun Ilbo survey places the concern among a large majority of Wall Street experts, who see AI as a major risk rather than a purely positive force. The former official's view, as CNN frames it, is that the run-up resembles a bubble that cannot hold. The experts surveyed by the Chosun Ilbo did not, in the supplied text, offer a single unified prediction beyond flagging the risk.

The context is a market that has climbed on AI optimism while a growing share of professionals warn of a correction, and the CNN report ties that correction to a possible recession before 2028. What happens next depends on whether the bubble deflates gradually or bursts suddenly, and the articles do not say which outcome they expect beyond the former official's warning. The Chosun Ilbo survey suggests the concern is widespread rather than isolated to one voice. Neither article, in the text provided, gives a timeline for the burst beyond the 2028 election horizon.

stories.Headline: Armin Ashenberg argues universities must teach graduates to collaborate with AI as automation reshapes the job market
stories.Summary:
Dr Armin D Ashenberg of the School of Law at Western Sydney University wrote an opinion piece first published with full links on The Conversation. The piece was also published by Western Sydney University on 16 November 2026. It addresses concerns about artificial intelligence taking people's jobs and reducing job opportunities for university graduates. AI software companies such as OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Anthropic are pursuing AI systems capable of matching or exceeding human performance across a broad range of intellectual tasks. The article asks what this means for graduates and universities and which jobs are most at risk.

A federal government report published in July rated jobs typically involving cognitive tasks as those with the highest exposure to AI automation, including accountants, clerks and receptionists. Jobs rated as lowest exposure tended to require more physical work, such as tradies, carers and truck drivers. The report found that as of February this year AI had not had significant impacts on the Australian job market, including graduate opportunities. This month the Reserve Bank of Australia noted some signs younger workers in more AI-exposed industries are struggling to find work in Australia. The number of graduate jobs in some law firms has been slashed, with low-level tasks passed onto AI, and consulting firms have also cut graduate roles in recent years but claim it is not because of AI.

Just last week Qantas announced it will outsource 850 jobs to India while investing more in AI. A 2024 study compared the reasoning skills of humans and AI language models through tests including maths puzzles designed to assess whether people and AI models could recognise that an answer, which seems right at first, is actually wrong. In the example given, a scarf costs 210€ more than a hat, the scarf and the hat cost 220€ in total, and the correct answer for the hat is 5€. Researchers found earlier AI systems performed worse than human participants in the study's reasoning test, while more recent AI models performed better. An OpenAI model recently disproved a longstanding conjecture in geometry dating back to 1946.

Ashenberg's own research analysed AI's responses on university criminal law exams in 2023 and 2025, finding average exam scores improved from 52.5% in 2023 to 76.3% in 2025. Unlike the 2023 study, the 2025 models on average performed better than an average university student on critical thinking capabilities. These were specific tests and do not prove AI could displace humans and take over an entire profession, but the results challenge the assumption AI weaknesses will remain unchanged. Robotaxis carry passengers in a growing number of cities, delivery robots bring meals to customers and autonomous excavators dig on construction sites. In a 2026 pilot study health-care professionals, mostly nurses, accepted half the deliberately wrong AI recommendations and passed over about one in six correct ones.

In a study looking at how the UK public uses AI for medical advice, researchers found people sometimes left out important details when consulting chatbots, so the chatbots sometimes mixed useful suggestions with misleading ones. The article is part of a series on how AI is reshaping higher education, taking a deeper look into how AI has disrupted degrees, how universities are responding and what the technology means for the sector's future. The article states that if a sufficiently capable AI could control reliable, affordable robots then electricians and plumbers could also face competition. It adds that despite significant progress in robots' ability to carry out complex physical tasks it is still unclear how soon they will be able to do more of the work tradies do. For now, students who choose vocational pathways such as apprenticeships may face a lower risk of AI-related job disruption.

The article argues the possibility of humans working with AI should be central to how universities prepare students for the workforce, because if a worker can't improve the quality or efficiency of AI's output an employer may have little economic reason to involve them. It says graduates may need to understand what a good result looks like when using AI, recognise when AI falls short, and have the knowledge and skills to improve AI's output. It says they also need to learn how to collaborate with AI, how to direct it, question its output and persist until the result is better than what it produced initially. It states universities can't simply replace disciplinary knowledge with AI skills, and students will need the knowledge and skills their degrees have always required as well as the ability to collaborate effectively with AI. It concludes that a technology designed to make our lives easier may actually require us to work harder to stay relevant in the job market.

stories.Headline: AC Milan appoints Rúben Amorim as head coach as AI posts falsely claim Paolo Maldini returns
stories.Summary:
Recent national headlines warned that New Orleans was replacing 911 professionals with AI, and the reports were wrong, but the misinformation spread quickly amid the firestorm surrounding this new technology. The U.S. is not handing its emergency response system over to computers, and AI is making emergency communications faster and more resilient while trained 911 professionals remain in charge. Viral posts on Instagram and Threads claimed that AC Milan legend Paolo Maldini had returned to the club as head coach of its men's first team. The posts were designed to resemble genuine football transfer and appointment announcements, complete with the familiar excitement of a "Here we go!" update.

The creators included a disclaimer reading "CONCEPT ART • AI | FICTIONAL SCENARIO," indicating that the announcement is an AI-generated concept rather than an actual development. AI can identify and translate other languages almost instantly, whereas bringing a human translator on the line takes precious minutes, and it can support realistic training simulations that better equip new hires for the demands of the job. It can analyze far more calls for quality assurance than supervisors could review manually, helping ensure call-takers perform at their best. AI can also help relieve the burden of routine, non-emergency calls coming to 911 centers, roughly two-thirds of all calls handled by 911 centers according to the 2025 Pulse of 911 survey, freeing telecommunicators to focus on calls where lives are on the line. The Enhancing First Response Act (S. 725) would correct the longstanding federal misclassification of 911 telecommunicators as secretarial and administrative personnel rather than the protective service professionals they truly are.

Having passed the Senate unanimously, the legislation now awaits action in the House, and Congress should encourage responsible innovation by passing bipartisan funding legislation to support the nationwide transition to an all-digital Next Generation 911 system. John Provenzano is CEO of NENA: The 9-1-1 Association, a nonprofit professional organization representing tens of thousands of 9-1-1 first responders across the U.S. He wrote that emergency calls are not ordinary customer-service transactions and that 911 has always depended on a direct personal connection. He said someone reporting a heart attack, hiding from an attacker, or helping an injured child may need calm reassurance, lifesaving instructions, or sound judgment amid confusion and changing facts. He wrote that human intuition and empathy are essential features of 911 that AI cannot replace, and that AI will not change the fundamental social contract that has existed since the beginning: when a citizen calls for help, 911 will answer. He called on Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.)

to bring the bill up for consideration during the lame-duck session under suspension of the rules. Provenzano wrote that the question is not whether AI is categorically "dangerous" or "safe" but whether we can harness its potential while ensuring the safety, reliability, privacy and public trust that underpin emergency response. He wrote that realizing that promise will require thoughtful implementation, clear standards and continued investment in both people and infrastructure. The football article said that with realistic-looking graphics and the emotional appeal of a legendary football figure returning home, such posts can easily confuse fans who come across them while scrolling through their feeds.

It said that for supporters who are emotionally invested in their clubs, the prospect of a beloved former player returning to the dugout can be particularly tempting to believe. It said that a quick check of official club announcements and credible sports publications can save fans from falling for an elaborate digital prank. Provenzano wrote that the 911 system Americans rely on today has come a long way since the first call made nearly 60 years ago. He wrote that over the decades 911 has repeatedly adopted new technologies to better serve the public, from mobile phones and text messages to digital data-sharing and streaming video, and that the system has evolved alongside Americans' technology preferences.

He wrote that AI is the next step in this evolution and that the industry's experience in safely implementing previous technologies will guide it now. AC Milan officially appointed Portuguese manager Rúben Amorim as head coach of its men's first team on June 16, 2026, following the departure of Massimiliano Allegri. The former Manchester United and Sporting CP manager was welcomed by the Italian club as part of its plans to rebuild the team. Paolo Maldini has never pursued a coaching career, and after hanging up his boots he remained associated with AC Milan in an administrative capacity, serving as the club's technical director until June 2023.

He also briefly took up the role of technical director at the Italian Football Federation (FIGC) in July 2026, but resigned after just 16 days. The football article said that AI-generated content is increasingly blurring the lines between football news and digital fiction, and that fabricated stories can acquire the appearance of genuine breaking news. It said that while AI can recreate the excitement of a dream managerial appointment, it cannot make that appointment real. It said that Maldini's return to AC Milan might make for a wonderful fictional football story, but Amorim is the man in the hot seat.

stories.Headline: AI tools help defenders find software flaws at scale but fixing them lags
stories.Summary:
In August, researchers found flaws in the PHP programming language, which underpins roughly 70% of the world’s websites, that could’ve allowed hackers to steal data or install malware on a huge scale. The flaws prompted a warning from the National Security Agency and a global effort to patch the bug. Other flaws have recently been found in systems ranging from Linux to OpenSSL to FreeBSD. Project Glasswing, a cybersecurity initiative started by Anthropic PBC, found more than 129,000 verified software vulnerabilities between April and July alone, many of critical severity. Anthropic independently found thousands more.

Project Glasswing granted select companies and security researchers access to a specialized version of the Claude AI model. An AI tool that Microsoft Corp. tested on the Linux kernel earlier this year took, on average, about 22 minutes and just $3.60 to verify each suspected flaw. A report by Google’s threat-intelligence team found that monthly vulnerability disclosures roughly doubled over the first half of the year. Only about 0.2% of all those found had actually been exploited by hackers. One study found that companies fully fixed only 26% of known-to-be-exploited vulnerabilities last year.

The Bloomberg editorial board wrote that such reports may sound like portents of a future AI apocalypse but are in fact cause for guarded optimism. The board said many of these flaws have been lurking undetected for years, and discovering and patching them makes the broader system safer. It said AI-assisted defenders are proving especially adept at finding weaknesses in widely used software that traditional testing has missed. The board said problems in PHP had been evident as early as 2024, but it took AI to grasp their full significance. It said AI is transforming the economics of security research.

The board said defenders can now use agents to scan for weaknesses at unprecedented scale and speed and to scour places like old libraries and codebases that once would’ve been too costly or impractical to investigate. It said defenders appear to have at least a temporary advantage, and there’s little evidence criminals have achieved widespread success. It said the immediate challenge for cybersecurity pros will be to advance from finding flaws to fixing them. It said top AI models are quickly getting better at writing patches, yet deploying them widely and at the requisite speed remains a problem. It said at many organizations, 30 to 60 days remains the norm for critical flaws.

The board said the White House should expand its efforts to get frontier AI cyber capabilities to as many vetted defenders as possible while modernizing the existing vulnerability management process. It said federal procurement rules should insist on secure automated updating and other software best practices, along the lines of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s “Secure by Design” pledge. It said Congress must invest in defending critical infrastructure, including essential open-source projects. It said it isn’t hard to imagine a day when the entire defensive process unfolds behind the scenes, seamlessly and automatically, with internet users blissfully unaware. It said getting from here to there could be an eventful journey.

The editorial was published by the Marin Independent Journal on November 16, 2026, and by the Duluth News Tribune on November 14, 2026. The Marin Independent Journal credited the piece to the Bloomberg editorial board and said it was distributed by Tribune Content Agency, LLC. The Duluth News Tribune ran it as an Other View and listed its office at 222 W. Superior St, Duluth, MN 55802. stories.Headline: Higgsfield releases AI Ad Generator for small businesses to create video adverts without studios
stories.Summary:
Higgsfield released an AI Ad Generator for small businesses to create video adverts without using studios. This software allows owners to produce short clips for social media using only a web browser. The tool was highlighted in a report published on 13 November 2026. It targets business owners in cities like Harare, Bulawayo, and Mutare. The system turns product links or photos into finished video advertisements.

The tool requires a product link or up to five uploaded images to build a profile. Users can choose from over 40 ready to use avatars or describe a custom one. It offers nine ad modes, including UGC, Tutorial, Product Review, Unboxing, TV Spot, and Hyper Motion. Other modes include UGC Virtual Try On, Pro Virtual Try On, and a Wild Card option. Seedance 2.0 provides native audio and lip sync in 9:16, 16:9, and 1:1 shapes.

Higgsfield states that the tool writes the script, directs the shots, and delivers the final cut. The company claims a business can go from a product link to a video in two minutes. They say the generator removes the need for filming, a crew, and post production. No design or editing experience is required to use the creative suite. The software supports multiple languages, though English is the default setting for the avatars.

Small businesses in Zimbabwe are affected because traditional production is often too expensive for them. These firms often lack the budget for cameras, presenters, locations, editors, and professional crews. Many owners also lack the specific skills needed for writing scripts, lighting, and cutting video. Consequently, many small firms rely on a single photo and a caption for their marketing. Video is now the format that customers expect for products like clothes and hardware.

Interest in these tools follows the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy launched in March 2026. The Zimbabwean government urged the private sector to invest in technology and partner with start ups. The government also planned to offer incentives to businesses that integrate AI into their operations. This strategy encouraged companies to use AI for practical purposes like marketing to see quick benefits. AI tools aim to close the gap for firms that cannot afford professional agencies.

Users must now test the tool with their own products to verify the vendor claims. Business owners should check if the generated voices sound credible to their specific local audiences. They must also ensure that prices and measures are shown as their customers expect. The articles leave the specific pricing plans for the Higgsfield service open and unstated. It remains for users to verify which specific languages are supported beyond the default English.

stories.Headline: US, China and Russia leaders meet to discuss preventing AI from triggering nuclear war
stories.Summary:
Presidents Donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin will meet for a trilateral summit during the APEC leaders meeting in Shenzhen, China. This high level gathering occurs during a period of profound flux in the international order. The three leaders intend to discuss the Ukraine War, trade, and tensions over Taiwan. They will also address strategic stability and the risks of artificial intelligence. The summit tests if great power diplomacy can build a safer international order.

The proposed dialogue requires a standing trilateral mechanism involving diplomatic, military, nuclear security, and technological officials. It seeks to protect nuclear command and control systems from cyber interference and maintain reliable crisis communications. The plan preserves human authorization over nuclear use and establishes reporting procedures for autonomous systems. This follows a 2024 commitment by America and China to maintain human control over nuclear decisions. It addresses the February 2026 expiration of the New START treaty between Washington and Moscow.

Jianli Yang proposes this dialogue to prevent AI from making nuclear war more likely. He states that the three powers must move beyond bargaining toward building a durable order. Yang argues that no government should gamble with humanity's survival using dangerous technologies. He believes the mechanism should recognize the distinctive nuclear and technological capabilities of each nation. He suggests that reciprocal restraints could prevent catastrophic miscalculations between the three nuclear powers.

Other officials warn that AI could introduce authoritative errors or accelerate provocative military decisions. Experts fear autonomous weapons might escalate conventional confrontations before political leaders fully understand the situation. The United Kingdom, France, and India are affected as they would eventually need to participate. US military planners warn that the AI rivalry between Beijing and Washington could trigger a war. China's expanding nuclear arsenal further complicates the strategic stability of the global order.

The US leads in frontier research and computing, while China combines AI capabilities with massive manufacturing. Russia provides energy resources, nuclear expertise, and military experience with drones and electronic warfare. China's Ministry of State Security allegedly used Alice Huang to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Alice Huang reportedly ran Megaspeed, a company that rented computer processing power to firms in China. China's National Intelligence Law requires citizens to assist the state through coercion or threats.

The leaders must decide if they can cooperate against dangers that threaten their own existence. They may establish common definitions, confidence building measures, and limited reciprocal restraints over time. The articles leave open whether mutual suspicion and difficult verification will make the dialogue mere theater. It remains unclear if the leaders can resolve underlying territorial disputes through this specific mechanism. The text does not say if the US will present evidence regarding Alice Huang.

stories.Headline: White House AI task force urges agencies to grant 12 months of liability relief to firms that report cyber incidents
stories.Summary:
The White House AI task force urged federal agencies to grant liability relief to companies on Thursday, November 13, 2026. This recommendation encourages agencies to avoid regulatory penalties for firms that voluntarily report cybersecurity vulnerabilities and incidents in good faith. The task force suggests this relief should last for at least 12 months, with possible extensions based on risk evaluations. This move follows the second meeting of the Trump administration's working group regarding the evolving cyber threat environment. The proposal aims to encourage reporting at a time when AI tools are being used by attackers against defenders.

The relief applies only to cybersecurity vulnerabilities and incidents, excluding issues like bad medical advice or failed internal safety tests. Agencies should implement these limitations where it is lawful, practical, and consistent with American interests, including public health and safety. The plan requires agencies to write the relief into formal guidance and depends on Congress renewing the 2015 Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act. This soon-to-expire law provides liability protection for companies that share threat data, which the task force supports for long-term reauthorization. The recommendation is voluntary, meaning federal agencies can choose to follow the guidance or ignore it entirely.

National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, and Pentagon research chief Emil Michael were present at the meeting. Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor also serves as a member of the task force behind this recommendation. These officials argued that current enforcement standards may be outdated and could have a chilling effect on critical information sharing. Cairncross and Michael described ongoing talks with industry leaders to create a voluntary process for reporting AI-related cybersecurity incidents. Under this framework, the government would analyze the reports and share defensive information back with the private sector.

The business community has complained that overlapping and contradictory cybersecurity regulations force companies to divert resources from incident response and defense. Startups may fear that reporting a breach to a regulator could provide that regulator with a case for punishment. Enterprise buyers could benefit if vendors disclose more, allowing them to ask pointed questions during their security questionnaire processes. Critics argue a voluntary regime relies on the same companies whose silence the government is currently trying to fix. Experts believe the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency should be deeply involved in AI security and critical infrastructure protection.

The task force noted that organizations with previously reasonable protections are now more vulnerable due to AI-fueled cyber threats. The National Security Agency and National Institute of Standards and Technology have tested frontier models in partnership with major labs. Commerce's CAISSI operates on a 10 million dollar budget, which is about one-eighth of the budget of its UK counterpart. CAISSI has stopped publishing test results and has seen two directors leave since April, while staff now report informally to the White House. The administration also envisions using experts from U.S. national laboratories to assist with incident response efforts.

The government is working with frontier AI labs to develop tools for better early detection, warning systems, and rapid remediation. Cairncross and Kupor are identifying actionable measures to boost security for critical infrastructure, focusing on small and medium-sized businesses. The task force is also developing initiatives to secure federal networks and hopes CISA establishes practical, non-duplicative reporting requirements. It remains unclear which specific regulators would offer the relief or exactly when such regulatory flexibility would begin. The articles leave open whether CISA participated in the task force meeting or has been involved in its work.

stories.Headline: Stanford researchers open source Memorilla to provide latent semantic memory for frozen LLMs
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Stanford University developed Memorilla, a latent semantic memory system for large language models, which was released in November 2026. This open source system condenses entire document collections into a fixed number of query dependent memory tokens for frozen models. It allows these frozen models to process extensive data with improved accuracy and efficiency while significantly reducing total token usage. The system reads a whole document collection and provides the model with just 16 memory tokens for each question. This approach achieves better average performance than other methods such as Mem0 and MemoRAG, according to the research team.

The system requires Linux with CUDA GPUs and Python 3.11, using NVIDIA H100 80GB GPUs for its training recipes. It utilizes a 194M parameter trainable memory module with a frozen Qwen3-Embedding-4B encoder and a frozen Qwen3-8B decoder. Training takes 19 hours on four H100 GPUs, downloading 310 GiB of data and embeddings across three distinct stages. The first stage uses 1.98M Wikipedia examples, the second adds 1.34M QA examples, and the third fine tunes on benchmarks. Checkpoints are available on Hugging Face at memorilla/Memorilla-Qwen3-8B under the Apache 2.0 license for public use and deployment.

The work comes from Jure Leskovec's SNAP group, with co authors from MIT, Penn, and the University of Toronto. The researchers stated that Memorilla learns what each question needs from the whole store rather than using retrieval chunks. They reported that the system achieves 84.33 per cent accuracy on FactKG, which is higher than the 80.43 per cent full context. The team noted that the memory module can scale to millions of tokens while consistently using only 16 memory tokens. They also claimed the highest reported average across eight benchmarks, with a score of 49.68 for the system.

The system affects frozen LLMs by removing the need for full context prompting, which slows down as history grows. It outperforms xRAG on PersonaMem-v2 with 44.60 per cent accuracy, compared to 30.90 per cent for the next best method. However, it performs worse on PubMedQA, scoring 59.00 per cent against 69.00 per cent for LLMLingua-2 due to small abstract sizes. MemoRAG leads on NarrativeQA ROUGE-L with 20.51 versus 19.31 and on PersonalizationV4 with 67.88 per cent versus 66.65 per cent. The system also helps agents, raising the average success rate on TextWorld games from 18.6 per cent to 24.2 per cent.

Full context prompting is slower than Memorilla, which answers in 0.74 seconds for 512 documents versus 19.9 seconds for full context. The system can compress books and movie scripts from NarrativeQA by over 4,000 times, replacing 67,385 tokens with 16 tokens. A memory cache can reduce processing for one million documents to 8.1 milliseconds, or 5.0 milliseconds using torch.compile. This cache costs 80 GiB at four million documents, where a question takes 33 milliseconds to process on one B200. The research team also released PersonalizationV4, featuring 149 synthetic users with 200 conversations each under a CC BY 4.0 license.

Users can install the system with uv on Linux and load the model using the MemoryVLLM.from_pretrained function for deployment. The first run requires downloading about 25 GB of models, and custom data needs parquet files with specific column names. Each checkpoint must run with the specific decoder it was trained with to ensure the evaluation documents remain accurate. The articles leave open whether any quantized variants of the memory module will be disclosed for users with smaller GPUs. They do not state if the system will be expanded to support decoders other than the Qwen3 series.

stories.Headline: VT Markets launches a ChatGPT and Claude plugin for real-time asset tracking
stories.Summary:
VT Markets, a multi-asset broker, announced on November 17, 2026 the launch of its official plugin for ChatGPT and Claude, which brings real-time asset tracking and economic intelligence directly into the conversational AI platforms. The integration lets traders, investors and market observers analyse global assets without leaving their chat interface or switching between financial dashboards. The plugin provides data and visual analytics across forex, commodities, global indices and equities, and users can surface price movements, highlight top gainers and losers, track market sentiment and generate visual charts on demand. It also lets users check upcoming central bank decisions and corporate earnings schedules so they can prepare for potential price movements ahead of major market shifts. The announcement was issued from Sydney through PR Newswire.

The plugin's listed features include multi-asset access across forex, commodities, global indices and equities, instant display of price action charts, top gainers and losers and broad market sentiment, live tracking of upcoming macroeconomic announcements and corporate earnings, and conversion of simple conversational queries into structured market summaries. VT Markets said the integration puts market intelligence where daily research happens and removes friction from financial analysis, equipping market participants worldwide to evaluate global assets, track macro trends and turn raw data into actionable insights instantly. Looking ahead, the company plans to roll out secure account connectivity for the plugins, which would allow traders to view their portfolios and prepare orders directly within the chat. The articles give no further dates for that rollout.

VT Markets is the company behind the plugin and describes itself as a leading multi-asset broker. The articles do not name any individual executive or give any personal statement beyond the company's description of the launch. VT Markets included a disclaimer stating that it does not represent the material as accurate, current or complete and that the information should not be relied upon as such. The disclaimer also says the information comes from a third party and is not a recommendation, an offer to buy or sell, or a solicitation to participate in any trading strategy, and it advises readers to seek their own advice. It adds that AI-generated content is for informational purposes only and does not constitute financial or investment advice.

The context given is that the plugin is designed to streamline daily research by placing market data inside the chat tools people already use. The articles do not report any figures on users, revenue or adoption, and they give no independent comment on the launch. The only stated next step is the planned secure account connectivity that would let traders view portfolios and prepare orders within the chat. Beyond that, the articles say nothing about further plans.

stories.Summary:
Nvidia is scheduled to report its quarterly earnings, and a South African analyst said the results could make or break the wider trade in artificial intelligence stocks, according to a report published on November 14, 2026. The article from ky3.com, dated the same day, was titled All About AI: Breaking down what's been going on with Nvidia, and it appeared in a news feed alongside unrelated local items. Those surrounding items covered a high school football score, a story about flaming letters at Logan-Rogersville games, the start of Missouri deer firearms season, a Springfield Cardinals garage sale and a cold weather forecast. No spokesperson for Nvidia, no investor and no other commentator is quoted in the material provided. The ky3.com page carries no byline in the text supplied and attributes no statement to a named source. Because the articles do not identify the analyst or the analyst's firm, the responsibility for the claim cannot be traced further from what is given.

The context the articles supply is limited to the framing that Nvidia's earnings matter for the broader AI trade, a connection stated in the headline rather than explained in the body text. The ky3.com item sits in a general news feed with local weather, sports and outdoors stories, and it gives no market reaction, no preview of analyst expectations and no indication of when Nvidia would actually report. stories.Headline: US, Russia and China plan joint statement to limit AI in nuclear weapons control
stories.Summary:
The United States, Russia, and China are planning a joint statement to limit artificial intelligence in nuclear weapons control. This agreement is being prepared ahead of a scheduled meeting on November 19, 2026. Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin, and Xi Jinping will attend this high level summit in China. Representatives from the three superpowers spent several weeks searching for a mutual issue to address. They sidelined other topics like Ukraine and the denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula to focus on this.

The proposed statement requires the three nations to remove artificial intelligence from their nuclear arsenal equations. This follows the 2025 NATO acquisition of the Maven system, which the Pentagon wants as core infrastructure in 2026. The UK recently invested 90 million pounds in Atlantic Net to locate Russian submarines using marine drones. Russia is projected by the Federation of American Scientists to have 13 strategic submarines by 2026. These submarines carry about 704 warheads, with each Borei class vessel holding 16 ballistic missiles.

The South China Morning Post reported that the three powers discovered a mutual interest in limiting AI. The articles suggest that these leaders are discussing limits on their own power to avoid catastrophic risks. Military analysts believe AI could act as a magic wand by locating hidden missiles and coordinating strikes. However, the text notes that humans are prone to believing they can win through lightning blows. This automation bias allows hyper intelligent advisors to reinforce the fantasies of delusional politicians and generals.

The Federation of American Scientists notes that Russia has 324 intercontinental ballistic missiles, including Yars, Topol M, and Voevoda. These mobile units use Peresvet laser systems to neutralize satellite surveillance, making them difficult for AI to track. Experts from the US Congress stated that the 44 interceptors in the Ground based Midcourse Defense cannot repel massive attacks. The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute warned in June 2025 that AI increases the vulnerability of strategic arsenals. Such technology could convince leaders that victory is guaranteed, even though ten surviving warheads could destroy major cities.

The articles cite historical errors, such as the 1983 Oko system mistake where sunlight was mistaken for American missiles. In January 1995, Russian radar mistook a Norwegian research rocket for a hostile missile, alerting President Boris Yeltsin. Other historical failures include the 1914 German plan for France and Hitler's 1941 hope to conquer the Soviet Union. Mussolini failed in 1940 to crush Greece in eight days, and the USSR struggled in Afghanistan in 1979. George W. Bush declared victory in Iraq in 2003, but the Taliban retook Kabul twenty years after 2001.

The leaders will meet on November 19 to decide if they will officially limit AI in nuclear control. The articles leave open whether the three rivals can actually reach a final agreement on this statement. It remains unclear if the Maven system or Atlantic Net will be restricted by any new treaty. The text does not say if other nuclear powers will be included in these specific limitations. The final outcome of the Putin, Trump, and Xi Jinping summit is not yet determined.

stories.Headline: Moody's chief economist Mark Zandi warns AI boom raises inflation and borrowing costs while diverting investment
stories.Summary:
Moody's Analytics Chief Economist Mark Zandi warned on Sunday in a post on X that the artificial intelligence boom is driving up inflation and borrowing costs while pulling investment away from the rest of the U.S. economy. Zandi wrote that AI has been a boon to economic growth and job creation, but he said its rapid expansion is bringing significant economic side effects. He said AI is adding to inflation by driving up electricity and consumer electronics prices, and he said AI investment is pushing up interest rates by soaking up capital to finance the AI build-out. He cautioned that the massive flow of money into AI infrastructure is coming at the expense of other investment. Zandi said that since ChatGPT debuted four years ago, AI has gone from a rounding error to accounting for nearly two-thirds of the growth in investment.

He added that growth in everything else has slowed by more than half since mid-2024. He concluded with a warning about the economic returns expected from the technology, saying the bet on AI had better pay off in higher productivity because the rest of the economy is not investing enough to deliver it. In September, JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said AI infrastructure spending could reach $1 trillion in 2027, adding about 1% to GDP growth annually while potentially contributing to inflation, and he cautioned that it was too early to identify winners and losers in the AI boom. In July, the International Monetary Fund warned that weaker-than-expected AI productivity gains could trigger a pullback in technology investment and a sharp correction in highly valued tech stocks, while raising its 2026 global inflation forecast to 4.7%. Last month, economist Peter Schiff warned that rising borrowing costs could weaken AI investment and expose broader economic vulnerabilities, while potentially benefiting gold and gold-mining stocks during an impending recession.

Former Federal Reserve adviser Danielle DiMartino Booth also suggested a recession may already be underway. Al Jazeera reported that Americans are pushing back against the rapid expansion of data centers powering artificial intelligence, raising concerns over noise, pollution and energy demands. The Benzinga article carried a disclaimer stating that its content was partially produced with the help of AI tools and was reviewed and published by Benzinga editors. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the warnings and forecasts described above.

stories.Headline: US AI chip export curbs threaten Southeast Asia data centre growth and send technology shares lower
stories.Summary:
The United States imposed new restrictions on exports of advanced artificial intelligence chips, a move that threatens the fast-growing data centre industry in Southeast Asia and sent technology shares sharply lower, according to the headline and the reporting summarized here. The curbs target the most advanced semiconductors, the same logic chips whose manufacturing base has shrunk dramatically over two decades. According to Bain & Company figures published by Data Centre Magazine, the number of companies making the most advanced logic node fell 84 percent, from 25 firms in 2002 and 2003 to just four between 2020 and 2026. That concentration leaves the global supply of AI chips dependent on a very small group of manufacturers.

The restrictions arrive as the region and the wider industry are committing enormous sums to new compute capacity. Bain estimates that up to US$6.5 trillion will be spent to build nearly 150 gigawatts of new compute capacity by 2030, while hyperscalers' data centre capital expenditure could top US$1 trillion by 2028. Data centre critical capacity is expected to grow 20 to 30 percent over the next five years, and global data centre electricity demand is estimated to more than double from 589 terawatt hours in 2026 to 1,228 terawatt hours in 2030. North America's virtual power plant market grew 13.7 percent last year to 37.5 gigawatts, a sign of how power infrastructure is being stretched alongside chip supply.

The articles do not name the officials who ordered the curbs or give the date they were announced, and they carry no direct statements from governments or companies about the decision. What the reporting does show is that capital, capacity, power and chip supply are all being strained at once, and that the pressure is unlikely to ease before 2030. For operators, the figures suggest that planning around the electricity grid and the semiconductor supply chain will matter as much as securing funding. The share slump reflects how directly the region's data centre boom depends on access to those advanced chips.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Uber exits Nigeria and launches London robotaxis with Wayve as drivers describe falling pay
stories.Summary:
On 2 September, Uber confirmed it was discontinuing its operations in Nigeria after 12 years in one of Africa's biggest markets, and it announced a similar exercise in Uganda. Uber said the decision followed a review of its business priorities and investment focus across Africa. The next day, 3 September, Uber and British AI company Wayve launched supervised autonomous ride-hailing services in London, matching passengers with electric vehicles equipped with Wayve's AI Driver technology. The vehicles initially operated with licensed safety drivers onboard, following global restructuring plans that included cutting about 3,300 jobs. Isiaka Agbaje, 42, a cab driver at the Murtala Muhammed International Airport in Lagos, said the ride-hailing business no longer pays his bills.

The move redirected savings and investments into autonomous vehicles and robotaxi partnerships, and Uber did not officially link its exit from the Nigerian market to investment in AI efficiency. Premium Times gathered responses from nearly a dozen cab drivers operating in Lagos, Nigeria's commercial nerve centre, Abuja and other parts of the country. Samuel Adeoti put Uber's commission at 35 per cent and gave a hypothetical example of a ₦10,000 trip, from which he said Uber deducted ₦3,500, leaving ₦6,500 with the driver. After spending about ₦5,000 on fuel, he said a driver would have just ₦1,500 left to cover other costs including car maintenance and dealings with the task force, police and road safety. In 2023, shortly after being sworn in, President Bola Tinubu introduced sweeping reforms in Nigeria's foreign exchange market and the downstream petroleum sector, abolishing what the government termed a wasteful subsidy regime and harmonising the foreign exchange market.

Lanre Mustapha, an ex-Uber driver, said the company failed to adequately address drivers' complaints about fares and commissions amid sky-high domestic prices. He said drivers had protested against low fares about six months before Uber left Nigeria, but the company failed to address their concerns. Mustapha said he migrated to InDrive and described uncertainty over account suspensions there as a major challenge, saying workers can wake up to find themselves permanently blocked without stated reasons. John Promise, 39, another driver on the platform, said drivers remained because they had no better options and did not want to lose access to their customers. Innocent Ogwuche, another ex-Uber driver, said he initially had a positive experience because of the app and safety features, but things changed when fuel prices increased and automated fares failed to keep pace with operating costs.

Ogwuche said Uber is not the one fuelling the car or doing the maintenance, and he lamented inadequate compensation for trips delayed by traffic. He said he repeatedly faced technical problems while accessing his driver account, which contributed to his decision to leave the platform. Abubakar Aliyu, a cab driver based in Abuja, said a union, the Amalgamated Union of App-Based Transport Workers of Nigeria (AUTTWON), represents ride-hailing and app-based transport drivers such as those on Bolt and InDrive. He said the union uses strikes, fare boycotts and court actions to push back against algorithmic control, but platforms often treat workers as independent contractors rather than employees. Aliyu said platforms use legal technicalities and grey areas to avoid collective bargaining agreements and demands for better service conditions, adding that the union is engaging rather slowly and faces challenges.

Earlier this year, the World Bank released a report titled World Development Report 2026: The Promise of Artificial Intelligence, which assesses how AI impacts 5.6 billion people in low- and middle-income countries. The report showed that AI offers a rare path to accelerate growth at a time when global development progress has dipped to its weakest pace in 75 years, and it can help bridge chronic gaps in health, agricultural guidance for farmers and basic administrative support for governments. It urged policymakers to follow a structured three-step approach: adopt existing AI tools, tailor the tools to local realities and develop the technology. The report cautioned that traditional work faces targeted white-collar disruption, entry-level hiring freezes and widening productivity gaps, and it warned that economic benefits from AI tend to flow toward business and capital owners rather than wage workers. It said mass automation is less immediate in developing economies, where only 4.5 per cent of jobs are highly exposed compared to 14.2 per cent in wealthy nations.

On 22 October, Uber announced a separate expansion of its AI adoption, making ChatGPT Work available to more than 30,000 employees globally after an initial pilot involving 1,000 workers. Through initiatives like Uber AI Solutions and Digital Tasks, Uber also lets drivers and contractors earn money by labelling data, recording voice prompts and evaluating AI responses during downtime. Digital labour sociologist Antonio Casilli describes this move as a "Great Digital Labour Convergence", adding that merging physical gig work with micro-task data labelling normalises underpaid, algorithmically managed work across more industries while threatening traditional employment protections. He argued that platforms serve as testing grounds where industrialists experiment with ideas they plan to roll out across all labour markets, and that even traditionally stable professions have begun to absorb gig-like features such as flexible scheduling, task-based pay, algorithmic oversight and precarious autonomy. In their book, 'Notes Towards a Digital Worker's Enquiry', Julie Chen, a professor of communications and digital labour, and other scholars examined how previously viewed "unorganizable" digital and precarious workforces are building collective resistance and identifying tactical chokepoints within platform capitalism.

stories.Headline: Bogdan Pătrăucean releases Wintoys 3.0 with an option to disable Windows 11 AI services
stories.Summary:
Wintoys 3.0, build 3.0.10.0, was released by developer Bogdan Pătrăucean and announced on Reddit, adding an AI components option under the Optimizations tab. The free tool is distributed through the Microsoft Store and runs on Windows 10 and Windows 11 through a WinUI 3 interface. The option disables background services such as WorkloadsSessionHost.exe, which hold machine-learning models in memory for features like Windows Recall and semantic search. Pătrăucean said those services can use 2GB to more than 8GB of RAM, including while the related features sit idle. On his 16GB Surface Pro 12, he reported that switching them off cut memory use from 11GB to about 5GB.

The option is limited to Copilot+ PCs with a neural processing unit, and on conventional desktops the entry is not expected to appear at all. Wintoys 3.0 also adds a separate Artificial Intelligence section for managing Recall, Click to Do, Notepad's writing tools and agentic search, with toggles depending on installed hardware and Windows features. Profiles exports and restores a Windows setup as a JSON file and requires the paid Wintoys+ add-on, a one-time purchase with lifetime access, while earlier functions remain free. A new Configuration mode applies settings as preferences or policies where the operating system supports it, improving synchronization with the Windows Group Policy Editor. The build also brings extra privacy controls, File Explorer preloading options, a reworked storage cleaner, clearer restart prompts and bug fixes.

Pătrăucean described the memory figures as individual observations rather than controlled benchmarks, and said actual savings will vary with hardware, software configuration and which AI workloads are active. He pointed to a Microsoft Q&A thread from July 2026 in which a different user described recovering about 5GB by halting the Windows AI Fabric service and its associated workload processes. He said the AI components option targets WorkloadsSessionHost.exe, which can run in multiple instances to keep models ready. He pitched Profiles at people setting up a fresh install or provisioning several machines. He said Configuration mode matters because policy refreshes can otherwise revert changes made by third-party tweakers.

The articles say disabling AI services can break the features that depend on them, and that users on work or organization-managed computers are advised to weigh the implications of each tweak because some changes may conflict with corporate configuration. The articles say Copilot+ machines ship with the AI stack enabled by default, and on 16GB configurations the resident models can consume a meaningful share of system memory. The articles say IT administrators may find the Group Policy synchronization the more consequential addition, since managed machines often have settings locked down by policy. The articles say the tool comes from an unverified third-party source rather than Microsoft's own settings app. The articles say Wintoys has been free since its launch and Profiles marks one of the first capabilities reserved for paying supporters.

The articles say Microsoft has worked to trim Windows 11's memory footprint, an effort the company has discussed publicly in recent months. The articles say Wintoys takes a more granular route by exposing individual components rather than waiting for Microsoft to retune them. The articles say the release lands as that Microsoft effort continues. The articles say Wintoys lets users manage system settings, uninstall applications, optimize performance and control privacy features. The articles say the update was detailed by the developer.

The articles say Wintoys 3.0 can be downloaded at no charge from the Microsoft Store. The articles say whether users who came for the memory savings will follow into the paid tier is an open question. The articles leave open the actual savings on other machines, since the figures are individual observations rather than controlled benchmarks. The articles leave open which toggles appear, since that depends on installed hardware and Windows features present on the system. The articles say users should review the implications of individual tweaks before applying them.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang resigns as NVIDIA CEO amid personal scandals and reports of restricted chip sales in China
stories.Summary:
Reuters published an investigation on November 13, 2026, regarding NVIDIA's business in China. The report found that Chinese demand for restricted hardware continued despite official company guidance. This news arrived during the same week that CBS News reported Jensen Huang's resignation. Huang stepped down as chief executive following reports of personal scandals and affairs. One affair involved a former executive at Megaspeed who allegedly has ties to Chinese intelligence.

NVIDIA guided to zero China revenue for four straight quarters, including Q3 guidance of 108 billion dollars. In Q1 FY2027, the company shipped no H20 compute products to China, compared with 4.6 billion dollars previously. Reuters found over 150 Chinese contracts worth 23 billion yuan, or 3.2 billion dollars, using H100, H200, and H800 chips. IDC estimates NVIDIA held 34% of Chinese AI-accelerator shipments in the first half of 2026. These projects include some that are running, some under construction, and some still planned.

CFO Collette Kress stated on August 26 that no China data center compute revenue was in the forward outlook. She described licensed Hopper 200 shipments to China as dilutive to corporate gross margins and under 1% of revenue. Jensen Huang said that unconstrained demand would be a lot higher than the 70% they could deliver. He explained that compute is revenue and that losing China barely dented the company's overall results. Kress has now stepped in as the interim CEO and longtime board member.

Analysts and reporters noted that the entire AI economy is built on top of NVIDIA. Rebecca Bellan stated that Huang is NVIDIA and expressed surprise at his resignation. Some believe the leadership change and U.S. scrutiny now imperil the restricted chip projects in China. This situation raises export-control risks for a company that told investors to expect zero China revenue. The stock closed at 162.85 dollars on November 13, down 26.41% for the month.

In 2025, Huang said NVIDIA's China market share fell from 95% to zero after U.S. export restrictions. The company reported Q2 FY2027 revenue of 96.22 billion dollars, which was up 105.8% year over year. Non-GAAP EPS reached 2.22 dollars, beating the estimate of 2.09 dollars, with data center revenue at 89.02 billion dollars. Intelligence circles reportedly knew about Huang's relationship with Alice Huang nearly a year before the public did. Trump was given warnings about the affair but reportedly did not mind.

The NVIDIA board is currently investigating Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese intelligence asset. Lawmakers are pushing for chip limits in the defense bill following the spy scandal. The company must now manage expenses under the caretaker appointment of the interim CEO. It remains open whether the board's probe will reveal if national security was threatened. The two companies are partnering to develop and scale industrial robots for smart manufacturing. They aim to connect robotic systems with operational applications in real world environments. This signing marks a more systematic and scaled phase of their existing cooperation.

Aptiv expects to deploy 100 TARSBOT A-Series robots by the end of 2026 across 8 process categories. These robots will cover 33 application scenarios, including production management, coordinated inspection, and flexible assembly. The parties plan to achieve mass production in 2026 using high performance computing platforms. A target scale of 1,000 units is set for China's first industrial embodied AI robot fleet. The first phase is currently being implemented at an Aptiv production site.

The two companies are responsible for validating applications in real industrial environments to support iterative development. They stated that insights from production will help develop the AWE general purpose foundation model. TARSBOT provides end to end embodied AI capabilities and experience in real production line applications. Aptiv contributes established engineering expertise, rigorous standards, and intelligent power distribution solutions. These combined efforts aim to support efficient and reliable deployment at scale.

Manufacturers worldwide are affected as they face growing demand for intelligent automation and greater supply chain efficiency. The collaboration aims to demonstrate that scalable deployment can be validated in practical industrial settings. Embodied AI is emerging as an important force in advancing next generation productivity for these manufacturers. The project provides a validated industrial reference for replicating AI across additional scenarios. This creates broader opportunities for smart manufacturing on a global scale.

The Jiading District Government of Shanghai provided support for the development of the industrial robot fleet. A first batch of robots has already entered operation at an Aptiv smart factory. High performance computing platforms provide reliable compute for motion control, perception, and decision making. The collaboration builds on the rich real world manufacturing environments found within China. These platforms support highly reliable operation in real industrial settings.

TARSBOT and Aptiv will continue to validate their robotic applications in real industrial environments. stories.Headline: AMD data center revenue jumps 97% as Google Cloud expands Epyc partnership
stories.Summary:
The Motley Fool published an article on November 15, 2026, by Harsh Chauhan, arguing that Advanced Micro Devices could be the best artificial intelligence stock to buy amid a sell-off. The PHLX Semiconductor Sector index had declined 12% over the past three months, and AMD was caught up in that vortex with significant volatility. Concerns about the sustainability of artificial intelligence infrastructure spending, which has been key to the semiconductor sector's growth, drove the weakness. AMD's stock fell $51.24, or 8.75%, to $534.06 as of 4:00 PM ET on 11/13/26 on the NASDAQ. The article said the recent weakness opened a great opportunity for investors to buy a top stock at an attractive valuation.

AMD's data center revenue jumped 97% year over year in Q3 to $8.5 billion, driven by tremendous demand for its Epyc server central processing units from hyperscalers and AI companies. Alphabet's Google Cloud division expanded its partnership with AMD to deploy its 5th-generation Epyc server CPUs, security fabric, and x86 software to power its cloud Tensor Processing Unit systems. AMD Epyc will serve as the foundation for Google's TPUs, allowing users to run inference applications. Google Cloud reported a backlog of $561 billion at the end of the third quarter, and the tech giant expects to recognize half of that backlog in the next two years. AMD expects revenue to increase by more than 80% in 2027, fueled by healthy growth in the data center business, where it sees the server CPU total addressable market jump to $220 billion by 2030.

The article's author, Harsh Chauhan, wrote that he would not be surprised to see AMD embark on a stunning long-term rally. He said AMD is emerging as one of the most important players in the AI chip ecosystem. He noted that AMD has partnerships with major hyperscalers and AI companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta Platforms, Microsoft, and others, in the data center segment. He wrote that these customers should ensure solid long-term revenue growth for AMD, which is precisely what analysts are expecting. Chauhan disclosed that he has no position in any of the stocks mentioned.

The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Advanced Micro Devices, Alphabet, Meta Platforms, and Microsoft. The article said the $52.2 billion revenue estimate for 2026 points to a 51% jump over last year, and the forecast for 2027 and 2028 is also quite solid. Analysts expect AMD's EPS to grow by nearly 70% annually over the long run, and AMD trades at 33 times forward earnings. Assuming AMD clocks even 50% earnings growth in 2029 and 2030, its EPS could reach $57.53 by the end of the decade, using 2028's projected EPS of $25.57 as the base. A price-to-earnings ratio of 20 at that time, in line with the tech-focused Nasdaq-100 index's forward P/E, would send AMD's shares to $1,150 in just over four years, twice AMD's current price.

The article noted that the past few months haven't been pretty for semiconductor stocks, as evidenced by the 12% decline in the PHLX Semiconductor Sector index over the past three months. It said AMD's data center segment has incredible room for growth and that Alphabet is poised to spend aggressively on its cloud computing infrastructure. The article stated that AMD is therefore going to be a direct beneficiary of Alphabet's enormous spending. It said AMD is well-positioned to capitalize on the massive server CPU opportunity. The article added that AMD's revenue growth will filter down to the bottom line as well.

The article said opportunistic investors should capitalize on the recent weakness in the semiconductor sector and buy the stock for long-term gains. Corporate filings released on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, revealed this surge was driven by a global artificial intelligence boom. The two companies benefited from strong demand for high bandwidth memory and other advanced memory chips used in AI data centers. This massive increase in liquid assets occurred as the companies capitalized on the growing needs of the AI industry.

Combined cash, cash equivalents, and short-term financial instruments reached 329.23 trillion won, or 246.33 billion US dollars, by the end of September. This total rose from 136.3 trillion won a year earlier and increased by 51.32 trillion won from 277.91 trillion won at the end of June. Samsung Electronics held 214.77 trillion won by September, nearly doubling its previous year record of 108.44 trillion won. SK hynix reported 114.46 trillion won in liquid assets, which more than quadrupled from 27.85 trillion won a year prior.

The companies are responsible for these financial gains through their cumulative operating profits in the first three quarters of this year. Samsung Electronics posted approximately 254 trillion won in operating profits, while SK hynix reported approximately 181 trillion won. These figures were detailed in their respective quarterly reports to explain the sharp rise in their cash reserves. The reports indicate that the financial growth is a direct result of the current AI-driven chip boom.

The broader context involves a global shift toward AI data centers that require specialized memory hardware. This trend has allowed these South Korean firms to accumulate vast amounts of capital in a very short period. The articles do not specify further future plans or next steps for the companies beyond the reporting of these current financial figures. stories.Headline: UN chief Guterres warns autonomous weapons cross a moral red line as Geneva talks open
stories.Summary:
Negotiations on possible rules for lethal autonomous weapons, also called killer robots, are underway at the United Nations in Geneva, NPR reported on November 16, 2026. The U.N. conference on Certain Conventional Weapons, or CCW, meets just once every five years. Supporters of controls say this week's conference is the last best chance to agree rules before it is too late. Warfare technology has advanced rapidly in the last few years, and some experts warn the world is months away from weapons that choose targets and decide to kill autonomously. In Ukraine and Gaza, AI-assisted weapons have already been used to take out targets, though these are still controlled remotely by humans.

Humanitarian organizations say the decision to kill, and responsibility for that choice, must stay in human hands. Ahead of the meeting, the United Nations, the International Committee of the Red Cross and the Pope all called for legally binding rules. U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned that allowing fully autonomous weapons to kill would be crossing a moral red line. The Red Cross worries the Geneva Conventions cannot be fully respected by autonomous weapons, because war is chaotic and situations change rapidly. Under the Conventions, soldiers who are wounded or surrendering can no longer be targeted.

Georgia Haines, a legal adviser with the Red Cross, said autonomous weapons may not distinguish a soldier still fighting from one wounded or surrendering. She said the risk is that, based on the technology being seen, they cannot understand contextual signals the way a human does. She said the risks are incredibly high that there will be a misidentification of a target. Human rights groups warn the technology behind AI-assisted weapons is becoming increasingly cheap and easy to use. They say greater military adoption raises the danger of proliferation and use by terrorist groups or law enforcement in repressive regimes.

In theory, a swarm of autonomous drones could be programmed to kill everyone wearing a red sweater, everyone carrying a poster or everyone speaking a certain language. At least 50 countries, including Ireland, Italy, Brazil, Mexico, France and Germany, are calling for a strict timetable to agree binding rules. The United States, Russia and Israel have indicated they are set to oppose legally binding rules. Washington proposes a five-year timetable to draft non-binding guidelines instead. The U.S. is traditionally a late adopter of international treaties and did not ratify the Ottawa Convention on landmines.

Under President Trump, doubts about international law have grown, and Washington has imposed sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court. This weekend, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, in a keynote speech to the Federalist Society, warned against quoting laws to men with swords. U.N. negotiations on limiting specific weapons are supposed to be conducted by consensus. Consensus was achieved in 1995, when countries agreed to a ban on blinding lasers, but other agreements have proved elusive. With landmines, countries frustrated by the delay took negotiations outside the U.N. process to create the Ottawa Convention.

This week, there may be a compromise: a longer or even open-ended negotiating period for rules individual states can adopt as binding or non-binding. For diplomats supporting such a solution, it is a way to ensure at least some progress. For campaigners, it is less than ideal, with one likening it to kicking a very dangerous can down the road. The articles leave open whether the Geneva talks will produce any agreement on autonomous weapons. They also leave open whether a compromise on the negotiating period will be reached.
