stories.Headline: Researcher maps four decades of AI growth in echocardiography research
stories.Summary:
An investigator conducted a bibliometric analysis of artificial intelligence research in echocardiography and published the results in the Journal of Cardiovascular Imaging. This comprehensive study mapped worldwide growth in the field by evaluating literature spanning more than four decades of cardiovascular imaging. The researcher analyzed 2,682 peer-reviewed and conference documents published between 1984 and November 10, 2025. These documents collectively accumulated 35,083 citations across global scientific databases. The analysis revealed a dramatic surge in publication volume and citation visibility following 2018.

The study required a dual-source search strategy querying both Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection through November 10, 2025. Scopus provided 2,472 documents, while the Web of Science supplied 1,928 records, resulting in 2,682 unique publications after deduplication. The research tracked 1,509 original research articles, 534 conference papers, and 300 review articles. In 2024, there were 572 records, and 2025 saw 573 records before the data collection ended. The analysis focused on diseases like heart failure, valvular heart disease, coronary artery disease, cardiomyopathy, and congenital heart disease.

The investigator stated that citation metrics measure scholarly visibility rather than translational effectiveness, diagnostic rigor, or patient safety. They noted that unadjusted observational comparisons reflect scholarly attention rather than underlying methodological quality or independent causal effects. The researcher explained that reliance on two databases may have underrepresented non-English literature and unindexed regional validation studies. They also mentioned that bibliometric databases remain susceptible to positive publication bias regarding successful algorithmic benchmarks. The author concluded that future research must transition toward rigorous multicenter prospective trials.

The study found that the United States led productivity with 1,404 publications, followed by China with 784 and the United Kingdom with 512. The Mayo Clinic ranked first in institutional output with 142 publications, while the University of California had the highest average citations. Top investigators included Francisco Lopez-Jimenez with 55 publications, Zachi I. Attia with 54, and Paul Andrew Friedman with 52. Open access publishing and dedicated funding were associated with higher citation counts for the researchers involved. The United States and United Kingdom formed the most productive partnership with 237 co-authored papers.

Echocardiography has been the most widely used clinical cardiac imaging modality since Inge Edler and Carl Hertz introduced ultrasound in 1954. Over subsequent decades, ultrasound instrumentation incorporated technological advancements that expanded daily procedural workloads and created highly complex diagnostic studies. Traditional manual acquisition and interpretation encountered structural limits under growing demands for precision cardiovascular medicine. Artificial intelligence emerged as a transformative methodology to provide computational solutions for automated view classification and myocardial quantification. These tools also offer diagnostic classification and structured electronic reporting across various clinical settings.

Future efforts must prioritize algorithmic explainability and dataset diversity across different ultrasound equipment platforms. Researchers need to integrate these technologies directly into clinical guidelines and real-world cardiovascular care. The study suggests a shift from retrospective single-center model development to more rigorous prospective trials. The articles leave open how these tools will specifically impact patient safety and diagnostic rigor in practice. They also leave open the exact timeline for the full integration of AI into standard clinical guidelines.

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence Accelerates Microbial Biosynthesis of Functional Bio-Based Nanomaterials
stories.Summary:
Microbial biosynthesis has emerged as an environmentally friendly alternative to traditional physicochemical nanoparticle production techniques, offering a versatile platform for generating functional nanoscale materials under mild reaction conditions. Conventional production routes, including chemical reduction, sol-gel processing, and laser ablation, routinely rely on hazardous reducing agents, toxic organic solvents, and high energy inputs that create environmental hazards and leave harmful surface residues. Microorganisms such as bacteria, fungi, algae, cyanobacteria, and actinomycetes circumvent these issues by deploying enzymatic pathways, metabolic by-products, and active biomolecules to reduce metal precursors and stabilize nanoscale structures. Recent synthetic evaluations demonstrate that these biogenic nanomaterials possess superior biocompatibility and surface functionality compared with their chemically manufactured counterparts. However, translating microbial synthesis into industrial production has long been impeded by complex biological dynamics, unstandardized parameters, and erratic batch-to-batch variation, prompting researchers to integrate artificial intelligence, machine learning, and data-driven materials informatics across every stage of the fabrication workflow.

Microbial nanomaterial generation operates through distinct biological mechanisms, primarily categorized into intracellular and extracellular pathways, alongside specialized biomineralization processes. In intracellular routes, metal cations traverse microbial cell envelopes through dedicated ion channels or electrostatic interactions with surface carboxyl and hydroxyl groups, undergoing reduction via intracellular enzymes, reduced cofactors such as nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, and thiol-bearing molecules like glutathione. Although intracellular synthesis yields smaller, highly monodisperse nanoparticles, product harvesting requires cell lysis that complicates downstream recovery. Extracellular synthesis circumvents this limitation by secreting reductive enzymes, extracellular polymeric substances, and redox-active metabolites into the surrounding culture medium, facilitating direct particle nucleation and capping without cellular disruption. Concurrently, biomineralization allows organisms such as magnetotactic bacteria to synthesize single-domain magnetic crystals of magnetite or greigite within membrane-bound magnetosomes, producing structures with tight size distributions and permanent magnetic dipole moments under strict genetic regulation.

The biochemical diversity across microbial classes dictates the morphology, yield, and catalytic activity of the resulting nanoparticles. Bacteria such as Bacillus, Pseudomonas, Escherichia, and Shewanella offer rapid growth and accessible genetic manipulation, using redox enzymes like nitrate reductase to yield metallic and metal oxide architectures. Fungi provide exceptional biomass yields and robust extracellular secretion rates, releasing high volumes of enzymes and secondary metabolites that simplify downstream purification while generating silver, gold, and zinc oxide nanoparticles. Photosynthetic microalgae and macroalgae utilize light and carbon dioxide to produce polysaccharides, polyols, and pigments that drive phyco-nanotechnology, yielding crystalline structures under sustainable cultivation regimes. Cyanobacteria contribute distinct phototrophic pathways that continuously supply reducing equivalents, whereas actinomycetes, particularly Streptomyces species, leverage diverse secondary metabolite profiles to assemble antimicrobial silver and gold particles with unique surface functionalization.

Despite the inherent flexibility of biological systems, native microbial synthesis remains exquisitely sensitive to extrinsic and intrinsic cultivation parameters. Small fluctuations in metal precursor concentrations, ambient pH, reaction temperatures, dissolved oxygen levels, nutrient feeds, and agitation rates trigger profound shifts in particle size, crystal structure, dispersity, and overall stability. For instance, alkaline reaction environments alter the ionization state of functional groups and boost biomolecular reducing capacity, favoring smaller, more uniform nanoparticles. Elevated temperatures accelerate reduction kinetics up to the threshold of thermal protein denaturation, while microbial physiological status during the logarithmic growth phase provides peak metabolic activity for efficient nucleation.

Because these environmental parameters exhibit complex, multidimensional interactions, traditional one-variable-at-a-time experimentation and standard response surface methodologies fail to resolve nonlinear interdependencies, leaving bioprocess optimization labor-intensive and frequently unrepeatable. Artificial intelligence and machine learning models are fundamentally transforming this landscape by replacing trial-and-error laboratory cycles with predictive modeling. Supervised learning algorithms, including artificial neural networks, support vector machines, Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting regressors, can map multi-parameter inputs directly to nanoparticle size, yield, and morphology. Hybrid algorithmic frameworks, such as neural networks coupled with particle swarm optimization, have successfully isolated precursor concentrations, feed rates, and agitation speeds as primary drivers of particle dimensions.

Furthermore, convolutional neural networks, graph neural networks, and transformer-based architectures automate feature extraction from electron microscopy and spectroscopy imagery, quantifying structural properties without subjective operator intervention. Integrating these predictive algorithms with high-throughput multi-omics profiles, spanning transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics, allows researchers to anticipate cellular states and systematically dial in desired nanomaterial specifications with minimal experimental iteration. Beyond primary synthesis, post-synthetic surface functionalization is critical for adapting microbial nanomaterials to demanding technological environments, as native biomolecular capping layers alone rarely satisfy rigorous industrial or clinical benchmarks. Polyethylene glycol coatings provide steric hindrance that limits non-specific protein adsorption, extending circulation half-lives and preserving structural integrity even under extreme thermal stress.

Natural biopolymers like chitosan introduce reactive amine groups that promote mucoadhesion and support covalent drug conjugation, while targeted protein functionalization utilizing antibodies, transferrin, and cell-penetrating peptides enhances receptor-mediated uptake in pathological tissues. Researchers are also constructing hybrid nanocomposites by embedding biogenic nanoparticles within bacterial cellulose scaffolds or coupling them with graphene oxide and reduced graphene oxide sheets, achieving synergistic mechanical strength, superior electrical conductivity, and amplified catalytic performance. Stimuli-responsive functionalization represents an advanced frontier in biogenic material engineering, enabling dynamic structural and functional adaptations in response to environmental triggers. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Ethics professor Domènec Melé argues AI shapes habits and desires but cannot replace human wisdom or communion
stories.Summary:
Dr. Domènec Melé, an emeritus professor of business ethics at IESE Business School and an emeritus member of the Royal European Academy of Doctors, published an article titled “Christian Spirituality and Artificial Intelligence: Discernment in a Global Technological Economy” in the journal Religions on 27 October, the academy reported on 16 November 2026. In it he reflects on how artificial intelligence and new technological environments affect the spiritual development of human beings. He writes that artificial intelligence has shown it not only expands human capabilities but also shapes habits, desires, attention and forms of relationship. He argues that processing information or generating plausible responses is not the same as wisdom, which requires integrating knowledge with experience, moral judgement and an orientation towards worthy ends.

Melé holds that fluid and personalised interaction may simulate attention or empathy but does not amount to communion, because communion requires reciprocal presence, vulnerability and the capacity for self-giving between persons. He notes that in an economy rewarding engagement or productivity, optimising means does not automatically settle which ends are worth pursuing. He says artificial intelligence can reduce repetitive burdens and broaden access to knowledge or assistance, but replacing activities whose value includes human participation, such as teaching, care, professional judgement or personal accompaniment, carries risks. He also warns of an unequal distribution of human presence, since those with greater resources may keep access to teachers, doctors or advisers in person while others increasingly receive automated substitutes.

The article further underlines the material footprint of the technology, noting that although it may appear immaterial to users, artificial intelligence depends on data centres, chips and electricity grids whose consumption of energy and water is considerable. Melé does not advocate rejecting technology or absolutising it, and he suggests technical creativity can be understood as a form of participation in the care and development of creation, while the power it confers is a responsibility entrusted to human beings rather than absolute dominion. In a context of concentrated infrastructure, data and capital, he argues that the social doctrine of the Church offers criteria of dignity, the common good, subsidiarity and solidarity to keep individuals and communities from becoming passive recipients of decisions taken elsewhere. He concludes that progress is genuinely human when directed towards the integral development of persons and, within the Christian horizon, towards communion with God and with others.

Over the past 30 years Melé has researched and written extensively on business and economic ethics, corporate social responsibility, Christian social ethics, spirituality in management, management philosophy and humanistic management. He has published more than 70 book chapters and scientific articles in journals including the Journal of Business Ethics, Business Ethics Quarterly, Business Ethics: A European Review, Business and Society Review, Philosophy of Management and Humanistic Management Journal. He is also the author of several books that have become reference works in humanistic economics, among them “Ethics in Business Management”, “Anthropological Foundations of Business Management”, “Business Ethics in Action. Seeking Human Excellence in Organizations”, “Christians in Society” and “Ethics in the Family Business”, the last co-authored with fellow READ emeritus member Miguel Ángel Gallo.

stories.Headline: Amazon withdraws Ashburn data center plan and will convey 25 acres to Loudoun County
stories.Summary:
On October 20, Amazon agreed with Loudoun County, Virginia, to withdraw its plan for four data center buildings totaling more than 800,000 square feet on its 122-acre Ashburn campus, the former George Washington University campus. Amazon had purchased the campus for around $427.3 million in March 2026. In July, Amazon filed a site plan called Bridgefield Tech Center, with four two-story data center buildings and three parking garages. Amazon sought a by-right approval, an administrative process with no Planning Commission, public hearing or Board vote. On November 17, Loudoun County supervisors are set to take a final vote on pausing new legislative data center applications for up to 12 months.

Under the October 20 deal, Amazon will convey about 25 acres to the county and seek to rezone the rest, mainly for housing. Amazon cannot construct data centers or host their supporting infrastructure on the Ashburn campus, and it will not sue to do so. The pause would cover rezonings and special exceptions, the longest gap Virginia law permits, but not administrative applications, including at least 17 grandfathered applications totaling over 11 million square feet. The Board can still consider grid reliability substations during the period. On September 15, supervisors voted 7-1-1 to pause Board consideration of certain legislative applications for data centers and electrical substations, and the written resolution was deferred from October 20 to November 17.

Board Chair Phyllis Randall announced the agreement, called Project Potomac Promise, and said the campus was just the wrong location for a data center, owing to the infrastructure it would need and residents' opposition. Amazon's Josh Weissman said the company had heard the community's pointed concerns and took them seriously. He said Amazon and the county have differing views on the site's legal potential, and it chose a shared vision over costly litigation. Neither Amazon nor Randall cited power supply as the reason for calling off the planned construction. Supervisor Juli Briskman had vowed on July 30 to fight the plan every step of the way.

Business Insider reported that some AWS sites had space for Nvidia GB300 racks but not enough power to run them, so finished racks were held in warehouses. Amazon called staging equipment best business practice and disputed that it lacked a path to bring the racks into its data centers. AWS CEO Matt Garman cautioned that over 100 data center moratoriums are being considered across the U.S. Governor Abigail Spanberger said the decision on approving or blocking data center projects should rest with the community and not the state. State Senator Russet Perry has drafted a three-year statewide moratorium on data center approvals. Loudoun County hosts about 233 data center buildings and 56.5 million square feet built or under construction as of March 1, 2026, plus 35.7 million square feet approved but not yet built.

In 2025, the county issued permits for over 10 million square feet of data center space, the highest in a year. A 2000 zoning ruling assigned data centers as office buildings, letting companies build them by right in office-zoned areas, and since March 2025 new data centers have required a special exception approved by a Board vote. The county generated $1.2 billion in tax revenue in fiscal 2026, 39% of its budget, with about 40%, or $1.3 billion, projected for fiscal 2027. In early October, county staff told supervisors that Amazon would need additional county approval before building, citing a zoning determination that data centers were not a permitted primary use on the property. AWS reported a $578 billion backlog and $46 billion in Q3 sales, up 39%, and Amazon's leases signed but not yet started rose to $164.9 billion in Q3 from $137.2 billion in Q2 and $96.4 billion at the end of 2025.

Amazon plans to spend meaningfully more in 2027 than the roughly $220 billion planned for 2026, and it purchased $77.3 billion of property and equipment, with $159.6 billion of property and equipment commitments. CEO Andy Jassy said AWS added 3.9 GW of power capacity in 2025 and expected to double it by the end of 2027, but still had capacity constraints that yield unserved demand. On October 2, Garman pledged more than $1 billion over five years to support communities near its data centers and confirmed Amazon would stop using NDAs with government agencies. On September 24, Oracle issued a force majeure notice to Blue Owl Capital over its 2.45 GW Stargate campus in Doña Ana County, New Mexico. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Experts warn AI cheating detectors will not be ready for this Thursday's national college entrance exam
stories.Summary:
Experts warn that specialized detectors designed to stop AI cheating will not be ready for the national college entrance exam this Thursday. The urgency for these safeguards grew after a thirty four year old man surnamed Han confessed on YouTube to cheating on a tax accountant exam. Han admitted that he used a micro camera to send exam questions to an AI and then viewed the answers on a smartphone. This incident has forced education officials to seek ways to identify smart glasses and other wireless devices during high stakes testing.

The Korea Communications Agency issued a tender on November 2 to develop a handheld radio detector for AI smart glasses. This device would allow proctors to pick up Bluetooth and Wi-Fi signals, but the technology is still under development. Some suggest using thermal cameras or a method from a Duke University research team that identifies glowing lenses through filming. However, the Radio Waves Act prevents the use of signal jamming except for military or counterterrorism operations. Authorities now plan to investigate potential AI cheating across 528 national exams and tighten checks for the 2027 college entrance exam.

Ryu Dong kyu, a professor of optometry at Shinsung University, believes the most reliable method is detecting wireless signals. He suggests that proctors should inspect glasses in person and use professional opticians to attach certifying stickers to approved eyewear. Yoon Sang ho, a professor at the KAIST Graduate School of Culture Technology, argues that manufacturers should build safeguards into the devices. Yoon believes it is technically possible to block modified devices or stop them from working when the camera light is covered.

The current situation leaves proctors relying on manual inspections because signal blocking is illegal and thermal cameras are impractical for every classroom. Education officials recently held training sessions on November 11 at the Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education to demonstrate smart glasses. These efforts aim to prevent a repeat of the tax accountant scandal before the nationwide exam begins. Future security will likely depend on the development of the handheld detectors and stricter manufacturing rules for smart wearables.

Articles.Title: Detectors that could stop AI exam cheating won’t be ready for CSAT

stories.Headline: President Lee proposes AI and critical mineral partnerships with Mekong and Asean nations
stories.Summary:
President Lee Jae Myung proposed expanded cooperation with Mekong and Asean nations on November 16, 2026. He made these pledges during summits held in Manila, Philippines, including meetings at the Philippine International Convention Center. The president sought partnerships regarding artificial intelligence, critical mineral supply chains, and countering transnational crime. He attended these events as part of a four-day trip to the Philippines and China. First lady Kim Hea Kyung accompanied the president on this diplomatic journey to Southeast Asia.

The Mekong partnership involves Vietnam, Thailand, Myanmar, Laos, and Cambodia in Pasay City, Metro Manila. Lee proposed the Asean-Korea AI companionship initiative and the Asean-Korea cultural and creative industries initiative. He pledged support for the Asean Community Vision 2045, a strategic road map adopted in 2025. Negotiations are underway to upgrade the Asean-Korea Free Trade Area to reach annual trade of $300 billion. Korea and the Philippines noted bilateral trade reached $21.3 billion as of September 2026.

President Lee stated that Korea is an ideal partner for the development journey of Mekong countries. He said Korea will share its experience as a former aid recipient that became a donor. Lee claimed Korea possesses full-stack AI competitiveness encompassing infrastructure, models, applications, and various services. He noted that Asean is a key partner for promoting peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula. The president expressed a desire to ensure everyone shares in the benefits of AI advances.

Philippine President Ferdinand Romualdez Marcos Jr. said the partnership is relevant amid strategic uncertainty and technological change. He noted that deep-rooted ties are reflected in shared strategic goals and vibrant people-to-people connections. Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul agreed to pursue cooperation in nuclear energy, defense, and intellectual property rights. Korean companies operating in Thailand and the Philippines are affected by these high-level diplomatic requests. The Asean community is affected by Korea's support for Asean centrality in the Indo-Pacific.

This year marks the 15th anniversary of Korea-Mekong ties and the third summit of its kind. The Mekong summit resumed after six years following a military coup in Myanmar in 2021. Asean and Korea established a comprehensive strategic partnership in 2024 to strengthen their regional bonds. Last year, Lee proposed a vision for Korea to be a contributor, springboard, and partner. Korea and the Philippines signed a memorandum on science and technology to expand smart farming.

The two sides welcomed a plan to hold a special summit in Korea in 2029. This future event will mark the 40th anniversary of dialogue relations between Korea and Asean. Korea and Thailand agreed to swiftly conclude a comprehensive economic partnership agreement to stabilize trade. Lee requested that Thailand resolve difficulties faced by Korean companies and expedite Korean-style industrial complexes. The articles leave open the specific results of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China.

stories.Headline: Amagasaki by-election candidates use AI-generated faces on posters as officials confirm no legal grounds to remove them
stories.Summary:
A city council by-election in Amagasaki, Hyogo Prefecture, on November 15, 2026, drew 12 candidates for one vacant seat, and at least four of them displayed posters with AI-generated faces rather than their own photographs. Former prefectural assembly member Hikoharu Konishi acknowledged that four candidates had used artificial images, and the Amagasaki City Election Administration Commission confirmed at least four posters were suspected of using generative AI. In one case, officials said the man depicted on the poster of candidate Hiroyoshi Hara was not Hara himself, and an election official who had met Hara said the person shown looked completely different. The controversy emerged during a closely contested race in which voters also chose a mayor on November 15, with incumbent Kazumi Matsumoto winning a second term and Hiromi Ikeshita securing the council seat. Some posters depicted men with tattoos on their arms, while others showed attractive, distinguished-looking older men alongside simple campaign messages.

Japan's Public Offices Election Act has regulated posters through requirements on dimensions and identification of responsible parties but has not required candidates to use photographs of themselves. After the July 2024 Tokyo gubernatorial election, when campaign poster boards displayed sexually explicit images of women and other material unrelated to candidates, lawmakers revised the law to require candidates' names to be clearly visible and to prohibit material damaging another person's reputation or violating public morals. The amended law contains no provision requiring a candidate's actual face to appear on a poster, and election authorities said they had no legal grounds to order the posters removed. Under the publicly funded election campaign system, public funding for poster production in the Amagasaki by-election was available up to approximately 610,000 yen per candidate, depending on reimbursement conditions. Each of the four candidates received enough votes to qualify for the return of the 300,000 yen deposit required to stand in the municipal election, though all four were defeated.

An Amagasaki election official said the commission could not intervene simply because a photograph or image was misleading, citing freedom of political activity and freedom of expression. Konishi, who with his secretary had submitted the candidacy registrations on behalf of the four individuals, reportedly responded that he found officials' requests for identity verification unpleasant. Speaking on behalf of candidate Koichi Sato, number 12, on November 14, the final day of campaigning, Konishi told voters the posters were the ones everyone in Amagasaki had been talking about and asked whether people genuinely felt suspicious about the images. He confirmed to Kansai Television that the images were produced using AI, saying of Sato's poster, "This was made with AI," and calling it "an image." Konishi said production costs were matters to be settled between candidates and contractors, that he had followed the Public Offices Election Act properly with the election commission's approval, and that outsiders should not make a fuss.

One Amagasaki resident said the artificial appearance immediately discouraged closer examination of the candidates' messages, and another said it made them wonder how committed the candidates really were and that it was difficult to sense any sincerity. Another resident said candidates should not engage in such unusual practices, while another questioned whether the individuals were seriously attempting to win office. Reporters searched Amagasaki for campaign vehicles and tried to contact the individuals by telephone but could not locate them or obtain interviews. Ono Planning Office, a local poster production company that has worked on more than 1,000 campaigns, restricts AI use to image correction and set its own guidelines in November. Company representative Satsuki Ono said AI can create a completely different face from the original material, that this is no longer simply correcting a photograph, and that charging nearly 600,000 yen for posters made with AI for practically nothing and paying only for printing could yield a substantial profit.

Election consultant Takuma Ohamazaki said that normally someone who runs for election incurs expenses and finishes with a financial loss, and that in this case he suspected some people may have ended up making money. Ohamazaki also warned that increasingly sophisticated AI could make future cases far harder to detect, saying the cat-and-mouse game between technological advances and the Public Offices Election Act will continue. Legal experts said Japan's election legislation has historically been designed to regulate specific, identifiable practices, making it difficult to anticipate abuses from new technologies, and that restrictions on political expression must be balanced against democratic freedoms including the right to participate in elections and communicate political messages. There has been no confirmation that the four candidates or their associates improperly received public funds or profited, and the allegations remain suspicions rather than established wrongdoing. Similar concerns circulated on social media, where users questioned whether obtaining publicly funded poster payments might have been one motivation for entering the election.

Further changes to the Public Offices Election Act are scheduled for March 2027, including a requirement to disclose when AI has been used in election-related materials. The planned disclosure requirement has drawn criticism because it carries no penalties for violations and does not necessarily require detailed explanations of which elements of an image were generated or altered. Experts questioned whether a simple declaration that AI was used would provide meaningful protection against misleading campaign imagery. Without clearer definitions of prohibited conduct or enforceable penalties, they warned, candidates may continue exploiting gaps between rapidly developing technology and election regulations. The Amagasaki controversy has highlighted a broader challenge facing Japan's democratic system.

stories.Headline: City leaders at Global AI Cities 2026 set out five priorities for making AI and digital infrastructure resilient
stories.Summary:
At Global AI Cities 2026, more than 300 local government leaders from over 50 cities gathered in Manchester to discuss artificial intelligence and digital resilience. The event was organised by Global Government Forum and co-hosted by Greater Manchester Combined Authority. Sarah Wray reported on the conference for Global Government Forum on 16 November 2026. The discussions were captured in the report Making AI work for people and places: Five priorities for cities. The report draws on insights from the event and includes examples from Romania, Westminster and Alberta.

The report sets out five priorities for cities, including fixing the fundamentals and prioritising according to criticality. It also calls for governing AI throughout its lifecycle and making digital infrastructure itself resilient. The report says resilience depends on people and partnerships as well as technology. Global AI Cities 2027 is to be held in Manchester on 24-25 May. The report is available to download.

Alexandru Georgescu, senior researcher at Romania's National Institute for Research and Development in Informatics, said local authorities are not actually ready for AI in itself. He said generative AI and large language models are not comparable to traditional software and need new processes and new cybersecurity practices, including adversarial testing and red-teaming. He said many large organisations are not ready to do this, let alone local administrations that probably have not budgeted for it. He said cities are agglomerations of critical infrastructures that serve wider regions and become targets for criminals, rogue states or state-sponsored organisations. He concluded that many local authorities are not adequately prepared and do not have the level of support they need from central authorities.

Gurpreet Muctor, chief data and technology officer for Westminster City Council, said a late 2025 cyber-attack took five months to recover from and forced the shutdown of all systems. He said the attack was perpetrated by somebody who impersonated a council employee and was still a manual process, not an AI attack. He said AI increasingly adds a new layer to that threat in the form of deepfakes that can impersonate council workers, politicians or senior officials. Richard Henderson, corporate chief information officer for the Government of Alberta, said many local governments make it too easy for hackers because they are not getting the fundamentals right. He said Alberta built AI-assisted tooling to scan 400 million lines of government code for vulnerabilities, work he estimated would have taken a human 125 years of development time.

Henderson advised cities not to wait for the most advanced tools and said they can probably build their own reasonable facsimile relatively quickly for not a significant amount. He said the only way to survive the deepfake threat is through good governance and protocols, such as an agreed challenge phrase to ascertain that someone is genuine. Georgescu said there is too much focus on the cutting edge when good enough is often adequate for both attackers and defenders. He said his institute prioritises based on criticality, identifying which systems would cause the greatest harm if compromised and hardening those first. He highlighted the most basic AI-related risk as someone pasting citizen data into a public LLM to save time, and said the human factor and security culture matter.

Georgescu said there is not enough talk about the lifecycle of AI products and systems and how decommissioning will be handled. He warned of AI agents stuck in systems and attached to data that an adversary could exploit long after the department that built them has moved on. Henderson said staff are not interested in waiting for discussions about AI and will use it whether organisations like it or not. One senior leader at the summit described facing a pandemic, a major snowstorm and an energy blackout, which highlighted the difference between having technology and having resilience. The city is now strengthening resilience through a city brain supported by AI, improved cybersecurity, closer partnerships with telecom providers, resilient government buildings, district-level citizen refuges with power and connectivity, and new platforms providing real-time information on infrastructure.

The articles do not state what specific measures, funding or deadlines follow from the report's five priorities. They do not name the city whose leader described the succession of crises. They do not give the outcome of the Westminster attack beyond the five-month recovery and system shutdown. They do not say what action, if any, Romania's central authorities have taken in response to Georgescu's comments. They do not give details of the Global AI Cities 2027 agenda beyond its dates and location.

stories.Headline: Foreign investors sell tech shares as Jensen Huang's Nvidia exit sinks Kospi 3.59 percent
stories.Summary:
Foreign investors sold off technology shares on Monday, November 16, 2026, causing the Kospi to tank. The main bourse lost 190.03 points to close at 5,100.5, which represents a 3.59 percent decline. This drop extended a losing streak to three sessions amid growing fears of an artificial intelligence bubble. The turmoil followed the ouster of Jensen Huang, who served as the chief executive officer of Nvidia. Investors remained cautious while awaiting an earnings report from Nvidia and the Nasdaq debut of Anthropic.

The market sell-off required significant adjustments for several major companies and financial instruments in South Korea. Samsung Electronics fell 4.47 percent to 196,800 won, while chipmaker SK hynix plunged 7.89 percent to 1.12 million won. Samsung Electro-Mechanics sank 8.19 percent to 785,000 won, and SK Square tumbled 9.71 percent to 688,000 won. Hyundai Motor slipped 1.48 percent to 265,500 won, and the local currency rose 1.9 won to 1,335.7 won against the dollar. Three-year Treasury yields shed 1.6 basis points to 3.743, and five-year government bond returns fell 1.1 basis points to 3.830.

Shinhan Securities analyst Kang Jin-hyuk explained that the market came under pressure from persistent concerns over Nvidia. He noted that these worries weighed heavily on semiconductor and other AI-related stocks during the trading day. Foreigners and institutions sold a net 1.38 trillion won and 451.26 billion won, respectively, while individuals bought a net 1.34 trillion won. Trade volume remained light at 209.27 million shares worth 15.8 trillion won, or approximately 11.8 billion dollars. Decliners far outnumbered advancers by a count of 612 to 263.

The broader context involves uncertainty regarding the global AI industry after the exit of a key figure like Jensen Huang. Investors are worried that the high-profile listing of Anthropic could divert necessary investment from other technology stocks. This environment has created a volatile atmosphere for AI infrastructure firms that previously grew using Nvidia cash. Market participants are now closely watching the upcoming earnings results to determine the future of AI spending. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Korea weighs radio frequency detectors and thermal imaging to stop AI cheating before nationwide exam
stories.Summary:
The Korean government and teachers are rushing to stop AI cheating before the College Scholastic Ability Test. These urgent efforts began just two days before the nationwide exam. Officials are weighing new security measures as experts warn AI may make traditional tests obsolete. The rush follows a scandal where a tax accountant exam topper confessed to using AI. AI cheating has also plagued the Seoul National University Test of English Proficiency since early 2026.

The government is considering radio frequency detectors and thermal imaging for 1,312 test centers. These measures are unlikely this year because there is too little time to equip all sites. Metal detectors are impractical because some centers hold over 500 students, making screening take eight hours. The Radio Waves Act prevents blocking wireless signals, which could also disrupt emergency communications in residential areas. Video recording is dismissed because obtaining consent from everyone is impractical.

Shin Jin-yong, director of the College Admissions Policy Division, said searching students risks treating them like criminals. He noted that some students with disabilities wear medical devices that could complicate searches. Vice Education Minister Choi Eun-ok convened an emergency video conference with deputy superintendents from 16 regional offices. Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin stated that delaying the exam could cause even greater disruption. He vowed to stake the ministry's reputation on ensuring the exam proceeds without incident.

Public school teachers in Gyeonggi and South Gyeongsang expressed anxiety over miniature cameras sold online. They fear public criticism if cheaters are found, similar to what happened with tax accountant proctors. The Korean Pragmatic Teachers' Federation urged the government to ease the mounting pressure on these supervisors. Some students, parents, and political figures called for the CSAT to be postponed. Singer San from Ateez urged adults to strengthen safeguards while encouraging hardworking students.

AI cheating has led to a retrospective review of 528 national exams. Miniature cameras smaller than a fingernail and smart glasses are now being used to cheat. The government is tightening checks on smart wearables ahead of the 2027 academic year. High school seniors in Daegu took a mock exam on September 2 to prepare. The Ministry of Education and Ministry of Science and ICT are discussing further measures.

The government plans to unveil additional anti-cheating measures on Tuesday. Experts like Kwon Oh-hyun argue that education authorities must adapt to assess thoughts and ideas. Ban Sang-jin suggests replacing test scores with a system that assesses a student's potential. Kim Seong-yeol argues for a shift away from speed-based exams toward essay-based questions. The articles leave open whether these changes will require extensive public debate.

stories.Headline: Los Angeles schools survey parents, students and staff to shape generative AI policy
stories.Summary:
The Los Angeles Unified School District is distributing a survey to parents, students and staff to help inform its policy on generative artificial intelligence in schools, LAist reported on November 16, 2026. The district wants to hear from community members about how the technology should be used in classrooms across the system. The survey is meant to gather input that will shape the district's formal policy on generative AI. The report was published by Elly Yu, who covers early childhood issues for LAist. The survey follows a surprise moratorium that LAUSD implemented in September on student use of generative AI on school-issued devices for this school year.

Before that moratorium, district policy allowed students 13 and older to use the technology under supervision. The school board has an ad-hoc committee on generative AI that examines the new technology and what its role should be in the classroom. The committee was formed as part of a resolution that was passed to limit screentime in the district. The ad hoc committee is scheduled to meet four more times this school year, on Dec. 9, 2026, Jan. 20, 2027, March 3, 2027 and April 7, 2027. The committee plans to make policy recommendations that the full board could vote on.

The survey of parents, students and staff is intended to help inform the district policy that emerges from that process. The committee's work and the survey together will feed into the recommendations the board may eventually consider. The context is a district still working out how generative AI fits into its classrooms after the September moratorium paused student use on school-issued devices. The ad-hoc committee's four remaining meetings this school year give the board a schedule for turning community input into recommendations it could vote on. The survey gives parents, students and staff a way to weigh in before those recommendations take shape.

stories.Headline: Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin admits Korea cannot guarantee detection of AI cheating before the CSAT
stories.Summary:
Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin admitted that authorities cannot guarantee the detection of AI cheating before the college entrance exam. This admission occurred on November 16 during a National Assembly Education Committee meeting held in Yeouido, Seoul. The minister spoke during a plenary meeting while answering questions from lawmakers about the security of the upcoming test. He acknowledged that countermeasures against miniature cameras and similar equipment would probably not be perfect for the examination. These statements were made just two days before the start of the College Scholastic Ability Test in Korea.

The government will now require candidates to surrender smart devices and block public Wi-Fi at all examination centers. Authorities also announced the formation of an interagency task force to handle the threat of AI assisted cheating. These new measures were announced on November 16 to protect the integrity of the largest annual national examination. The government is also ordering a retrospective review of 528 national exams following a major AI cheating scandal. These changes aim to prevent the use of sophisticated electronic devices during the high stakes university admission process.

Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin told People Power Party Rep. Park Jeong-hun that he could not identify every cheating case. He stated that he did not think the government could guarantee the detection of all AI assisted cheating attempts. The prime minister demanded vigorous effort to prevent violations and called for harsh punishment for those who cheat. He emphasized that the nation must prepare carefully as it approaches the biggest test day of the year. The minister's candid remarks have led some to describe his current position as irresponsible given the timing.

Some students and parents are demanding that the CSAT be postponed because of the intense fear of cheating. These groups worry that the fairness of university admissions will be undermined if the government cannot stop AI. Other affected parties include candidates in professional qualification exams, university essay tests, and various school based academic assessments. The public confidence in the system that determines educational opportunities for young people is now at serious risk. Many feel that the government responses lag far behind the rapidly evolving methods used by those who cheat.

AI cheating became more apparent after the top scorer on the certified tax accountant examination made several shocking revelations. In May, a candidate in Gwangju was caught using AI equipped glasses during a fire protection engineering certification exam. Prosecutors sought a summary judgment against that candidate for violating the National Technical Qualifications Act during the May test. Other cases have emerged in the Law School Admission Test, English proficiency tests, and various national professional qualification examinations. Online vendors have openly sold cheating kits, and button camera sets have reportedly sold out to prospective examinees.

The government must now procure and install additional equipment, which presents considerable practical difficulties with only two days remaining. Authorities must decide if they can comprehensively restrict communication between the examination rooms and all outside parties. Other countries have already revised professional exams, prohibited digital devices, or introduced measures to block all wireless communications. The articles leave open whether the current interagency task force can actually ensure a fair testing environment for students. It remains unclear if the government can restore public confidence before the College Scholastic Ability Test officially begins.

stories.Headline: EU science and ethics advisors urge public AI evaluation capacity
stories.Summary:
On November 16, 2026, the European Commission’s Group of Chief Scientific Advisors and the European Group on Ethics in Science and New Technologies issued a joint statement warning that traditional public policy guardrails cannot govern rapidly advancing artificial intelligence. The two senior advisory bodies called on the European Union to establish sovereign capacity to evaluate complex AI models rather than delegating safety assessments to commercial technology firms. The statement, titled ‘The next phase of artificial intelligence ,  Governing for safety, security and human agency,’ sets out four core principles for European policymakers. The advisors delivered the four primary recommendations to the College of Commissioners. The joint statement was published on 16 Nov 2026.

The first recommendation is to keep existing rules strong, with safety, cybersecurity and human agency remaining mandatory prerequisites for AI development. The advisors warn against regulatory backsliding and say political hesitation risks weakening statutory obligations under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, and that lobbying to dilute compliance deadlines must be resisted. The second is to calibrate development and deployment to degrees of danger, so the pace at which foundation models and autonomous systems are released correlates with potential hazards. Where models pose severe cybersecurity, biosecurity or critical-infrastructure risks, deployment must be contingent on verified mitigation rather than post-incident response. The third is to build independent public evaluation capacity, with the advisors urging the EU to develop public testing facilities and warning the bloc cannot remain dependent on self-attestations or proprietary safety benchmarks supplied by commercial developers.

The fourth is to establish an ecosystem for continuous learning, in which regulatory frameworks and scientific risk assessments evolve dynamically alongside advancing model capabilities, since static compliance checklists are obsolete and authorities must create adaptive monitoring loops that ingest empirical evidence from operational deployments. The Group of Chief Scientific Advisors, established under the Scientific Advice Mechanism, comprises seven eminent researchers appointed in their personal capacity to deliver evidence-based policy counsel. The European Group on Ethics in Science and New Technologies operates as an independent advisory body examining where scientific discovery intersects with fundamental European rights. Officials within the Directorate-General for Research and Innovation confirmed that the move reflects mounting concern that commercial market pressures threaten to bypass fundamental safety reviews. The GCSA and EGE argued that relying exclusively on commercial developers to determine whether their proprietary models trigger GPAI systemic risk thresholds introduces an inherent conflict of interest that undermines European safety objectives.

The advisors asserted that safety and market competitiveness are complementary, and that reliable, audited and trustworthy systems form the only durable foundation for widespread societal adoption in medicine, public administration and critical engineering. In independent coverage by Wisevoter, titled Scientists Urge Europe to Enforce AI Rules, observers underscored that the European advisory apparatus is pivoting attention away from theoretical rule-drafting toward concrete technical verification capabilities. European academic organizations welcomed the advisors’ insistence on public evaluation infrastructure. Policy commentators at European Interest had previously pointed out that public scientific research risks marginalization if access to frontier models and evaluation tools remains gated behind commercial licensing agreements.

University consortia emphasized that independent evaluation capacity within member states would provide academic researchers with transparent benchmarks and reproducible verification protocols. For universities, research hospitals and academic research offices, the recommendations highlight procurement due diligence and audit trails, expansion of research ethics committee remits, academic participation in public evaluation testbeds, and safeguarding scientific reproducibility. Both bodies have previously advised the Commission on computational technologies, delivering opinions on artificial intelligence in crisis management and publishing detailed guidance on the successful and timely uptake of artificial intelligence in science in the EU. The joint statement arrives as the operational burden of the AI Act, finalized in 2024, has shifted toward secondary rulemaking and practical enforcement.

Critical milestones currently under negotiation include the general-purpose AI Code of Practice and implementation frameworks that clarify downstream compliance obligations. The European Commission has introduced legislative proposals including the Cloud and AI Development Act (COM(2026) 502 final). The advisors warn that without substantial budgetary investment in public technical staff, automated evaluation tooling and independent laboratory verification, regulatory bodies risk becoming rubber-stamping entities for proprietary commercial claims. Following publication of the joint statement on November 16, 2026, the Directorate-General for Research and Innovation and DG CONNECT are scheduled to review the advisors’ recommendations.

Attention will center on whether the European Commission incorporates explicit funding for independent evaluation infrastructure into upcoming Horizon Europe work programmes and the implementation roadmaps for the Cloud and AI Development Act. In parallel, the European AI Office is preparing the final administrative drafts of the General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, where stakeholder negotiations over independent auditor access remain under way. Under existing voluntary frameworks, major model providers conduct internal red-teaming exercises and issue selective model cards. The articles leave open whether the Commission will adopt the recommendations and how the negotiations over independent auditor access will conclude.

stories.Headline: Bureau of Industry and Security requires licenses to export advanced AI chips to certain data centers
stories.Summary:
The Bureau of Industry and Security released an interim final rule on November 16, 2026. This rule requires licenses to export, reexport, or transfer advanced artificial intelligence chips to data centers. It targets facilities supplying significant computing power to companies headquartered in Macau or Country Group D:5. The rule also applies to companies whose ultimate parent is headquartered in those locations. These restrictions apply to chips shipped to data centers anywhere in the world.

The rule covers chips under ECCNs 3A090 and 4A090 providing over 12 million aggregate total processing performance. It requires licenses for shipments to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand. The rule formally rescinds the January 2025 AI Diffusion Rule and its associated authorizations. It applies to chips already in place, treating new restricted service as an in-country transfer. Data centers already supplying this power must obtain a license within 90 days of the effective date.

The Bureau of Industry and Security is responsible for enforcing these new semiconductor export controls. Officials stated the rule relies on existing power over chip shipments rather than direct remote access regulation. They explained that the diligence requirements prevent companies from evading controls through corporate spinoffs or restructurings. BIS will review license applications on a case by case basis for restricted destinations. They will consider the effectiveness of each country's export control regime and its cooperation.

Cloud providers, chip suppliers, and data center operators are affected by these new compliance requirements. They must now identify who runs workloads on chips and who owns those companies. Some reports indicate ByteDance, Alibaba, and Tencent used chips in Japan, Malaysia, and Thailand. Exporters must obtain know your customer information to prove they lacked knowledge of restricted end uses. A data center's refusal to provide this information is now considered a red flag.

The rule follows Executive Order 14434 and uses the term Super Intelligence instead of artificial intelligence. Previous BIS opinions from 2009 and 2014 stated that providing cloud computing capacity was not controlled. The Remote Access Security Act passed the House on January 12, 2026, to amend the Export Control Reform Act. A companion Senate bill, S. 3519, was introduced on December 17, 2025, to target foreign persons of concern. These legislative efforts aim to give BIS explicit statutory authority over network access to controlled items.

The rule takes effect on its publication date in the Federal Register with a 60 day comment period. The Secretary of Commerce may add more high risk destinations to the license requirement list. BIS may impose import restrictions or Entity List designations on parties that tolerate evasion. The Remote Access Security Act still awaits action in the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs. The articles leave open whether the Senate will pass the broader House definition of remote access.

stories.Headline: Prime Minister Han orders smart device checks and weighs Wi-Fi cutoff to stop AI cheating on national exams
stories.Summary:
Prime Minister Han Seong-sook directed eight ministries and agencies to prevent AI-assisted cheating during a meeting on Monday, November 16, 2026. The government will implement thorough smart device checks for students taking the College Scholastic Ability Test this Thursday. Officials are also considering a nationwide cutoff of public Wi-Fi at all testing sites to stop the use of wireless devices. These measures target advanced equipment that is difficult to detect, including AI glasses, ultrasmall cameras, and wireless earphones.

The Ministry of Education will lead a pangovernment emergency response team for the 2027 academic year CSAT to manage these screenings. Test-takers must hand in all smart devices, and the government will scrutinize results for implausibly high scores after the exam. Confirmed cheaters face stern penalties, including the nullification of their results, restrictions on future exams, and criminal investigations. Additionally, the Ministry of Employment and Labor and the Human Resources Development Service of Korea will overhaul national certification exams by installing smart screening gates.

Prime Minister Han stated that fairness in exams is a basic principle that upholds trust in society and must not be damaged. She urged officials to mobilize every capability to create a fair environment while ensuring that honest students do not suffer. Han also ordered the immediate voiding of results for the top scorer on this year's certified tax accountant exam who admitted to cheating. This individual will be barred from taking the exam for five years while the police conduct a rigorous investigation.

The government believes existing management is limited against new AI cheating techniques, leading to the creation of a pangovernment task force. This group will review how various ministries manage exams to establish common responses against smart device violations. Authorities will also operate a center for reporting cheating and investigate suspicious cases alongside the police. These broader efforts aim to protect the integrity of 528 national exams from the threats posed by advancing artificial intelligence.

stories.Headline: South Korean stocks fall for a fourth session as AI investment worries persist
stories.Summary:
South Korean stocks experienced a sharp decline late Tuesday morning on November 17, 2026, due to persistent worries regarding artificial intelligence investments. The benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index, known as the KOSPI, dropped 63.04 points or 1.24 percent to reach 5,037.46 by 11:20 a.m. This downturn marked the fourth consecutive session of losses for the index, which had fallen as low as 4,984.83 during the morning. These losses followed a Monday drop of about 2.5 percent for the Nasdaq Composite on Wall Street.

The market is reacting to the upcoming Tuesday earnings report from Nvidia and the planned Nasdaq debut of Anthropic on Thursday. Investors are particularly concerned about AI chip demand and infrastructure spending following the departure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang last week. Additionally, the U.S. government issued new rules on Monday that restrict remote access to advanced servers and computing chips. In Seoul, Samsung Electronics fell 2.49 percent and Samsung Electro-Mechanics dropped 1.4 percent, while SK hynix rose 0.4 percent and SK Square gained 1.02 percent.

Market participants are closely monitoring the outlook for the AI sector amid increased regulatory scrutiny from the United States government. The Korean won also weakened during this period, trading at 1,339.4 won against the U.S. dollar as of 11:20 a.m., which was a decrease of 2.9 won. Investors remain cautious as they await the financial results from Nvidia to gauge the future of the industry. The overall volatility reflects a broader uncertainty regarding the sustainability of current artificial intelligence spending and leadership changes.

stories.Headline: Malaysia plans full AI exposure in schools next year as PAGE urges a balanced approach
stories.Summary:
The Parent Action Group for Education Malaysia successfully conducted its 16th annual general meeting in September 2026 to continue its campaign for English language instruction. This educational lobby group previously advocated for the use of smartphones as teaching aids, though many teachers initially insisted that these devices remain at home. While some developed nations are now restricting technology, the Madani government has decided to implement full scale exposure to artificial intelligence within the Malaysian education system. This new curriculum is scheduled to begin next year for students entering Year One and Form One.

Several countries are currently spending significant funds to return to traditional learning methods to combat digital fatigue and protect cognitive focus. Sweden spent more than 2.1 billion krona, or 875 million ringgit, over two years to bring printed textbooks and teaching guides back into classrooms. Denmark committed 540 million Danish krone, which is 330 million ringgit, over ten years for physical books while making schools and after school clubs handphone free. Other nations including Finland, Italy, France, and Norway have restricted or banned phones, while Madrid, Spain, is capping primary student screen time to two hours per week.

Datin Noor Azimah Abdul Rahim, the chairman of the Parent Action Group for Education Malaysia, expressed concerns regarding the eagerness to put screens in front of developing children. She argued that implementation must be guided by child safety, equity, and educational outcomes so that students do not surrender their ability to think independently. She noted that professors at Harvard University are increasingly banning laptops, as an analysis by The Harvard Crimson in September 2026 found such bans had more than doubled. She believes pupils still need physical books and handwriting practice to avoid being distracted by digital notifications.

The group suggests that Malaysia should learn from developed countries that have come full circle by finding a healthier balance between digital and traditional education. The author warns that excessive self promotion without adequate preparation could lead to failure, citing the recall of 8,878 Chery Omoda 5 cars and 600 other vehicles. The goal is for students to use technology to solve problems and make informed decisions rather than depending on it to think for them. The group will continue to serve as a channel between concerned parents, the Ministry of Education, and other stakeholders.

stories.Headline: Reporter uses AI glasses to solve difficult CSAT math questions in 22 minutes
stories.Summary:
A Kyunghyang Shinmun reporter used AI glasses to solve 2026 College Scholastic Ability Test questions on November 16. The reporter tested the device on math, Korean, and science sections to see if cheating was possible. The AI solved difficult math killer questions in one to two minutes and easier items in five seconds. All thirty math questions were finished in 22 minutes, resulting in a score of 98. The reporter also solved twenty science questions in 12 minutes and 44 seconds, scoring 34 out of 50.

The reporter used Rokid Glass AI from the Chinese company Rokid, which was released last January. These glasses cost about 750 dollars, weigh 49 grams, and look like ordinary horn-rimmed glasses with a small camera. The reporter used the Gemini AI model, which required a 20 minute setup before starting the test problems. The device allows users to choose specific AI models and perform training with detailed prompts for better accuracy. The reporter touched the temple of the glasses to trigger the camera and display answers on the lens.

The reporter noted that the AI solved a tricky Korean question in one second, which was 300 times faster than them. They stated that detection of cheating would be harder if a user practiced controls or used the device selectively. The reporter observed that the battery drained from 75 percent to 30 percent during the 20 minute math session. They mentioned that head movements and touching the temple might look suspicious to a proctor in a real room. The reporter also found that the AI struggled with science inquiry items due to the need for separate training.

Education authorities are preparing to ban AI glasses from test sites to protect the fairness of the national exam. A top scorer in the certified tax accountant exam recently turned themselves in for cheating using an ultra-small camera. Police stated that smart glasses were not among the devices used by that specific individual in the tax exam. Other reported cheating methods include modified calculators, internal vibrating devices, and wireless bone-conduction earphones bitten with a molar. These developments affect the integrity of the CSAT, which is seen as a key gateway in Korean society.

The Human Resources Development Service of Korea detected smart glasses cheating in four of five national technical qualification test cases. Major generative AI models gave conflicting wrong answers to the same Korean question just one year ago. The 2026 CSAT Korean question used in the test had a wrong-answer rate of 77.7 percent among students. The reporter who conducted the test had previously scored in the top tier for Korean during their school days. The reporter had sat the 2021 CSAT in the math Type A track without elective subjects like Calculus.

Authorities cannot deploy radio-frequency or metal detectors to every nationwide test site within the three days before the exam. Professor Choi Kyung-jin of Gachon University said existing proctoring rules make it difficult to detect AI-enabled cheating. He stated that new rules are needed because the advancement of artificial intelligence is an unstoppable tide of the times. The articles leave open how the government will effectively police sophisticated devices with the current proctoring manual. It remains unclear if higher-performance products will be more difficult to detect than the affordable Rokid model.

stories.Headline: Top tax exam scorer admits using AI to cheat as Korea plans glasses checks for national tests
stories.Summary:
The top scorer of a national tax accountant qualification exam admitted to using AI to cheat in a YouTube video. He used a miniature camera to photograph questions and checked the answers on a smartphone. This event has caused educators and exam boards to worry that traditional supervision cannot keep up with AI tools. These cheating devices are becoming smaller, cheaper, and harder for proctors to detect during tests.

The Ministry of Education announced visual inspections of glasses before the College Scholastic Ability Test on November 19. Proctors received training on November 11 at the Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education building in Yongsan District, central Seoul. Some overseas platforms sell cheating sets with cameras, earphones, and batteries for around 60,000 won or 45 dollars. Other tools include AI pens that convert handwriting to digital text and smart rings that connect to glasses.

The Human Resources Development of Korea administers the tax exam and prohibits all electronic and communication devices at sites. Professor Park Ju-hyung of Gyeongin National University of Education said miniature earphones could also be used during interviews. Professor Kim Byung-chan of Kyung Hee University stated that old testing methods cannot effectively distinguish candidates' abilities. He believes exams should assess the thought process used to arrive at an answer.

An 18-year-old examinee surnamed Yoo worried that thick-framed glasses might raise suspicion during the visual inspections. Yoo suggested using radio-frequency detectors to find electronic devices that cannot be seen with the naked eye. Some online communities suggested using ultrasonic cleaners or electromagnetic pulse devices to block communications. However, experts say these technologies are not foolproof or are impractical for nationwide use.

Equipment for cheating has been readily available for years on various overseas online shopping platforms. Some users on the online community Blind suggested the tax accountant used AI glasses and a smart ring. Another social media user described a method using a camera and earphones to receive AI answers every five seconds. AI glasses currently on the market can be distinguished from ordinary glasses by their physical features.

Authorities will investigate potential AI cheating across 528 national exams and tighten checks for the 2027 College Scholastic Ability Test. Daelim University president Park Joo-ho suggested evaluating the ability to solve problems using AI or designing unanswerable questions. Experts say Korea may need to redesign exams to assess reasoning and the use of AI. The articles leave open whether technological detection or fundamental exam changes will be adopted.

stories.Headline: South Korea forms emergency team to stop AI cheating in national exams
stories.Summary:
An anonymous user on the online community DC Inside claimed to have used artificial intelligence to cheat on the 2024 Suneung exam. This individual allegedly used a miniature camera disguised as a shirt button and a smartphone to obtain an average percentile score of 98.6. These claims surfaced shortly after Han Won-seok, the top scorer on this year's tax accountant qualification exam, confessed to using similar AI tools. Han admitted to using a miniature camera and generative AI during both rounds of the national exam in April and July. He scored 397.5 out of 400 points and achieved perfect scores in three of the four subjects.

The current situation requires the Education Ministry to implement strict measures to prevent the use of hidden cameras and smart glasses. YouTuber Kim Min-woo, known as Mimiminu, has urged the government to postpone the upcoming Suneung to ensure proper security. He noted that the exam was previously delayed in 2017 due to the Pohang earthquake and in 2020 because of the COVID-19 pandemic. To combat these threats, Prime Minister Han Seong-sook vowed on Tuesday to root out AI cheating by activating an interagency emergency response team. The government plans to ban smart devices and deploy additional staff at testing sites to maintain the integrity of the process.

Several education experts have expressed deep concern regarding the ability of authorities to detect modern cheating devices. Kim Min-woo explained that tiny devices hidden in bracelets or buttons can solve complex questions very quickly. Kang Sung-tae, the founder of Gongsin.com, argued that checking for thick-framed glasses is insufficient because many smart glasses from China have discreet designs. He stated that he has warned for years that AI-assisted cheating was inevitable and hoped his warnings would raise awareness. These experts believe that the current screening methods are outdated and cannot stop sophisticated technology.

The South Korean government is now racing to curb these technological breaches before the college entrance exam takes place this Thursday. Authorities are focusing on identifying a wide variety of smart glasses and other wearable electronics that students might smuggle into the rooms. The Education Ministry must now decide if the existing laws allow for a schedule change to better prepare for these threats. If the government cannot guarantee a fair environment, the pressure to delay the exam may increase. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Tax accountant admits to using AI smart glasses to cheat as presidential office orders review of 528 national exams
stories.Summary:
A 34-year-old man surnamed Han admitted to using generative AI to cheat on the 2026 national tax accountant qualification exam. He turned himself in to police on Sunday and posted an apology video on YouTube on November 15. Han used AI smart glasses and a micro camera to send exam questions to a smartphone for answers. This confession prompted the presidential office to order a sweeping review of suspected AI cheating cases. The incident occurred just days before the national college entrance exam, known as the CSAT.

The review covers 528 national exams and includes the 63rd national tax accountant qualification exam where Han scored 100 in three subjects. Han earned 97.5 in public finance, while the 16,856 tax law test takers averaged 30.18 with no others above 90. The Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency assigned the case to the public crime investigation team for potential business obstruction. Under Article 314 of the Criminal Act, Han faces up to five years in prison or 15 million won. The Human Resources Development Service of Korea, or HRDK, will revoke his score and file a complaint.

Ha Joon-kyung, the presidential director of national policy, convened an emergency meeting on Sunday to address the cheating. Ha stated that the Ministry of Education and other agencies must examine every possibility to prevent AI cheating. The HRDK said it would consider using radio frequency detectors and proctors dedicated to checking for AI devices. The Korean Association of Certified Public Tax Accountants will launch a new evaluation system during practical training for apprentices. This system aims to screen out individuals who passed professional licensing exams by using cheating methods.

One tax accountant candidate called for a retest because the fairness of the exam had completely collapsed. A test taker surnamed Lee, who earned perfect LEET scores, faced online suspicion due to poor past CSAT grades. Lee previously took the CSAT five times starting in 2013 and once received a grade 7 in Korean. Other suspicions targeted three Yonsei University Mirae Campus dental hygiene graduates and candidates of the licensed customs broker exam. Suspicions also reached the certified appraiser, grade-5 national civil service, and Medical and Dental Education Eligibility tests.

Six cases of AI smart glasses cheating were caught through October in exams for gas craftsmen and various engineers. Cheating was also found in the financial investment analyst exam, the LEET, and university essay exams for early admission. Three Toeic takers and one TEPS taker were caught using AI, as were some middle and high school students. Equipment like 50,000-won micro cameras and 10,000-won earpieces are easily bought on overseas sites, including new AI pens. Critics say lax proctoring and a lack of rules on AI cheating contributed to these widespread problems.

The Education Ministry banned AI smart glasses on the CSAT, meaning violators will be barred for one year. Radio frequency detectors and revised enforcement rules banning smart glasses are not expected until the 2027 college entrance exam. The HRDK formed a task force in August and deployed 327 AI inspectors across two national qualification exams. Professor Choi Byoung-ho noted that Korea has virtually no AI cheating rules and requires a considerable budget for equipment. Professor Kim Byeong-chan suggested changing exam questions to evaluate the thought process rather than just the final result.
