stories.Headline: Uncountable co-founder Will Tashman says AI now links polymer synthesis, testing and scale-up data
stories.Summary:
Will Tashman, co-founder of Uncountable Inc., gave an interview published by AZoM on 16 November 2026 about AI in polymer development. He said AI's role has moved beyond suggesting new experiments and now depends on connecting synthesis records, analytical results, application testing and process history. He described AI contributing at every stage of polymer R&D, starting with modeling polymerization kinetics, chain extension or cross-linking. He said AI can then help predict how resulting materials perform once formulated or processed into a final product. He said the polymer manufacturers Uncountable works with want materials that perform better for customers.

Tashman said polymer development can involve 10, 15, maybe even 20 variables, including monomers, additives, catalysts and reaction-process parameters. He said Uncountable's screening tools use a sphere-packing approach to distribute experiments across the space being investigated. He described a resin publishing process in which the polymer team develops reactions in a permission-controlled environment and chooses what an applications group can see. He said that might include the resin's identity and selected measured properties such as glass transition temperature, solids content or NCO content, without revealing its composition. He holds a Bachelor of Science in Materials Engineering from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and co-founded Uncountable in 2016.

Tashman said much of the difficulty in bringing information together comes from how the work is distributed, with scientists recording reactions in spreadsheets or notebooks while other teams handle analytical testing. He said techniques such as GPC, FTIR and DSC often require specialists to run the instruments and interpret the results. He said Uncountable aims to bring the scientist designing the reaction, the analytical team receiving the testing request and the people reporting results into the same environment. He said analytical experts still apply their judgment, but their results and conclusions return directly to the scientist responsible for synthesis. He said a useful starting point for AI readiness is asking whether a team can connect a reaction to testing performed on its output.

Tashman said scientists accustomed to grids or familiar formulation designs may find it challenging to see several factors change at once. He said the important distinction is between an experiment easy to interpret by eye and a set of experiments designed to support efficient statistical analysis. He said simple ladder studies do not disappear, and broader mathematically designed screening should be followed by more focused studies once a team has narrowed its direction. He said a resin or polymer can be central to a company's intellectual property while also driving decisions across its wider R&D organization. He said teams need a way to share enough information for downstream work without automatically exposing the underlying composition.

Tashman said a polymer that performs well in a bench reactor may behave differently at pilot or production scale, which he called one of the main challenges Uncountable wants to help solve. He said capturing scientific processes in a structured way lets teams analyze how they evolve from laboratory work to pilot plants and full production. He said differences between reactors or production environments can affect performance even when the reason for a shift is not immediately clear. He said connecting process information with batch results allows teams to compare how related materials perform at different scales. He said teams can investigate whether particular recipes show changes in solids content or whether certain reactions exhibit greater exothermic behavior as scale increases.

Tashman said he expects changes starting with how teams explore their raw material space, with better tools helping scientists investigate a broader range of monomers, surfactants, solvents, catalysts and additives. He said he expects teams to shorten the time between running a reaction and reaching a useful conclusion. He said scale-up is another important opportunity, since understanding how to manufacture something reliably can take a substantial part of the overall development timeline. He said Uncountable's role is to help shorten both the initial exploration needed to identify a promising material and the later work required to turn it into a product that can be manufactured consistently. The article carries a disclaimer that the views expressed are those of the interviewee and do not necessarily represent those of AZoM.com Limited.

stories.Headline: Figure CEO Michael Tannenbaum says AI will cut DSCR loan processing from weeks to days
stories.Summary:
Figure Technology Solutions plans to cut DSCR loan processing from several weeks to days using artificial intelligence to automate underwriting, CEO Michael Tannenbaum told NMP. The push follows Figure's acquisition of Kiavi and a 135% surge in marketplace volume. Figure reported $5.8 billion in third-quarter loan marketplace volume, up 135% year over year. That figure included $677 million contributed by Kiavi following its Sept. 1 acquisition. Tannenbaum said the new DSCR product will automate document reviews, property valuations, and portions of the title process.

Tannenbaum said Figure can streamline the entire DSCR application process down to a matter of days from several weeks today. Figure's $717 million acquisition of Kiavi added an investor lending platform offering residential transition loans and DSCR loans for rental property investors. During its third-quarter earnings call, Figure outlined plans to introduce the new DSCR product in the fourth quarter and offer a white-label version through Figure Connect in the first quarter of 2027. Figure said it had onboarded 12 existing partners for Kiavi products, with more than 30 additional partners in its pipeline. Figure has not specified which loans would qualify for the accelerated process or whether certain transactions would still require traditional appraisals and manual reviews.

Tannenbaum said brokers will be getting the best-in-class DSCR provider through Figure's acquisition of Kiavi. He said that means the highest quality underwriting at speeds competitors cannot match. He said that speed leads to a decrease in closing time and an increase in the number of loans a broker can work at any given time. Tannenbaum said the new DSCR will automate almost every part of underwriting, and that Figure's process will automate a great majority of all document reviews. He said removing costly steps and reviews will create savings that can be passed on to brokers in the form of better unit economics.

In September, Charles Goodwin, vice president and head of bridge and DSCR lending at Kiavi, said the pricing gap between DSCR loans and conventional mortgages had narrowed to approximately 50 basis points from 75 to 100 basis points a year earlier. Goodwin said lenders are differentiating themselves on speed and service outside of pricing, and that many DSCR lenders now say they can close loans in as little as 10 days. Figure Connect generated $4.3 billion in volume, up 276% year over year, and accounted for 72% of Figure's standalone marketplace volume excluding Kiavi. Figure's standalone partner network reached 612, rising to 894 including Kiavi's broker partners. Adjusted net revenue climbed 83% to $283 million, while adjusted EBITDA increased 91% to approximately $164 million.

Figure is also expanding AI use in home equity lending, where its Sierra-powered Loan Officer Assistant has been involved in approximately $260 million in funded loans. Tannenbaum said the assistant handles the friction and loan officers handle the decision. He said the assistant shines during steps where borrowers drop off, including income verification such as bank linking and Social Security or pension income. Figure previously reported a 143% increase in funded-loan conversion when its AI assistant worked alongside human loan officers compared with originators working alone. Tannenbaum said loan officers remain essential because this is a considered decision, and that Figure's HELOCs go up to $750,000.

Tannenbaum said Figure will share more about pricing as it gets closer to launch. The company said it had already onboarded 12 existing partners for Kiavi products, with more than 30 additional partners in its pipeline. Figure outlined plans to expand access through its broker channel. The articles leave open which loans would qualify for the accelerated process and whether certain transactions would still require traditional appraisals and manual reviews. The articles also leave open whether automation savings would benefit brokers and borrowers, a question Tannenbaum answered by pointing to improved broker economics.

stories.Headline: PointClickCare's Rizhevsky urges operators to set one goal and map data flows before adopting AI in 2027
stories.Summary:
In 2026, nursing teams at Saint Therese of Woodbury in Minnesota and Pinnacle Living in Glen Allen, Virginia used PointClickCare's Chart Advisor, a real-time documentation intelligence tool, to gain faster visibility into resident risks and daily records. Kristin Stewart, Director of Nursing at Saint Therese of Woodbury, said the technology helped her see when and where falls occurred, which let her focus on questions about staffing levels, care times and coverage in areas such as the dining room. Pinnacle Living used the same tool to improve decision-making, spot patterns in its data and cut the time spent reviewing records. According to the article, Pinnacle spent 50% less time per shift reviewing and reconciling documentation for possible resident risk events, because relevant information now appeared in one place instead of being scattered across the resident record.

The article says operators using Chart Advisor could quickly read resident documentation and see flags about potential risks around falls, pressure injuries, elopement and psychotropic medication use. PointClickCare's Pharmacy Connect will soon include AI-Assisted Pharmacy Order Review, which compares medication order details with the pharmacy's directions and flags discrepancies before an order is confirmed, so teams can review what is flagged with less manual follow-up. Julia Rizhevsky, Vice President of Product Management and AI Strategy at PointClickCare, said the company's approach is that AI can flag, suggest a next step or make a recommendation, but the caregiver ultimately decides what action is taken. She described "explainability" as the ability to trace a flag or recommendation back to data in the chart, and she said 2027 will focus on giving operators better insight into the next step from a richer record of each resident.

Rizhevsky said operators who want those gains in 2027 should take three steps in the fourth quarter of 2026, starting with zeroing in on a specific operational goal, such as reducing time spent reviewing medication orders or reducing hospital transfers over a month, and treating it as an experiment for improvement. She said operators should bring in wellness staff, caregiving leaders and pharmacy partners, identify easily fixable problems such as duplication of work, missing data or time delays, and map how information flows between the parties. She suggested asking the people involved what piece of information they wish they had at each step, and then measuring results during daily stand-ups once a tool such as Chart Advisor is part of the new process. The article, a sponsored Views piece, says the opportunity with AI is huge and senior care is very much at the beginning, with rich data on one hand and manual, repetitive, error-prone processes on the other.

stories.Headline: GitHub lets users start AI Scan for up to 20 repositories at once
stories.Summary:
GitHub said on 16 November 2026 that users can now start AI Scan for repositories for up to 20 repositories at once, a change it described as a bulk start option for the feature. AI Scan for repositories finds security vulnerabilities on a repository's default branch, and it covers languages that CodeQL does not support while also finding additional issues in languages that CodeQL already analyzes. Findings from the feature appear in the code scanning backlog alongside CodeQL alerts, according to the GitHub blog post announcing the change. The bulk start option is in public preview, and AI Scan for repositories is available on github.com and on GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency.

The change means that users can start scans for selected repositories when they enable the organization-level setting, or they can do so from the code scanning organization alerts page. Users can also still start a scan for an individual repository from that repository's alerts page, so the bulk option sits alongside the existing single-repository route. GitHub said that a GitHub Copilot license is not required to use AI Scan for repositories, which removes a licensing step that might otherwise have applied. The post did not give a date for when the public preview will end or when the feature will become generally available.

GitHub itself is responsible for the feature and announced it in a blog post on its website, where it directed readers to learn more about AI Scan and to join the discussion in GitHub Community. The post also pointed readers to the company's biweekly newsletter for developers, which it described as offering tips, technical guides and best practices. The articles did not include any statement from an individual GitHub employee about the change, so no person was named as speaking on it. The post gave no further detail on how the bulk start option behaves beyond the 20-repository limit and the two places from which it can be started.

The context is that AI Scan for repositories adds a second kind of code scanning alongside CodeQL, which GitHub already uses to analyze code for security problems, and the bulk option is meant to let organizations begin scans across many repositories without doing each one separately. Because findings land in the same code scanning backlog as CodeQL alerts, teams see both kinds of results in one place rather than in separate lists. The feature is in public preview, which means it is available for use but not yet a finished release, and GitHub invited users to join the discussion in GitHub Community. The articles did not say what happens next beyond that preview status and the invitation to give feedback.

stories.Headline: CNCF reports inference traffic rises fourfold as Kubernetes becomes the standard for AI workloads
stories.Summary:
The article reports that the author revisited Salt Lake City for KubeCon/CloudNativeCon NA 2026, held on 2026-11-16, to look for practical approaches to delivering customer value amid AI-driven solutions. The Cloud Native Computing Foundation hosted the event and set its theme as "Cloud Native Without Limits." The article states that the community has more than 230 active projects and that AI adoption for building and consuming applications is increasing. Chris Anzyzcyk, chief technical officer of CNCF, said in opening remarks that at last year's KubeCon in Atlanta, OpenClaw was not released yet and MCP was less than a year old. He also said inference in cloud native was just getting started at that time.

Jonathan Bryce, executive director of CNCF, said AI compute was moving out of a phase where most of it was used for training and would massively ramp up inference. He said that in the last eight months there had been a 4X increase in inference traffic across the industry. He said inference is no longer just an opportunity but now a cloud-native production workload. The article states there are more than 350K CNCF contributors and 21.2 million cloud-native developers worldwide. According to the latest State of Cloud Native Development Q3 2026 report, fully three-quarters of those developers are already using AI coding agents.

The article states that two-thirds of self-described AI-driven organizations are standardizing on Kubernetes and related open-source technologies. The Kubernetes AI Conformance Program launched at KubeCon NA 2025 now has 42 major participating vendors agreeing to consistent standards. This year there are new Kubernetes AI Certifications for upskilling engineers, whether they are just starting out or are "Golden Kubestronauts" who already passed every course CNCF offers. Dan Ciruli, vice president and general manager for cloud native at Nutanix Inc., said Kubernetes has become the standard API for deploying a workload to a computer, including AI. He said the CNCF gave a safe haven for anyone from the smallest startup of two people to the largest companies on Earth to feel safe donating labor, code and IP.

Ciruli said that in turn gave everybody, from governments to financial services to hot startups, the confidence that they could consume it. Nutanix recently introduced its Nutanix Agent Gateway and an NKP Metal solution that allows Kubernetes clusters and workloads to run on bare metal as well as virtual machines in EKS, AKS or GKE for what it calls a "dual-native" experience. Matt DeBergalis, CEO of Apollo Graph Inc., doing business as Apollo GraphQL, asked how thousands of agents would be safely and sustainably connected to systems of record that run the business, such as customer loyalty or inventory. Apollo GraphQL supports the popular open source GraphQL query language and presented a new semantic domain model for deterministically interpreting AI prompts and controls for each record. Last year CNCF announced a Dynamic Resource Allocation capability that unlocked new possibilities for the community to optimize AI workloads running in Kubernetes.

This year, sandboxing, or running agents in secure instances to prevent escapes, hijacking and overprovisioning, was the watchword. Two new projects emerged: an Agent Substrate layer contributed by Google that optimizes resource consumption of thousands of agent sandboxes, and OpenShell, an Nvidia Corp.-contributed project for secure sandboxed runtimes. Startup Apelogic Inc., doing business as HyperShell, built an operational agent envelope based on OpenShell that defines guardrails on what systems an autonomous agent can access and what actions it can take. Cast AI started as a cloud cost optimization layer for rightsizing clusters on major hyperscalers and now automates and optimizes more AI workloads across CPUs and GPUs, memory and storage. Its new Kimchi code agent governs and deploys application infrastructures from a prompt, which allows developers to shift left agentic reviews before production tuning.

Floxdev Inc., which the author covered as a startup with Nix-based lean containerized environment deployments in 2025, put its Flox platform directly in the AI delivery path. The platform gives agents skills to stamp out identical complete environments that include all dependencies without reproducing any element of the software supply chain inventory that wasn't intended to change. The article says this moves agentic loops faster with lower compute costs, but the real value is when human engineers can reduce future maintenance and security remediation costs. This year's CNCF graduation of the OpenTelemetry project made OTel the lingua franca of application performance, scalability and reliability. The article states that observability was traditionally considered the domain of engineers and operators, but now everyone from data analysts to business executives may be using an LLM or an agent to interact with enterprise applications.

Splunk, a division of Cisco Systems Inc., added to its agent observability suite a specialized language model called Eval-G1 that can run prompt-and-response evals in sub-second times at sub-cent costs. The article says this gives engineers the ability to interrupt a faulty response in real time before it reaches customers. A new Evaluation Studio helps teams generate guardrails in a low-code graphical environment. A tokenomics feature from the recent acquisition of Galileo analyzes token spend versus system and business performance metrics. Morgan McLean, senior director of product management at Splunk and OpenTelemetry co-creator, said it has been exciting to see how OpenTelemetry, which started out as tens of thousands of adaptors for every application and client, has transitioned with the AI revolution so that frameworks now emit OTel natively.

McLean said Splunk and its competitors can just launch new observability features without putting 30 people on writing new integrations. Dynatrace LLC recently acquired Bindplane for OTel-native telemetry pipelines, BlueBox, which gives developers a custom agent for debugging and checks within a coding IDE, and Arize, which maintains the popular Phoenix open-source tool for AI evaluations. New Relic Inc. released a new Autopilot Kubernetes Agent, a virtual SRE that users can interact with via natural language to look across telemetry and APM data. The agent assesses the health of the cluster and application, triages issues with a complete stack trace, and recommends resolutions. Jemiah Sius, vice president of market strategy and developer relations at New Relic, said that especially when agents are brought into an environment, you can't just take telemetry and throw it over to a general-purpose LLM.

Sius said there are known deterministic patterns and historical insights about Kubernetes that New Relic has been working to resolve for years. The article states that a lot of the governance difficulty with agents, sandboxes and policies isn't a technical problem but is about user experience. It says human engineers don't like being "in the loop" for AI, aka "Meat Proxies," that continuously pass along approvals. Simone Morellato, senior director of product marketing at Rafay Systems Inc., said you can try to create a secure agent sandbox with a policy where everything is disabled by default until a human approves it. He said eventually someone gets tired of being in that approval loop, so you give an agent access to one thing and eventually end up giving them access to everything.

Morellato said at that point you are back at square one. Edera Inc., a hardened runtime container vendor the author covered last year, is finding new traction in this agentic age by strengthening the stack from the bottom up. It offers an agent runtime and OCAP bounded authority that acts as a switchboard for discretely defined agent capabilities rather than assigning agents credentials or access to MCP servers or APIs or other agents. The article says such access can be expanded or exploited for another HuggingFace-type incident.

Alex Zenla, Edera founder and chief technology officer, said you can consume capabilities in the system and publish capabilities. Zenla said that for an MCP server, Edera publishes each tool call as a capability, and when you spin up your agent you ask for the tool calls you want. Zenla said the agent then consumes just those capabilities, and Edera can enforce policies because it has one central pathway for everything to go through. Kolton Andrus, CEO of Gremlin Inc., said he loves the focus on reliability he saw in the talks and on the floor at KubeCon.

Gremlin was there demonstrating its new Foresight AI solution that proactively injects failure conditions in order to identify and remediate failure risks. Andrus said you can no longer wait for things to fall apart before taking action. He said everyone is moving 100 miles an hour trying to keep up with AI and waking up to the fact that reliability can't be an afterthought anymore. More to follow.

Articles.Title: At KubeCon 2026, the illusion of AI control meets the reality of implementation

stories.Headline: Stanford professors Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin launch Noeri with $110M to build self-improving AI for enterprises
stories.Summary:
Stanford professors Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin founded the AI lab Noeri in 2026 to build self-improving AI for enterprises. On November 16, 2026, the Palo Alto company announced it had raised 110 million dollars in new funding. Menlo Ventures led this investment round with participation from Madrona Venture Group, Kindred Ventures, Wing Venture Capital, and NEA. Strategic investors for the new lab also include Snowflake, NVIDIA, and Cisco Investments. The company is currently hiring researchers and engineers for its offices in Zurich and Palo Alto.

The system changes AI from frozen models into living systems that self-organize and self-improve through interactions on the job. Noeri's technology studies an enterprise's own data and workflows to improve the harness, skills, instructions, tools, and underlying parameters. The software works with open-weight and closed models, and customers retain ownership of their data and developed workflows. This approach allows smaller, specialized models to make sustained scientific discovery affordable by reducing the compute needed for search. The lab's mission is to enable a future where plural intelligence, meaning intelligence in the plural, co-evolves with humanity.

Co-founder and co-CEO Yejin Choi stated that the future of AI will be a healthy ecosystem of many diverse intelligences. Co-founder and co-CEO Carlos Guestrin said that specialization can move the curve for companies struggling with model costs and results. Guestrin noted that Noeri builds AI that becomes obsessed with the hardest problems of a company and teaches itself solutions. Venky Ganesan of Menlo Ventures said the founders are rare because they put world-class research to work inside companies. He explained that this combination of research and application is why his firm moved quickly to lead the funding round.

Large companies are affected because they spend heavily on AI but struggle to turn general-purpose models into specific results. These organizations typically must choose between paying more for the most capable models or accepting weaker results from cheaper ones. Noeri's AI acts as a co-discoverer for scientists and engineers working on complex technical systems, proteins, and new molecules. The system ensures every change is explained and sent to a person for approval, similar to a standard code review. This process allows the AI to find new solutions and refine known ones based on actual experience.

The technology is based on joint research by Choi and Guestrin regarding test-time training and on-the-job learning after deployment. Guestrin previously co-founded Turi, which Apple acquired in 2016, and he later led Apple's central machine learning and AI organization. He also co-created XGBoost, a widely used machine learning technology that powers various industries and accelerates scientific discovery. Choi is a MacArthur Fellow and a Schmidt Sciences AI2050 Senior Fellow who previously worked at the Allen Institute. Her research on agentic orchestration and pluralistic alignment helps small models outperform frontier models at a fraction of the cost.

Noeri is currently working with a varied group of strategic partners, including some of its investors, to help its technology generalize. The company aims to solve the open research problem of moving past the trade-off between model cost and performance. The lab continues to develop systems that align AI with the full diversity of human needs and values. The articles do not state when the first commercial products will be available to the general public. They also leave open which specific industries will be the first to adopt these self-improving living systems.

Articles.Title: Noeri Launches with $110M to Empower Companies to Build and Own Their AI

stories.Headline: ASE Technology Holding opens Luzhu plant to expand advanced packaging capacity
stories.Summary:
ASE Technology Holding opened the first phase of its new Luzhu plant on November 13, 2026. This facility is located in Kaohsiung and represents the company's first entry into the science park system of Taiwan. On that same day, the company also broke ground for the second phase of the project. This expansion is taking place within the Kaohsiung section of the Southern Taiwan Science Park. The new facilities are designed to expand the company's capabilities in the field of advanced packaging.

This strategic move allows the organization to scale its production capacity to meet growing industry demands. The project involves the construction of multiple phases to ensure a steady increase in operational output. These developments are situated in one of the most important technology hubs in the region. The company is responsible for managing the construction and the eventual operation of these high-tech sites.

While the provided text does not include specific quotes, the action demonstrates a commitment to strengthening its infrastructure. The company aims to leverage the benefits of the science park system for better integration. This investment signals a long-term plan to maintain a competitive edge in semiconductor assembly. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Eli Lilly gains $250 billion in market value as Nvidia loses $1.7 trillion
stories.Summary:
Eli Lilly gained over 250 billion dollars in market value while Nvidia lost more than 1.7 trillion dollars. This shift occurred between October 6, 2026, and the close of trading on Monday, November 17, 2026. The maker of Zepbound saw a 25 percent gain during this specific period. Meanwhile, the AI chip leader experienced a 32 percent drop in its value. These movements highlight a recent trend where weight loss drugs are beating artificial intelligence.

The market changes affected several major companies including Alphabet, which lost about 640 billion dollars in value. SpaceX shed about 450 billion dollars, and Micron lost about 300 billion dollars by Yahoo Finance calculations. Apple, Lilly, and Walmart were the stocks that collected gains during this time. Lilly now trades at roughly 27 times forward earnings, which is about two and a half times Nvidia's multiple. This follows an October period when AI stocks lost about 5 trillion dollars in less than a month.

Eli Lilly CEO Dave Ricks responded to claims that AI would soon eliminate major diseases like cancer and Alzheimer's. He wrote on X that such a rapid change is not likely to happen. Ricks stated that progress in these medical fields will likely be steady and incremental. This was a direct response to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who pitched his company's IPO. Amodei believes these illnesses will be relics of the past in less than a decade.

Other investors and analysts are monitoring the risks associated with these high stock prices. Michael Hartnett of BofA described healthcare as one of the groups most vulnerable to a downside. He identified semiconductors, discretionary stocks, and homebuilders as the groups most vulnerable to an upside. The current run for Lilly is stretched, sitting about 30 percent above its 200 day moving average. This volatility affects traders who remember previous streaks ending in drops of more than 20 percent.

The background shows that weight loss drugmakers were a major obsession early in this bull market. In the 15 months after October 2022, Lilly and Novo Nordisk gained about 92 percent on average. This growth was close to the 101 percent gain seen by the Magnificent Seven. However, Novo Nordisk later lost about three quarters of its value from a June 2024 peak. For two years, the GLP-1 trade watched big tech dominate the market before roles reversed.

The market now awaits the first earnings report for Nvidia since the exit of Jensen Huang. Analysts are watching to see if Lilly will continue to pull ahead of Nvidia over five years. It remains unclear if the current weight loss trade is the best one for investors to chase. The articles leave open whether the AI trade will recover or continue bleeding from every direction. Future price movements depend on whether these stretched valuations lead to another significant dip.

Articles.Title: Eli Lilly is trouncing Nvidia — and the weight-loss drug trade is beating AI again

stories.Headline: Audible launches an AI audio feature that summarizes books for listeners
stories.Summary:
Audible, which is owned by Amazon, launched an audio discovery feature on Monday that gives listeners a short spoken overview of a book before they decide to listen to it. The overview combines a summary of the book's themes, a roundup of what readers liked about it, and commentary from an Audible editor or the author, and it plays alongside the narrated sample. The summary audio is generated with AI, while the commentary is taken from recordings of past Audible interviews, according to the company. Audible says the expanded introduction is meant to help people choose their next listen, especially when they are on the go and do not have time to scroll through comments or reviews. The feature will first be available for select English-language titles in the United States, and it will arrive with new personalized collections based on each user's listening taste.

Audible says the overviews will also draw on other public materials, such as synopses and metadata, and the reader reactions come from publicly available reviews. The launch follows last month's release of AI tools that let users interact with characters, catch up through recaps, or ask questions about a story. Those Recaps and Ask a Question features are now expanding to more U.S. titles and will become more broadly available in December, but only for customers who bought a title or have it through their Audible membership. Andy Tsao, Audible's chief product and analytics officer, said picking your next listen should feel like getting a tip from a friend. He said the feature gives listeners a quick audio take on why a title might suit them, from editors, fellow listeners, or the author.

He added that some of the best listening experiences are rare finds and hidden gems, and the company wants those discoveries to happen more often and more easily. The article notes that pulling only positive remarks could limit users' exposure to negative reviews, though it says further testing would be needed to see if that is the case. The launch comes as Audible faces new competition in the audiobooks market, particularly from Spotify, which added audiobook listening hours to its paid subscriptions and expanded that service to more than 180 markets last month. Audible's approach echoes how Amazon already uses AI on its storefront, where the technology summarizes buyer reviews so shoppers can quickly grasp the pros and cons of an item. The article does not say what Audible plans beyond the December expansion of its other AI features.

Articles.Title: Audible turns to AI to help users discover audiobooks

stories.headline_source: Audible turns to AI to help users discover audiobooks

stories.Headline: Gary Marcus says the AI bubble has popped as Oracle falls about 61 percent
stories.Summary:
Gary Marcus wrote on November 16, 2026 that the AI bubble appears to have finally popped, pointing to Oracle's roughly 61 percent decline since he called the OpenAI deal "peak bubble" the previous September. Tech stocks kept falling sharply that day after a rout the week before, and even Axios acknowledged before the market opened that the jig was up. Ben Thompson of Stratechery published what Marcus described as an obituary for Jensen Huang, saying his demise ended many things including Nvidia's long-term prospects and the AI bubble. Marcus also cited a Wall Street Journal article reporting that Nvidia's days as an open checkbook for the AI economy were numbered.

The Journal article said interim CEO Colette Kress is expected to rein in deals after a stretch in which Nvidia aggressively financed computing deals and startup investments. Marcus argued that the LLM companies still lack a technical moat and still struggle to be profitable, which was true in 2023 and remains true. He said Nvidia could not sustain its growth indefinitely because you cannot sell chips endlessly if the buyers are not making profits from them. He also noted hints that some funny business in Asia may have made things look better than they were, and that circular financing made it hard to tell what was really happening.

Marcus wrote that it pretty much looks like game over for the current AI bubble, adding that the midterms no doubt contributed and that the free pass AI companies had in the first half of the Trump era is over. He said the critical question is whether any of this affects Thursday's planned IPO for Anthropic, or whether people simply leap from one fad to another as they did from crypto to NFTs to generative AI. He said the financial fundamentals do not justify the hoped-for valuation once liabilities are factored in, and that selling a deeply speculative IPO amid an AI stock crash will not be easy. He added that he cannot say whether there are enough hopeful suckers who are bad at reading profit-and-loss and liability statements.

Articles.Title: Game over, man? - Marcus on AI | Substack

stories.Headline: Mayo Clinic appoints AI program leader Matthew Callstrom as next CEO
stories.Summary:
The Mayo Clinic Board of Trustees announced this past Friday that Dr. Matthew R. Callstrom, a radiologist who has led the health system's AI program in recent years, will succeed Dr. Gianrico Farrugia as president and chief executive officer in the new year. Callstrom first joined Mayo Clinic more than two decades ago and has held a wide array of leadership roles across clinical practice, research and innovation since 2002. He has served on Mayo Clinic's Board of Governors and Board of Trustees, and most recently was medical director for Mayo Clinic Strategy. He previously served as interim chief strategy officer and as chair of the Department of Radiology at Mayo Clinic in Rochester.

Farrugia will remain CEO through December 31 and will work closely with Callstrom as he moves into the new leadership role. Farrugia has led Mayo Clinic for the past seven years, a period that included embracing cloud-enabled artificial intelligence and the launch of Mayo Clinic Platform. Callstrom's own work has led to hundreds of publications and patents, and he has served as president of the Society of Interventional Oncology. He earned degrees in chemical engineering and chemistry from the University of Minnesota Twin Cities, completed a postdoctoral fellowship at Harvard, and earned his medical degree from Mayo Clinic Alix School of Medicine, with residency and fellowship at Mayo Clinic in Rochester.

Richard K. Davis, chair of the Board of Trustees, said Callstrom's leadership across patient care, research, strategy and innovation prepares him exceptionally well to lead Mayo Clinic into its next chapter. Davis said Callstrom understands Mayo Clinic as a physician caring for patients, a scientist translating discovery into clinical care and a leader shaping strategy for the future. Farrugia called it the privilege of his career to serve as president and CEO and said Callstrom knows Mayo Clinic deeply and has the vision and experience to build on the progress made. Callstrom said he was deeply honored to lead Mayo Clinic in this moment and that the organization has always been at its best when it brings the full power of its clinical expertise, science and innovation to the needs of patients.

Callstrom has been vocal about AI's potential to enable advances in research and care when properly deployed. He said Mayo's aspiration for AI is to meaningfully improve patient outcomes by detecting disease early enough to intervene, and that what was once a hypothetical is now becoming reality thanks to AI and advanced computing. He previously explained why Mayo chose Cerebras as its first generative AI collaborator, citing its large-scale, domain-specific AI expertise to accelerate breakthrough insights for patients. He told Reuters that weighing all the factors for each patient requires a lot of experience, and that is where AI comes in to augment that.

stories.Headline: Dreamteam raises $53M to build AI-native CRM and signs over 100 customers
stories.Summary:
Dreamteam, a San Francisco-based startup founded in 2025 by former Freshworks executives, has raised $53 million in seed and Series A funding to build an AI-native CRM aimed at challenging Salesforce and HubSpot. The seed round was led by Together Fund and the Series A by Accel, with participation from Premji Invest, though the company declined to disclose the size of each round or its valuation. The company was co-founded by CEO Anand Venkatraman, Senthil Kanthaswamy, who spent more than nine years at Freshworks and most recently served as a product leader at Freshservice, and Ramesh Parthasarathy, who previously worked on AI and platform engineering at Freshworks. Venkatraman said he encountered problems with traditional CRM platforms over more than 25 years in enterprise software, including stints at Salesforce and Freshworks, because salespeople spent considerable time updating records while managers still struggled to get a reliable picture of their business.

Dreamteam's CRM is built around what it calls the Company Brain, which acts as virtual memory by pulling together information from emails, meetings and other customer interactions to build a shared record of customer relationships. Four built-in AI agents use that information to research prospects, draft follow-up emails, flag potential risks to deals and configure CRM workflows, with sales teams retaining control over what gets sent to customers. The startup has signed up more than 100 customers across 13 countries in the three months since it began actively selling, with most paying for the service, and it has replaced established platforms at several businesses, including Salesforce at healthcare company DMS Health and HubSpot at other customers. The advertising sales team at media streaming company Plex chose Dreamteam over HubSpot and other AI-native CRM alternatives, and Plex co-founder and chief product officer Scott Olechowski called its ability to integrate with AI tools already used across the company a game changer.

Venkatraman acknowledged that Salesforce and HubSpot are unlikely to disappear anytime soon, but said their entrenched positions do not guarantee they will dominate the next generation of CRM software, describing the shift as an electric-car moment for systems of record. Kanthaswamy said startups have a window of two to five years to gain ground before established CRM providers can fully adapt to AI, since rebuilding software around a fundamentally different architecture takes time. The venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz argued in a blog post earlier this year that existing CRMs are likely to remain the systems where customer records are stored, with a new generation of AI-powered tools capturing much of the value by working on top of them. Dreamteam plans to expand beyond sales into onboarding, customer support and upselling, and it already offers a feature called Magic Apps that lets users create custom applications and dashboards within the CRM using natural-language instructions without writing code. The startup employs more than 35 people, with engineering based in Chennai and go-to-market operations in the United States, and Kanthaswamy said it aims to reach eight figures in annual revenue by the end of 2027, though he declined to disclose current revenue.

Articles.Title: Freshworks alums raise $53M to take on Salesforce, HubSpot with AI-native CRM

stories.Headline: Math Ph.D. students find most peers less likely to stay in math after AI advances
stories.Summary:
Three math Ph.D. students, Anna Brandenberger, Hanna Mularczyk and Dora Woodruff, launched an online Google Forms survey after AI cracked problems that mathematicians had chased for decades, and the survey spread quickly through word of mouth and department mailing lists. Woodruff said they needed something that features the voices of graduate students and postdocs as well. The results, described in a preprint paper, drew 268 responses from nearly 60 institutions and paint a stark picture of a community in limbo. Respondents are largely frustrated and anxious that AI is taking the field for a ride, yet they are divided on what to do about it. Seven in 10 respondents say they are now less likely to remain in math, with broad consensus that AI will make tenure-track jobs harder to get.

Two-thirds report feeling less motivated to work on their research, with the growing possibility of a large language model beating them to their goals. About half are optimistic about AI's potential for mathematics, while a third oppose its use, either outright or for creative mathematical work. Among the optimists, four out of five say they are excited about AI in theory but strongly opposed to how things are unfolding in practice, and just 13 percent of all respondents are happy with the current trajectory. Woodruff said people have told her things like "I feel useless," and she noted that math is a lot of people's identities, not just their jobs. Some, she said, feel that not only does their work not matter, but their minds and their creativity do not matter.

She summed up what many early-career colleagues are thinking: in one year or two years, she does not know if she is going to have a job or funding. Even among the respondents who do use AI, which is nearly all of them, many describe feeling pressured to use it to keep pace, resulting in a generation reluctantly mastering the very technology they fear could make them obsolete. Woodruff cautioned that the voluntary survey is not representative of all young mathematicians, and nearly all of its responses arrived before OpenAI published AI-assisted solutions to hundreds of open problems in October. She said the survey shows that this headline-making year for math has come at a huge cost. She also said that a lot of people outside of math are looking at what is happening in math now, and that so far the field is not doing a particularly inspiring job.

Articles.Title: AI has put young mathematicians in an impossible situation

stories.Headline: Warsh opens first task force hearing on AI and the US job market
stories.Summary:
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh started a landmark hearing on Monday, November 16, 2026. He led the first meeting of a task force examining artificial intelligence. The event focused on how this technology could reshape the US job market. Warsh explored whether AI will fuel economic growth or disrupt employment. This hearing took place at the Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference.

The conference was hosted by the San Francisco Federal Reserve in California. Warsh established five task forces, including the one studying productivity and jobs. He assembled Marc Andreessen from Andreessen Horowitz and Microsoft executive Asha Sharma. Charles Jones, a Stanford professor on leave at Anthropic, also joined the team. These independent heads provide candid feedback to help the Fed set policy.

Warsh said the widespread adoption of this technology will significantly impact the economy. He stated that policymakers must be mindful that great opportunities rarely come risk free. The Chairman noted that overlooked risks could be highly disruptive and economically costly. He believes AI might change the speed of innovation compared to past technologies. Warsh wants to ask the right questions to understand the current reality.

Warsh questioned if the democratization of specialized knowledge will raise standards of living. He asked if AI will make achieving price stability harder or easier. The Chairman wondered if the surge in productivity will happen sooner in the US. He considered how the dual mandate is affected by these emerging technological shifts. Experts in their fields are being interrogated to provide these necessary answers.

Warsh compared super intelligence to the internal combustion engine and electricity from the past. He noted that previous general purpose technologies did not automate the creation of ideas. The Federal Reserve is now tracking a buildout of AI worth 700 billion dollars. Warsh believes that broadened idea generation could sustain growth above the long run average. He is analyzing the magnitude, scope, and timing of these potential changes.

One scenario involves inflation adjusted GDP growth rising while the US stays fully employed. Another scenario suggests widespread automation could push the unemployment rate higher through job displacement. A third scenario involves a stock bust and economic slowdown if AI returns disappoint. The articles do not state when the next task force hearing will occur. They leave open whether AI will actually deliver the expected productivity gains.

Articles.Title: Warsh kicks off first task force hearing on how AI could fuel growth or disrupt jobs

stories.Headline: Anthropic plans a Nasdaq debut to raise over 90 billion dollars
stories.Summary:
Anthropic plans to launch an initial public offering on the Nasdaq this week. The company intends to raise more than 90 billion dollars through this debut. This funding will come from the public offering and direct stock sales. Investors including Google and Microsoft are expected to participate in the sale. This move highlights the massive capital available to American artificial intelligence firms.

The offering contrasts with Z.ai, which raised 558 million dollars in January. Z.ai was the first generative AI firm on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. That company later raised 9 billion dollars through two additional share offerings. Anthropic earned over 16 billion dollars in the first half of 2026. Z.ai earned 142 million dollars during that same period of the year.

Kendra Schaefer of Trivium China says Chinese firms do not try to beat the U.S. on intelligence. She believes they know they cannot win that specific competition. Martin Chorzempa of the Peterson Institute says U.S. companies integrate AI more extensively. He states there is zero evidence that AI is spreading faster in China. Spy chief Chen Yixin called for more regulation to prevent misinformation and cyberattacks.

Public resistance to AI is growing in both the United States and China. American Democrats are calling to rein in the construction of new data centers. Chinese consumers called for a boycott of Lao Gan Ma over alleged layoffs. Workers in China are anxious about the technology's effect on their future jobs. The Communist Party fears AI could threaten its grip on national power.

Nvidia former chief executive Jensen Huang lost his job after a sex scandal. Alice Huang of Megaspeed was allegedly a spy who funneled chips to China. Washington imposed export restrictions on advanced chips to hinder Chinese technological progress. Alibaba used influencer Li Jiaqi to cut membership fees to .0015 cents. The Chinese government wants AI spread through the economy and society by 2035.

Lawmakers plan to add tighter chip export restrictions to a stalled defense package. The U.S. government continues to investigate Megaspeed for illegally shipping Nvidia chips. China may focus on low cost products rather than cutting edge intelligence. The articles leave open if China can build competitive models with fewer resources. It remains unclear if the U.S. will maintain a monopoly on superior AI.

Articles.Title: The Future of AI Is Not China

stories.headline_source: The Future of AI Is Not China

stories.Headline: Novelis’ Richard Leaton converts AI usage into hours and dollars to show generative AI returns
stories.Summary:
Richard Leaton, vice president of data, analytics and AI at Novelis, spoke with Bob West, data and AI security officer at Cyera, in the first part of a three-part CDO Magazine series about how leaders can prove generative AI is paying off. Leaton said the number of AI licenses a company buys measures only procurement, and that unused licenses are shelfware with an invoice. Instead, he tracks monthly active users and the kinds of work people do in the tool. Drawing on six industry studies, Leaton built a transfer function that converts usage into hours and dollars reinvested, tracked weekly on a 180-day rolling basis.

In that model, correcting an email earns few hours, creating a PowerPoint earns more, and building an agent that does the work earns more still. Leaton concedes the metric may be squishy because productivity gains are hard to tie to revenue or cost savings, but transparency about what it shows has kept finance comfortable. With agents, no human checks the data one last time, so Leaton puts data readiness and guardrails first. He then names process as the bottleneck to fix, since unrationalized processes make agents overspend.

The series draws three lessons: daily use says more about adoption than license totals or prompt counts, being clear about what an AI metric proves keeps finance on side, and ready data, guardrails and sound processes come before agents act alone. The article does not say when the conversation took place or what the second and third parts of the series will cover. It also gives no figures for Novelis' usage, hours or dollars. More to follow.

Articles.Title: How Can Leaders Prove Generative AI Is Paying Off? Novelis’ Richard Leaton Explains

stories.Headline: Horizon3.ai launches Adversarial Intelligence Frontier Lab and names Z. Berkay Celik as its director
stories.Summary:
Horizon3.ai announced on Thursday that it has established the Adversarial Intelligence Frontier Lab, a research facility that will investigate how artificial intelligence can help cybersecurity teams find weaknesses in computer networks, respond to intrusions and evaluate defensive measures in live environments. The AI-native proactive security company said the lab will draw on data from its NodeZero security tests to study the safe and effective use of autonomous offensive and defensive agents. Z. Berkay Celik, an associate professor of computer science at Purdue University, will serve as the lab's inaugural director. Celik co-directs the Purdue Security Laboratory and has worked with universities, companies and government agencies on research efforts, studying how complex software and systems can be compromised.

A central research priority for the lab is establishing safeguards for autonomous security agents, including methods for evaluating their performance, restricting their activities and reversing actions when necessary. Another initiative involves creating customer-specific cyberworld models that give red team and blue team agents a shared source of operational context and memory. Researchers will also investigate how advanced AI models could speed up vulnerability discovery and how malicious actors might coordinate groups of AI agents to conduct attacks. The lab will further examine whether offensive and defensive agents working together can shorten the process of exploiting a weakness, deploying a patch and confirming that it works.

The research will extend to critical infrastructure through Horizon3.ai's Cyber Resilience Centers of Excellence, which will operate under the lab and apply findings to industries where cyber disruptions could affect national security or economic activity. Horizon3.ai plans to base its research on evidence gathered from actual security assessments rather than relying primarily on digital twins or sensor telemetry, which the company says are common in existing AI security research. Its customer base includes more than 7,000 organizations, ranging from federal agencies and local hospitals to large banks and advanced manufacturers, and these customers conduct hundreds of thousands of NodeZero tests on production systems. According to Horizon3.ai, those tests generate an estimated 30 billion tokens of labeled, anonymized attack-and-defense data each day, documenting configurations of services behind customer firewalls, commands executed during attacks, their outcomes and the reactions of defensive security tools.

Snehal Antani, the company's CEO and co-founder, said Horizon3.ai has spent years collecting the attack-and-defense data required to research these systems. In August, Stephen Gates, a principal security subject matter expert at Horizon3.ai, said autonomous, proactive security testing could help agencies identify and prioritize the risks that pose the greatest threat, writing that NodeZero carries out real attacks using the same tactics adversaries use and is designed to run safely in production environments. In May 2025, Horizon3.ai received Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program High Authorization for NodeZero Federal, which provides autonomous penetration testing that meets government security and compliance requirements. The company also partnered with Intelligent Waves in 2024 to offer penetration testing to the Department of War and the intelligence community through Shadow, powered by NodeZero, an offering designed to run real-time network security assessments and verify fixes immediately.

stories.Headline: Trump administration considers tighter AI chip export controls to close loopholes for China
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump will not likely discuss the Nvidia scandal during his upcoming meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping. This visit occurs next week as Trump travels to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. The U.S. government believes the controversy should not affect the summit or the bilateral talks. Trump is scheduled to meet Xi on November 19 in Shenzhen, Guangdong Province. A first-ever trilateral summit including Russian President Vladimir Putin is also planned for this trip.

The scandal involves former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, a former executive at Singaporean company Megaspeed International. U.S. intelligence suspects Alice Huang had an affair with Jensen Huang and links to Chinese intelligence agencies. Megaspeed is suspected of shipping advanced artificial intelligence chips to China to circumvent U.S. semiconductor export controls. Trump previously allowed Nvidia to sell H200 chips in China despite security concerns over advanced technology. The U.S. government maintains that semiconductor export controls are not subject to negotiation with China.

A senior U.S. official stated that the administration does not expect the president to bring up Alice Huang. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent expressed frustration that the Commerce Department had not designated Megaspeed for export controls. Bessent noted that the State, Defense, and Treasury departments supported these controls several months ago. Another official stressed that export controls are national security matters decided through interagency consultation. The administration intends to keep the Nvidia situation separate from the diplomatic visit to China.

Congressional Democrats wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to demand an immediate halt to advanced chip exports. Lawmakers from both parties are pressing for tighter restrictions to protect the American edge in AI technology. Beijing has denied the espionage allegations and called the claims about Alice Huang unsubstantiated. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters that the U.S. should stop fabricating spy narratives. Some analysts believe the scandal could hinder discussions regarding an AI national security hotline.

Nvidia once held about 95 percent of the Chinese market before restrictions from the Biden administration caused sales to plummet. Jensen Huang previously lobbied Washington to loosen limits and frequently visited the White House during Trump's second term. In May 2026, Huang joined Trump on Air Force One for a state visit to Beijing. He and his wife, Lori, sat with Trump and Xi during a September meeting in Washington. The U.S. and China are currently competing to dominate the field of artificial intelligence.

The Trump administration is weighing options to close loopholes, such as tightening export licensing and restricting remote chip access. A Senate defense policy bill may authorize Congress to review licenses and track chips to prevent diversion. The U.S. may also compel allies to match restrictions on exports to Chinese chipmakers. It remains open whether Beijing will separate export controls from broader AI safety discussions. The U.S. does not expect Chinese retaliation if loopholes to existing computer chip measures are closed.

stories.Headline: Edgewater and Cornelis partner to support federal HPC and AI networking
stories.Summary:
Edgewater Federal Solutions and Cornelis Networks announced on Wednesday, November 16, 2026, that they have partnered to support federal agencies and research organizations evaluating networking infrastructure for high-performance computing and artificial intelligence workloads. The agreement adds Cornelis to the group of technology providers Edgewater works with on federal HPC and AI missions, according to Edgewater. Federal HPC and AI environments depend on networks that can move data efficiently alongside advanced processors and accelerators. Cornelis' Omni-Path fabric supports the Lynx supercomputing cluster at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. The partnership gives federal agencies access to Cornelis' HPC and AI networking technology along with Edgewater's support in fitting it into their broader operations through architecture planning, cybersecurity, implementation, integration, managed services and continued mission support.

The companies intend to help customers assess infrastructure options against security, workload, life cycle and mission requirements. Potential areas of collaboration include HPC and AI infrastructure planning, interoperability and architecture assessments, networking for advanced simulation and scientific computing, and secure integration into federal technology environments. Edgewater and Cornelis may also conduct technical briefings and workload assessments, including on Cornelis' CN6000 evaluation systems, and jointly develop offerings for federal opportunities. Rob Hays, vice president of business development at Cornelis, said federal HPC and AI programs judge infrastructure by the mission work it accomplishes. He said every minute an accelerator waits on the network is capacity an agency paid for and did not use, and that Edgewater knows how to design, secure and operate these environments.

He added that together the companies can help agencies get more from every compute investment. The Cornelis partnership builds on Edgewater's recent push into HPC. In October, the Frederick, Maryland-based company acquired RedLine Performance Solutions to add HPC and scientific computing expertise to its federal mission technology portfolio, and RedLine CEO Carolyn Pasti called it a natural evolution for the company and an exciting opportunity for its employees, customers and the missions it supports. Edgewater has also expanded across the Department of Energy's national laboratory network, securing a five-year contract to provide IT managed services for Argonne National Laboratory, including service desk operations and on-site and remote end-user support. Before that, Edgewater's EdgeScanAI, an OCR- and AI-based records management and reporting tool, received "Awardable" status on the Department of War Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office's Tradewinds Solutions Marketplace.

stories.Headline: Verizon CEO Dan Schulman says AI will automate much of its customer service
stories.Summary:
Verizon CEO Dan Schulman said in a Fortune interview published on November 16, 2026, that AI will automate much of Verizon's customer service. Schulman spoke with Fortune Editor-in-Chief Alyson Shontell on the new episode of Fortune 500: Titans and Disruptors of Industry. He took the CEO seat about a year earlier, after Verizon's board asked him several times and he said no several times. His wife convinced him to take the job, and he left retirement on his Montana ranch, where he has 900 head of cattle. He is now a year into a three-year overhaul of a company he calls a "big, lumbering giant."

Schulman said Verizon had been losing market share for five years or so and had gone from first in market capitalization in its industry to last. He said Verizon had the lowest P/E, which he described as what the Street thinks of future growth potential. He said Verizon has 150 million lines and the largest customer base. He said the company had processes requiring something like 35 signatures before moving forward, and that he blew that up, saying surely no more than three or four people need to sign. He said he told employees at his first all-hands meeting that layoffs were likely and that Verizon needed to spend billions of dollars investing back into the business.

Schulman said culture is the single most important thing in any transformation. He said Verizon had been playing not to lose instead of playing to win, with engineering at the center of the culture instead of the customer. He said the culture was very bureaucratic, very hierarchical, almost like the military, and very siloed, and that it was risk-averse and afraid of failing. He said he is a one on the integrity of financial results, cybersecurity and compliance, but an eight or a nine on trying new things. He said he got thousands of emails after the all-hands meeting from employees glad he laid out the truth.

Schulman said he thought AGI was three, four or five years away but now thinks most experts see it as soon as a year away, with the most skeptical at three years. He said quantum hits commercially probably in 2028 or 2029, and that humanoid robotics will be pretty darn good by 2035 at the latest. He said 85% of models today are done through recursive self-improvement, which he described as AI building the next model of itself. He said Verizon increased phone net adds ninefold from a year earlier while cutting acquisition costs by 41%. He said he is preparing for Elon Musk to become a bigger competitor and for SpaceX to deliver on its ambitions.

Lucas Perez Echeimberg wrote in a Deseret News guest opinion published November 15, 2026, that poor service isn't an AI problem. He is a Brazilian tax lawyer with a graduate degree in tax law from the Pontifical Catholic University of São Paulo and a student in Avila University Arizona's Master of Science in Artificial Intelligence, and he lives in Utah. He wrote that on January 21, 2025, President Donald Trump presented a joint venture of up to $500 billion in AI infrastructure formed by OpenAI, Oracle and SoftBank. He wrote that on October 30, 2026, Bloomberg reported America's tech giants are funding about $750 billion in AI spending this year, paid for by their advertising, consumer and retail businesses.

He wrote that Salesforce, a leading U.S. software company that also sells AI agents, surveyed 3,075 customer service professionals worldwide. Echeimberg wrote that the survey found adoption of AI agents in customer service rose from 39% to 66% between 2025 and 2026. He wrote that after adopting them, companies reported customer satisfaction was the most improved metric, ahead of rep productivity, average handle time, customer retention and first-response time. He wrote that Brazil's recent Decree No. 13,135, in force since November 2, allows AI but requires a live human by phone from 8 a.m.

to 8 p.m., seven days a week, and the option to reach a person at every step. He wrote that Connecticut's new AI law, SB 5, exempts customer-service bots, and that Congress is weighing the Keep Call Centers in America Act, which would require transfer to a U.S.-based human on request. He wrote that companies should have the freedom to decide how they use AI, and that lawmakers should look at how well companies serve their customers. Schulman said he did not want to come back into the CEO job, calling such jobs all-consuming at 10 to 14 hours a day.

He said he was the lead independent director of Verizon's board and that the board probably should have acted sooner. He said he came in with a little bit of a bad attitude but a year later is absolutely loving the job and is pretty hopeful about the future. He said Verizon is positioning its fiber network and facilities to capitalize on the AI infrastructure buildout, and he sees satellite service as a complement to Verizon's network rather than a replacement. Echeimberg wrote that AI can be regulated as long as the rules follow certain principles while still allowing nations some flexibility for the sake of their technological progress, and he cited the philosopher Luciano Florid in 2019.

Articles.Title: Verizon CEO Dan Schulman says AI will automate much of its customer service. Here’s which jobs he expects to bring back to the U.S.

stories.Headline: Fed official Warsh says AI can be highly disruptive and economically costly
stories.Summary:
Federal Reserve official Warsh said on November 16, 2026 that artificial intelligence can be highly disruptive and economically costly, according to a CNBC report that aired during the Halftime Report program. The remark was delivered as part of CNBC's coverage of the latest news out of the Federal Reserve, with correspondent Steve Liesman presenting the item on air. The report was published at 06:00 GMT and appeared in a video segment running one minute and fifty-one seconds. The segment was carried in CNBC's markets and business coverage alongside other items that morning.

The report does not specify any policy change, proposal or formal action attached to Warsh's remark, and it gives no figures beyond the length of the video segment. It also does not say which meeting or event Warsh was speaking at, or whether the comment reflected a formal Fed position. The only date given is November 16, 2026, the day the item was published and aired. No further numbers, names or dates appear in the article beyond those already noted.

Responsibility for the remark rests with Warsh, identified in the report as a Fed official, while the coverage was handled by CNBC's Steve Liesman, who joined the Halftime Report with the latest news out of the Federal Reserve. The article paraphrases Warsh's view as being that AI can be highly disruptive and economically costly, and it offers no additional statement from him beyond that characterization. It likewise carries no response from the Federal Reserve or from any other official quoted in the item. The report presents the comment without further elaboration on his reasoning.

The context given is limited to CNBC's rolling coverage of Federal Reserve news, with the Warsh item appearing among other market and business videos on the same page. Those surrounding items concern Nvidia's board and its CEO, and Altimeter's Brad Gerstner discussing Anthropic's IPO and Nvidia's leadership, but the article does not connect them to Warsh's remark. The report does not say what happens next, whether further comment from Warsh or the Fed is expected, or how markets responded to the remark. No follow-up statement or scheduled appearance is mentioned in the article.

stories.Headline: Supply chain analyst abandons AI assistant for Excel after inconsistent answers
stories.Summary:
A supply chain and analytics professional wrote that she dropped her AI assistant for Excel after it gave different answers to the same question on different days, in an article published on towardsdatascience.com on 16 November 2026. She wrote that she first used Claude Code 18 months earlier, when a single prompt adapted an algorithm she had designed years before to her current project and deployed it on her server, ready to connect to the customer’s Google Sheets. She described that as a game changer that gave her a semi-automated way to productise and deploy any optimisation algorithm she took months to develop. She wrote that she now wakes every day asking where her value is and how to avoid being replaced by AI. She set a goal for 2027 of not becoming what she calls a “meat proxy”, a human whose only job is to pass requests to an AI and its answers back.

She wrote that AI agents now handle a growing part of the analytics value chain, so she had to work out where she remains relevant as a supply chain and analytics expert. She wrote that her experience implementing AI for manufacturing and logistics operations taught her that these projects rarely meet automation expectations. She cited a planner who dropped his AI assistant for Excel because it answered the same question differently each day, and teams in one company who measure the same KPI in 36 different undocumented ways. She wrote that no agent could have solved these on its own and that this is the chance for analytics professionals to stay relevant. She wrote that she would share her experience managing agentic projects in mid-size and large companies to show the limits of AI in a corporate environment.

She wrote that she is a supply chain professional who learned data science to help manufacturing and logistics operations optimise their processes for profitability and sustainability, and that since 2020 she has shared real use cases in her blog where analytics helps solve an operational or business problem. She wrote that her first article presented a set of algorithms she built to reduce the walking distance of warehouse operators. She wrote that interest was huge at the time, with data science seen as an opportunity to use advanced mathematics to create value for companies. She wrote that since 2025 the focus has shifted to using AI to build workflows where agents are supposed to autonomously handle very complex business and operational processes. She wrote that in the projects she has seen these solutions fail to deliver on their promise, because the systems that run a company, such as ERP, CRM and WMS, are not plug-and-play solutions for models that require harmonised, cleaned data.

She wrote that the first obstacle companies face is mapping processes, what is now called ontology, and that in a typical consumer goods company the systems managing manufacturing, logistics, finance and HR are not a monolithic bloc with a central source of documented data. She wrote that most are legacy systems with many specific developments over the years to meet the needs of teams that generate and use data their own way. She described a project at a consumer goods company where her role was to design a tool to find the root cause of late store deliveries, starting with defining whether each delivery was on time or late by comparing the field Delivery Time in the ERP with Requested Delivery Time. She wrote that after 12 weeks of workshops with the logistics teams she discovered they used 36 different ways to define this boolean, and that the Brazil team flags a delivery as late only if the shipment arrives 10 days after the Requested Delivery Time because it uses sea freight with variable lead times. She wrote that these edge cases are not documented anywhere and require a human to ask other humans and translate their answers into a model of the data transformations performed inside and outside the systems.

She wrote that a manufacturing company contacted her after equipping its planning teams with AI assistants, and that its supply chain director wanted planners to create automated workflows with tools like Claude Cowork to pull data from an Excel file and answer strategic and operational questions. She wrote that the questions included how many units to produce next week to meet customer demand and how many production batches are needed to reduce inventory by 15%. She quoted the supply chain director saying “It became an operational chaos”, and wrote that a planner admitted she switched back to her Excel planning spreadsheet because AI can give different outputs for the same question from one day to another. She wrote that for the same question and the same input Excel file the agent generated two different Python scripts, and that workshops concluded the planners did not need AI. She wrote that deterministic tools such as inventory management rules in Python and dynamic algorithms like Wagner-Whitin can meet their needs, and quoted the director saying “We needed someone to challenge our requests, propose a structured process to generate insights from data and design robust tools we can rely on.”

She wrote that the director was surprised when she explained the assistant was also generating code to answer his planners’ questions, and that agents only had the context the planner shared in the prompt while she spent hours asking his team hundreds of questions. She wrote that in the FMCG example the requested delivery date is included in store orders and may be modified by customer service admins if the customer asks for a new date, that French teams have implemented a script that modifies the requested delivery date if the delay is below the service level agreement, and that American teams look at the actual ship date rather than the delivery date because they are not responsible for transportation. She wrote that these three points summarise 12 weeks of intense workshops, and that the supply chain director was surprised by the complexity of his distribution chain and admitted no one in the company expected measuring on-time delivery to be so complex. She asked readers whether plugging Claude Code into the SQL database of the ERP would help to get these insights. She wrote that she would conclude with her personal advice on how to build these skills using the free resources she shares on her blog.

Articles.Title: A Planner Dropped Her AI Assistant for Excel. Here's What Analysts Should Learn
