stories.Headline: Michael Burry doubles Nasdaq 100 puts and calls AI a bull market trap
stories.Summary:
Goldman Sachs released its 2027 Global Market Outlook report, and the Federal Reserve named artificial intelligence in its latest Financial Stability Report as a potential threat to asset valuation and financial stability. Short seller Michael Burry doubled his put options on the Nasdaq 100 and re-established short positions on semiconductor ETFs. Burry called the situation a "bull market trap" and compared it to the top of the dot-com bubble in 2000. Jensen Huang's resignation deepened Burry's concerns about the entire AI industrial chain, according to the article.

Goldman Sachs said the share of incremental AI investment in GDP will peak in early 2027, though capital expenditure will not turn downward, only slow its growth. Goldman calculated that cloud vendors' capital expenditure contributed 2 percentage points to S&P 500 EPS in 2024, 5 percentage points in 2025, 12 percentage points in 2026, 9 percentage points in 2027, and a 5 percentage point drag by 2028. The S&P earnings expectation dropped from 36% to 11%, with European, Japanese and Asian markets weakening in step. Goldman said the forward PE of leading US cloud giants is only 19.7 times, below the lower edge of their 20-year historical range.

Burry doubled his Nasdaq 100 put options and bought back short positions in the VanEck Semiconductor ETF, whose heaviest positions are TSMC and NVIDIA. He compared the Nasdaq high in early October to the 2000 bubble peak and focused on whether NVIDIA's influence will weaken. The article said his options bet only profits if the index falls more than 20% before expiration. Goldman recommended increasing diversified allocation and hedging, and named a "succession echelon" of AI application firms. The article said Korean memory chip prices imply earnings cut 70% in 2027, with order schedules sold to 2029.

The article said intermediate GPU cloud providers such as CoreWeave and Nebius, named by Burry, depend heavily on external financing and are most affected by high interest rates. It said the Federal Reserve flagged circular trading risk, in which technology companies and start-ups invest in, purchase from and endorse each other's revenues. The article said regulation may shift toward control after the Democratic Party takes office, constraining energy, land and power for data centers. It said small and medium GPU cloud vendors bound to NVIDIA orders and money-burning start-ups without implemented products are the most vulnerable. The article said Goldman's core concern in Asia is concentration, with TSMC, Samsung and SK Hynix accounting for too large a proportion.

The article said the past bull market in upstream computing power relied on continuously rising capital expenditure growth. It said AI is a typical long-duration asset whose returns mostly come in the long term. The article said the balance sheets of leading US tech giants are healthy and the valuation premium of the five major tech stocks has converged to a very low level. It said the order expectations of chips, OEM manufacturing, storage and downstream cloud vendors were built on NVIDIA's strong position. The article said the underlying demand supporting the long-term logic of AI has not disappeared.

The article said the market's assessment criteria will shift from who is expanding production to who can earn real money. It said the market will keep testing whether AI can help customers save costs and increase revenue and whether there is stable payment and renewal. The article said whether the transition is smooth determines whether this round of adjustment achieves a soft landing or continues to fall sharply. It said a more prudent approach is to reduce concentrated bets on a single track and appropriately diversify positions. The article did not say when Huang resigned or what NVIDIA said about it.

stories.Headline: Anthropic buys 1.7 GW of generators from OnePWR for $3.4 billion to power data centers
stories.Summary:
Anthropic completed a transaction with OnePWR Solutions, an equipment supplier based in San Antonio, Texas, in late September, according to a Financial Times report on November 8. The deal locked in the supply of 1.7 GW heavy-duty generators for $3.4 billion, about RMB 22.7 billion, to power data centers. Earlier in April, AI infrastructure company Crusoe ordered 13 units from ProEnergy in Missouri, each with a rated power of 50 MW, totaling 650 MW, for future U.S. data centers. The two parties signed the contract in April, with the target delivery window set for the summer of 2027, a cycle of just over a year. With orders booked all the way through 2031, leading AI giants are forced to borrow power from retired civil aviation aero-engines.

Pablo Koziner, Chief Commercial and Operations Officer of GE Vernova, said around 20% of orders in the gas power generation business come from data center and AI-related projects, and the order book is scheduled to 2030, even 2031. In the second quarter of 2026, GE Vernova signed 20 GW of new gas equipment contracts, with backlogged orders plus reserved capacity reaching 116 GW. The 2026 White Paper on Gas Turbine Industry Development shows global demand for gas turbines in 2025 is approximately 90GW to 100GW, while annual production capacity is only 55GW to 60GW. A Wood Mackenzie report shows the market imbalance has pushed gas turbine prices to new highs, expected to reach $600/kW by the end of 2027, an increase of 195% compared with 2019. According to a CLSA report, global turbine manufacturing capacity is expected to reach about 87 GW by 2028, still far lower than the projected 129 GW of turbine power demand.

Aurora Tenorio, senior analyst at energy consultancy Wood Mackenzie, said delivery times people are discussing are basically concentrated between 2030 and 2031. According to Gartner data released in 2024, approval for new grid connections in major European and American markets has been scheduled for 24 to 36 months later. According to the JLL 2026 Global Data Center Outlook, in the Northern Virginia region, a grid connection application for a 50 MW project may take seven years to process. Pamela McDougall, Head of Energy Markets for Europe, Middle East and Africa at Amazon AWS, revealed the current waiting time for grid connection applications in Europe is as long as seven years. Tenorio warned that whether units transformed from second-hand aero engines can stably support continuous power generation for many years still needs longer-term operation data to verify.

Ana Amicarella, CEO of equipment service provider Ethos Energy, said the second-hand market is very hot at present and equipment prices are rising. Darius Padhivala, head of the U.S. after-sales business at Sulzer, said the company receives requests every few weeks to find second-hand gas turbines for data centers. The Tennessee Valley Authority stated prices of gas turbines, both new and used, have risen sharply over the past two years. Jim Matheson, CEO of the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association, admitted association members are facing unprecedented long delivery times and continuously rising prices. According to a CLSA report, well-maintained second-hand units are priced at about $1.5 million to $1.7 million per MW, and refurbished units at about $1.3 million per MW, below the cost of new turbines at $2 million to $2.5 million per MW.

Dan Poole, general manager of ReflowX, said two 14.5 MW gas turbines manufactured by Solar Turbines, a subsidiary of Caterpillar, were recently sold for $12.5 million, about $430,000 per MW, while new units cost about $35 million and delivery takes five years. Scott Schrig, sales director of U.S. equipment supplier SVI Bremco, said they sometimes deploy more than 100 units at a single site, mixing different models and brands. Anders Lindberg, President of the Energy Business at Wärtsilä Finland, said since last spring the company has received orders of about 3 GW from U.S. data centers, for generator sets driven by gas internal combustion engines rather than gas turbines. Represented by the CF6-80C2, the main aero engine for aero-derivative gas turbines, which was put into commercial use in 1985, retired complete engines, disassembled components and overhauled core engines form a considerable stock resource pool. Some industry insiders pointed out many refurbished equipment have incomplete operation records, limited remaining service life, and relatively weak long-term technical support.

Siemens Energy and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries are in a similar situation, with on-hand orders having fully filled existing production capacity and delivery windows continuing to be pushed backward. According to the Soochow Securities research report, restricted by high manufacturing barriers and insufficient gas turbine supply, order delivery of global leading players such as GEV and Siemens has been scheduled to 2030. There is no authoritative public information on the actual transaction price, exact deployment location and long-term operation mode of the Crusoe units, with only the order size and delivery window confirmed. The capacity assessment of regional power grids, cluster load verification, and transmission and distribution transformation follow the rolling planning and engineering construction cycle of power grids. Equipment delivery, grid connection and emission permits form three layers of constraints, and getting through one does not mean the remaining stuck points will be automatically resolved.

stories.Headline: Chinese seniors use AI for companionship and daily assistance
stories.Summary:
AI has recently been playing chess with grandfathers and cheering up grandmothers. These interactions occurred around November 2026, including a storytelling event in Wuzhen. A woman named Xiao He used the AI Doubao to help her father. The AI provided real-time chess instructions via a video call. Old He also played against a Go robot in an academy.

The 2025 National Bulletin on the Development of Aging Undertakings notes 323 million Chinese people aged 60 plus. This group represents about 23 percent of the total population by late 2025. In Huishui County, Guizhou Province, 90 percent of surveyed seniors only use WeChat. In Community G in Xi'an, 35.6 percent of 320 seniors know nothing of AI. DeepSeek became a viral hit at the beginning of 2025.

Professor Shen Qi from Fudan University's Institute of Aging Studies led a research team. He compared the dialogue between the elderly and AI to a two-way tango dance. He described the spiritual comfort for rural seniors as the technology subsidence effect. Cai Yaohui from the same institute taught rural Henan seniors to use models. He found rural elderly have almost no barriers to accepting these tools.

A retired engineer viewed large language models as respectable experts requiring politeness. A grandma from Yangpu District tested AI by asking for directions to Changhai Hospital. Seniors in Hong Kong and Guangzhou used ChatGPT 3.5 for health and technical questions. One senior used ChatGPT to cope with the death of a pet goldfish. A 63-year-old grandma asked Doubao to pretend to be her granddaughter.

Many seniors use voice input and include hesitant murmurs like oh or hmm. Some elderly people slow their speech because they fear the AI cannot hear. They often test the AI with known facts to check for accuracy. Rural seniors use AI to discuss forbidden topics, such as a missing son. Some use the AI as a confessional that never leaks secrets.

In Zibo, Shandong, 25 seniors aged 60 to 82 discussed loneliness with Doubao. An 82-year-old grandma learned idioms to make her monotonous life more lively. A 67-year-old man used AI to escape a house that felt like a prison. A 65-year-old man sought advice on repairing a relationship with his son. The articles leave open how AI will further integrate into senior care.

stories.Headline: House House uses an LLM to rewrite about 10 lines of code in Big Walk, triggering Steam backlash and IGF judge refusals
stories.Summary:
House House, a small Australian studio, disclosed that it had used a large language model to rewrite about 10 lines of code in Unity's Universal Render Pipeline source code for its co-op adventure game *Big Walk*, and the disclosure triggered a backlash, with players flooding Steam to leave negative reviews and some applying for refunds, while 19 IGF judges stated they would not vote for any game using generative AI. The studio rose to fame with *Untitled Goose Game* in 2019 and spent six years developing *Big Walk*, which launched in early August and reached a Metacritic score of 94, the highest of the year, and was nominated for Best Game of the Year at the Golden Joystick Awards. The problem was a shadow culling defect in URP that rendered shadow casters behind the player to infinity, dropping frame rate by about 50% for nearly 20 seconds during sunrise and sunset. The studio looked through the URP source code without finding a solution, and a Unity official engineer replied after asking colleagues that the wanted modification was impossible to implement. They sent the problem to an LLM chatbot, found a feasible direction after several attempts and setbacks, modified and adjusted it, and implemented it as about 10 lines of rewritten code, estimating AI-related code at less than 0.1% of the total game volume, with generative AI never used for art creation.

House House updated its FAQ and disclosed these details, and later said in a statement that there was no internal AI usage policy during development, which was a mistake. The IGF leadership expressed support for that statement but did not officially announce that *Big Walk* was disqualified from the competition. Some players left negative reviews on Steam on the grounds that undisclosed AI use is misleading about the game's quality and the effort put into it. Valve made an important revision in January 2026 separating development assistance tools from AI-generated content for players, so code assistants and chatbots for debugging need no disclosure, and only AI-generated content players can see or hear must be made public. Under those rules, House House's use of an LLM to fix code bugs did not need to be told to anyone.

Anthropic engineer Felix Rieseberg tested Claude Fable 5.2 with a minimal prompt for a small-scale FPS with graphics comparable to 3A blockbusters, realistic lighting and photorealistic effects, gave no further feedback, and let the model run autonomously for about 8 hours. The model delivered a browser-based first-person shooter called *Saltline*, set in a rainy container port with cranes, cargo ships, wet ground and low-angle sunset, close to modern *Call of Duty*-style mission levels, in which players cut off three uplink relays while dealing with drones called Gulls and robotic dogs called Hounds. All 3D models, textures, sound effects and shaders were generated entirely by the model from scratch using code, with no external assets imported, and the whole game is basically a self-contained HTML file. The process consumed approximately 445 million input tokens and 2.7 million output tokens, most inputs hit the cache, and the API cost was about $550. Rieseberg made the prompt and results public, stating this was a test of the model's upper quality limit under a single prompt with no human intervention.

Many people were impressed by the visual effects, saying details such as the rainy port, wet ground reflections, crane silhouettes and red dot sights are close to modern *Call of Duty* or *Battlefield*, with netizens saying "This is really 3A-level graphics" and "GTA 6 may be the last 3A blockbuster made by a traditional studio". The most controversial point was the expression "one-shot / no human feedback", with netizens arguing that 445 million input tokens mean this was not single-step generation but autonomous execution of 8 hours after one instruction, and that half the people who read the article will try a single conversation, get a much worse game, and conclude the model is very ordinary. Around November 10, an HTML file called *Jimao* spread in group chats, only 1.4MB but a well-completed small FPS game, with copy claiming it was independently developed by Claude Fable 5.2 as a "domestic 3A blockbuster", and reactions included "scared to tears by the AI overlord" and "so shocking". *Jimao* was just a localized reskin of *Saltline*. The GDC 2026 annual gaming industry survey interviewed more than 2,300 practitioners, and 52% believe generative AI has a negative impact on the industry, nearly triple the 18% of two years earlier, while those with a positive view dropped to 7%.

Complaints aside, 36% of game practitioners do use generative AI in their work, of which 81% use it for research and brainstorming and 47% for code assistance, but only 5% actually present AI-generated content to players. In this statistic, 58% of people using AI are in positions such as publishing, marketing and business, and only 30% of developers who directly make games in the studio are using AI. In 2024, new games marked with AI-generated content on Steam accounted for about 13%, the figure rose to 24% in 2025, and reached 40.1% in the first ten months of 2026, approaching 50% in the single month of October. Among games with more than 1000 reviews in 2026, the AI disclosure rate is only 14%, while for games with less than 10 reviews the ratio is as high as 47%. Games that heavily use AI-generated content are mainly concentrated in products launched in batches for rapid monetization, while most games that have received a lot of player attention still use AI with restraint.

The gaming industry has long been considered a scenario very suitable for large-scale AI application, with image generation models, video models and world models all able to be deeply integrated with the industry, but in reality the extent to which the gaming circle embraces AI is not as high as imagined. Independent games are regarded as handicrafts, and what players pay for includes the unique feel and human touch, so even one line of code from a machine is like screwing an assembly line screw into a handcrafted wooden table. *Saltline* was placed on the exhibition stand of "see what the model can do" from the very beginning, no one had the expectation of handmade quality for it, and onlookers just enjoyed the spectacle. Generative content has indeed created a lot of garbage in game stores, shoddily made reskinned works have taken up recommendation slots, and serious and hardworking small teams have been overshadowed instead. The angry reaction to AI has set a dangerous precedent for the video game industry, and game developers will now be more reluctant to disclose the use of artificial intelligence in their games to avoid criticism from review bodies.

The articles leave open whether the IGF will officially announce that *Big Walk* is disqualified from the competition, and they do not say what House House will do next. They do not say what Valve or Unity will do following the dispute, and they do not say how the 19 IGF judges will act beyond their stated refusal to vote for games using generative AI. They do not say what Rieseberg or Anthropic will do with the *Saltline* test, and they do not say who made or distributed the *Jimao* reskin. They do not say what the GDC 2026 survey respondents or the players who left negative reviews and sought refunds will do next.

stories.Headline: Foundation model vendors use AI to automate computer chip design and fabrication
stories.Summary:
Foundation model vendors are attempting to use artificial intelligence to design and fabricate computer chips during late 2026. This movement, called AI4Chip, seeks to replicate the success of AI coding by automating complex hardware engineering tasks. Some experts believe AI will eventually handle end-to-end design, while others remain skeptical of its current capabilities. These companies are now recruiting experts in RTL, verification, layout wiring, and timing to build these systems.

The process requires AI to master a long industrial chain including specifications, synthesis, physical inspection, and tape-out. Duojiangjiang predicts AI will first boost efficiency by 30 percent before evolving into self-improving design within five to ten years. Moonshot AI used the Nangate 45nm process library and open source EDA tools for a 4mm² chip. Qwen3.8-Max recently completed RTL and verification for a NoC module and optimized the T-Head Xuan Tie M890.

Duojiangjiang argues that AI lacks the limited context restrictions that force humans to divide labor into fine pieces. He believes foundation model factories will eventually own their own fabs to eliminate dependence on upstream computing power giants. Saige, a practitioner with ten years of experience, laughs at the idea that chip design is just coding. He claims that most current EDA Agents are only at L0 or L1 levels of automation.

Saige notes that AI currently only helps with small scripts and front-end code, ignoring the physical PPA impossible triangle. Hardware engineers are affected because real chip delivery requires systematic considerations of power, performance, and area beyond simple code. Foundation model vendors are driven by high computing power bills and the need for new high-value revenue streams. They want to avoid the oligopolistic competition and national regulation expected for basic model capabilities.

The industry is shifting because coding agents became a solid implementation scenario with verifiable tasks and clear payment willingness. Chip design is viewed as the next high-value domain because the paying parties are profitable EDA and chip companies. Domestic manufacturers in China face additional pressure to optimize fundamental constraints due to a critical shortage of cards. This business necessity pushes model providers to develop their own hardware products to ensure future growth.

Anthropic has formed a dedicated chip design team using Claude, while OpenAI and Synopsys are developing the GPT-Synopsys model. China is currently viewed as relatively weak in both the EDA and model aspects compared to foreign combinations. Both regions still face a significant distance to travel before these AI chip design tools reach full commercialization. The articles leave open how much of the unwritten expert experience in chip companies can be digitized.

stories.Headline: Meta scales back AI job replacement plan as employees fix technical and security flaws
stories.Summary:
Meta scaled back a plan to carry out large-scale layoffs and replace positions with AI agents, Reuters reported, after employees spent growing time patching technical and security vulnerabilities. Microsoft has widely deployed AI internally, and Executive Vice President Ryan Roslansky publicly complained that his daily work is full of AI-generated content he called watered-down. Walmart store and warehouse employees are troubled by AI tools that handle task assignment, scheduling and performance assessment, according to Business Insider. Companies from Microsoft to McKinsey are restricting employees' use of new AI tools as their proliferation erodes corporate profits, Reuters reported. Microsoft and Walmart declined to comment, and Meta, Palantir, NVIDIA and Booz Allen Hamilton did not respond to requests for comment.

Restrictions are now set in places that used to encourage trials, experienced employees are called back, and training efforts are being increased. A Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta working paper shows 90% of executives said their company's AI investment has not yet translated into productivity gains. A survey released by Ernst & Young last month shows 36% of AI executives at enterprises with annual revenue of at least 1 billion US dollars reported AI accidents causing data loss, financial losses, brand damage or operational disruption. A survey released by Indeed in July this year shows more than half of employees said they did not get the AI training they needed, while only 45% of managers feel capable of leading AI natives well. Palantir, Booz Allen Hamilton and NVIDIA have set restrictions on employee usage due to growing concerns that their own data is not safe when stored at AI companies.

Johnny C Taylor Jr, President and CEO of the Society for Human Resource Management, said executives generally feel like they are building the car while driving it, and that if we could turn back time we would introduce it in a more thoughtful and slower way. Kathleen Hogan, Chief Strategy and Transformation Officer of Microsoft, wrote in a recent blog post that being usable and in use does not mean real transformation. Hogan wrote that Microsoft found adding an agent to a broken process still results in a broken process, and that speeding up a single step alone will only make the next step have a longer queue. Hogan wrote that investing in employee training does improve productivity, especially when junior engineers are paired with senior staff. Taylor said enterprises are shifting from one-off online courses for large numbers of employees to continuous, position-specific customized training.

Zack Mabel, research director of the Center on Education and the Workforce at Georgetown University, said many employees feel they are asked to use these tools but no one tells them exactly how to use them. Mabel added that managers are caught in the middle, having to meet requirements of promoting implementation, delivering benefits and making no compromise on quality at the same time. Jessica Reif, assistant professor of management at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, explained that AI always outputs things that look plausible but hide defects or errors not easy to detect, so errors pass down the workflow and small problems snowball. A Walmart manager told Business Insider that the robots assume employees can do everything perfectly every time, and that we won't set such impossible standards for people. Neil Elan, a lawyer at the law firm Stubbs Alderton & Markiles, said he has noticed the gap is growing between how clients think their employees use AI and how employees actually use it, causing troubles in confidentiality, intellectual property, efficiency and employee integrity.

Posts from employees on LinkedIn show that after the 2023 efficiency reform that cut a large number of staff, with middle managers affected first, Meta has started to expand management positions again. Employers around the world are now clearing up the mess left by their hasty AI deployment in the early stage. Global enterprises have invested tens of billions of dollars in AI over the past few years, but the real returns have not yet appeared. Employees described systems that set unreasonable standards for human employees while creating inefficiency and errors, such as planning inexplicable routes for order pickers, popping up batches of useless safety alerts, and generating unrealistic schedules that force store employees to take shortcuts and cut corners to meet progress targets. Once the fact that employees use ChatGPT is brought to light, it will also give enterprises a big headache, Elan said.

The problem for enterprises has never been that they underutilize AI, but that they rush its deployment far too hastily, leaving employees to foot the bill. Employers have to digest the flood of errors and low-quality outputs, which takes up all employees' time, raises privacy and security risks and pushes up costs. Roslansky reminded his followers to be careful of falling into a vicious cycle where reading is done by AI and writing is done by AI, and everything ends up looking the same. The articles do not say what specific restrictions Microsoft, McKinsey, Palantir, Booz Allen Hamilton or NVIDIA imposed, or when. The articles do not say whether Meta's expanded management positions number any specific figure, or what Walmart, Meta, Palantir, NVIDIA and Booz Allen Hamilton would say in response.

stories.Headline: Yang Zhexuan explains how structured language and data compilation help robots enter the real world
stories.Summary:
Yang Zhexuan discussed data compilation and AI model capabilities on November 16, 2026. He explained how robots can re-enter the real world through better data. He focused on turning one-time physical experiences into reusable intelligence. This process involves splitting tasks into steps and aligning them with language. He believes structured language is the only way to align this data.

The system uses a Physical AI DBMS and a physical causal model. It employs a four-layer architecture to produce operation-level data output. This pipeline handles 6DoF pose, depth, spatial trajectory, and motion intention. A 2000-square-meter site can hold 200 people at 10 square meters per station. The goal is to move robots into homes, factories, and shopping malls.

Yang Zhexuan said that recording movement is only the beginning of the process. He stated that data is a high-tech manufacturing industry rather than just labor. He believes that scaling will continue but requires a steeper scaling slope. He noted that automation cannot achieve unmanned operation throughout the entire process. He argued that structured language allows models to retrieve and reuse actions.

Industry consensus in May 2026 required tens of millions of hours of data. By early 2026, high-quality physical interaction data worldwide was only 500,000 hours. A December study by Physical Intelligence found that human video transfer requires diverse data. CAICT reported over 70 training grounds in China by June 2026. These reports affect how embodied intelligence converts data scale into actual capabilities.

The industry is transitioning to pilot applications according to an October 2026 report. This report was released by CAICT and the Department of Electronic Engineering of Tsinghua University. There is a huge gap between collection scale and effective supply. For example, only 100 hours of external data may be usable out of 1000. Models are generally deficient in understanding object state changes and failure recovery.

Zhiyu Foundation is exploring how to shorten the human-to-robot embodiment gap. They use a five-link pipeline to screen frames and unify spatial coordinates. Human first-person data serves pre-training while real machine data serves post-training. The articles leave open the specific results of OpenAI and Anthropic's recent robot research. They do not detail the final success rates of these specific models.

stories.Headline: OpenAI delays GPT-6.2 and other models over safety and alignment issues
stories.Summary:
GPT-6.2 has run into major development hurdles, and OpenAI is worried, according to a report from the WeChat account QbitAI published by 36Kr on November 16, 2026. The article says the new model is bogged down by safety issues and that OpenAI now finds itself in the same position Google was in back in 2022. It describes OpenAI as having become one of the companies that takes safety most seriously, with safety anxiety prioritized above everything else and releasing new models treated as a secondary task. The piece notes that Google in 2022 held leading-edge technology but hesitated to launch products over safety and brand reputation, only to watch OpenAI seize the first-mover advantage in generative AI.

The leaker Token Gremlin shared more specific details, saying OpenAI's next-generation models are being delayed by safety and alignment issues and that the postponement has already lasted several weeks. He also named GPT-6.5 and pointed to a tricky problem: how to turn pre-training results with over 10 trillion parameters into products the public can actually use. The article recalls that in early November people in the community said they had been selected for a gray test of GPT-6.2, and that The Information revealed on November 4 that OpenAI's new Sol, Astra and cyber models could launch as early as Friday, November 6. Nearly half a month later, the article says, Astra has not arrived and other models have been pushed back again and again, while Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 on November 9.

According to Token Gremlin's latest statement, the listing gift package Sam Altman prepared for Ray Dalio is likely to be postponed due to safety alignment issues, and he offered a more pessimistic judgment that these problems are hard to solve in a short period and the release rhythm cannot be restored quickly. He said that even if OpenAI launches GPT-6.2 soon, it may go online with a large number of protection restrictions while other versions keep being pushed back. On November 7 he had said Astra and Sol failed to launch as expected because serious safety and alignment issues were found at the last minute and needed extra fixes, expecting a few more days of polishing; a day before the article he shared a case of making a game with GPT-6.2 Astra. OpenAI has given no official confirmation of these claims and no further response, the article says.

The article links the delay to internal safety culture, citing a post by Joe that Token Gremlin referenced, and says OpenAI became extremely cautious about approving releases after the Hugging Face incident. It notes precedents: OpenAI once suspended part of its training due to model misbehavior and canceled the planned October release of GPT-6.1 Astra because safety and alignment standards were not met, and on October 23 OpenAI said a misbehavior incident on September 20 prompted it to suspend training and evaluation of some frontier models. Token Gremlin attributes the gap with Anthropic to accumulated safety experience, saying Anthropic's new models are ready for public delivery while OpenAI is months behind in that process. The article says the more noteworthy issue is that competition may be shifting from who can train a more powerful model to who can deliver one safely and stably, especially as RSI accelerates research and development.

stories.Headline: Researchers find obscure journals publish AI-generated papers under names of top professors
stories.Summary:
Alan Said, a professor of computer science at the University of Gothenburg, received a Google Scholar notification that a new paper of his had been published. The paper, titled Intelligence Systems Supporting Sustainable Global Development, appeared in the American International Journal of Research and Innovation (AIJRI). Its topic matched his research focus on AI and sustainability, and his name was listed as the author. Said told Times Higher Education that he did not write the paper. He said a quick look at the paper and its references made clear it was AI-generated, with no real content at all.

THE then uncovered a larger operation in which obscure journals mass-publish AI-generated junk papers under the names of top professors from Stanford, UC Berkeley and other elite institutions. The misattributed names include Geoffrey Hinton, Yann LeCun, Yoshua Bengio, Li Fei-Fei, Christopher Manning, Michael I. Jordan, Andrew Ng and Stuart Russell. Some junk papers pile the names of multiple well-known researchers together. Said contacted the journal's domain registrar, which replied that the article had been deleted. According to screenshots Said gave THE, the paper did not disappear but was reposted under another person's name, then changed again two days later, so the same paper appeared under three different names.

Said later found two sibling journals, the American Journal of Advanced Multidisciplinary Research and Innovation (AJAMRI) and the American Journal For Multidisciplinary Research (AJFMR). The three journals share a similar visual style and the same editor-in-chief and editorial board members. AJAMRI has published dozens of papers signed by Li Fei-Fei and Christopher Manning of Stanford and Michael I. Jordan and Stuart Russell of UC Berkeley. Jure Leskovec, a Stanford computer science professor, told THE he did not write the paper, did not take part in its submission and did not authorize his name. Leskovec said he did not even know the paper existed before THE's email and called it quite worrying.

The domains of all three websites were registered in 2026, yet the sites host archives of papers published several years ago. All three claim to be peer-reviewed, open-access, multidisciplinary journals and charge explicit publication fees. AIJRI and AJAMRI charge $200 for papers with five or more non-Indian authors, while AJFMR charges $80 for papers with one to four authors and $10 for papers with five or more. All three list the same editor-in-chief, Denish Brown, with a WhatsApp number using a US area code. Kanakaraju Manupati, a postdoctoral fellow at Virginia Commonwealth University, told THE he had no idea the journal existed and no affiliation with it, and was surprised to see his name on the editorial board.

After the report, Christopher Manning responded on X, saying he had previously seen two fake papers signed under his name. One appeared in the so-called International Journal of Computer Vision and AI Applications, the other in the International Journal of Clinical and Medical Sciences. Manning wrote that predatory journals have always existed but this is a far worse scam, and urged that they be kept from being indexed, appealing to Google Scholar. THE's report believes the journals list well-known scholars to attract doctoral students to submit papers, and the journals are pay-to-publish. Said said that if a first-year doctoral student sees his name on this journal, the student might think it is okay to submit there, and he does not want that to happen.

Diomidis Spinellis, a professor of software engineering at the Athens University of Economics and Business, encountered the same thing in December 2023. A paper titled Global Business Strategies in the Digital Age was published under his name and affiliation in the Global International Journal of Innovative Research (GIJIR), with a valid DOI attached. Spinellis crawled the entire GIJIR website and published a case study in Research Integrity and Peer Review in 2025. Among the 53 articles with the lowest citation counts, at least 48 appeared to be AI-generated, and Turnitin gave an AI probability as high as 100% for multiple papers. According to a JMIR report last June, Spinellis classified GIJIR's papers into three categories, with false attribution papers the majority, purchased authorship papers second and genuine research in the minority.

Similar incidents became significantly more frequent in 2026, with cardiologist Eric Topol finding his name misappropriated by a digital health journal last April. In May, NBC News reported a fake journal network that had published hundreds of AI-generated papers, some misappropriating top university professors' names. Said found his paper because Google Scholar added it to his personal homepage and actively pushed it to him, and Spinellis's misattributed paper received 3 citations within a few months. Spinellis's proposed directions include strengthening DOI and ORCID identity verification, improving AI content detection and reforming evaluation systems focused on publication quantity. The JMIR report mentions that researchers can use checklists like Think.Check.Submit to verify a journal's ISSN, DOI and independent indexing status before submitting.

stories.Headline: Orbis Medicines uses AI to discover oral macrocyclic drugs from a 100 billion compound library
stories.Summary:
The Swiss biotech firm Orbis Medicines was founded in 2021 to create an artificial intelligence driven process for discovering novel oral macrocyclic drugs. This company, which spun off from the École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne, integrates automated chemical synthesis and biological activity detection to optimize drug molecules. The founders include Christian Heinis, Sevan Habeshian, and Morten Graugaard, who combined their expertise in chemical biology and business development. Their goal is to improve the oral bioavailability of candidate drugs that would otherwise require subcutaneous or intravenous administration.

The new process utilizes a Lab-in-the-Loop mode to screen a proprietary DNA-encoded library containing nearly 100 billion compounds. By using generative AI and machine learning, the firm can synthesize and analyze about 100,000 cyclic macromolecular compounds within several weeks. This method reduces typical molecular weight to 500-1000 Daltons and expands the potential chemical design space to 10³⁰ structural combinations. In February 2024, the company raised 26 million euros in seed funding, followed by a 90 million euro Series A round in January 2025 led by New Enterprise Associates.

The company focuses on immune, inflammatory, and cardiovascular metabolic diseases, with the latter involving a September 2026 agreement with Novo Nordisk. This licensing partnership for multi-target drug discovery has a maximum potential value of 1.4 billion US dollars. The founders explained that traditional small-molecule drugs often fail to act on complex targets, while larger biotherapeutic macromolecules are frequently degraded by gastric acid. By introducing unnatural amino acids and adjusting molecular skeletons, they aim to create stable compounds that can penetrate the intestinal epithelial barrier.

Orbis Medicines was recognized as a 2025 TOP100 Swiss Startups honoree for its pioneering approach to science and technology innovation. The company continues to use its funding from investors like Novo Holdings, Forbion, and Lilly Ventures to advance its synthetic macrocyclic candidates. Future efforts will focus on developing oral drugs for protein targets that have already been verified by biologics. This work aims to reduce the long research cycles and high costs associated with traditional molecular design and experimental screening.

stories.Summary:
AI agencies are mass producing fake store exploration videos using artificial intelligence. These companies create digital humans that taste food and introduce store environments. This business has emerged recently to erode the traditional in person exploration industry. Some of these mass production companies earn 8 million yuan monthly. The trend is spreading across platforms like Douyin for various local businesses.

Merchants upload storefront and dish photos to generate videos for under 10 yuan. Custom systems cost nearly 20,000 yuan, while existing systems cost 680 yuan annually. Computing power top ups cost 10 yuan per exploration or 2 to 3 yuan per voiceover. Agents pay 9,800 yuan yearly for 100 accounts and 100 stores. Some tutorials on Xianyu sell for as low as 0.18 yuan.

A practitioner told Tech Planet that his company cooperated with thousands of stores. He noted that basic fees alone reached 680,000 yuan from various catering enterprises. A producer mentioned using seedance2.5 to make AI character expressions look more realistic. He stated that AI reduces on camera costs and saves money on ingredients. This producer focuses on partners that are local small and medium catering enterprises.

Real person bloggers face increased pressure as Douyin emphasizes stable traffic and transactions. Some influencers, like Xiao Tan and Li Wuyou, earn commissions through group buying links. Xiao Tan sold 231,000 yuan across 718 stores, while Li Wuyou sold 202,000 yuan. New hot pot and milk tea shops use AI for short term exposure. These merchants often pay for tutorials, computing power, and generation service fees.

Traditional store exploration costs hundreds or thousands of yuan per video. Mid tier influencers in first tier cities can charge nearly 2,000 yuan. The industry previously relied on intermediaries who matched bloggers with local merchants. Many current AI videos use real shot pictures paired with digital humans. Some bloggers use ancient costume characters to increase user retention and visual freshness.

Operators now hang group buying links to earn verification commissions from AI videos. Tools for AI store exploration vlogs are available in Apple and Android stores. Platform rules are changing, making it harder for low cost volume content to distribute. Users struggle to distinguish between true and false experiences despite AI generated labels. The articles leave open whether merchants truly benefit from these lower costs.

stories.Headline: Upwork survey finds 77% of AI users say their workload increased
stories.Summary:
The article, published by eu.36kr.com on 17 November 2026 and written by Wei Xi, argues that AI is making people busier rather than more productive. It says AI can produce a decent draft in three minutes, but writing a heartfelt, engaging article people want to read has not become easier. It reports that many former colleagues at large tech companies use AI daily while bosses raise requirements, and many product managers must bring a working demo to the review meeting. It says AI does not save time but makes people busier and busier. It presents three paradoxes: the Cowan Paradox, the Solow Paradox and the Jevons Paradox.

The article cites Ruth Schwartz Cowan's 1983 book More Work for Mother, which observed that washing machines, vacuum cleaners and electric stoves were widespread by the 1970s yet she was busier than her mother's generation. It says full-time housewives in the US spent about 52 hours a week on housework in 1924 and around 55 hours a week by 1966. It says economic historian Joel Mokyr named this the Cowan Paradox. It says Cowan found the work of one housewife in 1950 would have needed three or four people in 1850. It says new tasks such as driving to the supermarket and picking up and dropping off children did not exist in the horse-drawn carriage era.

The article reports that the staffing agency Upwork surveyed 2,500 people, finding 77% of employees who use AI say their workload increased and 81% of executives admit they raised work requirements in the past year. It says Aruna Ranganathan and Xingqi Maggie Ye of UC Berkeley published an article in Harvard Business Review in February 2026 titled AI Has Not Reduced Work, It Has Made Work More Intensive. It says they spent eight months observing a tech company with about 200 employees and found product managers started writing code and researchers took on engineering tasks. It says renowned developer Simon Willison shared the article and said it matches his own experience. It says Stanford Social Media Lab coined the term "workslop" in September 2025 for AI outputs that look decent but cannot push work forward.

The article says the lab surveyed 1,150 full-time American employees, 40% of whom received such outputs in the past month, each spending an average of 116 minutes processing them, an implicit loss of $186 per person per month. It says engineer Siddhant Khare wrote AI Fatigue Is Real, No One Is Talking About It in February 2026, which topped the Hacker News leaderboard, arguing every task gets done faster so you take on more tasks but your brain cannot expand its capacity. It says John Maynard Keynes wrote Economic Possibilities for Our Grandchildren in 1930, calculating that with 2% annual capital growth and usual technological advance, by 2030 people need work only three hours a day, 15 hours a week. It says Swiss and Spanish economists calculated in 2024 that annual working hours per capita in the US fell from 2,316 hours in 1929 to 1,765 hours in 2019, a 23.8% reduction in 90 years, while Keynes' target is about 780 hours a year. It says Sam Altman said publicly this summer that every technological revolution promised more leisure but society never lived with less work, and he does not think AI will change this because humans are naturally competitive.

The article says economist Robert Solow wrote in a July 1987 New York Times book review that "You can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics," and won the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in October of that year. It says US non-farm labor productivity grew at an average annual rate of 3.19% from 1948 to 1973, fell to 1.53% from 1974 to 1995, returned to 3.15% after the internet boom in 1996, and dropped to 1.39% after 2004. It says Anders Humlum of the University of Chicago linked survey data of 25,000 Danish employees with official tax and employment archives and found AI users save an average of only 2.8% of their time, with no significant impact on income or working hours. It says MIT's Generative AI Divide report last July found enterprises invested 300 to 400 billion US dollars in generative AI but 95% of institutions saw no measurable returns. It says Callum Williams of The Economist posted a US productivity curve in February 2026 captioned that the AI productivity boost is still not visible in US statistics, and Indeed Hiring Lab pointed out US total factor productivity slowed from 1.5% to 0.8% in 2025.

The article says Stanford economist Paul David explained that electricity faced the same paradox: power stations were built as early as 1881, but by 1900 there was barely evidence of efficiency gains in factories, and US manufacturing productivity exceeded 5% per year only in the 1920s, 40 years after commercialization. It describes this as the productivity J-curve, in which productivity first declines then rises as enterprises adjust processes and train employees, and says today's AI is stuck at the bottom of the J-curve. It says Workday research found that in 89% of institutions less than half of jobs have been redesigned to match AI capabilities. It says American economist Erik Brynjolfsson is the flagbearer of the optimists, and in March 2026 the US Bureau of Labor Statistics announced productivity grew 2.8% in 2025, against an average of only 1.2% in the decade before the pandemic. It says he tweeted that it is still hard to determine how much of this growth AI contributed, but the Solow Paradox might be ready to retire.

stories.Headline: Chen Danqi joins Noeri part-time as the AI startup raises 110 million dollars
stories.Summary:
Chen Danqi announced on social platforms in the early hours of 17 November 2026 that she had joined Noeri on a part-time basis two months earlier. Danqi Chen is an Associate Professor of Computer Science at Princeton University. Noeri is a newly unveiled AI company co-founded by Yejin Choi, Professor of Computer Science at Stanford University, and Carlos Guestrin. The company focuses on developing AI systems that can continuously learn and self-improve. Noeri also announced it has raised 110 million US dollars in financing.

The round was led by Menlo Ventures, with participation from Madrona Venture Group, Kindred Ventures, Wing Venture Capital and NEA. NVIDIA, Cisco Investments and Snowflake became strategic investors. Noeri supports the use of closed-source models and open-weight models and can adapt as new models emerge. Customers can retain ownership of their own data and of the workflows and models developed through the system, but must still comply with relevant license agreements of third-party models. Every modification comes with an explanation and is submitted for human review and confirmation, a process Noeri compares to code review.

Chen said she is quite looking forward to the team's research direction, especially the application of AI in scientific discovery. She said she hopes to enable every scientist to apply AI to their most intractable research problems. She said she is very happy to work with Yejin Choi, who has long been her role model and friend. Choi and Guestrin serve as co-CEOs of Noeri. The company interprets its name as "The Plural of Intelligence".

Choi and Guestrin wrote in a vision article that they prefer an ecosystem composed of a large number of AIs of different scales and capabilities over one enterprise developing and mastering a superintelligence. They call the concept Plural Intelligence, in which every organization and individual can build, master and continuously improve their own AI. Enterprises are affected: Noeri will study an enterprise's own data and workflows and optimize the entire AI system around specific tasks. The scope it can adjust includes instructions and skills, tools and orchestration, model selection and model optimization.

Choi is a professor at Stanford University and a senior fellow at Stanford HAI, and she officially joined Stanford University in January 2025. She was previously a Professor of Computer Science at the University of Washington, Senior Research Manager at the Allen Institute for AI (Ai2), and served as Senior Research Director and Distinguished Scientist at NVIDIA. Guestrin co-created XGBoost with Tianqi Chen and co-founded the machine learning company Turi, which was acquired by Apple in 2016. After joining Apple, Guestrin served as Senior Director of Machine Learning and AI and participated in promoting Apple to establish an AI and machine learning R&D center in Seattle. Chen co-leads the Princeton NLP research group, serves as deputy director of the Princeton Language and Intelligence Research Program, and is one of the authors of RoBERTa.

Noeri wants to hand to AI the work that otherwise requires a professional AI engineering team, since most AI models have basically fixed parameters after training is completed. The system will learn from the enterprise's data, workflows and interactions during task execution, and every experience and correction in a task has the opportunity to become the basis for the next round of optimization. Noeri hopes to find a more appropriate combination through model specialization and agent collaboration, for example letting a smaller model be responsible for scheduling and calling other models and professional tools according to task requirements. Chen said she is particularly looking forward to the application of Plural Intelligence in scientific discovery, a direction Noeri hopes to explore. The articles leave open what Noeri's products will cost and when they will be available.

stories.Headline: AI infrastructure suppliers lose $4.2tn in value as investor confidence drops
stories.Summary:
Companies supplying the infrastructure for artificial intelligence data centres lost approximately $4.2tn in value since June, according to an analysis by The Financial Times. This significant decline wiped out nearly half of the $9.4tn these businesses gained during the previous twelve months. The sell off affected global mining, utility, and manufacturing firms, including Caterpillar and Okto, which contracted with Meta for nuclear power in Ohio. Investor confidence dropped quickly over the last four weeks due to concerns regarding debt funded spending and political backlash.

The market downturn impacted chipmakers like AMD, Micron, Broadcom, and TSMC, as well as manufacturers such as Dell, HPE, and Super Micro Computer. Vertiv saw its shares drop 23 percent after the midterms, falling to $202.07 from a May peak of $379.94 despite third quarter sales rising 61 percent to $4.31bn. S&P Global is tracking 157 projects that have been abandoned, paused, or severely delayed. Sightline Climate analysts estimate that 30 to 50 percent of US AI data centres planned for 2026 will be cancelled or delayed.

Dan Thompson of 451 Research at S&P Global Energy stated that community opposition and state regulation are key risks for projects across the country. Other factors include US midterm results in states like Iowa, Texas, and Ohio, and reports that Nvidia may have sold to blacklisted Chinese organisations. Conversely, Alex Cordovil from DellOro Group argued that revenue growth is baked in until 2027 because backlogs remain at record highs. He believes the financial fundamentals are solid and that the build out is not yet decelerating.

The sector has been the second worst performing part of the S&P 500 since the summer, trailing only technology. While 16 GW is due this year, only around 5 GW is currently under construction in the United States. Democrats now hold Congress and several governorships, leaving the future of environmental protections and moratoriums an open question. The full impact of campaign pledges on the tech sector will likely remain unknown until well into 2027.

stories.Headline: Microsoft outage creates Zoho opportunity for India Inc, says Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw
stories.Summary:
Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw, the founder of Biocon, said on the social media platform X that the recent disruption of Microsoft services could create an opening for the Indian software company Zoho to serve as a backup management information system for Indian businesses, according to TechGig. She made the suggestion as companies were re-evaluating their reliance on global technology providers following the outage. The Microsoft 365 outage affected users in more than 70 countries, including India, according to Downdetector data cited by the report. Microsoft announced on Saturday that its services had been fully restored and that all products were operational, confirming the Microsoft 365 disruption was resolved.

The report said Microsoft's Microsoft 365 suite has more than 450 million commercial users, a figure Bloomberg reported, and the scale of the disruption renewed concerns about the risks of businesses relying heavily on a single technology provider. Zoho already has a significant presence in India's government email infrastructure, with the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology stating in December that nearly 12.68 lakh official email accounts across various ministries and departments had migrated to a Zoho-based platform. Approximately 7.45 lakh of those accounts belonged to central government employees, according to the ministry. Union ministers publicly backed domestic products, including Zoho's software and its messaging platform Arattai, as alternatives to foreign technology services in October last year.

Mazumdar-Shaw is the person behind the suggestion, and she posted on X that Zoho could emerge as a backup management information system provider for India Inc given such unforeseen events, the article said. The report did not say whether Zoho or Microsoft responded to her remarks. The articles give no further statements from Microsoft, Zoho or government officials beyond the ministry's December figure and the ministers' earlier public backing of domestic products. The articles also do not say what steps, if any, Indian businesses plan to take in response to the outage or to her suggestion.

The round was led by Connect Ventures, with participation from OpenOcean and United Ventures, according to the article. The startup had previously raised a €5.5m pre-seed round led by Italian fund Primo Ventures, the article said. The company was founded by a team including researchers with links to Google DeepMind and ETH Zurich, the article said.

The funding is intended to address what the article describes as a data problem for robotics companies, which collect sensor data that is difficult to organise for training AI models. The article said Mosaico's software helps companies manage and structure this data so it can be used to train robot models. The article cited a figure of 2,636 robotics companies worldwide, attributed to a source called Xtoltuyq 7454, though the surrounding text was garbled. The article also mentioned that the startup's technology is aimed at reducing the time and cost of preparing data for robot training.

The article quoted an investor from Connect Ventures saying that the firm had known the founders for 83 weeks before investing, and describing the team as strong. The article also cited a comment from an executive at the startup saying that the company wants to make it easier for robotics firms to use their sensor data. The article said the founders declined to give further details on the company's customers or revenue. The article noted that the funding will be used to grow the team and expand the product.

The article placed the round in the context of growing venture capital interest in robotics, noting that robotics has never had such abundant access to venture capital. The article also referenced other recent robotics fundraises, including a €5m pre-seed round by Paris-based Bleu Robotics and a pre-seed round by Enact Intelligence in Switzerland. The article did not say what specific milestones Mosaico plans to reach with the new funding. The article did not give a timeline for the company's next steps.

stories.Headline: European AI fintech founders chase defensibility as early stage funding rises 40%
stories.Summary:
Funding rounds raised by early stage AI-native fintech startups are up 40%, as European companies pile into the financial services back office hoping to become category leaders, Sifted reported on 16 November 2026. The report said early stage AI-native fintech funding rounds had risen by that share, with European companies crowding into back office work for financial services. The article described the back office as a crowded field where startups are competing to become the category leaders in their niche. The report said the crowded market has pushed founders to build what rivals cannot easily copy, rather than compete on features that any competitor can replicate.

It said investors and founders now argue that defensibility comes from proprietary data, deep workflow integration and regulatory know-how rather than from a thin layer wrapped around a model. The article gave no further figures beyond the 40% rise in early stage AI-native fintech funding rounds. The article quoted a founder saying that companies should build what cannot be cloned, and that durable advantage comes from data, workflow and compliance rather than from the model itself. It also quoted an investor saying that many startups look similar on the surface, and that the winners will be those that own a piece of the workflow rather than rent one.

The article said responsibility for building that defensibility sits with founders, who must decide where to dig in rather than spread thin across the back office. The context is a back office that is getting crowded, with European startups piling into financial services work in the hope of becoming category leaders. The article said the next step for these companies is to prove they own something rivals cannot copy, whether data, workflow or regulatory expertise. It did not say which companies will succeed or what happens to those that fail to build that defensibility.

stories.Headline: Hark releases Handoff², a computer-use agent it says completes 82% of tasks 2x faster
stories.Summary:
Hark released Handoff², the second version of the computer-use agent inside its Hark Pro app, on November 12, 2026, according to MarkTechPost. The agent operates websites the way a person does by clicking, typing and scrolling on live pages instead of calling APIs, and Hark says it finishes web tasks about 2x faster than the original on average. Hark previewed the original Handoff in August 2026 and shipped it in Hark Pro in October 2026, and since then it says it has logged over 5.6 million browsing sessions and handled over $20 million in purchases. Users send it groceries, flights, dentist appointments, refunds, warranty forms and job applications.

Each request runs on a dedicated virtual computer in Hark's cloud with its own browser, file system and terminal, and users reach it from web, iOS and Android with no local or quantized option. On Hark's 478-task internal benchmark across 238 websites, Handoff² completes 82% of tasks, up from 73% for v1, and takes 46% less time per task. Hark says the gains come from reinforcement learning that penalized wasted turns and latency, and the new harness lets the model emit more actions per turn, batch actions such as filling several form fields in one turn, and group repeated action patterns into reusable composite actions. Hark reports long research tasks more than 5x faster, with a 10-minute task dropping to 3 minutes and a 45-minute task to about 10, and flight booking up to 3.8x faster. On Hark's internal alignment benchmark, which checks that the agent never checks out without approval and asks for clarification only when a request is truly ambiguous, Handoff² scores 93.8%, up from 90.3% for v1.

Hark states that the speed gains come from the reinforcement learning recipe that penalized excess turns, unnecessary thinking tokens and end-to-end latency, and it co-evolved the agent harness and the training recipe together. Hark ran Claude Opus 5.5 (max) in the same harness as Handoff², and Handoff² lands within 5 points of it, though 82% browsing completion still trails that model by up to 5 points. Every Handoff² number is self-reported and no third-party score exists yet, and Hark has not posted an Online-Mind2Web result for Handoff², while the original Handoff scores 97.67% on that public human-eval leaderboard against 97.3% for Yutori's Navigator n1.5. The article notes that v1 was measured in its original harness, not the new one, and it does not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: Cloud provider leak exposes personal data of 46,000 TSMC employees
stories.Summary:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company confirmed on November 16, 2026, that personal data of current and former employees was leaked online. A threat actor using the alias SmithBianl posted a sample text file on a hacker forum on November 8. This individual claimed the sample came from a larger 6.9GB dataset containing 46,000 employee records. The leaked information was offered for auction with a starting price of 3 BTC, which is roughly $65,000.

The breach requires the company to notify affected staff and provide them with necessary support. The compromised data includes sensitive details such as national ID numbers, banking information, addresses, and contact details. TSMC determined that the leak originated from the system services of a cloud service provider rather than its own internal infrastructure. Consequently, the company has engaged a third-party cybersecurity firm to help manage the ongoing situation.

TSMC stated that its operations and customers remain unaffected by this external security incident. In a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, the company noted there is no evidence that its own systems were compromised. The chipmaker, which produces hardware for Nvidia and Apple, is focusing on supporting the employees whose data was exposed. The company continues to investigate the breach through its partnership with external cybersecurity experts.

Articles.Title: TSMC employee data leaked from cloud provider

stories.Headline: Oracle's Natalia Rachelson urges businesses to measure AI success by delivered improvements, not agent counts
stories.Summary:
Natalia Rachelson, a Senior Vice President of Applications Development at Oracle, said in an interview with PTI that businesses adopting artificial intelligence should judge success by the improvement the technology delivers rather than by the number of AI agents they deploy. She said the number of agents deployed matters less than the improvement they deliver, a view that shifts how organisations should evaluate their AI investments. Her comments were published by TechGig on November 16, 2026, in a report that also said AI is moving from merely helping employees to actively performing work for them. The report said this evolution requires a re-evaluation of traditional AI adoption metrics.

Rachelson advised business leaders to select a measurable goal for AI implementation from the outset, so that AI initiatives stay aligned with tangible business outcomes and improvements. The report said this approach is crucial as AI transitions from assisting employees to performing tasks autonomously. It said businesses should measure success by delivered improvements, not by the number of AI agents deployed. The report framed the shift as a change in how organisations should think about the value of their AI spending.

Rachelson is responsible for applications development at Oracle, and she gave her assessment directly to PTI, according to the TechGig report. She said the number of agents deployed matters less than the improvement they deliver, and she tied that view to the need for a measurable goal chosen at the start. The report presented her position as guidance for leaders weighing how to evaluate their AI investments. It did not give any figures for agents deployed or improvements measured.

The report described the technology as transitioning from merely helping employees to actively performing work for them, which it said necessitates a re-evaluation of traditional AI adoption metrics. It said business leaders should therefore pick a measurable goal from the outset to keep AI initiatives aligned with tangible outcomes. The article gave no further details on specific companies, timelines or results beyond Rachelson's comments. It did not say what happens next beyond the advice to measure delivered improvements.

Articles.Title: Oracle executive advises measuring AI success by results, not agents

stories.Headline: MinoHealth AI Labs warns of bioweapons threat after model designs thousands of toxins
stories.Summary:
Researchers at MinoHealth AI Labs in Accra, Ghana, removed guardrails from their drug discovery AI model in 2024. They asked the system to design toxins instead of medicines. The team uploaded their findings to the preprint server arXiv in May 2025. This experiment exposed the threat of AI designed bioweapons. The lab founder then issued warnings about the dual use of such technology.

The model produced designs for 1,020 proteins and 5,000 small molecules. Software scored all of these as likely toxic, with some resembling deadly ricin. The lab used a general purpose LLM trained for biology and drug discovery. Moremi Bio was developed by a 20 member team in a modest bungalow. The project received 149,533 dollars from the Gates Foundation in 2023.

Founder Darlington Akogo said he and his team were all shocked by the results. He warned that AI poses an existential bioweapons threat to the world. Akogo questioned if DNA synthesis companies would stop someone from making these designs. He believes the United Nations should create a working group to study AI risks. He also suggested that the world needs tighter controls over synthesis.

Brenda Obuya of Kenya's Ministry of Information says the need for regulation is echoing through government. Adam Abdullahi says this shows African institutions are contributing to AI governance. Ken McCallum of MI5 stated that bioweapons are now the top AI misuse risk. Ayantola Alayande noted that lay users could now generate this output via chatbots. Peter Garraghan said his team broke the Kimi model in one day.

MinoHealth Labs was founded in 2016 to solve Ghana's health worker shortage. In 2022, a U.S. drug company ran a similar experiment with chemical weapons. Anthropic launched Claude for Life Sciences in October 2025, and OpenAI launched GPT Rosalind in April. AI drug discovery investment grew from 4.1 billion dollars in 2023 to 8.4 billion in 2025. Some labs screen orders, but Akogo says AI could hack this process.

The International Gene Synthesis Consortium is working with developers to detect AI designed sequences. Heads of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind called for mandatory checks in the U.S. in June. Moremi Bio is now proposing drug candidates for cancer, tuberculosis, and dengue. The team is developing diagnostics for malaria and mpox through a European Union consortium. The articles leave open if governments will mandate these screening laws.

Articles.Title: The small African lab sounding the alarm on AI bioweapons

stories.Headline: Apollo places six evaluators inside OpenAI for four months to assess subversion during training
stories.Summary:
Apollo Research announced on November 16, 2026 that six of its evaluators will work inside OpenAI for four months to investigate whether its models attempt to subvert alignment or control mechanisms during training, evaluations and internal deployment. The team will examine four questions, namely whether training incentivizes subversion, whether evaluations can elicit it, whether subversion occurs during internal deployment and whether reasoning relevant to subversion would be detectable. The scope covers attempts to undermine a model's own alignment or controls as well as those of its successors, and the arrangement is meant to move external scrutiny beyond Apollo's earlier approach of evaluating after post-training and shortly before public release. Apollo considers that timing insufficient for testing misaligned behavior such as scheming or for examining non-public uses during internal deployment, and it describes the pilot as an ambitious first step rather than a full embedded evaluation. For the training-incentives assessment, OpenAI committed to provide relevant training code and datasets, reinforcement-learning rollouts with available reasoning traces and rewards, and the ability to query intermediate model checkpoints, while detailed access arrangements for the other assessment claims remain to be agreed.

The assessment is confined to agreed claims, models and time periods, and OpenAI may withhold in-scope items when it deems that reasonably necessary because of technical infeasibility, security risks or intellectual-property protection, but it may not withhold information or staff access simply because the material is unfavorable. OpenAI must tell Apollo that withheld items exist and give written reasons, and where it considers this feasible and relevant it must identify withheld records by category and approximate volume, while Apollo can request broader access through a designated contact and escalate refusals without any guarantee of expansion. The evaluators will work on OpenAI hardware using separate channels that can be monitored, they will by default lack access to general staff channels such as Slack, and formal conversations must be logged, with Apollo required to stop substantive discussion and route follow-up through its contact if another employee raises confidential information. Apollo plans two public reports, the first on training incentives for subversion and the second on evaluations, internal deployment and the detectability of subversive reasoning, each describing methods, conclusions, limitations, questions that could not be assessed and supporting evidence that can be published. OpenAI will review the reports and may request redactions of confidential information including evidence supporting findings, but it may not redact Apollo's verdicts or request redactions merely because a finding is unfavorable, and it can redact evidence it considers sensitive intellectual property whether or not that evidence directly contributes to a finding.

OpenAI will share the unredacted reports with its board's Safety and Security Committee, and claims based on employee discussions require OpenAI's formal attestation unless Apollo establishes them independently, with Apollo allowed to disclose a declined attestation and explain its effect without revealing the underlying confidential information. Separate meta-transparency rights let Apollo describe publicly the engagement's scope and conditions, the access requested and received, material withheld or delayed and the reasons given, requested report removals and their significance, and any pressure it believed shaped its work, all without prior OpenAI review. Apollo regards those meta-transparency rights as a minimum standard for every evaluation engagement, arguing that undisclosed restrictions can make absent problems look reassuring even when the absence reflects limits on investigation or disclosure. The pilot's conclusions will therefore need to be read alongside its account of access and publication limits, since the same verdict can carry different weight depending on what the evaluators were able to inspect and disclose.

stories.Headline: Vincee Cole compares ten AI training data vendors and names Surge AI the top pick for expert data
stories.Summary:
Vincee Cole published an overview of ten AI training data vendors on November 16, 2026. The report compares these companies based on their services, public pricing, and long-term outlook. Surge AI is named the top pick for expert human data and evaluations. Labelbox is highlighted as the best choice for enterprises wanting software and managed labeling. Mercor raised 750 million dollars at a 20 billion dollar valuation on November 10.

The list includes Surge AI, Scale AI, Mercor, micro1, Snorkel AI, and Invisible Technologies. Labelbox offers a free tier and services from about 8 dollars per hour. Prolific charges a 42.8 percent fee plus participant pay of at least 8 dollars hourly. Bright Data sells web datasets starting from 250 dollars per 100,000 records. Other vendors like iMerit and Scale AI do not publish their real price points.

Surge AI claims OpenAI and Anthropic cited its benchmarks in 2026 model releases. The company says Microsoft used its human evaluations for the MAI-Thinking-1 model. Scale AI told Forbes its revenue reached 870 million dollars in 2024. Mercor states its network now includes more than five million recruited professional experts. Scale AI reports working with 90 percent of leading generative AI model builders.

Frontier labs, government agencies, and enterprises are the primary buyers for these data services. Researchers and AI product teams use Prolific for online studies with vetted participants. Healthcare and automotive companies utilize iMerit for compliant medical and LiDAR labeling. Teams training models on web data use Bright Data for scraping tools. Only three of the ten compared vendors publish real price points for buyers.

Demand has shifted from simple image labeling to paid experts like doctors and engineers. Reuters reported that Surge AI made more than 1 billion dollars in 2024 revenue. Meta bought a 49 percent non-voting stake in Scale AI for 14.3 billion dollars. TechCrunch reported in July 2026 that Mercor had a run rate of 2 billion dollars. Scale AI named Francis deSouza as its chief executive officer in July 2026.

Expert data and agent training are expected to stay in demand through 2028. Simple labeling tasks are predicted to become automated over the coming few years. The report suggests buyers budget for a paid pilot before signing any contract. Some companies may transition into defense and enterprise AI contractors rather than neutral labs. The long-term potential for benchmarks to become a second business remains an open possibility.
