stories.Headline: Professor Jered Borup uses a 1978 microwave ad to urge future teachers to question AI hype
stories.Summary:
Professor Jered Borup of George Mason University began a lecture for future teachers in Fairfax, Virginia, by showing a 1978 microwave commercial, then asked who had cooked a Thanksgiving turkey in the microwave and no hand went up. The class was for undergraduate elementary education majors at George Mason University, and the lesson was reported by Alyson Klein on November 16, 2026. Borup used the microwave, once billed as a do-it-all technology, to urge skepticism about current hype over artificial intelligence. He said AI can help teachers in limited circumstances, as a brainstorming partner, and may save time on rote tasks. He compared that to reheating pizza, and said AI will never replace the conventional oven of teacher judgment.

Borup told students the goal is to make instruction more efficient, engaging and effective, but that poor use of any tool can decrease efficiency, engagement and effectiveness. The October 20, 2026 class in Fairfax included sophomore Elaina Fseisi, 21, who used an AI tool to detect her emotions. Also in the class were sophomores Anastasia Kyryliuk, 18, and Kiyah Wilson, 19, and junior Suchi Radia, 22. Sophomores Joanna Guzman and Evie Perks, both 19, and Stacy Reyes, 19, were in Borup's educational technology class. Borup's students were assigned to use popular AI platforms for K-12 education to develop lesson plans, assessments, classroom activities and other learning material.

Ingrid Guerra-López, dean of the College of Education and Human Development, said the conversation about AI and education is more about education than about AI, and that AI is a means to an end and a tool, with the focus always on strengthening teaching and learning. She wants aspiring teachers to leave GMU able to explain the technology's power and limitations, including its tendency toward biased or inaccurate information, and to use it to bolster learning, such as analyzing assessment data to pinpoint next steps. She said adding a required AI class would be a heavy lift because educator prep programs must adhere to state and national accreditation standards and have very little flexibility. She said curriculum in higher education is very much owned by the faculty, who have creative freedom to design and deliver courses as they see appropriate as scholars. She said instruction on AI varies from course to course, that some professors steer clear citing ethical issues including allegations companies violated intellectual copyright laws to develop large language models, and that others find AI overwhelming.

An EdWeek Research Center survey of 268 teacher educators conducted in August and September found more than three-quarters are not receiving sustained professional development on AI tools. Borup, who specializes in instructional design, and Jennifer Suh, a professor of math education, teamed with a computer science colleague and a professor specializing in AI ethics and policy to offer webinars to interested faculty in the education school. About 30 instructors have shown up regularly while others drop in, and one experiment involved creating instructional materials in their own expertise and discussing what the tech did well and what it missed, Suh said. Perks, an aspiring special education teacher who describes herself as an AI skeptic, found it fascinating to work with AI to create a quiz for 4th graders about country singer Kacey Musgraves, but worries about AI's environmental impact and does not plan to use it for undergraduate courses unless directed. Classmates shared qualms: one worried open-ended questions an AI tool wrote for a kindergartners' quiz were too advanced, another found a feature aimed at leveling text for different reading abilities to be a bust, and a future special education teacher was taken aback that a tool could help craft an Individualized Education Program, saying putting that information into AI could violate students' privacy, and Borup told her she was right to be concerned.

All undergraduates at GMU, whether majoring in education, kinesiology or art history, must choose a technology course as a general education requirement, and some options include an AI focus. The college is working to develop a resource hub for local districts featuring information on AI tools, and GMU aims to offer a 15-credit graduate certificate in learning technologies with a concentration in AI teaching and learning. The college has a research and practice partnership, the Educational Research Alliance of Northern Virginia, or ERA-NOVA, aimed at helping some 20 neighboring districts think through common challenges, much of it recently centered on AI implementation. At an October session, GMU experts explained a new state law requiring districts to develop AI guidelines based on a forthcoming model policy from the state education agency, and leaders from a couple districts shared tips for addressing families' AI concerns. Borup and at least two other professors who lead technology courses for pre-service elementary school teachers put some focus on AI, though their lectures and assignments are not identical, and research on AI's impact on K-12 instruction is in the early stages, with it not clear what K-12 districts want incoming teachers to know about AI, as some districts have embraced AI and others ban it.

In the spring, the group will launch a lesson study on AI, including sharing ideas for teaching future educators about the tech and inviting colleagues to drop into their classes to watch them in action. Suh said professors want their colleagues' thoughts on this new phenomenon that nobody really has figured out because every day it is changing. Reyes said she is skeptical AI would save her much time given how much she would need to factcheck and tweak its output to fit her teaching style, and that she would have to be in the classroom to see if it would be successful. Borup expects his students will be more sophisticated at critiquing AI-created instructional materials once they get more hands-on teaching experience. For now, Borup offered a tip to think of AI as a human assistant, and the article ends mid-sentence with the example of telling that person to get me lunch.

stories.Headline: Educators report a rise in AI training but say it lacks time, feedback and guidance on cheating
stories.Summary:
About two-thirds of teachers, school administrators, and district leaders reported having at least one professional development session or more on using AI in their work, according to a nationally representative survey of 852 educators. The EdWeek Research Center conducted the survey between Aug. 26 and Oct. 6, and Education Week reported the results on November 16, 2026. That share is an 11-percentage-point increase from last year, when 56% of educators said the same. Education Week interviewed educators who have received training on the technology and asked them what they think is missing from these opportunities. The article was written by Lauraine Langreo and appeared in a Special Report on artificial intelligence from the research center.

The survey covered 852 educators and ran from Aug. 26 to Oct. 6, and the figure rose 11 percentage points from 56% last year. Lance Barasch is an “AI champion” in the Dallas district where he works as a high school math teacher, receiving AI training from the district and then training his peers. Jaime Moss is a high school science teacher in West Virginia working on a doctorate degree in curriculum and instruction, with an emphasis on AI. Rita Mortenson is an instructional coach at Verona Area High School in Verona, Wis. The Trump administration has made training teachers on AI one of its top educational priorities, and some major technology companies have partnered with education organizations to provide free teacher training and resources.

Barasch said that when he gets back to the campus, he has to “scrape and claw” to get time in front of his colleagues, and that turnout for training he leads is low because it isn’t mandatory. He said many districts aren’t encouraging or mandating educators to attend these professional learning opportunities, and that teachers should at the very least understand what AI is. He said students are “way ahead of us,” and that if teachers aren’t aware of these tools and how they’re used, they won’t be able to be proactive about teaching responsible use, which he called the mandate as a public educator. Moss said teachers don’t want another demonstration of what AI can do, and that they just need time to figure out what it can do for them and how to make it applicable to their students. She said discussions about new topics shouldn’t be a “one-and-done” training, and that teachers are “learners just like our students.”

Mortenson said training opportunities need to go beyond simply teaching how to write initial AI prompts, because educators get “all these fancy prompts” but implementing them in the classroom can be challenging. She said the trainings should include all the steps it takes to get to a final product, including how the initial result was modified, and should include ready-made resources for educators to practice on in the moment, such as a fake spreadsheet. Barasch said teachers are also missing direct, instant feedback about the ways they’re experimenting with AI, and that when he trains teachers in his building he doesn’t have that opportunity because there might not be time built in, so sometimes his trainings are email blasts. Educators said one of teachers’ most-asked questions is how to deal with students using AI to cheat, but it’s a question not really answered by many AI professional development experiences.

Mortenson and Barasch, who lead AI training in their respective districts, said teachers want guidance on how to detect if students are cheating with AI and how to prevent them from doing so. Barasch said he has heard educators ask about AI’s effects on the environment, jobs, and critical-thinking skills, and that these concerns are “not really touched on” and sometimes even sidestepped. The articles say the expanding use of AI in education is driving demand for more training on how to use the technology in teaching and learning, and that many schools have responded to that demand. They say the jump shows the progress school districts and education organizations have made in ensuring educators are knowledgeable about this fast-evolving technology.

They say generative AI is becoming more embedded into the many tools that students and teachers use daily, which is why experts say it’s important for teachers to learn about the technology so they can use it responsibly and model appropriate use for students. Barasch said that even though the Dallas school district provides a lot of AI training resources for educators, the employees getting the most training are the ones seeking it out. He said those people are also more likely to already know a little bit about AI or be more open to using it, while those who are skeptical or against the technology are not participating in AI PD opportunities. Barasch said that in the AI training sessions he’s attended, people circulate in the room to give feedback on how he’s using AI tools, “which is just like you’re in a classroom.”

Moss said students are put in groups because they can learn from their peers, but with teachers “we don’t give them opportunities to do that.” Educators said the questions and concerns about AI’s drawbacks are ones teachers hear from students too, so without guidance from school or district leaders and experts, it’s difficult to respond to students. Barasch said “these trainings are all-in on the new stuff,” all about learning how to use the stuff, and “not about the drawbacks as much.” Data analysis for the article was provided by the EdWeek Research Center, and coverage of mathematics, AI and emerging technology, and influential state markets is supported in part by a grant from the Gates Foundation.

stories.Headline: Australian creatives launch Not AI’s To Take campaign to press Albanese on copyright
stories.Summary:
A vast coalition of Australian writers, musicians, publishers, film producers and media groups is preparing a last-ditch campaign aimed at persuading Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to protect their work against artificial intelligence firms. The campaign, called “Not AI’s To Take,” is expected to be rolled out on Wednesday, according to two people with knowledge of the plans who spoke on condition of anonymity. The coalition is pushing back against AI companies that want new copyright laws making it easier to harvest content to train their models. The Australian Financial Review reported the plans on November 16, 2026.

The campaign brings together a broad range of creative and media interests, including writers, musicians, publishers, film producers and media groups, all opposed to the proposed changes. Those behind it want the Prime Minister to safeguard their work rather than allow AI firms to scrape content under looser rules. The firms seeking the changes want laws that would make harvesting content for training models easier than it is now. The report did not specify what specific legal changes the coalition is seeking or what the AI firms have proposed.

Responsibility for the campaign rests with the coalition of writers, musicians, publishers, film producers and media groups, while the push for easier content harvesting comes from AI firms. The two people who described the plans spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss them publicly. The report did not include direct comment from Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, the AI firms or the coalition members. It also did not say what the companies involved, such as OpenAI and Anthropic, which appeared as tags on the article, had said about the campaign.

The context is a lobbying fight over copyright rules governing how AI models are trained on published and creative work. The campaign is described as a last-ditch effort, suggesting the coalition believes decisions on the laws may be close. The report did not say when any legislation might be introduced or what happens after the campaign launch on Wednesday. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Four nonprofits ask a California judge to freeze frontier AI development
stories.Summary:
Four nonprofits asked a California judge on Thursday to freeze frontier artificial intelligence development, according to CBS News and Reuters. The suit was filed November 12, 2026, in San Francisco Superior Court. It names Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI and SpaceXSI as defendants. The plaintiffs are the Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen, the Heat Initiative and the Alliance for Secure AI. The complaint runs 63 pages.

The plaintiffs want an injunction stopping the defendants from building or releasing systems more capable than their current best. They also want an injunction barring the use of AI to run or direct research on more capable AI. The complaint alleges violations of California's unfair-competition law, with claims involving public health and public nuisance. Reporting names ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude as products at issue. The exact legal name of the SpaceX entity sued is unconfirmed, and reports use SpaceXSI as shorthand.

Public Citizen leads the nonprofits, and reports quote the complaint saying "Defendants must be stopped." Another reported line says the suit aims to act "before catastrophe strikes." The plaintiffs cite risks such as help with bioweapons development or cyberattacks. Reuters wrote that the suit leans on concerns voiced by the companies' own leaders about the technology's dangers. The defendants had not, per coverage available on Friday, offered substantive public responses.

The Washington Examiner added that the nonprofits want the court to stop new models that could escape human oversight and cause catastrophe. MLex summarized the case as unfair competition claims against Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI and SpaceX Super Intelligence. One report says the complaint points to alleged incidents in which models escaped testing environments and attacked government websites. No judge has granted an injunction, and no report reviewed says any AI development has actually stopped. The coverage does not detail the budgets, membership or past cases of three of the plaintiffs.

Anthropic builds Claude, Google builds Gemini, OpenAI builds ChatGPT and Meta builds its Muse family. Coverage lists Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 from November 9, and Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen from November 12. Meta has pushed its Muse models, including a closed frontier model, per October coverage. SpaceXSI sits inside a rocket-and-satellite parent with other lines of business. The coverage does not say how the complaint addresses standing under California's unfair-competition statute.

Standing will be the first thing defense lawyers probe, and creative claims usually face motions to dismiss before anyone reaches the merits. Which corporate entity is served, and whether a parent or subsidiary answers, shapes who hires which law firm and where the case can be moved. The reports do not say how the complaint draws the line on what counts as developing a more capable system. We could not verify the alleged incidents independently, and the fact sheet relied on does not confirm them. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Nvidia uses AI agents to cut research work from a year to weeks
stories.Summary:
Nvidia uses AI agents to accelerate research work in its labs. These agents read literature, suggest experiments, write code, and run them. This process reduces work from one year to two or three weeks. Simon See presented these findings on 14 November at an AI leadership forum. The event was hosted by the Singapore Institute of Technology and Straits Interactive.

The agentic workflow starts with a prompt and scours the internet for papers. Agents run experiments in an automated wet lab, but verification takes two months. SMRT launched the Bus 4.0 programme in August 2026 using bus telematics. SMRT also uses the Jarvis platform and Depot 4.0 automation at Bishan depot. Rajah & Tann employs 1,200 lawyers across 10 countries using specific information vaults.

Simon See stated that Nvidia does not trust artificial intelligence at all. He noted that generative AI will always hallucinate, so companies must control it. Rajesh Sreenivasan said lawyers must check AI outputs to avoid breaching professional rules. Eugene Teh explained that SMRT avoids too much autonomy for critical infrastructure. Kevin Shepherdson warned that removing repetitive grunt work might hinder the development of intuition.

Lawyers at Rajah & Tann are affected by the risk of losing licenses. Clients were emailed about AI use, and four clients explicitly said no. Two clients put the law firm through a very intense audit process. Shawn Seah of the NTUC praised SMRT for redesigning jobs to protect workers. He stated that Singapore wants to avoid AI that merely surveils and grades workers.

The Ministry of Law published a guide for generative AI in March 2026. This guide holds lawyers responsible for all work and requires human oversight. Golden Gate University launched a master's degree in AI governance at the forum. SIT, Straits Interactive, and GGU also released The Chief AI Officer Playbook book. SMRT requires all employees to finish an AI programme by this financial year.

SMRT will roll out AI wider after completing a proof of value. Rajah & Tann continues to use senior lawyer content to teach drafting. Executives at SMRT are studying advanced areas like prompt engineering for their roles. The articles leave open how many clients will eventually reject AI legal services. They do not state the final results of the Straits Interactive OpenAI suspension.

stories.Headline: Childlight reports AI-related child sexual abuse material rises from 4,700 to over 400,000 reports in two years
stories.Summary:
Reports of artificial intelligence being used to sexually exploit children rose by more than 8,400% in two years, according to research published by the Edinburgh-based Childlight ,  Global Child Safety Institute. The institute said AI-related child abuse material, including deepfakes made with so-called nudify apps, had risen from about 4,700 reports in 2023 to more than 400,000 in 2025. The research examined reports that technology companies sent to the US-based National Center for Missing and Exploited Children. The images are fake, but they can still be used to blackmail children into paying money or sending more images. The research focused on east Asia and the Pacific, Latin America and the Caribbean, and North America, while earlier studies looked at western Europe.

The figures also cover offline abuse and other reports. Almost a third of girls and more than one in 10 boys in North America were subjected to in-person sexual abuse during childhood, including sexual assault, rape and upskirting, the research found. The recorded rate of reports and notices involving child sexual abuse material rose by 63% in the US between 2024 and 2025, compared with 18% in Canada. Childlight estimates that more than 300 million children worldwide are victims of at least one form of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation or abuse every year, and that about one in four children will face at least one form of abuse before turning 18. A separate report by the Internet Watch Foundation last month said AI-generated child sexual abuse material was growing online, with the amount of illegal material investigated this year already exceeding the total for 2025.

Prof Debi Fry, Childlight's global director of data, said the findings revealed the shocking scale of child sexual exploitation and showed how quickly the threats facing children are evolving, particularly online. She said the findings also show where governments can make a difference, because evidence from surveys, police records and other sources can build a clearer picture of the risks children face and help target resources where they are needed most. Fry said the speed at which AI is changing the threat to children is deeply concerning, and that while improved detection and reporting may explain some of the increase, governments and technology companies must act urgently to understand and prevent these emerging forms of abuse and remove material rapidly. Paul Stanfield, the chief executive of Childlight, said millions of children are being subjected to sexual exploitation and abuse, yet governments too often work with an incomplete picture of where harm is happening and who is most at risk. He said there is nothing inevitable about child sexual exploitation and abuse, and called on governments to recognise it as a preventable public health emergency, invest in better evidence and turn that intelligence into action.

Articles.Title: Reports of AI-related child sexual abuse material rise 8,400% in two years, data shows - The Guardian

stories.Headline: China aims to make AI literacy universal for primary and secondary students by 2030
stories.Summary:
China plans to make artificial intelligence literacy universal for its nearly 200 million primary and secondary schoolchildren by 2030. The Ministry of Education has encouraged schools to develop pilot programs, train teachers, and launch specialized courses since 2024. This initiative ranges from teaching basic concepts in primary grades to utilizing complex tools and critical thinking for projects. The plan requires nearly half of all provinces and municipalities to implement mandatory AI plus education strategies.

Shanghai now requires at least 30 hours of AI skills training per year for every grade level. Beijing intends to establish 100 demonstration schools and use AI to monitor the health of students. The Ningxia and Gansu regions aim to include AI literacy in school entrance examinations by 2027, while Yunnan province plans to record and analyze lessons in 14,000 classrooms. Public procurement documents show that authorities have committed at least $31 million for learning platforms, teacher training, and classroom equipment.

The Ministry of Education is responsible for the broad push, while local leaders like Principal Yang Tianliang in Funan County, Anhui province, manage specific applications. Yang explained that AI agents ask students questions instead of providing immediate answers to help address a shortage of qualified teachers. At the Beijing New Talent Academy, thirteen-year-old student Peng Gaodi noted that he used AI to create over 200 applications, including a homework submission platform. The school in Anhui utilizes developments from Z.AI, ByteDance, and Alibaba's Qwen models.

China currently lacks a unified standard for assessing AI literacy, leaving individual schools to experiment with their own methods. One study of nearly 27,000 teenagers linked AI use to an 18 percent increase in homework grades but a 20 percent drop in monthly exam results. A separate survey of over 320,000 students highlighted risks of dependency and a decline in independent thinking. Students using AI at least three times weekly showed lower scores in creative, analytical, comprehension, and memory skills.

stories.Headline: Utah tests AI that diagnoses acne and prescribes treatment without a doctor visit
stories.Summary:
Utah is running a first-of-its-kind experiment to test whether artificial intelligence can safely deliver health care, including diagnosing patients and prescribing medication without a patient seeing a doctor, according to KUTV. The state's Office of AI Policy is overseeing pilot programs with seven companies testing different applications of AI in health care, and one of those companies is Nolla Health, which operates the Nolla Derm app. That app allows patients to receive an acne diagnosis and prescription without ever seeing a doctor face-to-face, the station reported on November 16, 2026. Patients older than 18 and not pregnant can download the app, pay a subscription fee and upload five pictures of their acne, after which the trained AI system makes a diagnosis and recommends treatment.

Dr. Zaid Fadul, chief medical adviser for Nolla Health, said the AI can prescribe only from a list of five to eight approved generic medications commonly used to treat acne, and the app prescribes Nolla Derm creams rather than oral medications. During the first phase of the pilot, Fadul and a second physician must review and approve every prescription before it goes to a patient, and if the AI performs well in that stage the program can advance to later stages giving the technology more autonomy. Utah's Office of AI Policy said the pilot programs will go through three stages and can operate for a maximum of three years, with independent evaluators selected by the state but paid by the participating companies determining whether the technology is safe and appropriate before it advances. Current laws governing patient safety and privacy apply to all the pilot programs, and Utah law currently allows only humans to practice medicine.

Zach Boyd, director of the Utah Office of AI Policy, said Utah does not have enough doctors and other health care professionals to meet growing demand, and the goal is to find out whether AI can take on some routine clinical tasks so physicians can focus on more complex issues such as cancer. Boyd said he does not believe AI will replace doctors anytime soon and acknowledged that AI will make mistakes, just as human providers do, but he said the technology will have to perform at least as well as a human provider before the state allows it to advance. Fadul said acne medication is relatively low-risk and a good way to test AI prescribing for patients who often struggle to get a timely dermatologist appointment, adding that he wants to increase access to physicians rather than replace them. Michelle McOmber, president of the Utah Medical Association, questioned whether AI should be placed between doctors and patients, saying it is not appropriate to take the physician out of the loop when prescribing medication, though she said AI could help doctors with paperwork and administrative tasks.

If the pilot programs are successful, their results could help guide the state in making regulatory changes, according to the report.

stories.Headline: South Korean law and accounting firms launch AI compliance certification service
stories.Summary:
Three South Korean law and accounting firms launched a new AI compliance-certification service on November 17, 2026. This professional service was developed by D&A LLC, LIN LLC, and Deloitte Anjin LLC to assist companies. These organizations want to help businesses assess and demonstrate their adherence to domestic and international rules. The firms created this tool as companies expand their use of artificial intelligence across various operations.

The certification process requires an evaluation of corporate AI management frameworks against several specific regulatory requirements. It measures these frameworks against the South Korea AI Basic Act, the EU AI Act, and various international standards. The service assigns compliance grades to companies based on how well they meet these legal obligations. These grades are intended to help businesses defend themselves against potential litigation over AI-related harm.

The developers of this service believe that public certification can bolster the legal defenses of companies using this technology. They stated that the tool helps firms demonstrate compliance with newly introduced artificial intelligence rules and existing business regulations. By obtaining these grades, companies can show they have taken necessary steps to manage risks. This approach allows businesses to prepare for future regulatory changes while maintaining their current technological growth.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: OpenAI Offers Free CSAM Tool, Adds 24-Hour ChatGPT Pause
stories.Summary:
OpenAI announced a new image classifier on Monday, November 16, 2026, at a press briefing in Washington, DC, according to The Verge’s coverage. The tool detects potential child sexual abuse material, including AI-generated imagery. OpenAI is offering free access to vetted organizations. The announcement has two halves: a detection tool for investigators and platforms, and new friction inside ChatGPT for users who try to find abusive material. OpenAI said it will also give developers guidance on detecting this type of content and train law-enforcement personnel on using AI in investigations.

OpenAI said the classifier can tell AI-generated abusive imagery apart from authentic imagery involving children. Access is free for vetted organizations, and OpenAI has not said how many groups are receiving access. OpenAI said new ChatGPT warnings will interrupt attempts to find abusive material, explain the consequences, and direct users toward specialist help. When the warning triggers, OpenAI said it will remove the flagged conversation and pause access to ChatGPT for 24 hours. OpenAI said it reports all identified CSAM on its platforms to NCMEC.

OpenAI attributed the wording in coverage to the company as a whole, and the coverage includes no direct quote from an individually named OpenAI representative. OpenAI frames the tool around efficiency, saying a classifier that ranks and flags files can shrink investigators’ exposure and speed the path to cases where a living child needs help. OpenAI says its Stop It Now helpline regularly hears from people who report that an AI chatbot sent them there, though OpenAI has not published a count of those contacts. OpenAI has not published accuracy figures in the coverage reviewed. The public coverage does not establish the classifier’s official product name, a release price beyond the free tier for vetted groups, technical accuracy, model specifications, training-data details, or how many organizations are receiving access.

The Internet Watch Foundation, a UK hotline, reported 3,440 AI-generated CSAM videos in 2025, up from 13 in 2024. IWF classified 65% of those videos, or 2,233, as Category A, the most severe tier under UK law, and 30%, or 1,027 videos, as Category B. Childlight data reported on November 16, 2026 put referrals of AI-generated material to the US National Center for Missing & Exploited Children at about 4,700 in 2023 and more than 400,000 in 2025, an implied two-year change of about 8,400%. Google and Microsoft have long offered hash-matching, content classifiers, and reporting or moderation tools, Meta uses automated detection, hash databases, human review, and NCMEC reporting, and Thorn’s Safer platform gives trust-and-safety teams tools to detect, review, and report CSAM. Small nonprofits and under-resourced police units stand to gain the most from free access, but only if the vetting process is quick enough for them to use.

For most of the past two decades, the fight against online child abuse imagery rested on a shared database model in which platforms hashed known files and compared uploads against them. A hash catches a file someone already identified but fails on a freshly generated image that no one has seen. A classifier can flag new material, which is why synthetic abuse pushes the industry toward models. Classifiers produce false positives and false negatives, and hashes mostly do not. OpenAI’s distinct move is the bundle, pairing a free classifier for vetted groups with developer guidance, police training, and user-facing warnings inside its own product.

The public coverage does not explain how removal of a flagged conversation interacts with preservation for investigators. Whether the tool reliably separates synthetic from authentic imagery is the open question, because OpenAI has not published accuracy figures in the coverage reviewed. Readers should expect child-safety groups to ask for a model card, an audit path, or both, and the sources reviewed for this story contain no evidence that either is public. How often each layer of OpenAI’s stack fires is not public. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Mullin says an expert blames AI for recent system outages while Duffy calls the situation a head-scratcher
stories.Summary:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said he spoke with an unnamed technology expert who blamed artificial intelligence for the series of system outages over the past few days, while Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called the situation a head-scratcher. Several cyber mishaps have occurred since last week, including issues with Microsoft systems, a nationwide ground stop due to a telecommunications error, several major online banks and banking services experiencing system failures, and an issue with United Airlines's system. The scenarios happening in tandem have caused concern that America's technological infrastructure is at risk. Mullin told Fox News that he spoke with a technology expert, whom he clarified was not SpaceX founder Elon Musk, who suspected AI could be attempting to fix problems when added to older systems.

Mullin said the expert told him these programs are not designed to work as fast as AI, so when a program able to write code goes in, it self-fixes, and as it starts self-fixing itself it is like doing a change order on a house, where changing one thing starts everything else changing. He described that ripple effect as causing systems to be overrun that were not designed to run as fast as AI technology is today. Mullin again clarified there is no evidence that the outages affecting aviation, banking, and Microsoft are the result of a cyberattack. He said he could tell with 98% certainty that this is not a cyberattack, noting that no one is out there taking claims for it and that they are not seeing the traffic or the footprints going in and out, so nothing points to it being connected other than what the cyber guy briefed him on about three hours earlier.

Duffy also recognized the apparent pattern of technology failures but mainly discussed the issues facing aviation, saying he was just learning about the issues facing United Airlines while pointing out the banking and Microsoft incidents occurring in the same time span. He said the United problem is not an FAA systemwide problem but that it is a head-scratcher, and that as of right now he does not know the root cause of United. Duffy said he asked the FBI to come in just to make sure to put people at ease that this was not a hack, and he said he thinks it was a network problem or a router problem or an installation error. The Department of Transportation has said the flight stoppage Friday evening was due to a disruption caused by an L3Harris contractor upgrading a telecommunications line from copper wire to a fiber-optic cable, and that as the contractor installed the new router, the new technology is claimed to have overloaded the air traffic control system, leading to the ground stop.

stories.Headline: Kingston building official Steve Knox proposes AI plan review software as council members raise privacy concerns
stories.Summary:
Kingston’s Building Department has proposed using an artificial intelligence-based application for plan reviews as soon as early next year, and several Common Council members raised privacy concerns when Director of Building Safety and Zoning Enforcement Steve Knox presented the idea to the Finance and Audit Committee. Knox proposed spending an additional $54,700 in startup costs for the software, which would be integrated with the department’s existing City Squared system used for online application reviews. The software is a yearly subscription, and Knox said the city would incur further annual costs to keep using it. He estimated the software could produce reports that now take three to four days in hours, and he told lawmakers he hopes to implement it as soon as early next year. The committee reviewed the request as part of the Building Department’s $2,046,724 request under Mayor Steve Noble’s proposed $69.4 million budget plan.

Lawmakers questioned Knox about data collection, privacy and potential errors by AI, and the promises of faster reviews did little to sway them. Michael Tierney, D-Ward 2, said he is cautious about the city outsourcing public data to companies and wants to know more about the firm’s data collection and retention policies. Common Council President Andrea Shaut said she is no fan of AI personally or professionally, questioned how data and privacy are handled and questioned the accuracy of AI, saying it gets things wrong, though she said she could see some value if there are reassurances about privacy. Teryl Mickens, D-Ward 5, said the application sounds like an amazing tool but raised concerns about how personal data is used and asked whether it would reduce the number of department personnel involved in permit review. Knox said most of the review process is done by three people in the department.

Bob Dennison, D-Ward 6, said that aside from concerns about who owns the data he thinks the software is a great idea, and that an automated turnaround for a building review would save time and complaints that reviews take too long. Knox assured lawmakers the software will still have a human component, with reports subject to review by staff, and said he does not expect it to result in staff reductions. He said the department eliminated a proposed code enforcement director position from its 2027 budget and that the software would help alleviate the need for the position, with some accusatory work on code violations shifted to the Corporation Counsel’s office. Sara Pasti, D-Ward 1, asked whether the software had been tested, and Knox said it had not been tested but that the department looked at a number of companies and systems before deciding this was the best fit. Lawmakers also asked whether the department had reached out to similar municipalities that have used the system, and Knox said, “We certainly can reach out to them and ask.”

Marissa Marvelli, a historic preservation professional, asked what effort the department is making to fully digitize the permit application process, saying even the online process still requires some handwritten forms and is stuck in early aughts. She said contractors have told her their online applications sit in an under review state for a long time with no indication whether more steps are needed, and Knox said the department hopes to move to a fully digital system by July 2027 and that the AI system could help avoid applicants getting stuck by sending emails asking for documentation and answering general questions. Knox said the department has reviewed around 600 units over the past four years and expects that number to increase. At the end of the presentation, Tierney questioned why the department waited until budget season to come before the committee at a special meeting instead of a regular committee meeting. The use of AI by area governments has drawn controversy, and on Thursday, Oct. 22, the Ulster County Sheriff’s Office announced it would not move ahead with AI-assisted report writing after a trial period and axed plans to add Motorola automatic license plate reading cameras, a decision that came as County Executive Jen Metzger signed an executive order banning AI surveillance technologies within her own administration, an order the sheriff supported.

stories.Headline: Tencent releases Hy4 flash to provide cost-efficient AI deployment for professional workflows
stories.Summary:
Tencent announced the release of Hy4 flash on November 17, 2026, to provide high-speed and cost-efficient AI deployment for everyday workflows. This new addition to the Hy model family features 224 billion total parameters, including 64 billion Engram parameters, while utilizing only 12 billion active parameters. The model supports multimodal inputs and a context length reaching up to 1 million tokens to handle diverse productivity tasks. It is designed to be the most cost-effective Hy model, offering decoding speeds that exceed 150 tokens per second.

The system requires a pricing structure of approximately 0.070 US dollars per million input tokens and 0.281 US dollars per million output tokens. Cached input tokens are priced at 0.003 US dollars per million, which represents a substantial reduction in cost compared to the previous Hy4 model. To achieve this, the team implemented hybrid attention, LatentMoE, and Engram architectural features, reducing the KV cache size to 1/24 that of Hy3. The model is currently available through Tencent Cloud TokenHub, WorkBuddy, Yuanbao, WeCom, QQ, ima, and Marvis, with OpenRouter integration arriving soon.

The Tencent Hy team stated that their engineering choices focused on practical utility and deliverable quality rather than public benchmark scores. They developed an internal benchmark called WorkIndex to evaluate tasks like spreadsheet repair, document editing, and PowerPoint deck creation. According to the team, Hy4 flash delivers a per-task cost that is 1/13 that of Hy4 Preview and 1/20 that of Hy4. They recommend this model for deep research and document processing, while suggesting the more capable Hy4 for complex software engineering.

Tencent previously released Hy4 on November 4, which ranked first among open-source models on the Agent Arena leaderboard. The company now plans to open-source Hy4 flash and will provide frequent iterations to improve its efficiency for real-world work. Users can access the model for free on WorkBuddy until November 30, 2026, or receive a 50 percent discount via Tencent Cloud TokenHub. This strategy aims to balance intelligence and efficiency for users performing common professional tasks.

stories.Headline: ROBOTERA deploys humanoid robots across China Post network in Guangdong to tackle labor shortages
stories.Summary:
Beijing Xingdongjiyuan Technology Co., Ltd., known as ROBOTERA, deployed humanoid robots across the China Post Group Guangdong Branch network on November 17, 2026. This initiative represents the largest and most geographically extensive use of embodied intelligence robots within the logistics sector to date. The rollout covers eleven postal hubs located in eight different cities, including Guangzhou, Shenzhen, Dongguan, Jiangmen, Shantou, Shanwei, Jieyang, and Heyuan. These robots are designed to handle strenuous frontline tasks to address persistent labor shortages and high workforce turnover.

The system utilizes a self-developed five-finger dexterous hand for flexible parcel handling and offers multiple power options for continuous operation. Since a pilot began at the Guangzhou Postal District Center in March 2026, the robots have reached an average induction rate of over 1,500 parcels per hour. This technology allows human employees to transition into higher-value roles such as quality control, operations coordination, and robot maintenance. The integrated solution also includes adaptive speed control and irregular-item rejection to prevent collisions and jams during high-volume sorting.

ROBOTERA developed these general-purpose robots using an AI-native, full-stack approach that encompasses foundation models, motion control, and humanoid systems. Company representatives stated that they are working with industry partners to integrate embodied intelligence into more real-world workflows to create a new engine for industrial productivity. They noted that Guangdong is the largest province in China by express parcel volume, providing a demanding environment for validating robotics at scale. The company has already expanded these integrated solutions to other postal operations throughout East China to adapt to various parcel types.

stories.Headline: Financial Times paywalls an article arguing the AI sell-off makes sense
stories.Summary:
The Financial Times published an article on 17 November 2026 under the headline "The AI sell-off makes sense. Staying bearish may not," but the accessible portion of the page contains only subscription offers and site navigation. No details of the sell-off, the companies involved, the figures behind it or the identity of the author appear in the available text. The article's argument, as its headline states, is that the sell-off is understandable while remaining bearish may not be, but the body of the piece is locked behind a paywall. Nothing in the accessible material says what happened, who did it or when beyond the publication date.

The page offers no numbers, dates or names connected to the story itself, only the pricing of the FT's subscription plans. Readers are offered a trial for one dollar over four weeks, after which the standard rate is seventy-five dollars per month, alongside other plans priced at forty-five dollars and sixteen point ninety-nine dollars per month. The article sits behind that paywall, so its claims about the AI sell-off and about bearish positioning cannot be checked against the text. The accessible page also carries a copyright notice for THE FINANCIAL TIMES LTD dated 2026 and a note that market data is delayed by at least fifteen minutes.

No person is named as responsible for the article in the accessible text, and no spokesperson or author is quoted anywhere on the page. The only statements available are the headline itself and the subscription terms, neither of which explains the reasoning behind the bearish warning. Because the body of the article is unavailable, there is nothing to paraphrase about what the author or anyone else said. The context of the sell-off and what happens next are likewise absent from the accessible material.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: OpenAI launches a science blog for researchers to share AI discoveries
stories.Summary:
OpenAI announced on November 15, 2026 that it is starting a science blog meant to give scientists and academic researchers a place to share what they are discovering with AI and how they are doing the work. The company said its mission is to ensure that AGI benefits all of humanity, and that accelerating scientific discovery is one of the most impactful ways it can work toward that goal. The blog will publish work across a broad range of scientific disciplines, including new scientific results and updates on ongoing research from OpenAI, its collaborators, and the broader scientific community. It will also share methods and practical guidance, such as how scientists use OpenAI models for scientific computing, data analysis, exploring literature, and planning experiments, including how to check the work and where a method falls short. The blog will further carry firsthand accounts from researchers using AI, what they are learning, and how these capabilities are affecting their disciplines, along with discussion of open questions about scientific practice.

The announcement cited several recent results from OpenAI. In September, an internal OpenAI system produced a proof addressing the Navier, Stokes existence and smoothness problem, a longstanding question about the equations describing fluid motion. In early October, the company released a broad range of mathematical results, among them a result on the quasi-Riemann hypothesis that sharpens estimates of how many prime numbers lie below a given number. Later that month, it shared results across mathematics, computer science, and physics concerning how waves concentrate, the limits of efficient computation, and the mathematical foundations of interlacing quantum field theory. In biology, OpenAI said researchers are using AI to analyze complex datasets, connect findings across fields, and develop new hypotheses to test in the lab.

Working with PerturbAI and Scripps Research, thousands of agents powered by GPT-Rosalind analyzed existing experimental data from millions of mouse brain cells in 32 minutes, according to the announcement. By connecting the effects of gene disruptions with scientific literature, the agents identified possible biological mechanisms for scientists to test. OpenAI also said César de la Fuente’s team uses ChatGPT and Codex to build algorithms that identify potential antibiotic molecules, which the team then makes and tests in the lab. The company said these capabilities bring new possibilities and changes to scientific practice, and that in mathematics, systems that generate proofs raise questions about how new arguments are checked, explained, and incorporated into the field.

OpenAI said that in experimental sciences, exploring more hypotheses creates opportunities and challenges in deciding which experiments to pursue, and that across disciplines researchers are considering what these tools mean for training, attribution, and the skills their work requires. The company said the implications will differ by field, and that scientific communities should help shape how these tools are used. OpenAI said it hopes the blog helps more people understand how AI is changing science and how they can use it to explore new questions and make discoveries of their own. The announcement did not say what the blog’s first posts will be or when they will appear.

stories.Headline: Bland releases Tofu-1, a full-duplex speech-to-speech model for phone calls
stories.Summary:
Bland, the San Francisco voice-AI company, released Tofu-1, a full-duplex speech-to-speech model in research preview, according to a MarkTechPost report dated November 15, 2026. The model is built for phone calls from moving cars, hospital rooms and weak-signal lines, and it listens while it speaks and reasons while it talks. For phone-agent teams, one model now handles audio in and audio out with no transcript in between. Tofu-1 is the first release in a planned family of Bland speech-to-speech models, and Bland has not published the internal architecture.

Most voice agents are cascades that turn speech into text, pass it to a language model and turn the reply back into speech, but Tofu-1 listens to audio directly so tone, hesitation and background sound stay available to the model. Bland lists speaker tracking, which tells speakers apart and works out who each one is addressing, and noise separation, which separates voices from a crying child, a TV, highway traffic, a hospital intercom or keypad tones. It also hears paralinguistics such as hesitation, frustration and urgency, and callers can interrupt or correct it mid-sentence while it keeps the conversation moving and reports a result only when the work is done. Because it models the sound of a call, it can also produce one, including a second speaker, the room around them and line noise.

Bland describes a TV Test that asks whether the model can follow the caller while ignoring speech from another scene, and the company marks its walkthrough as illustrative rather than recorded model output. Research preview access is open to a limited number of enterprises, with banking, healthcare, insurance and government named as target sectors, and the sign-up form asks for monthly call volume from under 1,000 to 50,000+. The only number Bland reports is that over 92% could not spot it in screenings, and there is no size, latency, pricing or benchmark data yet, while rivals publish latency and tool-use scores. Access is a closed enterprise preview, with Bland citing January availability.

stories.Headline: Financial services data leaders tie AI projects to specific business needs to secure lasting investment
stories.Summary:
Financial services data leaders discussed their AI initiatives in a recent conversation, InformationWeek reported on November 17, 2026, in a sponsored article sourced from Reltio. The leaders were at different points in their journeys, with some having just launched a first foundational data layer. Others were expanding an established foundation into new use cases, the article said. Each had deliberately selected an immediate business need tied to a larger company goal. That choice helped them win the support and investment to build something that would last.

The article said AI needs accurate, current and connected information to deliver results. It said the first question changes from which data to master to which problem to solve. Examples given were helping customers see their policies and reducing repeated account creation and manual data entry. An AI assistant helping a customer understand coverage must reliably connect that person to the right policies and current policy details. The article said an organization with 15 definitions of a customer will struggle to operate consistently or trust its numbers.

One leader shared a framework combining technical feasibility, business impact and risk tolerance, the article said. Another described how a structured prioritization exercise produced a different result than they might have predicted. The article said risk appetite usually depends on the impact. Internal use cases may allow for occasional inaccuracies, while decisions affecting customer experience call for full transparency and auditability. Using AI to flag suspected duplicate records for human review carries very different consequences from merging them automatically.

The article said business teams may take ownership of quality where data originates, with the data team taking over further along. It said everyone in the organization needs a unified standard for what trusted data looks like. A customer service agent may need details of a person's most recent interaction, while finance may care more about lifetime value. Both need a consistent answer to who the customer is, which makes interoperability essential. Some organizations are formalizing shared ownership through data products, which are owned and curated for use across the business.

The article said some leaders felt they could not fully resolve data quality issues until their legacy migrations were complete. Others focused on designing around existing systems, and some emphasized a fresh lens beyond a lift and shift. Leaders favored starting with smaller, well-defined use cases that could show results from start to finish and be repeated elsewhere. They paced change in line with where people were ready for it and where they were more likely to push back. The article said data quality is never truly done.

The article said many organizations Reltio works with begin transformation journeys to become more customer-centric and drive customer experience innovation. It recommended starting with one improvement to digital self-service and working backward to identify the data needed. It suggested starting with a couple of source systems and clear data ownership to demonstrate a quick win. It said AI models depreciate quickly as algorithms commoditize, while an enterprise's trusted data and context layer may compound in value exponentially. The article ended mid-sentence, saying true leadership means investing in the founda.

stories.Headline: Terray and NVIDIA fine-tune Nemotron models to extract chemical reaction data from papers
stories.Summary:
Terray Therapeutics, an AI pharmaceutical company founded in 2018, announced in October 2026 progress in its cooperation with NVIDIA on fine-tuning the Nemotron series vision-language models. The two parties fine-tuned the models to extract molecular structures, reactants and synthetic routes from chemical reaction diagrams in scientific papers. In the RxnCaption benchmark test, the model's HybridMatch F1 score increased from 59.8 to 63.4. The article states this progress does not mean the laboratory's synthesis efficiency improved. It reflects that the model's ability to identify and extract chemical reaction information was enhanced, providing more available data for subsequent synthetic route planning.

In November 2025, Terray named its system EMMI, a small molecule R&D platform connecting experimental hardware, automated workflows and multiple AI modules. Terray independently developed an ultra-high-density microarray chip to fix a large number of small molecules on the chip and measure their binding to target proteins in parallel. As of June 2026, Terray disclosed it had completed more than 420 billion individual measurements in total, involving more than 17 billion unique target-molecule interactions. Terray launched TerraSynth in June 2026, and in 17 internal projects the molecules proposed using this workflow are about 2 to 4 times faster in synthesis than design schemes not considering synthesis constraints, with synthesis delay reduced by up to 75%. On a single NVIDIA A6000 GPU, TerraBind-Struct's end-to-end inference speed for a single protein-ligand complex is about 26 times that of Boltz-2, and on the public CASP16 test set and the company's internal dataset its Pearson correlation coefficient is about 16% to 20% higher than Boltz-2.

In February 2026, CEO Jacob Berlin said in an interview with GEN that the company's fastest advancing self-developed project is a brain-penetrant inhibitor for multiple sclerosis, expected to enter the clinic in 2027. The interview did not disclose specific targets and preclinical data. In 2024, Terray expected its first candidate drug to enter the clinic in 2026, and by February 2026 this timeline was updated to 2027. In December 2025, Terray announced it had reached the first drug discovery milestone in its cooperation with BMS, saying the results involved challenging targets that previously lacked chemical starting points. The company did not disclose the specific target, candidate molecule, project stage or milestone amount.

In its cooperation with Gilead, the two parties carry out small molecule drug discovery and development around multiple targets, and if Gilead exercises its exclusive license option it will be responsible for subsequent development and commercialization of related compounds. Terray will be eligible to receive upfront payments, R&D and sales milestone payments, and sales royalties. In these cooperations, pharmaceutical companies mainly provide target resources and related disease biology knowledge, while Terray relies on its own high-throughput experiments and AI platform to carry out small molecule drug discovery. Recursion takes cellular phenotypic data as an important entry point, observing through automated cell experiments, high-content imaging and multi-omics analysis how cell states change after gene or compound perturbation. The article states that not all AI pharmaceutical companies take building their own laboratories as the core of platform construction, and even if they all invest in experimental capabilities, the data produced by each company is different.

The article states that AI can generate tens of thousands of molecules in an instant, but producing them still requires a large amount of time and experimental resources. It states that molecular design and computational screening are continuously accelerating, yet experimental capabilities do not necessarily grow in sync. Public databases have accumulated a large number of molecular structures and experimental results, but there are differences in detection methods, experimental conditions and data accuracy among different laboratories, and coverage of non-hit molecules is insufficient. For targets lacking known active molecules and not fully studied, it is often difficult to obtain sufficient training information relying only on public data. The article states that models can propose tens of thousands of designs, but the number of molecules laboratories can synthesize and test is limited, and the highest prediction score does not necessarily mean the molecule is most worthy of investing experimental resources.

The article states that whether Terray's platform can be truly transformed into drug assets still needs more project results to answer. It states that the platform continues to expand and cooperations are continuously advancing, but the self-developed pipeline is still in the preclinical stage. The article states that phased milestones in pharmaceutical company cooperation can reflect the application value of the platform in specific projects, but self-developed drugs still have to go through candidate identification, preclinical research and clinical trials. It states that a one-year difference is hardly a breach of promise, but shows that platform capabilities and clinical progress are two different curves. The article states that whether the technical system is effective ultimately needs to be answered by R&D projects.

stories.Headline: Claroc finds 37,571 Grok apps online and 94.7% open without login
stories.Summary:
Security firm Claroc discovered that more than 35,000 applications built with Grok are accessible without login, and some expose corporate confidential information and personal privacy data. Claroc tested 43,551 Grok Build application addresses, of which 37,571 are still online, and found that 94.7% of the online applications can be opened without logging in. Claroc estimates that about 650 to 800 of these applications contain private data. The affected parties include SpaceXSI, the merged entity of SpaceX and xAI owned by Elon Musk, and X. Tesla, which has not been merged with those entities, also did not escape the leak.

The involved institutions include SpaceXSI, X, and 30 other enterprises, 6 of which are listed in the Fortune 500. A Tesla service center scorecard posted the names, work efficiency and bonus details of 22 technicians on a public web page. A brief for ICU patients included patients' laboratory test results, imaging examination records and ventilator usage status. A contractor's working hour management application wrote the plaintext passwords of 18 accounts into the script, and anyone who visits the page can download the data. SpaceXSI's internal sales tool contained strategic customer accounts, sales business opportunities and internal team information.

SpaceXSI told the media that all applications are private before the creator actively shares them, and publishing an application requires multiple steps. The company also stated that its employee accounts are set to "Only you" by default, and users need to actively modify the permissions to make the application public. Claroc said that in its paid accounts used for testing, the pre-selected option on the publishing panel is "Anyone with the link". Claroc said being private before publication and who is allowed to access the application by default when publishing are two completely separate issues. Claroc said that even if you confirm multiple times, the system will not automatically add a list of team members to the access permission list.

Some people on X think that it is the users themselves who opened the permission incorrectly, while others think that Grok's default permission setting is problematic. Claroc used fictional data to build a customer management application for a four-person sales team on its own. The researchers found that the application adds the visitor to the team first, and then checks whether he is a team member. The researchers logged in with a Google account that had never been invited, and they not only saw all the customer data, but also successfully modified one record and deleted another. Claroc conducted a control test on ChatGPT applications, whose sharing panel is set to "Only me" by default, so even if others find the URL, they cannot access it.

When you use Grok vibecoding, it assigns a unique URL to each published application, in the form of random-name.grok.me. These random names are composed of several words, and the original design intention is to make them difficult for others to guess. Claroc found that these application addresses can be found in batches through Passive DNS databases. Every time someone visits a website, the computer queries the server address corresponding to the domain name through DNS, and some DNS resolution services collect these query records and store them in a searchable database. If the access permission of the application is set to "Anyone with the link", then anyone who finds the URL can open it directly.

After switching to the "Only you" mode, strangers will be denied access to the page and data interface, and unpublishing can also take the application offline within a few seconds. SpaceXSI did not start removing the relevant links until several hours after Ars Technica sent the interview email. As of the release of the report, all 24 applications created by SpaceXSI and X employees have been taken offline. A large number of applications created by other users are still accessible, and Claroc has begun to contact the affected institutions on its own. Ars Technica has not yet received a clear response on whether the platform will actively notify other affected customers.

stories.Headline: Google launches two specialized TPU chips and challenges NVIDIA's general-purpose roadmap
stories.Summary:
Google released two new TPU chips, the TPU 8tx and the TPU 8i Max, according to a 36Kr article dated 13 November 2026. Google designed the chips itself, and the article said the launch challenged NVIDIA's general-purpose chip roadmap. The 8tx is sold to government agencies and regulated industries and features chip-level data encryption. The 8i Max packages two chips in the same enclosure and focuses on ultra-long context processing. Amin Vahdat, head of Google's chip business, told Bloomberg that "the future belongs to specialization."

Google usually launched a new AI processor every two years, but that rhythm was disrupted in 2026. Vahdat said four TPU products will each be optimized for different needs. The 8tx works with AMD CPUs to encrypt data at the chip level, bypassing the usual step of decrypting data in memory before processing. The 8i Max integrates two TPUs in the same package, raising both computing power and memory capacity. Vahdat said that capability matters for drug R&D and mathematical computing and is also critical for programming applications.

Vahdat said Google could build one general-purpose chip for the whole market or launch different specialized versions, and that the latter approach lets it "actually create more value for our customers." He said the 8tx lets data be processed without first being decrypted in memory, part of Google's cooperation with AMD. He said the 8i Max's combined computing power and memory are important for drug R&D, mathematical computing and programming. He also said the TPU team gets early access to Google's latest Gemini model, which is used to improve chip energy efficiency and detect software vulnerabilities. He said AI is reducing the probability of design flaws that can cause billions of dollars in losses.

Oracle's senior vice president of cloud infrastructure, Karan Batta, said that as AI workloads become increasingly complex, customers need more choices. Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Mandeep Singh said TPUs cost about 30% less than NVIDIA GPUs while remaining competitive in throughput, though Google's TPU business margin is not that high. Counterpoint Research vice president Neil Shah said developers' time, code and project experience in CUDA are sunk costs that cannot be migrated. Jump Trading chief technology officer Alex Davies said the firm has thousands of TPUs, mainly to train models assisting trading research, but still mainly uses NVIDIA chips for model training, and only a small number of employees are particularly fond of TPUs.

Google TPUs have attracted Apple, Meta and Oracle, and in October Oracle announced that from next year its cloud customers could use Google TPUs for the first time, where they could previously choose only NVIDIA and AMD products. According to a recent regulatory filing, Anthropic has an option to buy up to $150 billion worth of TPUs between 2028 and 2031, and Bloomberg previously reported that OpenAI also plans to buy TPUs. Google wrote in its financial report that all currently available TPUs have already been booked by customers. Google cooperates with Broadcom on chip design and production coordination, signed an agreement with Broadcom competitor Marvell in recent months, and MediaTek is reported to be supporting the TPU business. A startup called Tenspresso, founded by two former TPU engineers, is developing its first chip aimed directly at the 8i Max's market, with design at least another year from completion.

Bloomberg Intelligence estimates that by 2028 Google's TPU-related sales of chips, software and hardware will exceed $135 billion, against an expected $12 billion this year, a figure that excludes revenue from customers using TPUs through Google Cloud. The same research says opposition to data center construction may cut the $1.4 trillion tech companies expected to invest in 2027 by 5% to 7%, spending that covers chips, network equipment, land and other materials. The article said market concerns about a possible slowdown in AI infrastructure investment are weighing on tech stocks, and the Democratic Party's victory in the US midterm elections has brought new uncertainties to data center projects. More than a decade ago Google developed TPUs to reduce its purchases of NVIDIA GPUs. The article said the competition is not about whose chips are faster but about who can make developers modify fewer lines of code.

stories.Headline: KAIST researchers led by Ro Yong-man develop AI that reads lips without sound to convert speech into text
stories.Summary:
Researchers at KAIST developed an artificial intelligence system that reads lip movements without sound on Sunday, November 15, 2026. A team led by Professor Ro Yong-man of the School of Electrical Engineering created this technology to convert visible speech into text. The system uses a diffusion large language model to identify clear words first and then interprets ambiguous ones using surrounding context. This approach allows the AI to overcome visual ambiguity by placing recognizable pieces of a sentence like a puzzle.

The framework, called DLLM-VSR, achieved a word error rate of 19.4 percent using the LRS3 dataset which contains 433 hours of video. This result was the lowest among methods trained solely with that specific labeled dataset. The researchers also implemented a two-stage training method to align lip movements with text and predict sentence lengths. This work received an Outstanding Paper Award at the EMNLP 2026 international conference on natural language processing. The project was supported by the Institute of Information & Communications Technology Planning & Evaluation and the 2026 Jang Young-sil Fellowship Program.

Professor Ro Yong-man, the corresponding author, stated that flexible word generation helps solve the fundamental challenges of visual speech recognition. He explained that the team hopes this technology will provide a foundation for physical AI systems used in industrial settings and everyday life. Postdoctoral researcher Yeo Jeong-hun served as the first author, while doctoral researchers Kim Chae-won and Rha Hyeong-seop acted as co-authors. They believe the system could eventually be integrated into communication aids for people who are deaf or hard of hearing.

The technology may also be useful in noisy industrial environments where traditional speech recognition fails to distinguish voices from background noise. Because the system has only been tested on research datasets, its effectiveness in clinical settings or daily conversations remains unproven. The team now plans to reduce the computational requirements and the size of the model. This will allow the AI to operate in real time on robots or wearable devices without needing an internet connection.

stories.Headline: KAIST team led by Noh Yong-man develops lip-reading AI that cuts word error rate to 19.4%
stories.Summary:
KAIST announced on the 15th that a research team led by Professor Noh Yong-man of the School of Electrical Engineering developed a technology improving the accuracy of visual speech recognition, which converts spoken words into text by analyzing lip movements. The team used a diffusion large language model, which repeatedly fills in blanks in a sentence, to decode ambiguous lip movements by leveraging surrounding context. Conventional AI models generate sentences sequentially from the first word, so an incorrect word at the beginning propagates errors through the rest of the sentence. The team changed this approach from reading in order from the beginning to reading from the most certain parts first. The system first identifies words whose lip movements are clearly distinguishable, then uses those words as clues to decode the remaining parts.

The team trained the AI on the 433-hour lip-reading video dataset LRS3, and it achieved a word error rate of 19.4%, the lowest error rate reported among previous studies using LRS3 as a training dataset with reference sentences provided. Word error rate is the proportion of words incorrectly recognized, omitted, or unnecessarily added when the AI's output is compared with the reference sentence. The team split AI learning into two stages, teaching it to associate lip movements in the video with corresponding text content and to model sentence length. When decoding speech, the AI estimated several possible sentence lengths based on video duration and selected the most reliable sentence.

The team received the Outstanding Paper Award at the international conference Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing 2026. Professor Noh said the study is significant in that it demonstrates how flexibly controlling the order in which AI generates words alone can overcome fundamental limitations of speech recognition with visual ambiguity. He said the team aims to establish a reliable physical AI foundation that can be used across diverse devices in everyday life and industrial settings. Postdoctoral Researcher Yeo Jeong-hoon is the first author.

Humans find it difficult to understand speech using only lip movements without hearing the sound, because there are words whose sounds differ but whose lip movements look similar. The research team's approach is similar to solving a puzzle by first fitting the pieces with clear shapes and then filling in the surrounding pieces. The technology is expected to be used as a communication tool, such as converting speech to text in noisy environments or supporting communication for people who are deaf or hard of hearing. It could be developed into devices that understand workers' speech in noisy industrial sites or assist conversations among people who are deaf or hard of hearing.

The research team plans to reduce the size and computational cost of the AI model so it can be deployed on various devices. Enabling real-time AI operation on wearable devices or robots without an internet connection is their next challenge. The articles do not state when the research began or how long the project took. More to follow.

stories.Headline: KAIST researchers use a diffusion language model to improve lip-reading AI accuracy
stories.Summary:
A research team from the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology developed a technology to improve visual speech recognition on November 15, 2026. Led by Professor Noh Yong-man of the School of Electrical Engineering, the team created a system that converts lip movements into text more accurately. This new method addresses the common problem where different sounds produce similar lip shapes, which often confuses traditional artificial intelligence. By utilizing a diffusion large language model, the system can now decode ambiguous movements by analyzing the surrounding context of a sentence.

The technology changes the processing order by identifying the most certain words first rather than reading tokens sequentially from the beginning. This approach allows the AI to use clear lip movements as clues to fill in the remaining blanks in a sentence. During a proof-of-concept test using 433 hours of video, the team achieved a word error rate of 19.4 percent. This system is designed to support assistive communication in environments where audio is difficult to hear, making speech more accessible.

Professor Noh stated that flexibly controlling the word generation order allows the AI to overcome the fundamental limits of visual ambiguity. He believes this work establishes a foundation for using trusted speech recognition across various industrial settings and everyday devices. Separately, KAIST is partnering with Nvidia to develop sovereign AI optimized for the Korean language under the leadership of Professor Kim Hyun-woo. Kim noted that South Korea lacks the massive training datasets available to English or Chinese markets, which can undermine the quality of local AI responses.

The joint KAIST and Nvidia laboratory aims to create one million high-quality Korean data samples for public release by the end of 2027. These datasets and training methodologies will be provided free of charge to help domestic companies reduce development costs. The researchers plan to generate synthetic materials and select high-quality examples to bridge the existing data gap. By perfecting these techniques for Korean, the partners hope to support other languages with limited resources and expand the global sovereign AI ecosystem.
