stories.Headline: Stanford review finds AI boosts task completion but not durable learning across 52 causal studies
stories.Summary:
On November 10, 2026, Stanford University's SCALE Initiative released an expanded evidence review examining 52 causal studies on artificial intelligence in education. The review found that AI tools frequently enhance real-time task completion and student confidence. It found that durable learning gains remain highly inconsistent. The review cautions university researchers, institutional review boards, and evaluation teams that passive cognitive offloading often undermines conceptual retention compared to structured pedagogical scaffolding. The report is titled The Evidence Base on AI in K-12: A November 2026 Review.

The report was published by the AI Hub for Education within the Stanford Center for Opportunity Policy in Education, the SCALE Initiative. It was authored by Seth Walker, Lily Fesler, JP Martinez Claeys, Chris Agnew, and Susanna Loeb. The synthesis expands a March 2026 baseline of 20 papers by adding 32 newly published causal studies released between October 2025 and June 2026, bringing the total evidence base to 52 rigorous investigations. The Stanford repository enforces strict methodological criteria, including only randomized controlled trials and well-identified quasi-experimental designs. The March 2026 review included zero student-facing causal studies in operational U.S. elementary and secondary schools, while the November update captured the first five domestic K-12 trials, though most research remains concentrated in adult and higher education contexts.

The authors highlighted a notable shift in setting toward the first five domestic K-12 trials. The core finding across the 52 evaluated studies is that educational outcomes diverge sharply based on whether AI provides cognitive scaffolding or enables cognitive offloading. When tools deliver Socratic guidance, clarify misunderstandings, and structure problem-solving steps, students achieve modest gains in conceptual mastery comparable to human tutoring. When students use models to offload intellectual tasks such as generating complete essays, code, or mathematics solutions, durable learning declines. In-session task completion accelerates, but unassisted post-tests reveal marked performance deficits compared with peers using traditional learning materials.

In multiple randomized experiments, students using AI reported elevated confidence, decreased anxiety, and perceived mastery, yet their objective exam scores failed to demonstrate measurable academic advantage. Generative fluency often conceals genuine comprehension deficits. Generative platforms reduced teacher preparation time for lesson plans, reading level adaptations, and grading rubrics without compromising curricular quality as assessed by subject-matter experts. Automated diagnostic systems providing feedback to novice tutors improved pedagogical technique and pupil outcomes. In classrooms where teachers relied heavily on automated instructional prompts, spontaneous teacher-student interaction declined, occasionally dampening student motivation.

Across evaluated platforms, students rarely logged the dosage required for measurable academic impact unless usage was mandatorily integrated into structured class periods. Following the rollout of foundational models in 2023, vendors widely promoted AI as an automated one-on-one tutor capable of rapid learning acceleration. Commercial claims overwhelmingly rested on correlational customer surveys lacking control groups. The Stanford SCALE Initiative established the AI Hub for Education Research Repository in early 2025. Independent coverage by Education Week underscored the tension between school district technology procurement and the finding that homework offloading undermines student retention.

Analysts emphasized that districts have deployed significant funding without established pedagogical guardrails governing home use. Reporting in Chalkbeat highlighted equity concerns, noting that under-resourced schools often lack the staffing needed to guide student AI interactions effectively. Researchers quoted across both outlets echoed Susanna Loeb's conclusion that AI is not a uniform intervention, but a medium whose efficacy is defined by how educators structure student engagement. Educational AI studies must incorporate delayed, unassisted post-tests to distinguish real skill retention from transient tool assistance. Investigators should formalize outcome measures and analytical models in advance by completing a study protocol preregistration, preventing selective reporting in a field facing commercial pressure.

Institutional review boards must adjust evaluation standards, and protocol assessments in classroom environments must evaluate cognitive risks and control-group fairness alongside privacy protections when students are exposed to task-offloading software. Experimental reproducibility requires detailed sharing of prompt templates, model versions, and interaction logs. Researchers should support their findings with an open data availability statement and maintain compliance via institutional responsible conduct of research training programs. The Stanford AI Hub for Education will continue updating its repository monthly.

stories.Headline: A systematic review finds AI achieves high accuracy in cancer imaging but needs prospective multicenter validation
stories.Summary:
A systematic review of 180 peer-reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2025 found that artificial intelligence systems, particularly those using deep learning, show consistently high performance in cancer detection and prognostic modeling across imaging modalities and tumor types. The review was published in Discover Artificial Intelligence, volume 6, issue 1, Article 1531, by N. A. R. Mohamed in 2026. Scienmag reported on it on November 15, 2026, in an article by Nathaniel Bowman. The study selection followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines to identify original research applying AI to major oncological imaging tasks. Early research focused on convolutional neural networks for basic pattern recognition, and the field has since evolved toward architectures integrating imaging with clinical and genomic information.

The review covered computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, positron emission tomography, mammography, histopathology, dermoscopy and endoscopy, and assessed each study with the QUADAS-AI framework. Several high-quality cohorts reached area under the receiver operating characteristic curve values above 0.90 for cancer detection, and certain curated whole-slide histopathology datasets reached an AUC of 0.99. Mammography-based deep learning models for breast cancer screening reported AUC values between 0.89 and 0.96, while lung cancer screening studies using 3D convolutional neural networks trained on over 42,000 CT scans achieved an AUC of 0.94. Approximately 20 percent of studies lacked clear documentation of recruitment methods or exclusion criteria. Only 21 percent of included studies performed external validation using independent datasets, and only 14 percent incorporated multicenter datasets.

The authors emphasize that prospective, multicenter trials are the necessary next step to verify robustness in routine clinical workflows and reliable performance across populations and technical environments. The reviewers identified persistent limitations in reporting standards concerning patient selection, data flow and timing. They note that deployment must occur without increasing the reporting burden on clinicians or introducing workflow complexities. The review states that ongoing monitoring of system performance is essential, as models may require periodic updates against evolving scanner technologies and changing clinical protocols. The authors identify future priorities including robust outcome-based clinical endpoints, federated multicenter validation strategies and continued development of explainability frameworks.

The review notes that saliency mapping and feature attribution techniques have been used to improve clinician trust by visualizing the diagnostic basis of predictions. Regulatory science frameworks increasingly emphasize structured reporting standards such as CLAIM to ensure clinical deployments are safe, effective and consistent. Federated learning approaches were noted for mitigating privacy and data-sharing constraints, allowing collaborative training across institutions without centralized patient data. The review states the highest clinical evidence currently supports AI as an adjunctive tool in breast and lung cancer screening, metastatic detection in digital pathology, and classification of dermatologic and endoscopic lesions.

The review says AI could reduce workload pressure on radiology and pathology services while maintaining standards for patient care and early disease intervention. Benchmark datasets such as BRATS facilitated advancement of U-Net and V-Net architectures, with more recent transformer-based models like UNETR further improving accuracy of 3D tumor segmentation and characterization. Handcrafted feature extraction allowed researchers to predict tumor phenotypes, survival outcomes and potential responses to immunotherapy in patients with lung cancer and glioblastoma. Vision transformers and self-supervised pretraining methods have emerged as particularly influential in enhancing representation learning for volumetric and cross-domain data.

These methods reduce dependence on large, manually labeled datasets, which have traditionally been a bottleneck in training and generalizability across institutions and scanners. Multiparametric MRI applications for prostate cancer provided automated lesion localization and Gleason grade prediction. The review notes that integrating tools into picture archiving and communication systems and existing electronic health record workflows requires overcoming medico-legal, technical and process-oriented hurdles. The ability to predict responses to therapies such as neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy in rectal cancer without excessive manual intervention highlights the practical utility of advanced architectures.

The research landscape is shifting toward large-scale foundation models and more tightly coupled molecular-oncology frameworks. The review leaves open how prospective, multicenter validation will be conducted and how reporting gaps in patient selection, data flow and timing will be closed. It also leaves open how regulatory, workflow and monitoring requirements will be met as scanner technologies and clinical protocols change. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Collin Hansen warns pastors that AI cannot replace scripture and prayer
stories.Summary:
Collin Hansen, editor-in-chief of The Gospel Coalition website, raised the question of whether pastors can trust artificial intelligence in an essay titled "Why AI Will Write Your Next Sermon," and he discussed the issue further in a telephone interview with columnist Terry Mattingly, whose piece was published on November 15, 2026. Hansen said AI had become a nearly daily part of his life over the past couple of years, as it has for many others, and that he has found help with home repairs, diet and exercise plans, meal preparation, trip planning, personal health assessments, and even baseball swing and pitching advice for his son. The deeper question, he said, is how AI will handle the problems pastors face as the faithful wrestle with parenting and careers, marriage and morality, sin and forgiveness, questions that affect work in the pulpit as well as private hospital conversations and prayers. Hansen said the software professionals who build these platforms struggle to separate factual questions from those focusing on ethics and morality, and he warned that pastors who seek AI help with sermons need to understand that. He asked whether AI means people do not have to study and remember the Bible as much, and said that doing so turns what used to be Bible study into some kind of science that can be chopped into pieces and processed, perhaps with another AI program.

He said the computer system does not recognize what happens in counseling, evangelism, apologetics and deathbed ministry, where there is a difference between asking AI to supply the answers you need and your own personal, intimate familiarity with the scriptures, and he said those distinctions will be lost on people who think these tools will make things more efficient. Religious leaders and pastors need to pause and ask what they are being efficient for, what they are trying to accomplish, what they will say to these people and how they will pray for them if they are not formed in the scriptures and in prayer themselves, he said. The article cited the third annual "State of AI in the Church" survey, conducted by AIforChurchLeaders.com, ChurchTechToday.com and others, which found that AI has moved from novelty to normal, with 93.5% of church leaders actively engaging with or exploring AI in their ministries. Two years ago 13% totally opposed the use of artificial intelligence in church work, and now only 2.4% say that, while 43% of church leaders reported using AI every day, double the 2024 rate, and 78% used AI weekly or more, up from 43% in 2024. The survey also found that 64% of participants used AI when doing sermon research or writing, and that a mere 9% of churches have a formal policy on using AI agents.

A Lifeway Research survey of Protestant pastors yielded more modest numbers, with less than 50% saying they are using AI, only 10% describing themselves as regular users and 32% experimenting with it, while 18% were intentionally avoiding AI and 20% claimed they were simply ignoring AI trends; 62% of pastors in that survey worry that users are not being honest about how they were using AI in ministry, and 55% affirmed that God has always shared His Word through people and AI isn't a person. Hansen said everyone knows AI programs can help users who are not gifted writers or speakers appear more literate, but it is also clear that these platforms struggle to separate questions about facts and those about doctrine. He said AI knows better how to answer Bible questions than a seminarian or an average pastor, but that a person will not get good, ethical, trusted advice from AI unless they ask for it. If pastors ask about the Ten Commandments, he said, they will hear the mean ethical take of an AI engineer in Silicon Valley in the year 2026, a human pretending to be an objective computer, and they will not hear the God who thundered on Mount Sinai.

stories.Headline: Career experts advise job seekers to build networking relationships before asking for help
stories.Summary:
Online job applications have become easier to send but harder to get noticed through, because employers increasingly use automated screening tools to evaluate large numbers of applicants, according to the Associated Press. Employment experts say that having inside connections from professional networking can help job seekers stand out when the robots threaten to reject a resume outright. LinkedIn career expert Catherine Fisher said networking is important whether or not someone is searching for a job, and that it is not just a nice-to-have because it sets a person apart and gives an edge. The advice was reported by Newser on November 15, 2026, in an article that also carried an unrelated item about Kalshi dropping Donald Trump Jr.

The experts offered several tips, starting with developing relationships before asking for help. Indeed career strategist Matt Berndt said networking is about relationship-building and that a common mistake is approaching it transactionally, meaning people reach out only when they need something. Instead of asking about job leads straight off, he suggests approaching contacts for specific career information or advice, such as asking about the job market and compensation where a contact works if you are thinking about relocating. Another way to start a conversation is to follow people on social media and comment on their posts.

Nisha Chittal, chief of staff at Vox, said first messages to a hoped-for professional contact should be brief and to the point. If you are inquiring about openings, she advises against asking vaguely about upcoming opportunities that would match your qualifications, and suggests instead asking whether the contact has or knows of openings for a specific position. Chittal also said a quick no to an online application does not necessarily close the door, because a personal recommendation is worth a shot since many recruiters are bombarded with applications and appreciate hearing about promising candidates. She said that generally if you have that kind of referral, someone will give the application a serious look, and that it is a tough environment to be job searching right now, so anything that makes a personal connection helps when there are many hundreds of applicants for a job.

stories.Headline: Shai Gilgeous-Alexander corrects reporter who cites false AI stat and warns against trusting AI
stories.Summary:
On Friday, the Oklahoma City Thunder lost 113-112 to the Los Angeles Clippers at Intuit Dome in an NBA Cup game, their third straight defeat, despite Shai Gilgeous-Alexander scoring 40 points. During the postgame press conference, a Los Angeles reporter asked Gilgeous-Alexander a question built on a statistic about his first-half assists that the reporter had taken from an AI-based search engine. Gilgeous-Alexander, the reigning back-to-back NBA MVP, corrected the reporter by saying the figure was a false stat. After Gilgeous-Alexander gave a routine answer about his efficient 40 points, the reporter admitted in a joking way that the incorrect stat had come from AI. The reporter then quipped, "Gotcha, don't trust AI," and Gilgeous-Alexander replied as he walked off the podium that people should definitely not do it.

The exchange changed nothing about the result, which saw the Clippers score the final seven points to escape with the one-point win, and Gilgeous-Alexander missed a shot at the buzzer. The loss was Oklahoma City's third in a row and dropped the Thunder in the NBA Cup, while Gilgeous-Alexander's 40 points came in a losing effort. The articles give no further numbers, dates or names beyond the 113-112 score, the 40 points, the two MVP awards and the Intuit Dome setting. Coverage of the moment spread through HoopsHype, ClutchPoints, Awful Announcing, Thunder Wire and other outlets, with headlines calling Gilgeous-Alexander the NBA's preeminent Anti-AI King. The articles do not say whether the reporter or his outlet faced any discipline, correction or policy change after the exchange.

The reporter is responsible for the incorrect statistic, having relied on AI search results without cross-checking the information, as Awful Announcing noted most people hardly do. Gilgeous-Alexander said the stat was false and, when the reporter joked about not trusting AI, told him not to do it and definitely not to do it. The articles do not name the reporter or identify his outlet beyond describing him as an LA reporter. The Thunder star's response drew praise online, with fans saying they love when players put media in their place and calling him the man. The articles do not quote the reporter beyond the few words of the quip.

The context is a difficult stretch for Oklahoma City, which the articles describe as a growing injury crisis and a depleted roster, with fans noting half the team is out. Gilgeous-Alexander has admitted the Thunder are maybe having their toughest stretch ever, and coverage says coach Mark Daigneault cannot ask him to become everyone as supporting players must step up. The articles do not say what happens next for the reporter or his outlet, and they give no follow-up beyond the exchange itself. Oklahoma City's next game and any response from the team or the reporter are not covered in the articles provided.

stories.Headline: SAP engineers contribute to Nvidia OpenShell to make enterprise AI agents auditable and controllable
stories.Summary:
SAP and Nvidia are deepening their collaboration to make autonomous AI agents in enterprises safer, more controllable and fully auditable from the ground up, according to a report published by e3mag.com on November 17, 2026. The two companies announced the Nvidia Open Agent Safety Platform and the widespread availability of Nvidia OpenShell, an open-source secure runtime environment that is to be deeply embedded in the newly consolidated SAP Business AI Platform. Thomas Pfiester, Head of Customer Engagement and Adoption and a member of SAP's Extended Board, took the stage at the 2026 DSAG Annual Congress in Cologne on Tuesday, October 6, where he outlined SAP's vision of the Autonomous Enterprise and presented the cloud as the foundation and AI as the engine for measurable business results. When e3mag.com asked afterward how an existing SAP customer keeps AI agents under control, Pfiester referred to the partnership with Nvidia without going into further detail, and a statement from Andre Lamego, Senior Vice President and Chief Product Officer for the SAP Business AI Platform Fabric, shed light on the technical background.

The arrangement goes well beyond a simple product integration, because SAP engineers are contributing directly to the Nvidia OpenShell codebase as part of the co-development effort. SAP's development work focuses on four specific core areas of the OpenShell project, including the decomposition of the runtime environment into independently deployable components by separating the supervisor layer from the actual agent execution layer to enable isolated scaling. For native Kubernetes operation, the contributions include operator support, the management of confidential access data for private container registries, customer-specific storage requirements and the orderly deletion of sandbox resources. SAP is also working to minimize the environmental and technical footprint of the gateway container image, expand driver support for heterogeneous computing infrastructures and embed monitoring of the supervisor's operational readiness and structured logging in line with established observability standards. At the governance level, the Joule Studio runtime environment serves as the highest authority, checking business authorizations, role-based policies and the relevant process context before a request reaches the actual execution layer, while OpenShell complements this with an isolated runtime sandbox that precisely controls what an agent is allowed to see and do and where inference data flows.

The collaboration is supported by the goal of achieving FedRAMP and FIPS certifications for regulated industries, as well as by participation in the newly founded Open Secure AI Alliance. SAP is making Joule Studio's runtime environment available to its customers and partners free of charge through the end of October 2026. According to the report, that free period is a classic bait-and-switch tactic common in the software industry, and existing customers fall for a costly illusion if they believe the use of autonomous agents will remain free of charge indefinitely. Once the grace period expires, the usage-based billing system, which relies on consumption-dependent AI Units, BTP Capacity Units and AI token prices, will kick in behind the scenes.

stories.Headline: Startup Fortune advises teams to version AI agent prompts in Git and tag every release
stories.Summary:
On 15 November 2026, Startup Fortune published a guide on versioning prompts for AI agents before a bad edit reaches production. The guide says prompts, tool descriptions, few-shot examples and the model name all change agent behavior, so all of them belong in Git. It says a release file names the live prompt version, and a rollback means editing a single line. It says the first version takes about two hours. It says nothing crashes when a prompt edit breaks an agent, which just gets quietly worse at something nobody was watching.

The guide says to keep the system prompt, tool descriptions and exact model ID in a Git repo and tag every release. It says to have the app read a small release pointer so a rollback is a one-line change, not a redeploy. It says to build an eval set of 20 to 30 real cases from your own logs and run each case at least three times. It says to block any prompt change that fails a must-pass case or drops the overall pass rate against production. It says to stamp the prompt version on every trace, and after any revert add the failing conversation to the eval set.

The guide says xAI said an unauthorized change had been made to the system prompt of its response bot, and that it would start publishing its system prompts on GitHub so people could see every edit. It says the fix xAI chose is one you can copy today. It says the prompt often sits in a dashboard text box, a Notion page or a string buried in a Python file, and someone tweaks it on a Tuesday because one customer complained. It says tool descriptions are the sneakiest, and rewording "look up an order" to "look up an order or refund" makes the agent call that tool for refund questions it used to hand to a human. It says to pin a dated model snapshot where your provider offers one, not a moving alias.

The guide says Microsoft 365 Copilot was hit by EchoLeak, tracked as CVE-2025-32711, through a crafted email its victim never opened. It says teams can limit the damage with narrow credentials, per-task tool lists, domain allowlists and human approval for irreversible actions. It says Langfuse's prompt management lets you attach labels to prompt versions, and your code fetches whichever version carries the "production" label. It says LangSmith keeps commit hashes for prompts and lets you pull by tag. It says a solo founder with one or two agents doesn't need either, because a Git repo and a release file will do.

The guide says in May 2025 xAI's Grok began answering unrelated questions on X with remarks about South Africa. It says Air Canada was ordered to pay about C$812 in February 2024 after its chatbot invented a refund policy. It says OpenAI began rolling back a GPT-4o update on April 29, 2025, after the model turned noticeably flattering, and later published a post on what its testing had missed. It says Promptfoo, an open-source tool, is built for this, describing prompts, test cases and assertions in a YAML file and running it from the command line. It says thirty cases at three runs each is about a hundred calls, a modest bill on most models.

The guide says to send the new version to a slice of traffic first, say 10 percent of conversations, or run it in shadow mode where it answers but the customer still sees the old reply. It says to run a rollback drill once, on a quiet afternoon, pushing a deliberately bad version to staging, flipping it back and timing it. It says to look at the eval set monthly, adding cases from new failures and dropping ones about features you've removed. It says not to change the prompt and the model in the same release, and to treat a model upgrade as its own versioned change. It says not to share one prompt across several agents, and to give each agent its own folder and its own tags.

Articles.Title: How to Version Prompts for AI Agents Before a Bad Edit Hits Production

stories.Headline: Economist Daniel Susskind urges parents to teach literacy, numeracy and critical thinking
stories.Summary:
Daniel Susskind, an economist at King's College London and a senior research associate at Oxford's Institute for Ethics in AI, published "What Should My Children Do: A Human's Guide to the Age of AI," Business Insider reported on November 17, 2026. The father of three speaks to audiences all over the world about how AI is changing work. The most common question he gets is what his children should do. Business Insider's Books Insider feature, written by Dan Slater, covered the book. A live Q&A between Slater and Susskind was set for 1:30 PM ET on November 17 in Business Insider's studio.

Susskind advises parents to focus on three basic skills even if AI does them better: literacy, numeracy, and critical thinking. He defines numeracy as basic fluency with numbers and data. He argues that one third of a student's time at college and university should go to learning about AI and how to use it. His strategy runs on two tracks, AI and non-AI, so students learn to use the technology and also to flourish without it. He writes that losing literacy, numeracy, and critical thinking would be "a disaster, leaving people unprepared for what lies ahead."

Susskind opens the book with an admission that no one, including himself, can predict the future. He writes that at the dawn of the internet era, no one could have guessed that search engine optimizer or social media manager would become jobs. He says coding, long seen as the safe bet, is no longer a certainty. He argues that AI can now offer everyone what Oxford's tutorial system once offered a privileged few, but better. He writes that the latest systems explain ideas, question students, and guide them through problems better than so many teachers he has watched, himself included.

Susskind says students should learn to use AI so they can "stand on the shoulders" of the technology and do tasks that would otherwise be unthinkable. He suggests English classes where students make sense of a basic poem without AI and a more demanding one with AI. He adds that students might prompt AI for intentionally misleading readings of a poem and critique each of them. He writes that there is a huge scope for creativity in making this change. He admits AI is warping and ingesting white-collar work far faster than blue-collar work.

Susskind's counterintuitive advice for early-career white-collar audiences is to stay the course. He writes that the future will likely see more domain experts, experienced humans who know what problems need solving, paired with AI that excels at solving them. He says it is crucial to move into a field because the underlying problems grip you, not the traditional job. He advises becoming a lawyer to help people navigate the legal system, not for the image, the lifestyle, or even the work itself. He says the roles most at risk include some of the most historically high-valued ones, where humans are merely a means to an end rather than an end in themselves.

Susskind counsels looking for work where people truly want a human involved, whether for aesthetic, empathetic, or moral reasons, such as artists and writers, athletes and musicians, nurses and carers, judges and politicians. He suggests education move away from building workplace competence and toward cultivating personal character as AI progresses, possibly toward outperforming humans at every economically useful task. That would mean moving moral questions into classrooms in a structured way, asking what is the right way to act and which laws and institutions are just. Slater writes that his 11-year-old son is a math enthusiast who works with tutors and participates in a competitive math team. In early October, OpenAI released 722 AI-generated math papers claiming solutions or progress on hundreds of open problems, and mathematicians are still checking the work.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Amazon faces voter backlash over its planned $17bn Ohio AI data centre
stories.Summary:
Amazon’s planned $17bn artificial intelligence data centre in Ohio is facing a voter backlash, according to the Financial Times, which reported the threat on 17 November 2026. The article names Amazon as the company behind the investment and places the project in Ohio, but its text is otherwise behind a subscription paywall. The report gives no further detail on who the voters are, what form their opposition has taken or when any decision is due. Beyond the headline and the date, the available article carries no other facts about the project or the dispute.

The article does not say what the $17bn covers, how many jobs the data centre would create, where in Ohio it would stand or what approvals it still needs. It gives no dates for construction, no figures on energy or water use and no names of local officials or campaign groups involved. Because the body of the story is locked, the only numbers available are the $17bn figure and the publication date of 17 November 2026. Nothing in the text explains what the voter backlash requires the company or the state to change.

The article does not identify who is responsible for the project beyond Amazon, and it carries no statements from the company, from voters or from public officials. No spokesperson is named and no comment is paraphrased, because the accessible text contains none. The only attribution is to the Financial Times itself, which published the report on its website. Any claim about what Amazon or its critics have said would go beyond what the article supports.

The context is limited to the headline’s framing of a large AI data centre bet running into local political resistance, and the article does not develop that theme in the text available. It does not say what happens next, whether the project is paused, reviewed or proceeding, or when further news is expected. Readers without a subscription cannot see the analysis behind the headline. On the material available, the story cannot be carried further without inventing detail.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Tim Cowen proposes robots.txt terms and antitrust action to curb platform power over publishers
stories.Summary:
Tim Cowen, the chair of the antitrust practice at Preiskel & Co LLP, recently addressed the struggle publishers face when negotiating artificial intelligence rights with dominant platforms. He argues that publishers are often forced to accept unfair commercial terms because they depend on these platforms to reach their audiences. Cowen believes that companies like Meta act as monopoly distributors, which gives them undue bargaining power over content they did not create. This power imbalance makes it difficult for publishers to refuse content collection without risking their visibility to readers.

To address this, Cowen proposes a framework where publishers use robots.txt files to set separate terms for search indexing and other AI uses. His plan allows web crawlers to index sites for free while requiring explicit permission and payment for any other material usage. He suggests that regulators should use the U.K. Competition Act, EU Article 102, and the Digital Markets Act to ensure fair licensing payments. Additionally, he wants authorities to stop Google from bundling its Gemini AI service with its monopoly search product to give rivals a fair chance.

Cowen stated that distributors should not be able to impose their will on content creators who lack meaningful negotiating power. He explained that the Movement for an Open Web provides a consortium for businesses to challenge these dominant platforms collectively. According to Cowen, the commercial value of digital content varies by time and importance, so individual website owners should set their own prices. He believes that public availability of a website does not mean the owner surrenders authority over how that material is subsequently used.

Articles.Title: Publishers Push to Keep Search Access While Setting AI Terms

stories.Headline: ChatGPT AI predicts Bitcoin could reach $220,000 to $280,000 by January 1, 2027
stories.Summary:
Bitcoin traded near $64,000 to $65,500 in mid-November 2026 after a sharp multi-week decline that erased much of its recent gains and triggered heavy liquidations. Sam Altman's ChatGPT AI predicted a historic bullish reversal could be on the cards by 2027. The prediction was published by Alex Ioannou on Sunday, November 15, 2026 at 12:00 PM CST on Yahoo Finance, citing 99bitcoins.com. Bitcoin had broken lower from the mid-$70,000s and tested the low $60,000s, with a cascade of long liquidations accelerating the move. The article described the forecast as pure speculation and entertainment, not a realistic base-case outlook.

The ChatGPT AI predicted Bitcoin could reach between $220,000 and $280,000 by January 1, 2027, with a stretch target above $320,000 in the most aggressive outcome. Key support sits in the $60,000 to $62,000 zone, with a deeper demand area nearer $55,000 to $58,000 if selling pressure intensifies. Overhead resistance is layered at $68,000 to $70,000 and then the more significant $75,000 to $80,000 region that previously acted as both support and resistance. Reclaiming $70,000 on a weekly close would be an important first confirmation in a standard recovery. The catalyst would require a sovereign wealth fund or national treasury to formally announce a multi-billion-dollar strategic Bitcoin reserve allocation.

The article said the move would be framed as a long-term reserve diversification decision, prompting other large official and quasi-official entities to follow. It said the resulting structural demand would overwhelm available supply and ignite a powerful new leg higher. It said the catalyst would require extraordinary coordination among major technology and infrastructure players that is currently highly unlikely. It said momentum had turned firmly negative on intermediate timeframes, yet the depth of the decline pushed many oscillators into oversold territory. It said that condition historically can precede sharp relief rallies once forced selling exhausts.

The article said US spot Bitcoin ETFs saw strong cumulative inflows earlier in the cycle, and institutional players continued to build infrastructure. It cited expanded custody offerings from traditional banks and specialized solutions such as the Blockstream, Thales custody system. It said reports of large holders and funds adjusting positions, including increases in related equities and ETF exposure by major firms, show sophisticated capital has not abandoned the asset class. It said Bitcoin has repeatedly shown it can recover from steep corrections when structural demand returns. It said the combination of maturing institutional infrastructure and the theoretical potential for large-scale official adoption keeps the door open for a powerful rebound.

The article said the over-the-top bullish scenario still leaves room for a dramatic recovery by January 1, 2027. It said the landmark catalyst is a highly unlikely but not impossible supercharged outcome of genuine institutional progress. It said the scenario builds on recent developments such as major banks expanding digital-asset custody services and large institutions quietly increasing Bitcoin-related exposure. It said under the extreme sovereign-reserve catalyst, intermediate levels would be cleared rapidly, allowing measured-move extensions and multi-cycle projections from the current base. It said the past week's price action was unambiguously painful and had tested investor resolve.

The article directed readers to follow 99Bitcoins on X for the latest market updates and to subscribe on YouTube for daily expert market analysis. It said the prediction remains pure speculation and entertainment. It said the catalyst would require extraordinary coordination that is currently highly unlikely. It said the door stays open for a powerful rebound without stating what would confirm the extreme scenario beyond the sovereign reserve announcement. It left open whether any sovereign wealth fund or national treasury would actually announce such an allocation.

stories.Headline: Leopold Aschenbrenner's Situational Awareness fund buys back AI stocks and takes a $440 million stake in SharonAI
stories.Summary:
Leopold Aschenbrenner's artificial intelligence-themed hedge fund Situational Awareness, which nearly collapsed in July, loaded back up on AI stocks as it returned to financial markets at the end of the third quarter, according to a new regulatory filing reported by CNBC on November 17, 2026. As the fund got back on its feet, Aschenbrenner took an equity position in Australian neocloud company SharonAI valued at more than $440 million, along with equity stakes in AI-centric plays Cleanspark, IREN, Bitdeer Technologies and Fermi. The Cleanspark stake is worth almost $39 million, while the IREN and Bitdeer stakes are more than $21 million and more than $20 million respectively, and the Fermi stake has a value of more than $11 million. The fund also owned call options at the end of September in neocloud Nebius, memory chip name Sandisk, the Roundhill Memory ETF and data center power play Bloom Energy, with Sandisk and Nebius being key holdings that almost took out his fund over the summer.

All of these Situational Awareness holdings have been routed since September 30, with SharonAI at the top of that list after a 58% loss in October and an 11% fall so far this month. IREN was down 41% in October while Nebius declined 35%, and last week Nebius plummeted more than 16% in a single day after the company issued a weak full-year forecast. It is not known whether the hedge fund manager got out of those positions during the October AI selloff, because the 13F filing is just a snapshot of what the hedge fund held at the end of the quarter. The near-collapse of his hedge fund over the summer forced him to sell all of its public equity positions to Ken Griffin's Citadel, and the fund had $45 billion in assets at its peak before that tumbled to around $10 billion, consisting mostly of private stakes.

Aschenbrenner, who launched the fund in 2024 after rising to fame that same year with his AI manifesto also entitled Situational Awareness, re-entered financial markets a bit in September, sources told CNBC at the time, and the Monday filing shows he picked up right where he left off. Stocks tethered to the AI trade took a hit in the most recent quarter as investors grew concerned about a slowdown in development of the technology, fears spurred by comments from industry leaders such as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman back in September. In recent weeks, investors have worried about how Democratic wins in the midterm elections could hinder data center development, whether some technology companies are using too much debt to finance the AI buildout and what role Nvidia will play in that financing with Jensen Huang now out as CEO at the company. Losses in Nvidia as well as other AI-related stocks dragged down the three leading U.S. indexes during Monday's session as investors continued to assess the fallout of Huang's departure.

stories.Headline: Quantum X and Everest Cloud sign MOU to bring quantum and AI services to six South Asian markets
stories.Summary:
Quantum X and Everest Cloud signed a memorandum of understanding on November 6, 2026, to bring Quantum X's quantum computing and AI infrastructure products to customers across six South Asian markets, according to a press release from Quantum X. Everest Cloud is the Kathmandu-based cloud services brand of Digital Network Solutions Pvt. Ltd. The non-binding agreement gives Everest Cloud's customers access to Quantum X's EntangleX platform and broader AI and data infrastructure solutions in Nepal, India, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Sri Lanka and the Maldives. It also establishes a reciprocal arrangement under which Quantum X will promote Everest Cloud's services to U.S. customers, with both companies planning joint sales and technical integration.

The MOU has a two-year initial term and is non-binding, and the parties intend to sign a definitive Channel Partner Agreement within 90 days. Under the reciprocal, non-exclusive arrangement, each party earns commissions on revenue from customers it refers, with registered leads protected for twelve months and the option for either party to resell the other's products. The go-to-market plan includes joint sales calls, co-branded proposals, bundled offerings, joint marketing and technical integration between the two platforms, overseen by dedicated partnership managers and quarterly senior leadership reviews. Quantum X has not attributed a revenue estimate to the partnership and will report on referred customers as they are secured.

Emil Assentato, Chief Executive Officer of Quantum X, said the next phase of quantum and AI will be decided by access rather than hardware alone, and that Everest Cloud already serves the banks, telecom operators, universities and data centers EntangleX was built for. Ujjwal Roy, Head of Strategy and Chief Scientist of Quantum X, said working with Everest Cloud gives EntangleX a trusted local channel into these markets while giving U.S. organizations access to reliable cloud infrastructure from the region. Arun Khatri, Chief Executive Officer of Digital Network Solutions Pvt. Ltd., said the partnership opens the U.S. market to Everest Cloud and gives its clients access to quantum computing and advanced AI infrastructure through a trusted local partner. Khatri said the MOU lays a strong foundation for the company's vision of becoming a "Local to Global" company from the Himalayas.

The partnership gives EntangleX its first international route to market, through a cloud provider serving enterprises, banks, telecommunications operators, government bodies, universities and data centers across the six markets. IBM, Tata Consultancy Services and the Government of Andhra Pradesh have announced plans to deploy an IBM Quantum System Two in Amaravati, and India's National Quantum Mission is funding research and startups nationwide, while Amazon Web Services and IBM already offer quantum computing as a cloud service. EntangleX is a hosted circuit simulation and labs platform, live at entanglex.co as a minimum viable product, where users can build circuits gate by gate in a visual editor, send larger simulations to a hosted job queue and use Agentic Labs to turn a plain-language description of an experiment into a draft circuit. SliceX, Quantum X's platform for GPU slicing and security within the slices, has proven its ability to slice, but completion of the security issues between the slices is still subject to funding.

stories.Headline: Tax partners say AI token models complicate corporate value and tax treatment
stories.Summary:
Corporate capital structures have long centered on debt and equity, but artificial intelligence and token-based business models are beginning to complicate that framework, according to a Bloomberg Tax article published on November 17, 2026 by Megan Lisa Jones, a tax partner at Holland & Knight, and Fotis Konstantinidis, a managing director at Stout. Technology companies can now combine stock with tokens, token warrants, digital incentives, access rights, and governance mechanisms, while AI businesses develop new ways to monetize services. The result is a structure in which economic value may no longer reside entirely in corporate equity, and where tax treatment can be far less settled than for traditional stock and debt. A token does not necessarily represent ownership in a legal entity, and its value may instead depend on network growth, utility, scarcity, trading demand, or contractual rights.

The article says the IRS treats digital assets as property rather than currency under Notice 2014-21, so a sale or exchange of a token generally produces gain or loss, and receiving tokens as compensation, as payment for goods or services, or through staking or an airdrop can result in ordinary income. The guidance explains how a holder is taxed when it receives or disposes of a digital asset but does not say what a particular token is, and there is no comprehensive authority on whether a token is stock, debt, a partnership interest, an option or forward contract, or simply property. A token that is a security under the Howey test is not necessarily stock or debt for tax purposes, and a corporation generally does not recognize gain when it issues its own stock, but there is no comparable rule for tokens. Tokens issued to employees and service providers raise questions of timing, valuation, and withholding, including whether a Section 83(b) election is available, and in an acquisition tokens delivered to selling holders are unlikely to count as stock of the acquirer.

The authors say the law in this area has not caught up with the technology, with no comprehensive statute, regulation, or ruling addressing whether a token is debt or equity, and existing guidance deals only with specific fact patterns such as hard forks, airdrops, and staking. They advise companies to expect to take positions without clear authority, document the basis for them, and revisit them as guidance develops, and say tax advisers should be involved when the token is designed rather than after it has been issued. For management teams and boards, they write that the most important question may be the simplest, namely what business problem the token is solving, followed by understanding the economic rights being created and how those rights interact with existing shareholders. The article says the opportunity is real because AI and digital assets may allow companies to create forms of ownership, participation, and economic incentive that were difficult to implement through traditional capital structures alone, but that greater flexibility comes with greater complexity.

Articles.Title: AI-Monetized Digital Assets Muddle Corporate Value, Tax Treatment

stories.Headline: Redwood AI plans Quantum.IQ expansion for Canadian and U.S. defence compliance
stories.Summary:
Redwood AI Corp. announced on November 15, 2026 that it plans to expand its Quantum.IQ post-quantum cybersecurity platform to enhance operability with certain Canadian and U.S. defence compliance capabilities. The work is being undertaken by the company's cybersecurity and compliance software development team, comprised of employees and consultants. The Vancouver, BC based company made the announcement through ACCESS Newswire. The expansion responds to potential customer requirements under Canada's Canadian Program for Cyber Security Certification and the United States' Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification. Redwood trades on the CSE under AIRX, on the OTCQB under RDWCF, and on the Frankfurt exchange under Y0N with WKN A422EZ.

The company's initial development focus is on capabilities intended to support Level 1 requirements under the CPCSC and CMMC programs. Redwood is developing functionality for the Quantum.IQ platform intended to help users maintain inventories of applicable cybersecurity controls, organize supporting documentation and assemble evidence used in compliance workflows. The planned capabilities are intended to draw from live technical data generated through the platform, reducing reliance on manual evidence collection. The planned capabilities would extend the platform beyond cryptographic asset discovery, quantum-readiness assessment and post-quantum migration planning. Where higher levels of assurance require independent third-party assessment, Redwood expects those requirements would be addressed through relationships with appropriately qualified or accredited assessors rather than through the platform itself.

Louis Dron, Chief Executive Officer of Redwood AI, said cybersecurity compliance is becoming increasingly connected to the ability of companies to participate in defence supply chains. Dron said that for many organizations this is no longer simply about adopting cybersecurity best practices. He said organizations need to understand their environment, demonstrate that required controls are in place and produce evidence to support that position. Dron said that by expanding Quantum.IQ's capabilities in this area, the objective is to help organizations address cybersecurity requirements they face today. He said the objective also includes preparing their systems for the transition to post-quantum security.

The company believes that as these requirements become increasingly integrated into North American defence procurement, organizations will need to demonstrate that appropriate cybersecurity controls are in place to participate in applicable contracting opportunities. The development forms part of Redwood's broader strategy of applying artificial intelligence and post-quantum cybersecurity technologies to security challenges facing government, defence, critical infrastructure and other mission-critical operations. Redwood AI describes itself as a technology company developing advanced artificial intelligence and cybersecurity solutions for defence, public safety and life sciences. The company applies artificial intelligence across quantum cybersecurity, scientific research and advanced chemistry applications. Redwood AI's technology is designed to help organizations prepare for quantum-enabled cybersecurity threats while enabling faster, more efficient development of new therapies and chemistry-driven applications.

Post-quantum cybersecurity is focused on preparing digital systems and cryptographic infrastructure for a future in which sufficiently capable quantum computers could compromise certain encryption methods widely used today. "Q-Day" refers to the point at which sufficiently capable quantum computers could break certain forms of conventional encryption currently used to protect sensitive communications, business information and financial data. Experts have warned that Q-Day could potentially arrive within the next five to ten years. Concerns extend to "harvest now, decrypt later" attacks, in which adversaries collect encrypted information today with the intention of decrypting it once sufficiently capable quantum computers become available. Enterprise users spent approximately US$300 million on quantum initiatives in 2025, surpassing the combined spending of research laboratories and governments for the first time, according to research from Boston Consulting Group.

The same research found that 62% of 275 major global companies across 11 industries were spending at least US$1 million annually on quantum initiatives and had established dedicated quantum programs. Companies are investing in both potential commercial applications of quantum computing and defensive efforts to protect systems against the future ability of quantum computers to break existing encryption technologies. Redwood's forward-looking statements note risks including delays, cost overruns or technical challenges in developing, testing, integrating or deploying the planned capabilities. Risks also include changes to, delays in, differing interpretations of, or the company's inability to satisfy requirements under the CPCSC, CMMC or other applicable standards. The company states that the platform is not itself an assessment, certification or guarantee of compliance, procurement eligibility or contract award.

stories.Headline: The Hallway rebuilds its agency model around AI-powered CERTNTY OS
stories.Summary:
The Hallway, an independent advertising agency, has rebuilt its business around a new operating system called CERTNTY OS, which it designed to help marketers make better investment decisions and deliver more effective communications faster. The launch, reported on 15 November 2026, marks the culmination of an 18-month transformation during which the agency expanded its capabilities across media, data and measurement, invested in AI-powered products and introduced a new positioning called Calculated Creativity. Founder and CEO Jules Hall said the industry in which The Hallway started no longer exists and that agencies still operating as though nothing has changed are heading for extinction, particularly larger agencies where change is harder. He said marketers face more complexity than ever, including fragmented media, overwhelming amounts of data, greater scrutiny of budgets and a fundamental shift in the economics of production, yet businesses still need to grow and marketers still need to show their investment is delivering. Rather than bolt AI onto an existing agency model, he said the agency asked what it would build if it were starting The Hallway today.

The new model connects strategy, creative, media and measurement through a single operating system, and over the past 18 months the agency added media specialists led by head of media and connections Phoebe Keogh. CERTNTY OS combines proprietary processes, commercial intelligence and AI-powered tools across three stages of marketing investment: MODEL, which combines customer, audience and commercial intelligence to identify growth opportunities and inform investment decisions; MAKE, which connects strategy with creative development and AI-enabled production; and MEASURE, which connects brand, behavioural and commercial performance to assess effectiveness and inform future investment. Keogh said the advertising is the visible output but only part of the job, and that understanding how customers discover a brand, what influences their purchase decisions and which part of the customer experience will create the greatest impact is just as important. She said most marketers understand the value of building a brand, but the harder question is how much to invest, where to invest it and how to demonstrate the commercial return, which is the problem CERTNTY OS was built to help solve.

The agency pointed to its work with Webjet as an example of the connected approach, beginning with customer research, brand strategy, identity, customer value propositions and staff engagement and extending to investment modelling, media strategy and the Go Somewhere creative platform. Analysis with Webjet found that customers arriving directly or through organic search were more likely to purchase and generated higher transaction values, insights that supported a significant shift from performance-led spending towards brand investment. In its FY26 reporting, Webjet recorded a 9.7% increase in new site visitors following the relaunch and an improvement in customer acquisition costs of 29% compared with the corresponding six months a year earlier. Webjet CMO Oonagh Flanagan said every channel has been thought about and connects back to Go Somewhere, and that the data, thinking and strategic mindset The Hallway brought went far beyond what a traditional creative agency would have done. As The Hallway approaches its 20th anniversary, Hall said creativity remains its greatest competitive advantage but the way it is applied, produced and measured has fundamentally changed, and that AI lets the agency do things that were not commercially viable a few years ago.

Articles.Title: The Hallway rebuilds agency model around AI-powered CERTNTY OS

stories.Headline: Can AI Replace Club Fitters?
stories.Summary:
Earlier this year, Club Champion leaned heavily into artificial intelligence with its proprietary AI Co-Pilot system, and a Plugged In Golf writer recently watched the system in action to see whether it could replace fitters completely. The fitting was one of his friends fitting another, and the fitter was Drew Koch, a Plugged In Golf staff writer and master club fitter with Club Champion. The golfer was Alex, who is 51 and a very solid player looking for a driver to replace his eight year old PING G400. Alex came in viewing his driving as consistent and reliable but not a big strength. The fitting started with Alex making ten swings with his current gamer while Drew talked him through what he was seeing in the numbers.

All of the Trackman data was then fed into AI Co-Pilot, and the system generated five shaft recommendations ranging from a 60 gram stiff flex to a 40 gram senior flex. Shaft testing started with the Fujikura Ventus Blue 5-S, and after a couple of swings Drew saw it was a poor fit for Alex's smooth transition. The data from those swings went into AI Co-Pilot, the recommendations changed slightly, but Drew went off script and pulled the Fujikura Ventus White in 4-R, which was not on the list but was in line with the smooth, 40 gram option the system suggested. Results with the Ventus White were excellent, with club and ball speed up and smash factor crossing the 1.5 threshold several times. Drew fed that data into AI Co-Pilot, which generated more new ideas but began to hone in on Alex's preference for something lighter and softer, and a couple more shafts were tested but nothing outperformed the Ventus White.

With the shaft choice locked in, Drew asked AI Co-Pilot which head would be a good fit, and the system returned two options: the PING G440 LST that Alex was already using to test shafts and the Titleist GTS2. Both options performed well, but there was little question that the PING was the better option for Alex. Alex picked up roughly 8 MPH of ball speed, over 7 yards of carry, and over 18 yards total while painting the center line. The author wrote that AI Co-Pilot, with well over 50,000,000 data points in its system, shows the range of possible solutions, simultaneously narrowing the field and keeping options open. He added that unlike human fitters, AI is not going to get stuck in a rut of solving the same problem the same way every time, and with access to every fit from every fitter it is constantly finding the newest, best solution.

The author said that while AI Co-Pilot started with a wide net during the shaft fitting, once it had enough data it was able to speed them toward the final answer with the club head. Toward the end of the fitting, Alex noted that he was getting tired, and having to only test two driver heads was extremely helpful in making the fitting efficient. The author argued that in an AI fitting there is no conversation, just ten shots and a bunch of numbers, and the AI does not understand who the golfer is as a player, what they are trying to achieve, what brands they love, or what sound they hate. He said the AI cannot pull the plug on a bad combination the way a human fitter can, seeing one bad swing as just one data point where an experienced human fitter sees a golfer fighting a shaft that is never going to work. He noted that in the fitting he watched, the best combination did not come directly from AI Co-Pilot's list of suggestions, and Drew was able to get to it faster because of his experience and knowledge of Alex's swing.

The author wrote that he is sure some people once worried that launch monitors would replace club fitters, and the same with interchangeable heads and shafts, but neither did and AI will not either. He said all of these things are tools that a skilled club fitter can use to deliver a better fit for the golfer. He concluded that if you want the best fitting, you want the best human fitter using the best technology, meaning the best launch monitors, the most hittable combinations, and the smartest AI, all of which he said can be found at Club Champion. The article was published on November 17, 2026, by Matt Saternus, editor in chief at Plugged In Golf, who founded the site in 2013 and has over 16 years of golf industry experience. Saternus lives in the northwest suburbs of Chicago with his wife and two daughters.

More to follow.

Articles.Title: Can AI Replace Club Fitters?

stories.Headline: Springer Nature reports 6.3% revenue growth as AI and open access lift research publishing
stories.Summary:
Springer Nature reported financial results for the first nine months of 2026, with growth in its academic publishing business driven by increased journal output, expanding open access agreements and continued investment in AI-enabled publishing technology. The publisher reported group revenue of €1.47 billion for the nine months to September, up from €1.43 billion in the same period last year, representing underlying growth of 6.3%. Adjusted operating profit increased to €427.8 million, with underlying growth of 7.7%. Its Research division remained the principal driver of performance, generating revenue of €1.15 billion, with underlying growth of 7.4%, while adjusted operating profit in the division rose to €369 million, reflecting underlying growth of 8.4%.

The company reported a 12% increase in published research articles during the period, compared with estimated market growth of approximately 8%, with growth recorded across its fully open access, Nature and Springer journal portfolios. During the first nine months of 2026 it signed 23 new transformative agreements with national consortia, government bodies and research institutions, bringing its total number of transformative agreements to 105, covering more than 4,500 institutions worldwide. The company also launched 54 journals during the period, including Nature Progress Oncology, npj Nephrology, BMC Sustainability and Scientific Reviews, a multidisciplinary sister publication to Scientific Reports, and the launches included 17 titles in its Discover portfolio. More than 62% of manuscript submissions were processed through SNAPP, the publisher's integrated AI-enabled publishing platform, during the first nine months of 2026, and the company reported progress with Nature Research Assistant, its AI-powered research tool, which is currently in beta testing with more than 25,000 users.

Frank Vrancken Peeters, CEO of Springer Nature, said the performance in the first nine months of 2026 was again led by the Research segment, and that this continued momentum is driven by leadership in open access, the use of AI-enabled tools and continuous investment. He said the company has updated its guidance and now expects underlying revenue growth for the Group of at least 6% in 2026 with at least 30bps of margin expansion. Springer Nature said it had completed its 2026 contract renewals, while negotiations for the next renewal cycle, which began in September, were progressing as expected.

The company said AI-enabled technology remains a central element of its publishing strategy, with investment focused on improving editorial workflows, strengthening research integrity and supporting researchers. Nature Research Assistant is scheduled for launch in early 2027 and continues to achieve customer satisfaction scores above 80%, including for newer features such as Manuscript Adviser, introduced earlier this year. Beyond publishing workflows, Springer Nature reported growth in its text and data mining services and new ARC3 licensing partnerships with corporate customers, which enable organisations to access scientific content within AI-powered environments. Its books business also recorded revenue growth across print and digital formats, and the publisher introduced the first titles from its new Nature Books imprint at the Frankfurt Book Fair in October. The company completed the disposal of its consumer media businesses, selling Scientific American to LabX Media Group in June and Spektrum to GeraNova Bruckmann in July, which it said represents a further concentration of its portfolio on its core research publishing and related activities.

This funding will come from the public offering and a separate private placement. These financial activities were reported by Bloomberg on November 15, 2026. The reports describe a significant effort to secure a large amount of capital.

One method is the initial public offering and the other is a private placement. These figures represent the total financial goal for the company and its supporters. The oversubscription rate shows that demand for the shares is seven times higher than supply.

The sources for this information are people familiar with the matter. These sources indicate that the IPO has seen very high levels of interest. They report that the company is working with backers to raise the funds. The reports highlight the specific financial targets for the public and private offerings. These individuals provided the details regarding the oversubscription of the stock.

Investors and backers are the primary parties affected by this large fundraising effort. The high oversubscription suggests that many investors are eager to buy into the company. The separate private placement allows specific backers to provide additional capital. This strategy aims to maximize the total amount of money raised for the firm. The market response indicates a strong appetite for Anthropic shares.

The articles provide a snapshot of the company's current financial strategy. They focus on the specific mechanisms used to raise the 90.4 billion dollars. The background is centered on the high demand for the initial public offering. This demand is evidenced by the seven times oversubscription rate. The company is utilizing both public and private markets for its growth.

The next steps involve completing the IPO and the private placement process. The articles do not state when the funding will be fully secured. stories.Headline: Manas AI reduces early cancer drug discovery time from eight years to three months
stories.Summary:
Dr. Siddhartha Mukherjee, an oncologist and CEO of Manas AI, announced on Saturday at the Hindustan Times Leadership Summit 2026 that artificial intelligence is accelerating early cancer drug discovery. He explained that the time required for this initial phase has dropped from nearly eight years to just three or four months. This American startup uses machine learning combined with physics and chemistry to build new drug molecules from atoms to block disease proteins. For example, identifying a target spot on a pancreatic cancer protein now takes two hours instead of a decade. The company pairs molecular design with robotic lab testing to complete design and test cycles every three weeks.

These efforts produce experimental cancer candidates that are up to 200 times stronger than current competitor drugs. Dr. Mukherjee also co-founded Immuneel Therapeutics with Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw in Bengaluru to create customized blood cancer treatments. These treatments cost roughly 35,000 dollars in India, which is significantly lower than the 500,000 dollars charged in the United States. Dr. Mukherjee stated that while AI saves time and money early on, it does not yet reduce the cost of clinical trials or regulatory timelines. He urged India and China to implement technological and regulatory reforms to streamline testing rules without compromising safety.

He noted that cancer cannot be cured all at once because every type of cancer is biologically distinct. While progress is strong for leukemia, lymphoma, and breast cancer, stomach and pancreatic cancers remain very difficult challenges. The World Health Organization and its research agency reported in 2026 that there are 20.6 million new cancer cases and 10 million deaths globally each year. In India, that report estimates 1.56 million new cases and over 900,000 annual deaths, with 3.32 million people living with the disease. Additionally, the Indian Council of Medical Research projected 1.57 million cases for 2025 and noted that one in nine Indians faces a lifetime risk of cancer.

Articles.Title: AI cuts early cancer drug discovery from 8 years to 3 months: Dr Siddhartha Mukherjee

stories.Headline: National Insurance Crime Bureau reports AI mentions in questionable claims rise over 1,400%
stories.Summary:
The National Insurance Crime Bureau, a nonprofit based in Oak Brook, Illinois, published its 2026 threat assessment on November 16, 2026, reporting that mentions of AI in questionable claims rose by more than 1,400% from 2025 to mid-2026 across auto, liability, cargo and workers' compensation lines. The report identifies three converging threats: AI-enabled identity schemes, organized crime networks that mix digital and physical tactics, and professional networks of attorneys, medical providers and auto repair firms working together to inflate claims. Fraudsters are using widely available tools to generate fabricated medical records, synthetic identities and doctored accident photographs at a volume that existing claims workflows were not built to handle. A separate Verisk study published in March 2026, based on surveys of 1,000 US consumers and 300 claims professionals, found that 36% of consumers would consider digitally altering a claim image or document even if it broke insurer rules, rising to 55% among Generation Z. On the insurer side, 76% of claims professionals said manipulated media submissions had grown more sophisticated over the past year, while only 32% were confident their organization could identify a deepfake.

The report also found more than 1,600 transnational, interstate and state-level organized crime rings operating in 2025, running schemes that span staged accidents, vehicle theft and complex multi-party fraud. The NICB describes predatory legal and medical networks as systematically exploiting the litigation system, turning low-severity incidents into mass litigation and driving settlement values well beyond the underlying loss, and it has focused legislative efforts on fraud in litigation funding. The FBI estimates non-health insurance fraud costs the US at least $40 billion annually, and fraud losses inflate loss ratios, which in turn drive premiums. In commercial cargo, total supply chain crime incidents across the US and Canada held roughly steady in 2025 at 3,594 events against 3,607 in 2024, but estimated losses reached nearly $725 million, a 60% year-on-year increase, according to Verisk CargoNet's January 2026 annual analysis. The average value per theft rose 36% to $273,990, confirmed cargo theft cases rose 18% year-over-year, and California, Texas and Illinois accounted for just over half of all incidents, while New Jersey, Indiana and Pennsylvania each recorded significant increases.

Pranay Mittal, vice president of Travelers Investigative Services, said in a statement issued alongside the NICB report that shared insight is the industry's strongest defense because every insurer holds a piece of the picture, and that working with NICB and other fraud-fighting partners helps investigators spot patterns sooner and focus investigations with greater precision as new threats emerge. Aimee Stidham, president of the International Association of Special Investigation Units, a global nonprofit headquartered in Albany, New York, and claims SIU manager at Hiscox USA, said in a statement issued alongside the report that the fight against insurance fraud is no longer undertaken by any single organization, and that today's most effective anti-fraud initiatives are driven by collaboration, intelligence sharing and a shared commitment to protecting policyholders.

The NICB is integrating business intelligence across its member companies, authenticating digital evidence and building infrastructure to flag emerging fraud patterns earlier, while its field agents work alongside law enforcement to disrupt cargo theft operations directly. For brokers placing cargo or logistics cover, the articles say policies underwritten against 2023 or 2024 loss assumptions may no longer reflect current exposure, and carriers are tightening terms, adding exclusions and demanding stronger chain-of-custody controls from clients, conversations that now fall to brokers to initiate. Policyholders and industry professionals can report suspected fraud to NICB at reportinsurancefraud.org.

stories.Headline: US government creates Super Intelligence Force to manage advanced AI risks
stories.Summary:
The United States government recently established the Super Intelligence Force to manage the risks associated with advanced artificial intelligence. Jay Clayton, a former U.S. attorney, was appointed by the president to lead this new organization as the national AI czar. In this specific role, Clayton is tasked with creating comprehensive plans to respond to threats enabled by super intelligence. This move marks a shift for Washington, which had previously been largely disengaged from the regulation of the industry. The initiative aims to protect national security, individual privacy, and the future of human civilization.

The transition to an AI economy requires a focus on retraining workers and supporting those who lose their jobs. Policymakers are encouraged to invest in the community college system to develop new curricula for AI training programs. There is a call to reintroduce and expand wage insurance, a tool used in the 1962 Trade Adjustment Assistance program. Additionally, the authors suggest bolstering the earned-income tax credit to increase the financial rewards for working people. Business leaders are urged to use AI to complement human tasks rather than replacing entire occupations.

Glenn Hubbard, a Columbia University professor and former chairman of the Council of Economic Advisers, co-authored these recommendations. He and Luke Pardue, the policy director of the Aspen Economic Strategy Group, argue that ignoring mundane economic shifts could lead to social instability. They believe that failing to support displaced workers could trigger a political backlash similar to the one following global trade with China. The authors suggest that the Super Intelligence Force should coordinate public and private efforts to manage this labor transition. They point to the Workforce 2020 program at AT&T as a successful model for proactive employee retraining.

The current economic climate is characterized by a large-scale transition that will likely happen faster than previous industrial shifts. There is already a growing bipartisan opposition to the construction of data centers necessary for the diffusion of AI. If the government and business leaders fail to manage this transition, the authors warn that all of society will suffer the consequences. Future efforts should mirror the Committee for Economic Development, which helped America transition to a peacetime economy after World War II. The goal is to ensure maximum participation in the economy to maintain a sense of purpose and identity for all citizens.

stories.Headline: Downing Street says Andy Burnham writes most of his own speeches after aide is photographed using ChatGPT on a train
stories.Summary:
Downing Street said on Nov 15 that Prime Minister Andy Burnham writes most of his own speeches, after the Mail on Sunday published photos that appeared to show one of his aides using AI to prepare a speech. The Mail on Sunday said the aide, with a glass of prosecco in hand, used ChatGPT to rework a speech for the Labour leader while on board a train. The images were said to have been taken on Nov 13 by a fellow passenger before Burnham gave a speech to the Welsh Labour party conference in Cardiff. The newspaper said the aide used the AI app to ask how to make the speech more emotive.

A Downing Street spokesperson said an aide sought feedback on a speech draft that had already been written, and the spokesperson insisted that the PM writes most of his own speeches. The Press Association news agency reported that the suggestions from ChatGPT did not make it into the final speech. The government said the AI suggestions were not used in the final speech. The Mail on Sunday said the aide used AI to make a draft more emotive before Burnham’s speech to Welsh Labour in Cardiff.

The story concerns Andy Burnham, the British Prime Minister and Labour leader, and an unnamed aide who was photographed on a train on Nov 13. Downing Street played down the photos published in the Sunday newspaper, with a spokesperson quoted by the domestic Press Association news agency. The newspaper posted the snap of the aide using ChatGPT to rework a speech of the Labour leader while on board a train. The images were said to have been taken before Burnham gave a speech to the Welsh Labour party conference in Cardiff.
