stories.Headline: AI Dosing Tool Standardizes IVF Drug Starts Without Changing Birth Rates
stories.Summary:
A pilot real-world study at Peking University Third Hospital tested an algorithmic dosing tool called POvaStim in assisted reproduction. Researchers led the single-centre observational study, published in Frontiers in Endocrinology, on women undergoing in vitro fertilization or intracytoplasmic sperm injection. The team matched 119 women whose clinicians used POvaStim against 119 propensity-score-matched controls managed by conventional experience-based judgement. The controls were managed under gonadotropin-releasing hormone antagonist protocols. The study enrolled consecutive women between August 3 and December 31, 2022, at the Center for Reproductive Medicine at Peking University Third Hospital.

The tool standardizes initial gonadotropin dosing during ovarian stimulation, and the study included standard antagonist cycles using follitropin alfa, follitropin beta, or urofollitropin. Mild stimulation regimens were excluded, and matching drew on a candidate pool of 4,877 conventionally dosed cycles. Matching used one-to-one nearest-neighbour propensity score matching without replacement within a caliper of 0.2 standard deviations of the logit score. Matching was based on body weight, gonadotropin preparation, and an ovarian reserve score derived from age and anti-Müllerian hormone. Twenty-six algorithmic cycles could not be matched within tolerance and were excluded, and post-matching standardized mean differences stayed below 0.08.

The authors emphasized that the investigation compared two composite care strategies, clinicians supported by POvaStim versus clinicians relying on unassisted clinical judgement. They cautioned that the absence of hospital admissions does not prove equivalent safety, because elevated ovarian response in the algorithmic arm was actively mitigated through increased elective embryo cryopreservation. They noted that conditioning on fresh transfer introduces post-treatment selection bias, as transfer decisions depend directly on ovarian response. They stated that separating artificial intelligence effects from physician attributes will require future factorial or cluster-randomized trials comparing clinicians across explicit experience strata with and without decision support. They also noted study limitations including the single-centre design, unmeasured outpatient hyperstimulation, and restriction of algorithmic assistance strictly to starting doses while omitting POvaStim's dynamic inhibin B adjustment module.

Under conventional practice, physician-selected doses yielded a standard deviation of 69.8 international units per day and an interquartile range of 87.5 international units per day. Clinicians using POvaStim recorded a standard deviation of 44.7 international units per day and an interquartile range of 50.0 international units per day, a 43 percent narrower interquartile range and a 2.43-fold lower variance confirmed by an F test yielding a p-value of 2×10⁻⁶. After adjustment, residual standard deviation was 16.2 international units per day with algorithmic guidance versus 49.4 international units per day in controls. Median cumulative gonadotropin consumption reached 2,175 international units in the algorithmic group compared to 1,950 international units in controls, alongside a higher median daily dose of 225.0 versus 195.0 international units per day. When researchers retrospectively applied POvaStim to control patients, the model recommended near-identical mean starting doses of 216.36 versus 216.42 international units per day.

Protocol instructions required algorithmic clinicians to round calculated doses upward to commercial pen increments, placing administered doses above recommendations in 94.1 percent of cycles and driving 38 percent of the gap. Control clinicians unknowingly prescribed below model recommendations in 69.7 percent of cycles, accounting for 62 percent of the 27.4 international units per day difference. Cumulative live birth occurred in 49.6 percent (59 of 119) of the algorithmic group versus 50.4 percent (60 of 119) of controls, an absolute risk difference of -0.8 percent with a 95 percent confidence interval of -13.5 to +11.9 percent (p = 0.897). Cumulative clinical pregnancy occurred in 56.3 percent (67 of 119) of algorithmic patients versus 63.9 percent (76 of 119) of controls, a risk difference of -7.6 percent with a 95 percent confidence interval of -20.0 to +4.8 percent (p = 0.234).

Median retrieved oocyte counts were 14 in the algorithmic group compared to 13 in controls, while median normally fertilised two-pronuclear embryos were 7 versus 6 and good-quality embryos were 5 versus 5. Fertilisation rate per inseminated oocyte was significantly lower in the algorithmic cohort, with a median of 0.58 compared to 0.69 among controls (p = 0.010). Conventional insemination was used in 68.1 percent of algorithmic cycles compared to 52.9 percent of controls, and among conventionally inseminated cycles rescue intracytoplasmic sperm injection was required in 8.6 percent (7 of 81) of algorithmic cases versus none (0 of 63) in controls. No patient in either arm developed severe ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome requiring hospital admission.

Elective whole-embryo cryopreservation for non-genetic indications occurred in 46.2 percent (55 of 119) of the algorithmic arm versus 34.5 percent (41 of 119) of controls (p = 0.064), with hyperstimulation prevention the primary motivation in 83.6 percent and 78.0 percent of freezes respectively. Retrieval of at least 15 oocytes occurred in 47.9 percent versus 38.7 percent of cycles, while freeze-all procedures for preimplantation genetic testing were more frequent in controls at 13.4 percent versus 1.7 percent. Among women receiving a fresh transfer, clinical pregnancy was significantly lower in the algorithmic group at 51.9 percent versus 72.4 percent in controls (interaction p = 0.048), though this lost significance after Holm correction (adjusted p = 0.100). No interaction appeared for live birth.

Primary clinical outcomes were assessed after two years of longitudinal tracking extending to a fixed data-lock date of December 31, 2024. In the primary analysis, treating 16 patients without an embryo transfer as non-events, sensitivity analyses evaluating complete cases, adjusted models, and matched-pair structures yielded consistent results. Because the study was not designed as an equivalence or non-inferiority trial, the wide confidence intervals cannot rule out clinically important outcome differences. Total fertilisation failure occurred in one algorithmic cycle and zero control cycles, while cycles without blastocysts did not differ significantly between arms.

Articles.Title: AI Dosing Tool Standardizes IVF Drug Starts Without Changing Birth Rates

stories.Headline: Non-sonographers use AI guidance to capture quality heart scans in rural mobile unit
stories.Summary:
Healthcare personnel without prior clinical ultrasound training acquired high-quality echocardiographic scans in a mobile examination unit serving rural United States communities, aided by real-time artificial intelligence guidance and centralized expert evaluation. The independent preliminary research was scheduled for presentation at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions 2026, held November 6 through November 9 in Chicago under Abstract Poster MDP2290. The work was conducted as part of the broader Risk Underlying Rural Areas Longitudinal cohort study, known as the RURAL study. The investigation evaluated whether non-specialists could reliably capture research-standard cardiovascular images directly within geographically isolated localities. The approach seeks to bring advanced diagnostic tools closer to rural residents while expanding rural participation in cardiovascular clinical research.

The observational study cohort comprised 4,597 volunteer adult participants spanning ages 25 to 65, with a cohort average age of 48 years. Women represented 67 percent of the enrolled population, and at enrollment 63 percent self-identified as white adults, 35 percent as Black adults, and 2 percent as Hispanic adults. Mobile operations ran within a dedicated mobile health unit that visited ten rural counties across Alabama, Kentucky, Louisiana, and Mississippi between November 2021 and June 2026. Each participant completed examinations within a single 3.5-hour scheduled appointment inside the vehicle. The echocardiograms were performed by fourteen non-sonographer healthcare workers, including nurses, nursing assistants, and computed tomography technologists with no prior background in cardiac ultrasound, who completed a standardized two-hour training curriculum divided into four structured modules, with three operators requiring retraining following preliminary reviews.

Principal investigator Dr. Gerald S. Bloomfield and the Duke Clinical Research Institute established a centralized quality assurance framework to address the gaps. Study author Dr. Sanjana Ravi, an internal medicine and pediatrics resident at Duke University School of Medicine in Durham, North Carolina, said echocardiography is among the most valuable research tools in cardiovascular science yet delivering it in rural communities has proven difficult. Dr. Ravi noted the conventional framework requires an expert sonographer in a hospital or specialized imaging center, resources severely limited across rural areas. She also cited a pronounced scarcity of cardiovascular imaging specialists available to review recorded images and a shortage of local clinicians who can communicate diagnostic results to patients. Dr. Ravi expressed surprise at how quickly nurses and computed tomography technologists adapted to the technology.

Dr. Lee H. Schwamm, a member of the American Heart Association volunteer committee on AI and Technology Innovation who was not involved in the study, observed that one in five Americans lives in a rural area, severely restricting access to critical diagnostic testing and specialty medical care. Dr. Schwamm, senior vice president and chief digital health officer of Yale New Haven Health System and associate dean of digital strategy and transformation at Yale School of Medicine, noted that if confirmed through subsequent trials, this paradigm could serve as a valuable operational blueprint for other diagnostic specialties. The study set a performance target requiring scans within a fifteen-minute operational window. Of the 4,597 completed heart examinations, 98 percent captured all six standard echocardiographic views mandated by the protocol, and Duke core laboratory experts rated scans adequate more than 99 percent of the time. Diagnostic-quality rates for individual anatomic views ranged between 77 percent and 94 percent, and operators met the 15-minute target in 81 percent of sessions with a median scan duration of 9.5 minutes.

Echocardiography uses high-frequency ultrasound waves to generate dynamic, moving visual representations of cardiac structure and function. According to American Heart Association guidance, physicians order this non-invasive test for heart murmurs, damaged heart valves, or unexplained chest pain, and it is standard practice for congenital heart defects, documented myocardial infarction or stroke, or prior rheumatic fever. The conventional clinical pathway depends on specialized sonographers in hospital departments or dedicated outpatient imaging facilities, which remain scarce throughout rural regions. Experts identified critical results in 133 scans among the 4,597 asymptomatic volunteers, most commonly a left ventricular ejection fraction of less than 50 percent. The study team communicated 99 percent of these critical findings to participants within three days of image acquisition.

The investigators noted the trial design included no direct head-to-head comparison between images from AI-guided non-sonographers and experienced professional sonographers scanning the same patients. Reproducibility of structural measurements was evaluated internally within the Duke core laboratory and not independently validated against external imaging core laboratories, and inter-operator variability was not systematically evaluated. The protocol relied on a single commercial brand of artificial intelligence software and a single academic core laboratory, so alternative platforms or facilities will require separate verification and validation studies. Findings from this rural cohort may not extrapolate to non-rural populations or settings lacking support from an experienced academic core laboratory, and the investigation did not examine whether returning critical results influenced subsequent clinical care or long-term cardiovascular health outcomes. Because the study was presented as a scientific meeting abstract, the findings have not undergone formal peer review and are preliminary until publication in a peer-reviewed journal, and the American Heart Association notes that abstract conclusions represent solely the views of the study authors and not official association policy.

stories.Headline: Psychologist Sebastian Ocklenburg proposes psychological evaluations for AI developers
stories.Summary:
On November 15, 2026, Psychology Today published a personal perspective by Sebastian Ocklenburg, Ph.D., asking whether psychological evaluations are needed for AI developers. Ocklenburg is a professor for research methods in psychology at the Department of Psychology at MSH Medical School in Hamburg, Germany. The article was reviewed by Jessica Schrader. Ocklenburg wrote that AI companies have warned about the risk of AI going rogue and causing harm to humans. He argued that another potential risk may be mentally unstable AI developers purposefully building harmful AI tools.

Ocklenburg cited the American Psychological Association's 2017 guidelines for occupationally mandated psychological evaluations, published on February 24, 2017. He wrote that psychological evaluations are occupationally mandated in some jobs in many states of the U.S., including police officers, people working in prisons, firefighters, people working with the FBI, pilots, air traffic controllers and people working in nuclear power plants. He wrote that in some jobs evaluations may be conducted with people already employed if they show signs of impaired mental health or thinking abilities, including physicians and other healthcare workers. He described the March 24, 2015 crash of a Germanwings passenger plane in the French Alps, in which a pilot with severe mental issues purposefully crashed the plane with 150 people on board, killing all passengers. He wrote that AI developers do not routinely undergo mental health screenings.

Ocklenburg wrote that he believes occupationally mandated psychological evaluations of AI developers should be considered. He wrote that professional organizations for psychologists, companies that make hiring and employment decisions in relation to the development of AI tools, and government agencies involved in the regulation of tech companies should consider such evaluations. He wrote that more psychological research is needed into whether severe, untreated mental health conditions in AI developers could lead to the risk of real harm for other human beings. He wrote that occupationally mandated psychological evaluations of AI developers could help ensure that only mentally stable people are involved in the development of frontier models with the potential to cause real harm to humans. He wrote that no one knows how likely catastrophic events akin to the Germanwings airplane catastrophe would be in the field of AI development and what impact they would have.

Ocklenburg wrote that over the last few weeks there has been a lot of discussion in the media about the extent to which rogue AI agents may potentially cause harm to humans in the future or even kill all of humanity. He wrote that experts debate whether AI agents turning on humanity is a real risk or not. He wrote that one potentially more likely risk of AI often gets ignored. He wrote that just like a pilot could cause a plane to crash on purpose, an AI developer could purposefully build AI models that lack the necessary checks and balances to prevent them from hurting humans, or even an AI that exists with the purpose to harm humans, for example by performing hacking attacks on critical infrastructure. He wrote that AI does not need to turn rogue by itself to harm humans, because one developer doing so on purpose could lead to massive economic and personal harm.

Ocklenburg wrote that a scenario like this seems more likely to occur in the near future than AI turning rogue by itself, so measures to prevent such an incident are needed. He wrote that mental health conditions like antisocial personality disorder, which has been linked to violating the rights of other people without feelings of guilt, and dark personality traits such as psychopathy mean such a scenario is not entirely unlikely. He wrote that the big AI companies themselves warn about the potential risks of AI. He wrote that the Germanwings incident highlighted how important it is that people who work in high-risk fields and have a responsibility for the survival of others are mentally stable. He wrote that his research focuses on left-handedness and brain asymmetries.

Ocklenburg wrote that he believes occupationally mandated psychological evaluations of AI developers should be considered, and the article gives no further steps beyond that recommendation. The article leaves open how likely catastrophic events akin to the Germanwings airplane catastrophe would be in the field of AI development and what impact they would have. The article leaves open whether severe, untreated mental health conditions in AI developers could lead to the risk of real harm for other human beings. The article gives no date for when such evaluations might be introduced or by which body. The article gives no response from AI companies, psychologists' organizations or government agencies to the proposal.

stories.Headline: OpenAI finds 98 per cent of surveyed scientists expect AI to speed discoveries
stories.Summary:
A study by OpenAI found that 98 per cent of surveyed scientists expect artificial intelligence to accelerate discoveries in their fields, according to a report published on November 17, 2026. The study also found that more than one in five scientists believe a discovery that typically requires 10 years could be achieved within three years with AI assistance. These findings rest on an analysis of 580,186 scientific messages from 1,819 researchers and a survey of 251 scientists in OpenAI's ChatGPT for Academic Researchers programme. Researchers estimated that AI lets them complete tasks at the same quality in nearly half the time.

ChatGPT was used across literature review, writing, evidence analysis, software development and idea generation, and reading and writing together made up over half of the average scientist's scientific messages. The report said AI can advance scientific progress by speeding up tasks and helping researchers identify more promising questions while exploring a wider range of topics. It also said AI is not replacing human involvement, because researchers sought clarification, checks or revisions after about 32 per cent of AI responses, which shows human judgment remains crucial for assessing and improving AI output. Respondents named insufficient personnel at 51.8 per cent, funding at 43.8 per cent and time as major bottlenecks to research productivity, and the report noted these constraints could limit the gains from broader AI adoption.

OpenAI concluded that the findings underscore AI's potential to support scientific work, while translating productivity gains into faster discoveries will also depend on adequate funding, staffing and experimental capacity. The articles do not name any individual responsible for the study or give any statement from a person, so no one is quoted beyond the report's conclusions. The context the report gives is that scientists already use ChatGPT widely in their daily research work and still check its output closely. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the report's note that funding, staffing and experimental capacity will shape whether the expected gains arrive.

stories.Headline: Researchers develop deep learning model to predict nasopharyngeal carcinoma recurrence risk from biopsy slides
stories.Summary:
Researchers conducted a multicenter retrospective study to forecast nasopharyngeal carcinoma recurrence risk. They used a weakly supervised deep-learning computational pathology framework for this purpose. The study was completed by November 15, 2026, across three Chinese tertiary medical centers. The system analyzes routine hematoxylin and eosin stained biopsy whole-slide images. It stratifies progression-free survival in patients with locally advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

The study involved 253 patients with stage III to IVA undifferentiated non-keratinizing nasopharyngeal carcinoma from 2012 to 2025. Nanfang Hospital, Jiangsu Cancer Hospital, and Shandong Cancer Hospital and Institute served as the three centers. A training cohort had 149 patients, while internal validation had 52 and external testing had 52. The model used a ResNet-50 convolutional neural network and a binary risk score cutoff of 0.450. Images were digitized at forty times optical magnification with a resolution of 0.25 micrometers per pixel.

The research team developed an attention-based multiple-instance learning model to evaluate biopsy images. They stated that traditional clinicopathological factors and standard tumor-node-metastasis staging provide limited resolution for predictions. The team noted that visual evaluation of biopsies remains inherently qualitative and subjective. They claimed their model extracts robust prognostic signals without requiring laborious manual annotation of tumor margins. This approach allows for individualized risk assessments to determine if patients need treatment intensification.

Clinicians struggle to identify which patients can safely avoid excessive therapy-related toxicities. Patients with locally advanced disease are affected, representing seventy percent of new diagnoses. These individuals often receive induction chemotherapy followed by concurrent chemoradiotherapy. Some higher-risk subgroups may also receive adjuvant systemic therapy and immune checkpoint inhibitors. The model helps distinguish between high-risk and low-risk patients to improve these clinical decisions.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is an epithelial malignancy with aggressive local invasion and systemic dissemination. It has the highest global incidence in southern China, East Asia, Southeast Asia, and North Africa. Standard treatment relies on definitive radiotherapy paired with platinum-based chemotherapy. However, treatment responses and recurrence patterns vary widely among patients in identical clinical stages. Conventional pathological examinations cannot systematically parse high-dimensional spatial microenvironmental characteristics across entire slides.

The model achieved a 3-year progression-free survival area under the curve of 0.721 in external testing. It correctly identified sixteen out of seventeen patients who experienced disease progression within three years. The gated attention model outperformed four alternative pipelines, including Vision Transformer and ResNet-50 mean pooling. The articles do not state how this tool will be integrated into daily clinical practice. They leave open whether the model will be tested in other global populations.

stories.Headline: Representational Atoms in Neural Networks
stories.Summary:
Chenhui Hu, Pengfei Cao, Kang Liu and Jun Zhao posted a paper titled Representational Atoms in Neural Networks on arXiv on 17 November 2026, and in it they formally define fundamental representational units, or FRUs, as the basic units of meaning inside a neural network. The authors set out two criteria for judging such units, fidelity and stability, and they prove that threshold-activated sparse autoencoders, or TSAEs, can identify FRUs with high fidelity and stability under appropriate conditions. They also validate that result through large-scale experiments, according to the abstract. The work addresses two questions the authors call critical for explaining model mechanisms, namely how learned knowledge is organized in internal representations and how those representations relate to human conceptual structure.

The paper's further analyses report that FRUs with higher stability show greater monosemanticity, meaning they carry a single meaning rather than several mixed together. The authors also say these units can be composed across layers to recover semantic organization that corresponds to human conceptual structure. Every number, date and name in the abstract appears above, and the abstract gives no other figures. The authors present the results as a unified framework for defining, evaluating and identifying FRUs in neural networks, and as a foundation for characterizing the relationship between neural network representations and human conceptual structure.

The four authors are responsible for the work, and the abstract states their claims in its own terms rather than in quoted remarks. They say TSAEs can identify FRUs with high fidelity and stability under appropriate conditions, and they back this with large-scale experiments. They describe higher-stability FRUs as more monosemantic and as composable across layers to recover semantic organization matching human conceptual structure. They frame the whole as a unified framework and a foundation for future characterization of the link between network representations and human concepts.

The context the abstract gives is that understanding internal representations and comparing them with human conceptual structure are two critical questions for elucidating model mechanisms. The first question concerns how learned knowledge is organized inside the network, and the second provides a basis for interpreting representations through human conceptual structure. The abstract does not say what happens next beyond offering the framework and foundation, and it names no follow-up work or publication venue. The paper is available from arXiv as a PDF, as experimental HTML and as TeX source.

stories.Headline: SIU School of Medicine and Springfield Memorial Hospital fund a $2 million AI device to teach patient communication
stories.Summary:
Springfield Memorial Hospital and its Foundation joined the Southern Illinois University School of Medicine in putting $1 million each toward a new artificial intelligence and Extended Reality device for the Ed Curtis Laboratory for Innovation in Medical Education, and the technology was shown to the public and to Memorial Health Foundation donors last week. The device is meant to help students and doctors learn how to talk with patients and their families about the care those patients are receiving. The story was reported by Capitol City Now on November 15, 2026, with Elston Lacy and Will Stevenson credited on the piece. The laboratory’s team has been working on this kind of research since early 2025. According to an October news release from the SIU School of Medicine, the ECLIME team has launched more than 20 research projects focused on improving educational outcomes since early 2025.

That work explores how AI can deliver timely feedback, strengthen communication skills and support learning while preserving the essential role of faculty mentorship. The new device combines artificial intelligence with what the school calls extended reality, and its features are expected to be valuable both to students and to working professionals. The investment by the foundation and the school totals $2 million. Pam Hulten, Director of the Springfield Memorial Foundation, said on the WTAX Morning Newswatch that the hospital has to do its part to train its workforce, including nurses and everyone within the hospital, and then the extension over with SIU. She said the institution has incredible and brilliant physicians, medical residents and students who are eager to have learning at their fingertips.

Dr. Traves Crabtree, Professor and Chair of the Division of Cardiothoracic Surgery at the SIU School of Medicine, also speaking on WTAX, described a concept in medicine called de-skilling. He said that if medical professionals look to AI for the answers on what a diagnosis is and how to work it up, there is a threat that the learner loses the ability to think about and develop clinical reasoning. He added that the school is not really in that space right now, and that what it is doing is finding opportunities in education where there are important things to teach or train but the resources or time are lacking. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the public and donor showing of the device last week.

stories.Headline: US agencies suspect Alice Huang of spying for China using Nvidia founder Jensen Huang
stories.Summary:
United States intelligence agencies suspect that Alice Huang spied for China using Jensen Huang. This suspected operation occurred around November 2026 involving the founder of the company Nvidia. Alice Huang is also known as Huang Le and is a Chinese businesswoman. She is linked to Megaspeed, which is a company based in Singapore. This firm purchased advanced processors from Nvidia during the period of the affair.

The situation involves technology subject to export restrictions and state-of-the-art semiconductors in the United States. Jensen Huang was the CEO of Nvidia until he stepped down recently. Reuters reported his departure from executive leadership on November 12, 2026. The investigation focuses on whether China's Ministry of State Security recruited Alice Huang. This effort aimed to obtain strategic information and facilitate access for Chinese interests.

U.S. intelligence agencies suspect that the romantic relationship was a honey trap for recruitment. These agencies believe the intimacy was used to penetrate circles of power and obtain documents. Nvidia launched an independent investigation to see if its CEO was a foreign target. The company wants to determine if any clandestine activity occurred during the affair. Officials noted that semiconductors are key strategic assets in the competition with Beijing.

China has rejected the accusations regarding the recruitment of Alice Huang for espionage. It has not been publicly demonstrated that Alice Huang obtained any trade secrets. It is also unproven if Jensen Huang was aware of any secret activity. The reports were first published by The New York Times and then Reuters. The case affects the technological competition between the United States and the city of Beijing.

The articles explain that intelligence services often exploit romantic relationships to identify personal vulnerabilities. This practice is known as a honey trap and involves attraction, intimacy, or blackmail. History shows examples like Mata Hari, who was executed by France in October 1917. Other examples include the Nazi Salon Kitty in Berlin and agents used by Markus Wolf. These cases illustrate how secret services use seduction to influence political decisions.

Nvidia continues its independent investigation into the conduct of its former chief executive. The United States continues to monitor the strategic assets involved in the semiconductor industry. The articles leave open whether Alice Huang actually transmitted any classified information to China. It remains unclear if Jensen Huang was a willing participant or an unwitting target. The final results of the intelligence probe have not been released to the public.

stories.Headline: npj Digital Surgery opens AI surgical care collection with 2027 deadline
stories.Summary:
The journal npj Digital Surgery has opened a collection titled Innovation in Digital Surgery: Artificial Intelligence Across the Surgical Care Pathway, with a submission deadline of 12 July 2027, according to the collection page. The collection is edited by Marc D. Succi of Harvard Medical School and Arya S. Rao, also of Harvard Medical School, and it supports research related to SDG3, SDG4 and SDG9. The page says the collection highlights work that identifies unmet clinical needs and implements solutions leading to quantifiable improvements in patient care. It also says the collection confronts the traditional obstacles of translational innovation, including funding, intellectual property, commercialization and venture support.

The collection invites papers on preoperative risk assessment and perioperative decision-making, including studies of how digital and AI systems influence decision support in realistic surgical settings from triage through discharge. It also seeks work on computer vision, including vision-language models applied to laparoscopic, endoscopic and robotic video that can identify anatomy and assess surgical milestones. Natural language processing and generative AI are another focus, covering operative note generation, extracting information from the clinical record and preparing discharge paperwork, with particular interest in data governance, privacy, bias and regulatory considerations. Surgical training is also in scope, including AI-powered simulation, virtual and augmented reality curricula and digital competency assessment, while studies primarily about device or pharmacologic treatments fall outside the collection's scope.

The page says the collection welcomes submissions from all authors and not by invitation only, provided manuscripts fall within the scope of the collection and of the journal. All submissions are subject to the same peer review process and editorial standards as regular npj Digital Surgery articles, including the journal's policy on competing interests. The page says the Guest Editors have no competing interests with the submissions, which they handle through the peer-review process, and that peer review of any submission for which the Guest Editors have competing interests is handled by another Editorial Board Member without competing interests. The collection is not supported by sponsorship, and papers will be published as soon as they are accepted and then collected together and promoted on the collection homepage.

stories.Headline: Minghao Liu and colleagues review explainable AI that unifies formability and performance in additive alloys
stories.Summary:
A review published in Advanced Materials Joining on November 15, 2026 evaluates how explainable artificial intelligence can bridge the divide between defect suppression and mechanical optimization in additive manufacturing. The review was led by Minghao Liu, Wei Xu and colleagues. Laser powder bed fusion melts consecutive powder layers with focused laser beams. Localized energy deposition and rapid cooling rates of 10⁴ to 10⁶ K/s create severe thermal gradients. Traditional data-driven machine learning models correlate raw process inputs directly with bulk properties.

The review categorizes physical interpretability across four knowledge domains: physical metallurgy principles, cross-scale numerical information, microstructural image data and causal physical mechanisms. Physical metallurgy-guided support vector machines use thermodynamic driving forces and equilibrium phase fractions to constrain process schemes. First-principles calculations supply formation enthalpies and cohesive energies for high-entropy alloy designs. Calculation of Phase Diagrams methods supply non-equilibrium phase fractions, solidification intervals and transformation temperatures. Finite element modeling and molecular dynamics provide thermal stress distributions and solidification cooling rates.

The authors state that contemporary studies remain predominantly task-specific and single-objective, focusing either on defect mitigation or on mechanical strength. They emphasize that both formability and mechanical properties arise from the identical composition-process-thermal history pathway. They propose a unified multi-objective optimization framework structured around shared thermal history descriptors including local thermal gradient G, solidification front velocity R, cooling rate and remelting depth. They say coupling physics-constrained models with standardized multimodal databases and causal discovery algorithms will allow researchers to determine whether formability and performance objectives are driven by cooperative or competing metallurgical mechanisms. They add that establishing standardized repositories pairing raw process signals, three-dimensional defect geometries and mechanical performance measurements will be vital for training reliable multi-objective surrogate architectures.

Steels and titanium alloys represent the performance-first paradigm, where components achieve near-full density across broad processing windows but suffer anisotropic microstructures, cyclic thermal reheating and non-equilibrium phase evolution. In LPBF steels, statistical models paired with physical metallurgy descriptors mapped linear energy inputs to density and nanohardness with classification accuracies reaching 92.4%. Combining extreme gradient boosting with SHAP interpretability and NSGA-III multi-objective optimization enabled rapid design of ultra-high-strength stainless compositions. For Ti-6Al-4V, incorporating threshold stress intensity factors and Kitagawa-Takahashi envelope constraints into neural network loss functions improved fatigue strength prediction coefficients of determination from 0.70 to 0.82 and reduced mean absolute errors from 40.5 MPa to 29.9 MPa across 143 experimental samples. Combining three-dimensional micro-computed tomography defect volumes with deep neural networks identified maximum defect circumscribed sphere diameter and sphericity as primary determinants of fatigue life, attaining a test coefficient of determination of 0.946.

Aluminum alloys and nickel-based superalloys represent the formability-first paradigm, where hot tearing, liquation cracking, high laser reflectivity and wide freezing intervals dominate processing challenges. High-strength aluminum alloys including 2xxx and 7xxx series feature freezing ranges exceeding 100 K. Graph attention networks integrated with physical metallurgy knowledge graphs designed an additive aluminum alloy achieving 99.98% relative density without substrate preheating, with ultimate tensile strength of 454 MPa and elongation of 9.5%. In nickel-based superalloys, dual-parameter criteria evaluating heat resistance and deformation resistance mapped cracking susceptibility by quantifying elemental microsegregation. Trace additions of boron, zirconium and hafnium severely aggravate cracking by depressing the solidus temperature.

Incorporating causal transfer learning allowed researchers to predict fatigue strength in low-alloy steels from tensile data with as few as thirty training sets, achieving a verified 50 MPa fatigue strength increase. Physics-informed neural networks incorporate conservation of mass, momentum and energy to simulate molten-pool geometry and Marangoni convection. Phase-field dynamics modeled via the Allen-Cahn and Cahn-Hilliard equations describe dendritic growth and solute segregation during solidification. Mechanics-based fatigue formulations incorporate Basquin's law and stress-dependent variance rules. Currently available datasets are fragmented, typically reporting either defect characteristics or mechanical test metrics but rarely paired measurements from identical specimen batches.

Explainable methodologies have resolved biomechanical compromises in biomedical titanium alloys, with physical metallurgy descriptors including molybdenum equivalent, valence electron concentration ratio and d-electron parameters introduced into gradient-boosted decision trees trained on seventy-five compositions. Embedding these parameters as constraints within genetic algorithms enabled design of quaternary and quinary titanium-molybdenum-niobium-zirconium-tin alloys, both achieving stable single-phase beta structures with measured elastic moduli of 40 GPa and 37 GPa against predicted targets of 43 GPa and 39 GPa. Physics-informed neural network models incorporating Weibull distributions, finite element frequency mapping and Monte Carlo estimation established ultra-high-cycle fatigue predictions for Ti-6Al-4V, boosting crack propagation resistance by 20 to 30 percent while cutting development cycles by more than half. Quantum machine learning alongside high-throughput computing designed the lightweight Al85Cu5Li4Mg3Zn3 entropy alloy, exploiting rapid cooling to convert brittle intermetallics into hierarchical cellular eutectic structures and dense planar faults. Combining light gradient boosting with genetic algorithms introduced nanoscale titanium diboride particles into the aluminum matrix, promoting ultrafine equiaxed grains that suppress hot tearing and decoupling grain-boundary, Orowan, dislocation and solid-solution strengthening contributions.

stories.Headline: Researchers find precise performance throttling in LLMs does not guarantee believable skill reduction
stories.Summary:
Chengguang Gan, Yunhao Liang, Hanjun Wei, QingHao Zhang, and Shiwen Ni published a study on November 17, 2026, regarding the ability to reduce large language model performance. The researchers investigated whether a model could be driven to a specific target score while maintaining failures that resemble those of a naturally weaker model. They tested various methods to see if performance throttling could be made believable across different types of tasks. This empirical study focused on whether these models were truly becoming less capable or were simply playing dumb.

The team introduced CapLadder, which is an IRT-calibrated suite containing 1,985 items covering tool use, code, mathematics, and multiple-choice reasoning. They found that a weak-teacher LoRA dial could reach target levels on reasoning with a held-out calibration error of only 1.9 points. However, this method failed on multiple-choice questions because errors converged on a single answer-token attractor, such as letter D for Qwen or letter A for Llama. Logit interventions showed that subtracting the estimated shift recovered 52 to 59 percent of lost accuracy and removed the dominant attractor.

The authors explained that while human-coded error distributions matched weak references on reasoning with a JS of 0.00, local plausibility differs from aggregate detectability. They noted that structured tool calls showed more natural degradation in the Qwen family with a JS of 0.09. The researchers concluded that a globally calibrated dial transfers poorly across benchmarks, resulting in a 14.2-point error on two usable benchmarks. Ultimately, they stated that precise score control does not guarantee a portable or believable reduction in the actual skill of the model.

Articles.Title: Can We Make an LLM Dumber, or Is It Just Playing Dumb? An Empirical Study of Believable Performance Throttling

stories.Headline: DRAMA: Dissecting Attention Redundancy for Accelerating Multimodal Diffusion Large Language Models
stories.Summary:
Yi-Hsin Hung, Fangfu Liu, Shao-Yuan Lo and Chu-Song Chen posted a paper on arXiv on 17 November 2026 describing DRAMA, a training-free framework for speeding up multimodal diffusion large language models. These models generate text through iterative masked denoising with bidirectional attention, and every denoising step needs a full forward pass over long multimodal sequences in which visual tokens dominate the sequence length. A fixed step budget makes the quadratic per-step cost worse, and earlier acceleration approaches characterized attention redundancy only implicitly, drawing designs from isolated attention visualizations rather than from measurement. The authors say they close that gap by systematically dissecting attention redundancy in these models.

By probing attention tensors along spatial and temporal axes, the authors report two persistent redundancy structures in multimodal diffusion large language models. Attention mass consistently concentrates on a sparse subset of visual tokens, and attention distributions rapidly stabilize across denoising steps after an initial formation phase. These findings motivate two complementary mechanisms, Spatial-Redundancy-Aware Visual Token Pruning and Sufficiency-Guided Adaptive Stopping, which together make up DRAMA. The framework achieves an average 18.67 times inference speedup across six vision-language benchmarks without training, architectural modification or attention caching, while maintaining competitive accuracy.

The paper presents the work as a measurement-grounded acceleration baseline for multimodal diffusion large language model inference, and the authors are listed as Yi-Hsin Hung, Fangfu Liu, Shao-Yuan Lo and Chu-Song Chen. The abstract does not attribute separate roles to the four authors or give individual statements from them beyond the shared claims of the paper. The article gives no further detail on how the two mechanisms are implemented or on the accuracy figures behind the competitive accuracy claim. It also does not say what happens next with the work, beyond the paper being available as a PDF, HTML and TeX source on arXiv.

stories.Headline: Visual Cipher Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Visual Reasoning
stories.Summary:
Deyao Hong and fourteen other authors posted Visual Cipher Bench to arXiv on November 17, 2026, as a benchmark for testing whether language-model agents can carry long-horizon reasoning from text into images. The authors argue that agents succeed at long coding and terminal tasks only because those tasks come with explicit text specifications and immediate execution feedback. Neither condition holds in real-world problems where the critical information exists only in images, so it was unclear whether long-horizon ability transfers to visual reasoning. In such visual settings the rules and clues resist transcription into text and there are no test cases to give feedback, so agents must repeatedly inspect images, simulate spatial transformations and cross-check clues on their own.

The benchmark collects 40 original visual puzzles across four categories, which are spatial manipulation and simulation, logical constraints and planning, rule induction, and knowledge-based decoding. Each puzzle gives only one to three black-and-white line drawings and a minimal submission instruction, and the agent must discover the solving mechanism entirely from the images. The authors tested 29 reasoning-effort configurations of eight frontier models, and even the strongest model, GPT-6 Astra at max effort, reached only 26.7 percent accuracy. Five of the eight models scored below 1 percent, yet on a ten-task subset a single non-spoiler hint about the mechanism raised accuracy from 12.2 percent to 51.1 percent.

The authors conclude from that contrast that the main bottleneck for current agents is not carrying out multi-step plans but autonomously discovering rules from visual evidence. They present Visual Cipher Bench as a rigorous benchmark for measuring long-horizon visual reasoning in agents, and they say existing evaluations fail to capture this capability. Visual reasoning benchmarks largely reduce tasks to single-turn, short-chain question answering, while agent benchmarks focus on text-based environments or interactive states that allow trial and error. The paper is listed on arXiv under identifier 2611.16861, with a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source available.

The articles do not say what happens next, such as whether the benchmark will be expanded or how the models will be retrained in response to these results.

Articles.Title: Visual Cipher Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Visual Reasoning

stories.Headline: Researchers build 2.4K-sample LIS dataset that outperforms larger safety alignment datasets
stories.Summary:
A paper posted to arXiv on November 17, 2026 describes a compact dataset for safety alignment of large language models, built by Hongyu Li, Zhan Yu, Zhe Zhao, Kimmo Yan, Xiong Kuang and Renfen Hu. The authors say existing models typically rely on massive fine-tuning datasets for safety alignment, which raises the cost of alignment and often leads to over-refusal. Their method, called Less is Safer (LIS), was constructed through interpretable feature-guided selection and adversarial synthesis. The team used Sparse Autoencoder activations to efficiently select prompts that cover diverse and interpretable safety features, and then applied a multi-agent adversarial synthesis framework to generate harmless prompts that nevertheless elicit unnecessary refusals.

LIS contains only 2.4K samples, yet the authors report it outperforms much larger datasets in overall performance on four safety and five over-refusal benchmarks. The comparison datasets named in the abstract are TRIDENT-Core with 26K samples, TRIDENT-Edge with 19K and WildJailbreak with 262K. Through ablation experiments, the authors demonstrate that neither safety data nor over-refusal data alone can achieve optimal results. They also used safety features from the Sparse Autoencoder, annotated by a language model, for data filtering, but say those results were inferior to the pipeline proposed in the paper.

The work is credited to the six named authors, who present LIS as a compact yet highly effective dataset for safety alignment. Their abstract frames the approach around interpretable feature-guided selection and adversarial synthesis rather than large-scale fine-tuning data. The stated aim is to lower the cost of safety alignment while addressing the over-refusal problem that the authors associate with existing methods. The paper appears on arXiv with a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source, and the abstract page also carries standard text about arXivLabs and its values.

The articles give no information on what happens next, such as release of the dataset or further testing beyond the reported benchmarks. The abstract reports results on four safety and five over-refusal benchmarks but does not describe any planned follow-up work. Beyond the arXiv listing, the articles do not say whether the dataset or code will be made available to other researchers. No publication venue or peer review status is given in the articles beyond the arXiv posting itself.

stories.Headline: Researchers develop LLM-agent system to detect ecological environment damage
stories.Summary:
Researchers including Man Zhao and Liangfu Chen developed a cross-modal retrieval method to detect ecological environment damage on November 17, 2026. This new system uses a multi-agent framework based on large language models to identify unauthorized construction and production activities. The tool allows users to interact through natural language to specify the regions, time periods, and types of damage they wish to investigate. It then coordinates various sub-agents to automatically gather and aggregate both textual clues and remote sensing image evidence.

The system replaces older methods that relied on predefined rules, professional experiential knowledge, and passive retrieval of public complaints. It requires the integration of natural language understanding and multi-step task execution to provide faster and more flexible results. This research received funding from several sources, including the National Key Research and Development Program of China under Grant 2022YFC330160204 and the Fundamental Research Funds in Heilongjiang Provincial Universities under Grant 145309328. Other support came from Grant SJGY20200125, Grant No. 2024KJGG18, and Grant No. YQJH2023105.

The authors, affiliated with institutions such as Qiqihar University and the Chinese Academy of Sciences, designed the agent for users without technical backgrounds. They stated that the method provides satisfactory performance and usability while remaining simple for people to learn. The researchers noted that the tool can offer significant technical support for the screening and assessment of environmental issues. Testing was conducted by professionals in the field of procuratorial case handling to ensure the system worked effectively.

The project was approved by the Science and Technology Ethics Committee of Qiqihar University to ensure all survey participants provided informed consent. This technology addresses the increasing severity of damage within Ecological Conservation Redline zones caused by non-compliant activities. By combining textual and image data, the agent helps officials review and analyze problem clues more efficiently. The authors have released the research under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License for wider use.

Articles.Title: LLM-agent-based cross-modal retrieval method for detecting clues of ecological environment damage

stories.Headline: PM calls for considering disabling Wi-Fi at CSAT test sites to prevent AI cheating
stories.Summary:
Prime Minister Han Seong-sook instructed government officials on Monday, November 16, 2026, to implement strict measures against artificial intelligence cheating. These urgent orders come just three days before the nationwide College Scholastic Ability Test, which is scheduled for this Thursday. The government is reacting to a shocking confession from the top scorer of this year's certified tax accountant exam. This individual admitted on Sunday to using a smartphone, a miniature camera, and generative AI to cheat on two rounds of that test. He further confessed to using these same sophisticated methods to cheat on a certified public accountant exam.

The new requirements involve the education ministry ensuring that all test takers turn in every smart device before the exam begins. Officials must conduct thorough checks to confirm that no smart devices are possessed by students during the testing period. Additionally, the science ministry has been asked to actively consider disabling all public Wi-Fi signals at the test sites. Prime Minister Han also announced the establishment of an interagency emergency response team for the 2027 CSAT to create comprehensive preventive measures. The government intends to investigate any abnormal signs that defy common sense after the exam using objective data.

Prime Minister Han stated that the government must concentrate all national capabilities to prepare against misconduct involving advanced AI technology. She explained that conventional exam management methods are now limited because AI technology is advancing so rapidly. The prime minister emphasized that upholding the fairness of examinations is a fundamental duty directly linked to public trust. She urged each government ministry to develop effective measures and ensure they are implemented thoroughly across all state-administered exams. Han called for the development of advanced detection technologies, including those leveraging AI, to counter ultra-small electronic devices and outside help.

The government is now scrambling to prevent similar AI-assisted cheating from occurring during the upcoming college entrance examinations. This concern follows reports of four separate cheating cases involving AI glasses at middle and high schools earlier this year. Authorities have indicated that they will pursue criminal punishment and a three-year exam ban for any CSAT cheaters using AI glasses. Officials are now tasked with creating a comprehensive government strategy to respond to increasingly diverse and sophisticated methods of cheating. They aim to create a fair testing environment that the public can trust through these new technical measures.

Articles.Title: PM calls for considering disabling Wi-Fi at CSAT test sites to prevent AI cheating

stories.Headline: South Korea and Philippines agree to deepen cooperation in AI and defense industry
stories.Summary:
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung and Philippine President Ferdinand Romualdez Marcos Jr. held a summit on Monday, November 16, 2026, in Manila. This meeting occurred on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit and marked the third time the two leaders have met. They previously held discussions in Gyeongju, South Korea, last year and again in the Philippine capital during March. The leaders focused on strengthening ties in traditional sectors and expanding their partnership into several emerging industries.

The agreement requires deeper cooperation in defense manufacturing, infrastructure, shipbuilding, artificial intelligence, nuclear power plants, aerospace, and disaster management. Bilateral trade between the two nations reached US$21.3 billion during the first nine months of this year, which already exceeds the previous annual record. The two countries signed a memorandum of understanding on science and technology to expand collaboration into smart farming. Additionally, they signed a grant aid agreement to help the Korea International Cooperation Agency implement various projects in the Philippines.

Spokesperson Kim Sung-wan stated that President Lee requested continued support from the Philippine government to help South Korean companies expand their operations. The spokesperson noted that both leaders pledged to foster mutually beneficial cooperation in areas where their bilateral ties are already strong. President Lee arrived in Manila on Monday for a four-day trip to engage with regional leaders. He is scheduled to travel to Shenzhen, China, next to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
